### [1] [Simulator-Grounded Large Language Models for Industrial Causal Reasoning: Tool-Use, Structured Injection, and Plant-Portable Retrieval for Wastewater Treatment Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05151)
*Gary Simethy,Daniel Ortiz Arroyo,Petar Durdevic*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper compares three methods for grounding LLMs in a wastewater treatment simulator for causal QA: a live simulator oracle (99.5% accuracy), structured parameter injection (79%), and a lightweight Decoupled Recall-Reasoning retriever (75.8%). The DRR method trains in ~17 seconds per plant, transfers across plants (88%), and uniquely handles counterfactual queries about interventions, outperforming all retrieval-augmented baselines. An out-of-domain replication on ARC/OpenBookQA confirms the approach generalizes beyond wastewater.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wastewater treatment plant operators need causal reasoning grounded in their specific plant's dynamics — such as understanding why N2O emissions are rising or predicting effects of operational changes — rather than relying on generic pretraining text. Existing LLM grounding approaches lack systematic comparison in industrial causal QA settings.

Method: The authors compare three grounding approaches applied to a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model paired with the CCSS-IX wastewater simulator: (1) a live simulator oracle that queries the simulator directly at inference, (2) structured parameter injection using pre-computed static tables of simulator variables, and (3) a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever — a compact 110M-parameter model that selectively retrieves relevant numerical parameters, trained per plant in ~17 seconds. Evaluation uses a 198-question causal benchmark and a 60-question counterfactual benchmark. Out-of-domain validation uses the AI2 Reasoning Challenge with an OpenBookQA corpus.

Result: On the causal benchmark, Methods 1, 2, and 3 achieve 99.5%, 79%, and 75.8% respectively, all surpassing the best retrieval-augmented baseline at 48%. DRR transfers cross-plant to a biologically distinct facility at 88%, while Method 2's static table fails to transfer. On counterfactual queries, only Method 3 handles intervention-based questions, beating Method 2 by +16.3 pp (95% CI [+7.1, +26.4] pp) with 100% accuracy on timescale and operating-regime categories. On ARC with OpenBookQA, the selective-retrieval mechanism reaches 79% vs. unconstrained Llama-3.1-8B (76%) and full-injection (74%).

Conclusion: The three methods form a practical deployment ladder trading off accuracy against cost and latency. The lightweight, trainable DRR retriever offers the best balance: fast per-plant adaptation, cross-plant transferability, unique counterfactual reasoning capability, and out-of-domain generalization. This provides the first unified comparison of live tool-use, static parameter injection, and learned numerical-parameter retrieval for industrial causal QA.

Abstract: Wastewater operators need answers grounded in how their plant's variables interact and how fast effects propagate, not in generic pretraining text, when asking causal questions such as "why is N2O rising?" or "what happens if I cut aeration by 20%?". We compare three concrete ways to ground a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model in an architecturally interpretable wastewater simulator (CCSS-IX): a live simulator oracle (Method 1), structured parameter injection (Method 2), and a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever (Method 3). On a 198-question causal benchmark the three reach 99.5%, 79%, and 75.8%, forming a deployment ladder above the strongest retrieval-augmented baseline at 48%. The DRR retriever has 110M parameters and trains per plant in ~17 seconds; after cross-plant transfer to a biologically distinct plant it still reaches 88%, while Method 2's static table cannot transfer. On a 60-question counterfactual benchmark only Method 3 handles queries about what happens after an intervention: +16.3 pp over Method 2, paired 95% CI [+7.1, +26.4] pp, with 100% on the timescale and operating-regime categories. On the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) with an OpenBookQA fact corpus, the same selective-retrieval mechanism reaches 79% versus unconstrained Llama-3.1-8B 76% and full-injection 74%, a +3 pp out-of-domain replication that argues against a result specific to wastewater treatment. We provide the first single-simulator comparison of live tool-use, static parameter injection, and learned numerical-parameter retrieval for industrial causal question answering.

</details>


### [2] [Mean-Field Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05152)
*Hao Ai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A framework modeling LLM chain-of-thought reasoning as guided discovery on a clue graph, yielding a mean-field ODE that statistically fits empirical reasoning patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide theoretical explanations for LLM chain-of-thought reasoning behavior without oversimplifying model architecture or relying on analogies to physical systems, thereby deepening understanding and guiding optimization.

Method: The authors formulate LLM reasoning as a guided discovery process on a clue graph and derive a one-dimensional ODE for the fraction of discovered clues via mean-field approximation. Clue tokens are identified using normalized surprisal of a student LLM on teacher LLM outputs. Statistical regularities are extracted by averaging over many reasoning chains.

Result: The statistical regularities obtained are reproducible within the same dataset and can be effectively fitted by solving the proposed theoretical ODE.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully captures statistical regularities in LLM chain-of-thought reasoning through a tractable mean-field ODE model, offering a principled theoretical lens for analyzing and potentially optimizing LLM reasoning behavior.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with chain-of-thought reasoning have been widely applied in recent years, and theoretical explanations of their behavior may help deepen our understanding and guide model optimization. In this study, we introduce a framework that seeks statistical regularities and theoretical interpretations in LLM reasoning without simplifying the model architecture or making analogies to existing physical systems. We formulate LLM reasoning as a guided discovery process on a clue graph, and derive a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation for the fraction of discovered clues using the mean-field approximation. Experimentally, clue tokens are identified using the normalized surprisal of a student LLM on the outputs of a teacher LLM, and statistical regularities are obtained by averaging over many reasoning chains of thought. Our experiments show that the resulting statistical regularities are reproducible within the same dataset and can be fitted by the solving the proposed theoretical equation.

</details>


### [3] [Universal Pathologies, Conditional Consequences: A Triple-Robustness Analysis of RAG for Multi-Hop Traceability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05153)
*Meftun Akarsu,Burak Ozdemir*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A rigorous triple-robustness study (varying embedder, corpus, and judge across 4,440 runs) reveals that GraphRAG's over-citation problem is architecturally universal but its faithfulness consequences are corpus-conditional. The authors also show that single-judge LLM faithfulness evaluation is fragile, and propose a learned router for hop classification as a mitigation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior reports that GraphRAG underperforms vector RAG on citation precision have remained anecdotal and corpus-bound. The authors seek to systematically identify where and why GraphRAG fails, disentangling architectural effects from corpus-specific and evaluation-specific confounds through a controlled, multi-axis experimental design.

Method: The paper conducts a triple-robustness analysis holding the retrieval architecture fixed while independently varying three orthogonal axes: (1) embedder (local e5-small vs. Azure text-embedding-3-small), (2) corpus (DO-178C typed-edge requirements vs. Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and (3) judge (paired GPT-5.4 vs. GPT-4.1). The main matrix comprises 4,440 runs, supplemented by 600 cross-corpus runs and 1,200 paired faithfulness judgments. A learned router operating on dense embeddings alone is trained for hop classification, evaluated via macro-F1.

Result: Key findings include: (C2a) Over-citation is architecturally universal — GraphRAG emits 11–15 citation IDs per answer with citation precision of 0.12–0.23 and retrieval recall of 0.68–0.87 across all three settings. (C2b) Faithfulness consequences are corpus-conditional: in typed-edge DO-178C, GraphRAG faithfulness drops from 74% to 40% across hops; on Wikipedia chains it rises from 42% to 58% because over-cited paragraphs remain topically supporting. (C1) Stratum-conditional winners are corpus-conditional but embedder-robust: vanilla RAG wins 2-hop on DO-178C, GraphRAG wins 2-hop on MuSiQue, regardless of embedder. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness is fragile: same-judge self-kappa across embedders is only 0.137 for GPT-5.4, with verdict changes on 41% of items. (C4) A learned router on dense embeddings achieves macro-F1 of 0.86 for hop classification.

Conclusion: The authors argue that triple-robustness — varying embedder, corpus, and judge simultaneously — should be the minimum methodological bar for making trustworthy claims about RAG architectures. The findings expose GraphRAG's over-citation as a fundamental architectural flaw while demonstrating that its downstream harm is mediated by corpus topology. They also caution against reliance on single-judge LLM evaluations due to poor reliability.

Abstract: GraphRAG underperforms vector RAG on citation precision in many reports, but where and why have remained corpus-bound. We present a triple-robustness analysis that holds the retrieval architecture fixed and varies three orthogonal axes embedder (local e5-small -> Azure text-embedding-3-small), corpus (DO-178C typed-edge requirements -> Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and judge (paired GPT-5.4 x GPT-4.1) across 4,440 main-matrix runs, 600 cross-corpus runs, and 1,200 paired faithfulness judgments. (C2a) Over-citation is architecturally universal: GraphRAG emits 11-15 IDs per answer at citation precision 0.12-0.23 and retrieval recall 0.68-0.87 across all three settings. (C2b) Its faithfulness consequence is corpus-conditional: in typed-edge DO-178C, GraphRAG faithfulness collapses 74%->40% across hops; on Wikipedia chains the same pipeline rises 42%->58% because over-cited paragraphs remain topically supporting. (C1) Stratum-conditional winners are corpus-conditional but embedder-robust: vanilla wins 2-hop on DO-178C, GraphRAG wins 2-hop on MuSiQue, identical under either embedder. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness is fragile to retrieval state: same-judge self-kappa across embedders is 0.137 for GPT-5.4 (verdict change on 41% of items). A learned router on dense embeddings alone reaches macro-F1 0.86 on hop classification (C4). We argue triple-robustness is the minimum bar for trustworthy RAG architecture claims.

</details>


### [4] [RIG-RoPE: Relation- and Instance-Gated Rotary Positional Encoding with Duration-Aware Temporal Coordinates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05154)
*Donggen Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RIG-RoPE introduces relation- and instance-gated mechanisms with duration-aware temporal coordinates to address two key limitations of M-RoPE: cross-modal spatial interference from static H/W position assignments, and equal-step temporal treatment of tokens with vastly different information densities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing M-RoPE suffers from (1) inappropriate application of height/width rotations across tokens from different modalities or visual instances, where spatial displacement is not geometrically meaningful, and (2) treating all tokens as equal-step temporal counters regardless of information density differences between text, images, and video.

Method: RIG-RoPE augments each token with a modality indicator, visual instance ID, and scalar information-duration coordinate. H/W rotations are enabled only for query-key pairs from the same visual instance; otherwise, unknown spatial displacement is marginalized. Temporal coordinates use interpolated cumulative block durations: unit duration for text, dimension-aware logarithmic spatial scale for images, and logarithmic temporal extension over effective frames for video. The method requires no learned parameters and fits within tiled attention kernels with constant per-token metadata overhead.

Result: The paper establishes the theoretical formulation, including a gauge-invariance argument against cross-instance spatial rotation, an impossibility result for static IDs under shared H/W subspaces, and a duration-consistency argument against equal-step multimodal time. Empirical validation is deferred.

Conclusion: This is a preliminary report that formulates RIG-RoPE and outlines a validation path without claiming empirical superiority. The proposed mechanism addresses fundamental structural limitations in multidimensional RoPE for interleaved multimodal contexts.

Abstract: Rotary positional encoding (RoPE) is a core component of modern language models and has been extended to multimodal LLMs through multidimensional variants such as multimodal RoPE (M-RoPE), which split positional channels into temporal, height, and width subspaces. This report identifies two limitations of static multidimensional position assignment in interleaved multimodal contexts. First, height/width rotations may be applied to token pairs whose spatial displacement is not a well-defined geometric object, producing cross-modal and inter-instance spatial interference. Second, temporal coordinates are often treated as equal-step counters, so a text token, an image block, and a video segment can advance the temporal phase by comparable amounts despite different information density.
  We propose RIG-RoPE, a relation- and instance-gated RoPE mechanism with duration-aware temporal coordinates. RIG-RoPE augments each token with a modality indicator, a visual instance identifier, and a scalar information-duration coordinate. It enables H/W rotations only for query-key pairs from the same visual instance; otherwise the unknown spatial displacement is marginalized rather than set to zero. Temporal rotations use interpolated cumulative block durations: text tokens consume unit duration, images use a dimension-aware logarithmic spatial scale, and videos further apply a logarithmic temporal extension over effective frames. We provide a gauge-invariance argument for avoiding ordinary cross-instance spatial rotation, an impossibility result for static IDs under shared H/W subspaces, and a duration-consistency argument against equal-step multimodal time. RIG-RoPE adds no learned parameters and can be implemented inside tiled attention kernels with constant additional metadata per token. This preliminary report establishes the formulation and validation path without claiming empirical superiority.

</details>


### [5] [Beyond Sentiment: Comparing Traditional NLP and LLM-Based Multi-Dimensional Analysis for Political News Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05155)
*Maryam Fooladi,Federico Bottino*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis suffers from "neutral collapse" on political news (70% classified as neutral), while an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing platform captures bias, sensationalism, and political framing dimensions more aligned with social sciences and humanities research needs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional sentiment analysis models only provide polarity classification but fail to capture rhetorical, ideological, and framing dimensions essential to political discourse analysis in the social sciences and humanities (SSH).

Method: Comparative study applying RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis and an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis platform to a corpus of 50 political news articles from 17 international media outlets.

Result: RoBERTa classified 70% of articles as neutral ("neutral collapse"), with 23% of those neutral articles having negative probability scores above 0.30. The LLM-based approach successfully captured political bias direction/intensity, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing across multiple dimensions.

Conclusion: Traditional sentiment analysis alone is insufficient for political media analysis; LLM-based multi-dimensional frameworks provide a more epistemologically adequate computational approach for SSH research.

Abstract: Traditional sentiment analysis (SA) models, while effective for polarity classification, provide limited insight into the rhetorical, ideological, and framing dimensions of political discourse -- dimensions that are central to research in the social sciences and humanities (SSH). In this paper, we present a comparative study of RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis and an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis platform applied to a corpus of 50 political news articles from 17 international media outlets. The results reveal a critical limitation we term neutral collapse: RoBERTa classifies 70% of articles as neutral, effectively flattening substantively rich political content into an analytically uninformative category. We find that 23% of neutral-classified articles exhibit negative probability scores above 0.30. By contrast, the LLM-based approach captures political bias direction and intensity, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing -- yielding multi-dimensional analytical outputs aligned with SSH epistemologies. We argue that for political media analysis, traditional SA alone is insufficient, and that LLM-based multi-dimensional frameworks offer a more epistemologically adequate computational lens for SSH research needs.

</details>


### [6] [Scaffold-Mediated Post-Training: Co-Evolving Model Parameters and Procedural Scaffold Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05156)
*Fei Ding,Yongkang Zhang,Runhao Liu,Yuhao Liao,Zijian Zeng,Huiming Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes scaffold-mediated post-training where procedural scaffolds co-evolve with model parameters via discovery, distillation, and recompilation. Instantiates this as Skill Training, achieving 8.1pp improvement on FeatureBench with scaffolds, and 85.2% distillation retention rate—significantly outperforming standard SFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training optimizes only model parameters while inference-time scaffolds are designed independently, creating a disconnect that prevents models from automatically acquiring and internalizing complex reasoning strategies.

Method: Scaffold-mediated post-training framework (Skill Training) with three components: (1) procedural scaffolds organized as an evolvable graph structure, (2) co-evolution of scaffolds with model parameters through discovery, distillation, and dynamic recompilation, (3) progressive distillation to internalize scaffold knowledge into model parameters.

Result: On FeatureBench, automatically discovered skills improve passed rate by 8.1pp. After progressive distillation, the model achieves 27.7% passed rate without external scaffold, yielding an 85.2% distillation retention rate (post-distillation / with-skill passed rate), significantly outperforming standard SFT on identical data.

Conclusion: Scaffold-mediated post-training successfully bridges the gap between parameter optimization and procedural scaffolding, enabling models to acquire and internalize complex strategies that standard post-training methods cannot achieve.

Abstract: Post-training of large language models optimizes only parameters, while inference-time procedural scaffolds are typically designed independently of parameter training. This disconnect makes it difficult to automatically acquire and internalize complex strategies. We propose scaffold-mediated post-training: procedural scaffolds are organized into an evolvable graph structure that co-evolves with model parameters through discovery, distillation, and dynamic recompilation. We instantiate this paradigm as Skill Training. On FeatureBench, automatically discovered skills improve the passed rate by 8.1pp, and after progressive distillation the model still achieves a 27.7% passed rate without any external scaffold (distillation retention rate 85.2%, defined as post-distillation / with-skill passed rate), significantly outperforming standard SFT on the same data.

</details>


### [7] [Large Language Models Threaten Double-blind Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05157)
*Bulambo Mwendelwa Gloire,Prasenjit Mitra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs can deanonymize double-blind review papers using only titles and abstracts, outperforming humans by detecting latent conceptual signatures in problem framing and research focus, even without stylistic or citation cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Double-blind peer review relies on the assumption that anonymized manuscripts do not reveal author identity. With the rise of LLMs, this assumption may no longer hold, threatening fairness and the integrity of scientific review.

Method: The authors tested whether LLMs could identify authors from anonymized titles and abstracts of papers published after model training (i.e., no memorization). Candidate pools consisted of five domain experts. They systematically excluded stylistic and bibliographic cues to isolate semantic/conceptual signals.

Result: LLMs collapsed anonymity more efficiently than humans, concentrating belief onto a small subset of plausible authors. The effect persisted even when stylistic and bibliographic cues were removed, suggesting that stable, latent conceptual signatures — patterns in problem framing and research focus — drive the identification.

Conclusion: Double-blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference via LLMs. The research ecosystem must reevaluate how anonymity and fairness are maintained in an AI-augmented environment, as conceptual signatures alone suffice for author re-identification.

Abstract: Double blind peer review serves as the scientific community primary defense against status and affiliation bias. Its effectiveness rests on the assumption that anonymized manuscripts convey scientific merit without revealing their authors. While authorship can often be recovered using citation networks or stylistic markers, we show that this assumption is increasingly fragile in the presence of large language models (LLMs). Using only titles and abstracts from papers published after model training, we find that LLMs collapse anonymity more efficiently than humans, with belief concentrating onto a small subset of plausible authors drawn from pools of five domain expert candidates. This vulnerability persists even when stylistic and bibliographic cues are excluded, indicating that stable patterns in problem framing and research focus function as latent conceptual signatures of authorship. Together, these findings indicate that double blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference, necessitating a revaluation of how anonymity and fairness are maintained in an AI augmented research ecosystem.

</details>


### [8] [Safe Evolution with Circuit Anchors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05158)
*Yan Liu,Jie Fu,Tsung-Yi Ho*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper identifies that LLM self-evolution algorithms lack safety constraints, causing models to become capable but dangerous ("misevolve"). Inspired by biological Hox genes, the authors propose Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE), which anchors a tiny safety circuit (<2% of features) during evolution while allowing other features to adapt freely. CAE outperforms reward-based constraints across 3 model families and two evolution algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-evolution algorithms for LLMs optimize purely for capability without preserving safety, analogous to unconstrained biological mutation. The authors demonstrate this leads to "misevolution"—models becoming powerful yet dangerous. Nature solves this via developmental constraints (e.g., Hox genes anchoring body plans while peripheral traits adapt), but no analogous mechanism exists in LLM evolution pipelines.

Method: The authors propose Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE): (1) Use mechanistic interpretability to identify a "safety circuit"—a small set of features (<2% of total) that causally mediate safety behaviors. (2) During self-evolution/optimization, anchor this circuit by constraining its feature displacements within a small bound. (3) Allow all remaining features to evolve freely. This mirrors biological evolvability with constraint—preserving essential functions while adapting peripheral capabilities.

Result: CAE achieves superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss across 3 model families and two evolution algorithms. It substantially outperforms explicit reward-based constraint baselines in both effectiveness (safety retention) and efficiency (lower computational overhead).

Conclusion: Just as developmental constraints prevent biological evolution from producing nonviable organisms, circuit anchoring prevents model evolution from producing capable but dangerous systems. CAE offers a principled, efficient mechanism for safe LLM self-evolution grounded in both biological principles and mechanistic interpretability.

Abstract: In biological evolution, unconstrained mutation can lead to catastrophic outcomes: organisms may evolve enhanced capabilities while losing essential functions for survival. Nature's solution is \textit{developmental constraints}, where core regulatory genes remain anchored while peripheral genes adapt freely. We observe that current self-evolution algorithms for large language models lack analogous constraints. They optimize purely for capability, implicitly assuming safety will be preserved. Our experiments reveal this assumption to be dangerously wrong: models can \textit{misevolve} into powerful yet dangerous entities. Inspired by how Hox genes anchor body structure across $500$ million years of evolution, we propose \textbf{Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE)}. Using mechanistic interpretability, we identify a tiny \textit{safety circuit}, comprising less than $2$\% of model features, that causally mediates safety behaviors. We anchor this circuit during evolution, constraining it within a small displacement bound while allowing the remaining features to evolve freely. This mirrors the biological principle of \textit{evolvability with constraint}: preserving what is essential while adapting what is peripheral. Experiments across $3$ model families and two evolution algorithms demonstrate that CAE achieves superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss, substantially outperforming explicit reward-based constraints in both effectiveness and efficiency. Just as developmental constraints prevent biological evolution from producing nonviable organisms, circuit anchoring prevents model evolution from producing capable but dangerous systems.

</details>


### [9] [SemiAdapt-Instruct: Extensible Instruction Tuning via Latent Domain-Specialised Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05161)
*Josh McGiff,Salma Mekaoui,Robert Shanahan,Nikola S. Nikolov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SemiAdapt-Instruct is a modular framework that discovers latent instruction domains, trains per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel with parameter-free routing, and supports extensibility by adding new domains via single-adapter training—outperforming full fine-tuning while matching single LoRA performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs deployed in evolving environments face the practical challenge of extending capabilities without full retraining. Monolithic fine-tuning approaches lack extensibility, making it costly to adapt to new domains incrementally.

Method: The framework operates in three stages: (1) discovering latent instruction domains from heterogeneous data using independent discovery methods, (2) training per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel for each discovered domain, and (3) performing parameter-free routing at inference to select the appropriate adapter. New domains are incorporated by training only a single new adapter without modifying existing ones.

Result: SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full model fine-tuning across all configurations on ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge metrics, matches single LoRA fine-tuning performance, and demonstrates superior extensibility—updating a single adapter with new domain data beats all monolithic baselines. Independent discovery methods converge on the same specialisation-friendly domains.

Conclusion: Decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains enables extensible NLP systems where evolving domains require only targeted single-adapter updates, eliminating full model retraining.

Abstract: Instruction-tuned LLMs are deployed into environments where domains evolve, yet extending a fine-tuned model's capabilities without full retraining remains an unsolved practical challenge. We present SemiAdapt-Instruct, a modular framework that discovers latent instruction domains, trains per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel, and performs parameter-free routing, incorporating new domains via single-adapter training without modifying existing components. SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full model fine-tuning across all configurations on both ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, while matching single LoRA fine-tuning and delivering extensibility that monolithic approaches cannot provide. We empirically demonstrate this extensibility by showing that updating a single adapter with new domain data outperforms all monolithic baselines. Our study also finds that independent discovery methods converge on the same specialisation-friendly domains. These findings demonstrate that decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains enables extensible NLP systems where evolving domains require only targeted single-adapter updates, eliminating the need for full model retraining.

</details>


### [10] [PoolBench: A Benchmark for Pooling Strategies in Concept Representation Evaluation for Decoder-Only LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05162)
*Ayushi Agarwal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PoolBench isolates pooling strategy as a controlled variable for decoder-only LLM concept representation, evaluating 19 pooling methods across 3 models and 17 concepts. Hierarchical pooling (W4_hierarchical) significantly outperforms the widely-used last-token baseline. A key finding is that strong concept detection does not translate to strong steering, revealing a fundamental representational bottleneck rather than a pooling failure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pooling strategy is an under-examined, consequential design choice in concept representation work using decoder-only models. Practitioners must collapse token-level hidden states into passage-level vectors, but no shared protocol exists for comparing pooling methods across concepts, models, and tasks. Reported performance gains are confounded by simultaneous changes in dataset, layer, construction method, and pooling rule, making principled comparison impossible.

Method: The authors introduce PoolBench, a benchmark that isolates pooling as the sole experimental variable under a fixed evaluation protocol. It covers 17 concepts, 19 pooling strategies, and 3 open-weight decoder-only models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), evaluated on 37,693 real-text passages. Three evaluation axes are used: linear separability (D1/AUROC), steered concept prevalence (D2/SCP), and output-level disentanglement (D3). Statistical significance is assessed via Friedman rank test with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons.

Result: W4_hierarchical achieves a cross-model mean AUROC of 0.7799, significantly outperforming the P1_last_token baseline (0.7640; p = 2.0e-36). Rankings are highly stable across layers (rank correlation rho = 0.961–0.990). A critical negative result: strong detection (D1) does not imply strong steering (D2, D3), which are substantially weaker for most concepts. On mid-difficulty concepts, W4_hierarchical outperforms P1_last_token by 0.042–0.113 AUROC. Construction method choice (DiffMean vs. REPE, delta AUROC ≈ 0.15) has a larger effect than pooling (delta ≈ 0.016), establishing the correct practical hierarchy of design decisions.

Conclusion: Pooling strategy matters significantly and consistently, with hierarchical methods (W4_hierarchical) emerging as the strongest. However, the gap between detection and steering performance points to a fundamental representational limit rather than a pooling deficiency. The practical hierarchy places construction method above pooling in importance. All artifacts (corpus, activations, scorer models, steering vectors, code) are released as a reusable protocol.

Abstract: Pooling is a consequential but under-examined design choice in decoder-only concept representation work: practitioners must collapse token-level hidden states into a passage-level vector, yet no shared protocol exists for comparing this choice across concepts, models, and tasks. Reported gains are confounded by simultaneous changes in dataset, layer, construction method, and pooling rule, making principled decisions impossible. We introduce PoolBench, a benchmark that isolates pooling as the experimental variable under a fixed evaluation protocol. PoolBench covers 17 concepts, 19 pooling strategies, and 3 open-weight decoder-only models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), evaluated on a single audited corpus of 37,693 real-text passages. The primary axis is linear separability (D1/AUROC); steered concept prevalence (D2/SCP) and output-level disentanglement (D3) serve as diagnostic axes. The primary finding is decisive: W4_hierarchical reaches a cross-model mean AUROC of 0.7799, while the widely adopted P1_last_token baseline reaches only 0.7640 and is statistically significantly worse (Friedman+Nemenyi, p = 2.0e-36; 77 significant pairs among 18 effective strategies). Rankings are stable across layers (rho = 0.961--0.990). A key negative result: strong detection does not imply strong steering -- D2 and D3 are substantially weaker than D1 for most concepts, indicating a fundamental representational limit rather than a pooling failure. On mid-difficulty concepts, W4_hierarchical outperforms P1_last_token by 0.042--0.113 AUROC; construction method choice (DiffMean vs. REPE) has a larger effect (delta AUROC 0.15) than pooling (delta AUROC 0.016), establishing the correct practical hierarchy. We release the corpus, pre-extracted activations, scorer models, steering vectors, and evaluation code as a reusable protocol for pooling research.

</details>


### [11] [Where Privacy Risk Lives in English-Source Multilingual RAG: A Stage-Decomposed Audit Across Five Query Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05163)
*Yanhang Li,Zhichao Fan,Zexin Zhuang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Tests whether non-English queries make multilingual RAG systems more vulnerable to PII leakage, using a Qwen2.5-7B pipeline across five languages. Finds English has the highest leak rate under output-only filtering; an input judge reduces but doesn't eliminate leaks for Arabic and Swahili. Oracle document attachment blocks most residual leaks, but as a mechanism diagnostic, not a deployable defence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Challenge the common assumption that non-English queries inherently increase the attack surface for extracting personal information from multilingual RAG systems. The authors aim to empirically test this hypothesis rather than accept it uncritically.

Method: An English-source synthetic-PII corpus is queried in five languages (English, Arabic, Swahili, plus two others). The entire pipeline — translator, input judge, back-translator, and generator — uses Qwen2.5-7B. A two-stage defence is tested: (1) an LLM-based input judge that screens queries, and (2) a regex-based output filter. Two filtering regimes are compared: output-only filtering versus input judge + output filter. An ablation with back-translation is reported. A final mechanistic diagnostic attaches the gold corpus document to the input judge on a residual-leak subset (n=17) using oracle retrieval.

Result: Under output-only filtering, English yields the highest unstructured-PII leak rate; only English vs. Swahili shows clean separation under document-level bootstrap intervals. Adding the input judge leaves residual leaks only on Arabic and Swahili. Back-translating queries fails to close this gap (non-causal, since the back-translator shares model family). Attaching the gold document to the input judge blocks 15 of 17 residual cells in the multilingual-prompted-judge corner case.

Conclusion: The common assumption that non-English languages are uniformly riskier for PII leakage is not supported under this pipeline-conditional setup. English can exhibit the highest leak rates. The gold-document-attachment result is framed strictly as a mechanism diagnostic — not a deployable defence — due to oracle retrieval, lack of benign-query FPR measurement, and absence of answer-utility cost evaluation. Priority follow-up calls for independent machine translation plus non-Qwen judge replication with native-speaker queries.

Abstract: A common assumption holds that switching to a non-English language makes a multilingual RAG system easier to attack for personal information. We test this on an English-source synthetic-PII corpus with five query languages and a two-stage defence (LLM input judge + regex output filter), in a pipeline whose translator, judge, back-translator, and generator are all Qwen2.5-7B -- so every finding below is pipeline-conditional, not a causal ranking of language-inherent risk. Under output-only filtering, English has the highest observed unstructured-PII leak rate; only English-vs-Swahili separates cleanly under document-level bootstrap intervals. Once the input judge is added, residual leaks remain on Arabic and Swahili, and back-translating the query does not close the gap (an ablation we report but cannot use as a causal diagnostic, since the back-translator is also Qwen). On a separate n=17 multilingual-prompted-judge residual corner, attaching the gold corpus document to the input judge blocks 15/17 residual cells. We frame this last result as a mechanism diagnostic, not a deployable defence: it uses oracle retrieval, BLOCK/ALLOW rates are measured on adversarial queries only, and we measure no benign-query false-positive rate and no answer-utility cost. The supplementary material contains code, corpora, queries, and per-trial JSONLs; the priority follow-up is an independent-MT plus non-Qwen-judge replication with a native-speaker query set, scoped in the Limitations section.

</details>


### [12] [Cross-Architecture Steering Transfer in Language Models: A Systematic Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05164)
*Ayushi Agarwal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Independently trained LLMs develop shared internal representations (supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis), and this geometric similarity enables cross-model steering transfer — but only above a critical parameter scale threshold (~1.7B). Below this scale, alignment and functional transfer degrade sharply.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has shown that independently trained LLMs can share geometric representations of semantic concepts, it remains untested whether this similarity has functional consequences — specifically, whether concept directions from one model can steer another model's behaviour. The paper aims to fill this gap with the first systematic evaluation of cross-model steering transfer.

Method: The authors study five open-weight models across three parameter scales (0.8B–8B) and two architectural lineages. They train one Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) per model across 15 semantic domains and evaluate cross-model feature alignment across all 20 directed model pairs. They then test cross-model steering using concept vectors derived from one model applied to another, measuring win rates and comparing against same-model native vectors and a universal vector.

Result: A discontinuity emerges near 1.7B parameters: at ≥1.7B, 47–49% of cross-model feature pairs validate (Pearson r ≥ 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895–0.956). Below 0.8B, alignment degrades sharply. Cross-model steering vectors achieve a 71.0% win rate vs. 68.0% for same-model vectors; a single universal vector achieves 67.3% across 4 of 5 models. Transfer fails for sub-1.7B models and one generationally unstable model.

Conclusion: Shared LLM geometry is functionally exploitable for cross-model behavioural control, but only when sufficient representational capacity exists. The findings establish scale thresholds as critical for mechanistic interpretability — tools validated at 7B scale may not transfer to smaller models. This provides the first functional complement to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, demonstrating cross-model control without fine-tuning under identified scale conditions.

Abstract: Independently trained large language models may develop shared internal representations of semantic concepts despite architectural differences -- but whether this geometric similarity has functional consequences for cross-model behavioural control remains untested. We present the first systematic evaluation of cross-model steering transfer and show that shared LLM geometry is functionally exploitable, conditionally: concept directions from one model can steer a different independently trained model when sufficient representational capacity exists. We study five open-weight models spanning three parameter scales (0.8B--8B) and two architectural lineages, training one Sparse Autoencoder per model across 15 semantic domains and testing alignment across all 20 directed model pairs. We observe a suggestive discontinuity near 1.7B parameters: at >= 1.7B scale, 47--49% of cross-model feature pairs validate (Pearson r >= 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895--0.956), while alignment degrades sharply below 0.8B. Cross-model steering vectors (B3-TI) achieve a 71.0% win rate across 15 supervised concepts versus 68.0% for same-model native vectors; a single universal vector achieves 67.3% in 4 of 5 models without any per-model supervision. Transfer degrades for models below 1.7B and for one model with generation instability, confirming that functional exploitability requires sufficient representational capacity. Our findings underscore the importance of scale thresholds in mechanistic interpretability: tools validated at 7B scale may not transfer to smaller models without revalidation. We provide the first functional complement to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- geometric convergence across independently trained LLMs supports cross-model behavioural control without fine-tuning, under the identified scale conditions.

</details>


### [13] [A Study of ASR Adaptation and Representation Dimensionality Reduction in Persian Speech Emotion Recognition Using Whisper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05165)
*Ali Shendabadi,Parnia Izadirad,Mostafa Salehi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a parameter-efficient SER framework for Persian using Whisper encoder embeddings reduced via PCA, combined with attention pooling and a lightweight classifier. PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves performance and efficiency, while Persian ASR fine-tuning offers only modest SER gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SER in low-resource languages like Persian suffers from limited labeled data. The authors aim to efficiently leverage large pretrained speech models (Whisper) for Persian SER while minimizing trainable parameters and investigating whether language-specific ASR adaptation transfers to emotion recognition.

Method: Frame-level embeddings are extracted from the Whisper encoder, then dimensionality-reduced via PCA (avoiding learned projection layers). Reduced representations undergo attention-based pooling and classification with a lightweight prediction head. The authors also fine-tune Whisper on Persian ASR to assess downstream SER impact. Evaluation uses the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent protocol.

Result: PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition accuracy while reducing training latency and memory footprint. Persian ASR fine-tuning yields only modest SER improvements, indicating limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion-related representations under the tested conditions.

Conclusion: PCA is a simple yet effective alternative to learned projection layers for Whisper-based SER in low-resource settings. Language-specific ASR fine-tuning provides marginal SER benefits, suggesting emotion-relevant features are not substantially enhanced by ASR adaptation alone.

Abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) in low-resource languages remains a challenging problem due to limited labeled data. In this work, we study the use of Whisper for Persian SER with a particular focus on representation dimensionality reduction and language-specific model adaptation. We propose a SER framework in which frame-level embeddings extracted from the Whisper encoder are reduced in dimensionality using PCA, eliminating the need for learned projection layers and substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. The reduced representations are aggregated using an attention-based pooling mechanism and classified with a lightweight prediction head. In addition, we investigate whether fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task improves downstream SER performance. Experiments conducted on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent evaluation protocol show that PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition performance while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning yields only modest gains for SER, suggesting limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion-related representations under the evaluated conditions. These findings provide practical insights into the efficient use of large pretrained speech models for emotion recognition in low-resource languages.

</details>


### [14] [Conditional Cognitive Biases in LLMs: How Biased User Turns Modulate In-Context Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05166)
*Sachini Weerasekara,Sagar Kamarthi,Jacqueline Isaacs*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study evaluates how multi-turn conversational context with biased user turns affects bias expression in instruction-tuned LLMs. Using a novel 3-condition framework and 24,300 jury-validated prompts (9×9 bias interaction matrix), the authors find that biased conversational context systematically increases bias in 6 of 8 frontier models, driven by two competing dynamics: exposure amplification and alignment-related suppression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM bias evaluations typically use zero-shot, single-turn prompts, which fail to capture how biases emerge in realistic multi-turn interactions where users may express biased views. The authors aim to disentangle whether bias amplification stems from mere exposure to biased content versus the semantic content of that bias, and to understand the behavioral mechanisms governing context-conditioned bias expression.

Method: A three-condition experimental framework: (1) zero-shot baseline, (2) exposure to a biased user turn with explicit bias cues, and (3) exposure to biased reasoning without explicit bias markers. A benchmark of 24,300 jury-validated user prompts is constructed, covering all 81 cells of a 9×9 target-human bias interaction matrix (9 bias categories in both the LLM's target response and the user's expressed bias). Eight frontier instruction-tuned LLMs are evaluated under this framework.

Result: Biased conversational context systematically increases bias expression compared to zero-shot baselines in 6 of 8 frontier LLMs. Two competing dynamics are identified: (1) conversational exposure to biased reasoning generally amplifies downstream bias tendencies, and (2) explicitly stated bias cues often trigger alignment-related suppression behaviors that reduce overt bias expression.

Conclusion: Multi-turn conversational context significantly modulates bias expression in LLMs, revealing a tension between exposure-driven amplification and alignment-driven suppression. The released framework and dataset provide a foundation for studying context-conditioned cognitive biases and behavioral adaptation in LLMs.

Abstract: We present an evaluation of cognitive bias expression in state-of-the-art instruction-tuned LLMs under realistic multi-turn interaction settings. Our work introduces a novel three-condition experimental framework that disentangles the effect of exposure to a biased user turn from the effect of the turn's semantic content, alongside a benchmark of 24,300 jury-validated user prompts spanning all 81 cells of a 9x9 target-human bias interaction matrix. Across eight frontier LLMs, we find that biased conversational context systematically increases bias expression relative to zero-shot baselines in 6 of 8 models. We identify two competing behavioral dynamics underlying this effect: conversational exposure to biased reasoning generally amplifies downstream bias tendencies, while explicitly stated bias cues often trigger alignment-related suppression behaviors that reduce overt bias expression. We release our framework, codebase, and dataset to support future research on context-conditioned cognitive biases and behavioral adaptation in LLMs.

</details>


### [15] [CNM-BERT: A Drop-In Structural Embedding for Chinese Characters via Ideographic Description Sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05167)
*Thomas Sing-wing Wu,Liqian Yan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CNM augments BERT with recursive Tree-MLP encodings of Chinese character compositional structure (IDS trees), yielding large gains on rare/OOV characters (+9.8 structure accuracy) and consistent downstream improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard token-based encoders treat Chinese characters as atomic tokens, ignoring their internal orthographic composition (radicals, components). This causes degraded performance on rare and out-of-vocabulary characters, where models cannot rely on frequent co-occurrence patterns.

Method: CNM (Compositional Network Model) parses Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) into tree structures, encodes them through a recursive Tree-MLP, and fuses the resulting structural embeddings into BERT's representations via a lightweight augmentation — crucially, without modifying the backbone Transformer.

Result: On the Wu et al. (2025) structural-probing benchmark, CNM-BERT outperforms ChineseBERT (strongest baseline) by +9.8 Structure accuracy and +7.7 Radical F1 on long-tail/OOV characters. It also achieves consistent gains on CLUE, MRC, and NER tasks at both base and large scales.

Conclusion: Explicit injection of discrete compositional structure into Transformer encoders yields both robust OOV understanding and tangible downstream value, outperforming existing approaches that depend solely on contextual co-occurrence or implicit sub-character modeling.

Abstract: Token-based encoders like BERT treat Chinese characters as atomic identifiers, ignoring their recursive orthographic structure. Consequently, models rely on contextual co-occurrence, degrading performance on rare and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) characters. We propose the Compositional Network Model (CNM), a lightweight augmentation that injects discrete compositional structure into Transformer encoders. CNM parses Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS) into trees, encodes them via a recursive Tree-MLP, and fuses the structural embeddings into BERT without modifying the backbone. Evaluated on the Wu et al. (2025) structural-probing benchmark, CNM-BERT outperforms the strongest baseline (ChineseBERT) on long-tail and OOV characters by +9.8 Structure accuracy and +7.7 Radical F1. Furthermore, CNM-BERT achieves consistent gains across CLUE, MRC, and NER tasks at both base and large scales, demonstrating that explicit structural injection delivers both robust OOV understanding and tangible downstream value.

</details>


### [16] [ConWriter: Transition-Constrained Stateful Long-Form Story Generation with Lightweight Neuro-Symbolic Consistency Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05169)
*Jindong Li,Yang Yang,Zihao Liu,Yutao Yue,Menglin Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConWriter is a training-free framework for long-form story generation that uses scene-level incremental writing with dynamic memory, symbolic state reasoning, and uncertainty-aware risk signals to detect and repair narrative inconsistencies before they propagate through the story.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompting-based methods for long story generation suffer from accumulating errors across temporal consistency, factual accuracy, character coherence, commonsense reasoning, and stylistic uniformity as story length increases. The authors aim to address this by introducing consistency control mechanisms that operate during generation rather than post-hoc correction.

Method: ConWriter generates stories incrementally at the scene level, guided by four components: (1) static story requirements that define overarching constraints, (2) dynamic narrative memory that tracks evolving story states, (3) symbolic state reasoning for checking narrative transitions, and (4) uncertainty-aware risk signals that prioritize validation and perform localized repair when inconsistencies are detected. The framework is training-free and operates without fine-tuning any underlying model.

Result: Evaluated on the ConStory-Bench benchmark across four tasks (continuation, generation, expansion, completion) at 3k, 6k, and 12k target lengths using Qwen3.5-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5 series models. Only the first five cases per task were used due to the high cost of long-form generation and evaluation.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates that consistency-aware long story generation can be achieved without additional training by combining dynamic state tracking, symbolic reasoning over narrative transitions, and uncertainty-driven risk assessment to identify and repair inconsistencies before they cascade into later scenes.

Abstract: Long-form story generation requires models to preserve narrative consistency across extended contexts, yet existing prompting-based methods often accumulate temporal, factual, character, commonsense, and stylistic errors as the story grows. We propose ConWriter, a training-free framework for consistency-aware long story generation. ConWriter writes stories incrementally at the scene level, guided by static story requirements, dynamic narrative memory, symbolic state reasoning, and uncertainty-aware risk signals. Rather than treating long-story generation as a single free-form decoding process, ConWriter maintains evolving story states, checks whether new scenes satisfy required narrative transitions, and uses uncertainty-aware risk signals to prioritize validation and localized repair. This enables consistency control during generation, before local errors propagate into later scenes. We evaluate ConWriter on ConStory-Bench, covering four long-story tasks: continuation, generation, expansion, and completion. Due to the high cost of long-form generation and evaluation, we use the first five cases from each task and test 3k, 6k, and 12k target lengths across Qwen3.5-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5 series. Experiments follow the official ConStory-Bench evaluation protocol.

</details>


### [17] [DREAM: LLM-based Dynamic Role-playing via Event-Aware Memory Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05170)
*Zhihao Xiao,Mengting Li,Xintao Wang,Linfeng Li,Limin Shui,Mengqi Ji,Borui Cai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DREAM introduces a structured memory framework for role-playing agents, using an Event-aware Memory Graph inspired by the ABC cognitive model to organize character experiences into temporally ordered, causally linked events. It constructs dual-granularity character profiles and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing role-playing agents rely on static character descriptions and unstructured memory, which limits their ability to maintain long-term narrative consistency and causally grounded behavior. The authors aim to address the lack of temporal and causal coherence in current RPAs.

Method: DREAM transforms unstructured literary text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG) that organizes experiences into temporally ordered and causally linked events. It constructs dynamic, dual-granularity character profiles capturing stable personality traits and event-driven behavioral evolution, grounded in the Activating Event-Belief-Consequence (ABC) cognitive model. A new benchmark, Temporal Causal Memory (TCM), is also introduced for evaluation.

Result: DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance across three benchmarks: CoSER, LIFECHOICE, and the newly proposed TCM, outperforming multiple strong baselines.

Conclusion: Structured memory, as implemented in DREAM, effectively enhances the interpretability and long-term consistency of role-playing agents by grounding behavior in temporal and causal narrative structures.

Abstract: Role-playing agents (RPAs) have emerged as a key application of large language models, enabling immersive and high-fidelity character simulation. Accurate role-playing of established characters requires not only stylistic imitation but also temporally consistent and causally grounded behavioral reasoning. However, existing RPAs primarily rely on static character descriptions and unstructured memory, limiting their ability to maintain long-term narrative and personality coherence. We introduce DREAM, a structured memory framework for role-playing agents inspired by the Activating Event-Belief-Consequence (ABC) cognitive model. DREAM transforms unstructured literary text into an Event-aware Memory Graph (EMG) that organizes character experiences into temporally ordered and causally linked event graph. This representation enables the construction of dynamic, dual-granularity character profiles that capture both stable personality traits and event-driven behavioral evolution. We further propose the Temporal Causal Memory (TCM) benchmark to evaluate temporal consistency and long-range causal narrative coherence. DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance across CoSER, LIFECHOICE, and TCM, outperforming multiple strong baselines. Our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of structured memory in enhancing the interpretability and consistency of role-playing agents.

</details>


### [18] [Position: It's Time to Optimize LLMs for Self-Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05188)
*Itamar Pres,Belinda Z. Li,Laura Ruis,Zifan Carl Guo,Keya Hu,Mehul Damani,Isha Puri,Ekdeep Singh Lubana,Jacob Andreas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The authors argue that many persistent LM failures (sycophancy, poor logical generalization, confident errors) stem from evaluating models on single input-output pairs in isolation. They propose "self-consistency" as a unifying framework, showing that diverse improvement techniques are special cases of consistency optimization, and outline a vision for developing generally consistent LMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LM training pipelines treat each input-output pair independently, which makes it impossible to detect failures that only emerge when examining relationships across multiple model responses. The authors aim to reframe these disparate failure modes under a single conceptual lens.

Method: This is a position paper that introduces the self-consistency framework. The authors demonstrate that existing methods targeting adversarial robustness, factual coherence, and other properties can all be reformulated as "consistency optimization" procedures amenable to a common set of optimization tools. They then extrapolate to propose new properties achievable through consistency optimization.

Result: The paper identifies that techniques addressing seemingly unrelated LM deficiencies share a common underlying structure: they all optimize for some form of consistency across the model's response distribution. This unification suggests a path toward more systematic improvement of LMs.

Conclusion: Developing generally consistent LMs would require shifting from independent output evaluation to relational reasoning about responses. This paradigm shift could enable new capabilities but also raises important objections regarding feasibility, cost, and potential risks that warrant further discussion.

Abstract: Despite ever-increasing sophistication in language model (LM) pre- and post-training pipelines, many important failures persist: models overcondition on user framing ("sycophancy"), exhibit incomplete logical generalization, and produce confident but incorrect responses. We argue that these failures arise from a modeling assumption permeating all aspects of the pipeline: that behavior can be specified and evaluated independently on single-output pairs. Many model failures are difficult, if not impossible, to detect without reasoning about relationships between a model's responses across inputs. In this position paper, we propose self-consistency as a framework for understanding these failures. We first observe that a wide variety of techniques designed to improve specific aspects of LM behavior-targeting properties as diverse as adversarial robustness and factual coherence-can be understood as special cases of a common "consistency optimization" procedure and addressed with a standard set of optimization tools. We next outline a set of new model properties that could be achieved by optimizing for consistency, and conclude with a discussion of what it would mean to develop generally consistent LMs, including the capabilities they would enable and the objections they raise.

</details>


### [19] [Analysis of Numerical Localisation in LLM Translations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05232)
*Patrizia Kaye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Extending Tang et al. (2025) from numerical translation to localisation, this paper evaluates five LLMs on commodity hardware for times, numbers, and dates, finding that embedding localisation principles into prompt context yields statistically significant accuracy gains over direct translation or alternative strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The work is motivated by extending Tang et al. (2025)'s numerical translation research into the domain of localisation (rather than translation) of times, numbers, and dates, specifically targeting models deployable on commodity hardware.

Method: Five LLMs capable of running on commodity hardware were selected. A baseline accuracy was first established for each model on the localisation task. Three distinct improvement strategies were then tested and compared against this baseline and each other.

Result: Embedding localisation principles directly into the prompt context yielded a statistically significant improvement in accuracy over both direct translation and the other two alternative strategies tested, contrary to the findings of Tang et al. (2025) in the translation domain.

Conclusion: For localisation tasks on commodity-hardware LLMs, prompt-based embedding of localisation principles is the superior strategy, diverging from Tang et al.'s findings in numerical translation.

Abstract: The work of Tang et. al. (2025) on numerical translation is extended by analysing the capability of five large language models (LLMs) for the localisation of times, numbers, and dates instead of translation. Models were selected that could be loaded onto and run on commodity hardware and a baseline quality for each mode is computed, then three different strategies to improve on that accuracy were tested. In contrast to Tang et. al., it was discovered that on the tested LLMs, embedding the localisation principles into the prompt context provided a statistically significant improvement in accuracy compared to direct translation or the alternative strategies.

</details>


### [20] [Constraint-First Reasoning: A Training-Free Protocol for Exploiting Answer-Space Constraints in Mathematical Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05254)
*Hongbo Ma,Bangji Yang,Yunqian Selina Cheng,Jiajun Fan,Hanwen Zhang,Ge Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CFR is a training-free, two-stage prompting method that extracts problem constraints before solving, and uses a regex router to activate only when restrictive cues are detected. It improves CoT on math benchmarks but is a targeted intervention, not a general-purpose solution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often produce plausible but constraint-violating mathematical outputs (e.g., missing modular reductions, wrong answer formats). Existing CoT prompting lacks explicit mechanisms to enforce stated requirements throughout reasoning.

Method: Constraint-First Reasoning (CFR): Stage 1 extracts and summarizes constraints from the problem; Stage 2 solves while checking intermediate and final results against the summary. Routed-CFR uses a text-only regex router to detect restrictive cues and selectively activate the two-stage protocol; otherwise defaults to direct CoT.

Result: CFR improves direct CoT across AIME, CMIMC, BRUMO, and AIMO_AMC on multiple backbones. Analyses include convention-controlled routing, matched prompting baselines, paired tests, decoding robustness, constraint-quality audits, token accounting, and OlympiadBench evaluation.

Conclusion: CFR is a targeted test-time intervention effective only when constraints are recoverable and Stage 1 extraction is reliable, rather than a general-purpose replacement for mathematical reasoning.

Abstract: Large language models can derive a plausible mathematical object yet still violate explicit requirements--for example, by omitting a modular reduction, returning a non-integer, or using the wrong encoded answer form. We introduce Constraint-First Reasoning (CFR), a training-free two-stage prompting protocol: Stage 1 extracts and summarizes constraints entailed by the problem, and Stage 2 solves while checking intermediate and final results against that summary. Routed-CFR activates the two-stage protocol only when a text-only regex router detects restrictive cues; otherwise it uses direct chain-of-thought (CoT). Across AIME, CMIMC, BRUMO, and AIMO_AMC, the method improves direct CoT on multiple backbones. We further report convention-controlled routing experiments, matched prompting baselines, problem-level paired tests, decoding robustness, constraint-quality audits, total-token accounting, and an OlympiadBench evaluation. These analyses position CFR as a targeted test-time intervention whose benefit depends on recoverable constraints and reliable Stage 1 extraction, rather than as a general-purpose replacement for mathematical reasoning.

</details>


### [21] [Evidence Lock Before Commitment: A Frozen Interface Degrades LLM-as-Judge Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05353)
*Divyansh Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM judges that persist intermediate evidence and then rely exclusively on that record for final decisions perform worse than judges that retain access to the original candidate answers. Evidence locking reduces agreement with human preferences and increases order inconsistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-judge pipelines often extract criteria and evidence before rendering a verdict, assuming the intermediate record captures all necessary information. The authors question this assumption, testing whether persisting evidence and making it the exclusive input to the next call degrades judgment quality.

Method: Across 24,000 judgments on HelpSteer3, FeedbackQA, and CoVal, the authors compare four paradigms: standard pairwise judging, structured one-call judging, two-call evidence locking (evidence persisted then judged in isolation), and three-call pointwise locking. They use Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5 as judges.

Result: Evidence locking reduces agreement with human preferences by 4–6 percentage points and increases answer-order inconsistency by 8–10 points relative to structured one-call judging. Pointwise locking is similarly harmful. Structured evidence elicitation (without locking) remains close to standard judging. Results hold across both models and all three datasets.

Conclusion: Persisted evidence can support auditability, but it should not replace the source answers at decision time. Judges need continued access to the original candidate answers to maintain alignment with human preferences.

Abstract: LLM judges are often asked to extract criteria and evidence before choosing between candidate answers. This workflow assumes that the intermediate record preserves the information needed for a later verdict. For reasoning-capable models, visible field order does not reveal internal decision order, so we test an observable alternative: persist the evidence in one call and make it the exclusive input to the next. Across 24,000 judgments over HelpSteer3, FeedbackQA, and CoVal, we compare standard pairwise judging, structured one-call judging, two-call evidence locking, and three-call pointwise locking with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5. Evidence locking reduces agreement with released human preferences by 4 to 6 percentage points and increases answer-order inconsistency by 8 to 10 points relative to structured one-call judging. Pointwise locking is also harmful, while structured evidence elicitation remains close to standard judging. The result holds for both judges and all three datasets. Persisted evidence can support auditability, but it should not replace the source answers at decision time.

</details>


### [22] [The interface of intonation and lexical tone: Boundary phenomena in Mandarin varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05364)
*Cong Zhang,Yiya Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This chapter examines how intonation and lexical tone interact in Mandarin Chinese, centering on f0 as their shared acoustic cue. It focuses on boundary phenomena—where intonational and tonal functions converge at phrase edges—to explore how sentence-level functions (e.g., questions vs. statements) and speaker attitudes are encoded, alongside theoretical models and emerging analytical techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mandarin Chinese presents a challenging case for prosodic analysis because both lexical tone and sentence-level intonation rely on the same acoustic parameter—fundamental frequency (f0). Understanding how these two systems coexist and interact, particularly at prosodic boundaries where pragmatic and attitudinal meanings are concentrated, is essential for advancing phonological theory and modeling communicative functions in tone languages.

Method: The chapter takes a synthetic, review-based approach. It draws on empirical studies of intonation boundary phenomena in Mandarin varieties, examining acoustic (f0) patterns at phrase and sentence edges. It integrates findings on question/statement contrasts and paralinguistic attitude encoding, then discusses theoretical frameworks (e.g., autosegmental-metrical models adapted for tone languages) and emerging computational/experimental techniques used to disentangle tonal and intonational contributions to the f0 contour.

Result: Key findings reveal that intonation and tone interact most saliently at prosodic boundaries, where boundary tones can override, modify, or co-occur with lexical tones to mark sentence type (interrogative vs. declarative) and speaker attitudes. Multiple communicative functions are shown to be simultaneously encoded through systematic f0 variations at these boundary sites, with theoretical models incorporating layers of tonal and intonational specification to account for the data.

Conclusion: The interaction between tone and intonation in Mandarin is not a simple superimposition but a complex, layered phenomenon most evident at prosodic boundaries. Effective theoretical modeling requires multi-level representations that accommodate both local tonal targets and global intonational contours, and emerging techniques promise further refinement in disentangling these intertwined prosodic dimensions.

Abstract: This chapter explores the intricate interplay between intonation and tone in Mandarin Chinese varieties, focusing on f0, the primary acoustic cue for both intonation and tone. The main empirical base is intonation boundary phenomena, where intonation and tone intersect and influence each other in conveying a range of sentence-level linguistic functions -- such as question vs. statement -- and a rich array of speakers' attitudinal information. Theoretical models and emerging techniques are also discussed to account for the observed interactions of tonal aspects and boundary phenomena to convey multiple levels of communicative meanings.

</details>


### [23] [FormBharo: Designing and Evaluating a Voice Agent for Conversational Form Filling in Rural India](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06027)
*Aman Dalmia,Sanskriti Midha,Jigar Doshi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FormBharo is a voice agent that uses LLMs paired with rule-based validation to fill structured forms over phone calls for low-literacy, Hindi-speaking mothers in India. The paper introduces FormVoiceAgentBench, shows that real-speech transcription errors degrade form completion by ~41 points, demonstrates that rule-based controls help smaller models match frontier models, and reveals that component-level metrics fail to predict end-to-end performance, necessitating Pareto-optimal model selection across accuracy, cost, and latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social benefit enrollment in India requires form-filling, but the most vulnerable beneficiaries are often illiterate and need spoken interaction. This work is currently done by frontline health workers one-on-one, which is an inefficient use of their limited capacity. A scalable, automated voice-based solution is needed to conduct enrollment conversations in Hindi over phone calls.

Method: FormBharo pairs LLMs (for transcription, information extraction, and reply generation) with deterministic, rule-based validation and flow control to maintain structure under tight latency and cost constraints. Evaluation uses FormVoiceAgentBench, a benchmark with human-recorded Hindi audio across 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests and 960 simulated calls, measuring component-level (ASR transcription, slot extraction, reply generation) and end-to-end form completion under real acoustic conditions.

Result: (1) Form completion drops ~41 points when LLMs receive error-prone real-speech transcripts vs. reference ones. (2) Rule-based controls recover many turn-level extraction errors, letting smaller/cheaper models match or surpass frontier models. (3) Component performance does not predict end-to-end performance: GPT-5.5 leads extraction accuracy (99.8% on reference) but ranks lower on form completion. (4) No single model is best across accuracy, cost, and latency; Pareto-based weighted-sum scalarization selects a deployable configuration.

Conclusion: End-to-end evaluation is essential for voice-agent pipelines because errors propagate and cancel across components, making component-level metrics misleading. Combining LLMs with rule-based controls enables cost-effective deployment, and Pareto-optimal model selection across accuracy, cost, and latency is necessary since no single model dominates all three dimensions.

Abstract: In India, almost every social benefit starts with a form, yet the people who need these benefits most are often unable to read or write. Reaching them requires a spoken conversation. Today that work falls to frontline health workers who enroll beneficiaries one at a time, a poor use of stretched capacity. We built FormBharo ("fill the form" in Hindi), a voice agent that fills a structured form over a phone call under tight latency and cost budgets by pairing Large Language Models (LLMs) with deterministic, rule-based validation and flow control. It is being piloted with ARMMAN, an NGO running large-scale maternal and child mobile-health programs in India, to enroll low-income, Hindi-speaking mothers in antenatal and postnatal care. To our knowledge, it is the first voice agent piloted to fill an enrollment form for this population. We openly release FormVoiceAgentBench, a benchmark pairing human-recorded Hindi audio with 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests across 960 simulated calls, to evaluate our agent's components (transcription, extraction, reply generation) and end-to-end form completion under real acoustic variations. Form completion drops by up to ~41 points when LLMs receive error-prone real-speech transcripts instead of reference ones. The rule-based controls recover many turn-level extraction errors, helping smaller, cheaper models match or surpass frontier models on form completion. Component performance does not predict end-to-end performance: GPT-5.5 leads turn-level extraction accuracy on reference transcripts (99.8%) but ranks lower on form completion. Since errors both propagate and cancel across the pipeline, the optimal model choice of models emerges only through end-to-end evaluation. Finally, no single model is best across accuracy, cost, and latency at once, so we use a Pareto-based weighted-sum scalarization to select a deployable configuration balancing the three.

</details>


### [24] [Mood Matters: How Syntactic Sensitivity Undermines Safety Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05409)
*Alina Klerings,Jannik Brinkmann,Heiner Stuckenschmidt,Simone Paolo Ponzetto*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Non-imperative syntactic forms (e.g., past tense, conditionals) systematically bypass refusal mechanisms in aligned LLMs. Using causal mediation analysis, the authors show refusal is spuriously conditioned on syntactic features rather than pure semantics, trace this to linguistically biased post-training data, and demonstrate that increasing syntactic diversity in training mitigates the vulnerability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed that simply changing tense from present to past could elicit harmful responses. The authors aim to investigate whether this is part of a broader, more general failure mode: the vulnerability of LLM safeguards to non-imperative syntactic forms, and to understand the mechanistic root cause behind this phenomenon.

Method: The authors conduct behavioral evaluations across 16 models up to 70B parameters to demonstrate the syntactic vulnerability.
