They then apply causal mediation analysis to identify whether refusal is conditioned on upstream syntactic features. By steering these syntactic features, they trigger and suppress refusal. Finally, they trace the ill-conditioning to linguistically biased post-training data in open-source models and test whether increasing syntactic diversity mitigates the issue.

Result: The syntactic vulnerability was confirmed across 16 models. Causal mediation analysis revealed that refusal decisions are partially conditioned on syntactic features rather than pure semantics. Steering these syntactic features could both trigger and suppress refusal. The root cause was traced to linguistically biased post-training data, and increasing syntactic diversity was shown to mitigate the vulnerability.

Conclusion: Current alignment approaches introduce syntactic confounders that prevent a pure semantic grounding of refusal decisions. This suggests that post-training data with limited syntactic diversity causes models to rely on surface-level syntactic cues (e.g., imperative mood) rather than deep semantic understanding when deciding whether to refuse harmful requests.

Abstract: Large language models typically undergo post-training to align them with safety policies but there exist many sophisticated jailbreaks that sidestep established safeguards. For instance, prior work by Andriushchenko et al. (2025) has found that changing the grammatical tense from present to past can be enough to elicit harmful responses. In this work, we uncover a more general failure of non-imperative syntactic forms. We demonstrate that this syntactic vulnerability exists in 16 models up to 70B parameters, using behavioral evaluation. To investigate the root cause, we apply causal mediation analysis, finding that refusal is partially conditioned on upstream syntactic features. By steering these purely syntactic features we are able to trigger and suppress refusal. Finally, we trace this ill-conditioning to linguistically biased post-training data of open-source models and show that increasing syntactic diversity can mitigate the issue. Our findings suggest that current alignment approaches introduce confounders that prevent a pure semantic grounding of the refusal decision.

</details>


### [25] [Decolonizing Linguistic Policies in Automated Speech Recognition: A Framework for Cross-Culturally Competent Speech AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06141)
*Jay L. Cunningham,Mark Atta Mensah,Richard Martinez,Joao Vieira da Silva Neto,Efi Dawodu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper argues that ASR failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties constitute implicit colonial linguistic policies, introduces a Three Harms (3M) taxonomy and a seven-layer situatedness model, and proposes a participatory framework for culturally competent ASR development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent ASR failures for marginalized language varieties are framed not merely as technical shortcomings but as implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies. The authors aim to reframe these errors as sociopolitical harms requiring structural, community-centered intervention rather than purely engineering solutions.

Method: The paper draws on theoretical frameworks—linguistic capital (Bourdieu), raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing—to analyze how data curation, evaluation metrics, and model priors systematically exclude non-dominant language varieties. It introduces two conceptual tools: the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy (Misrecognition, Misalignment, Mistrust) and a seven-layer situatedness model capturing linguistic diversity dimensions in ASR systems. It then proposes a participatory framework and a minimum audit protocol for community co-design, evaluation, and governance.

Result: The analysis reveals that ASR systems’ design choices—training data selection, metric optimization, and architectural priors—function as de facto language policy, rendering non-standard varieties illegible and entrenching raciolinguistic hierarchies. The 3M taxonomy and seven-layer model provide a structured lens for diagnosing these harms, while the proposed participatory audit protocol offers actionable pathways toward culturally competent ASR.

Conclusion: Culturally competent ASR requires shifting from a purely technical framing to a sociotechnical, participatory paradigm where affected communities serve as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners. The proposed frameworks offer both a diagnostic vocabulary and a practical roadmap for decolonizing voice interfaces in public services, healthcare, and education.

Abstract: This paper focuses on automatic speech recognition (ASR) and ASR-mediated voice interfaces that shape access to public services, healthcare, and education. We argue that persistent failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties are not only technical errors, but also implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies. Drawing on linguistic capital, raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing, we show how data, metrics, and model priors determine whose voices become machine-legible. We introduce the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy---Misrecognition, Misalignment, and Mistrust---and a seven-layer situatedness model for linguistic diversity in ASR and ASR-mediated voice interfaces. We then propose a participatory framework and minimum audit protocol for culturally competent ASR, positioning affected communities as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners.

</details>


### [26] [Example-Guided Prompting for Document-Level Text Simplification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05447)
*Marina Litvak,Ariel Perstin,Ilan Shtilman,Michael Färber*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates using retrieved document-simplification examples to augment prompts for LLMs, improving document-level text simplification without fine-tuning. Experiments on OneStopEnglish show consistent quality gains over prompt-only baselines and competitive performance against supervised and planning-based systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt-based LLMs struggle with document-level text simplification because textual instructions alone provide insufficient guidance for complex, discourse-aware transformations, leading to inconsistent outputs.

Method: Example-guided prompting: retrieved parallel simplification examples (from a corpus) are incorporated into prompts to guide LLM generation. Evaluated on the OneStopEnglish corpus using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, compared against prompt-only baselines, supervised T5, and the planning-based PlanSimp system.

Result: Incorporating retrieved examples consistently improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation. The approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to T5 and PlanSimp. Benefits vary across LLMs, indicating that effective use of retrieved examples depends on a model's contextual integration capability.

Conclusion: Example-guided prompting is an effective, training-free strategy for document-level simplification. Its variable efficacy across models highlights the importance of contextual integration ability, pointing toward future work on optimizing example selection and model-specific prompting strategies.

Abstract: Document-level text simplification requires large language models (LLMs) to rewrite complex documents while preserving meaning, readability, and discourse coherence. Although prompt-based LLMs have shown promising performance, they often produce inconsistent simplifications because textual instructions alone provide limited guidance for complex document-level transformations. We investigate whether retrieved document-simplification examples can improve document-level generation by augmenting prompts with examples selected from a parallel simplification corpus. This example-guided prompting approach enables LLMs to exploit relevant simplification patterns without task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments on the OneStopEnglish corpus using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs show that incorporating retrieved examples consistently improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with representative supervised (T5) and planning-based (PlanSimp) document simplification systems. Furthermore, we find that the benefits of example-guided prompting vary across LLMs, suggesting that effective use of retrieved examples depends on a model's ability to integrate contextual information during generation.

</details>


### [27] [DBLAST: Dependent Block Drafting for Stochastic Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05448)
*Amirmohammad Karimi,Chao Gao,Negar Hassanpour*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DBLast introduces a dependent block drafter for speculative decoding that uses low-rank latent mixtures to model inter-position dependencies, trained with an acceptance-oriented objective. It improves accepted draft length over independent block sampling, particularly in high-entropy, non-greedy decoding settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing block and diffusion-style drafters assume conditional independence across positions within a draft block. This assumption fails in non-greedy speculative decoding where the target distribution is stochastic, causing accepted draft length to degrade as sampling entropy increases.

Method: The authors propose a dependent block drafter using a low-rank latent mixture over token positions to capture inter-token dependencies, paired with an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly optimizes expected verified length rather than standard token-level losses.

Result: Experiments with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks show consistent improvements in accepted draft length over independent block sampling, with gains most pronounced in higher-entropy decoding regimes.

Conclusion: Modeling dependencies across draft block positions and optimizing directly for acceptance yields substantial gains in speculative decoding efficiency, especially when target sampling is non-greedy and stochastic.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models' inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple future tokens and a target model to verify them. While recent block and diffusion-style drafters can predict several positions in a single pass, their training and sampling procedures are typically optimized for greedy decoding or assume that positions in the draft block are conditionally independent. This assumption becomes brittle in non-greedy speculative decoding, where the target distribution is deliberately stochastic and multiple continuations become plausible. We study this mismatch for block diffusion drafters and show that the accepted draft length degrades as the entropy of the target sampling distribution increases. We propose a dependent block drafter based on a low-rank latent mixture over token positions, complemented by an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly targets the expected verified length. Experiments with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks show that our approach, namely DBLast, consistently improves accepted length over independent block sampling, especially in higher-entropy decoding regimes.

</details>


### [28] [Different Perturbations, Different Mechanisms: Understanding Continued Pre-training for Zero-Shot Dialect Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05510)
*Aarohi Srivastava,David Chiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A systematic study comparing six perturbation-based continued pre-training (CPT) strategies across German, Italian, and Arabic dialect tasks reveals that character-level noise consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while preserving standard variety performance. Importantly, methods with similar downstream accuracy induce distinct internal mechanisms of robustness, involving different patterns of adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dialectal variation poses a significant challenge for multilingual LLMs. While perturbation-based CPT shows promise for robustness, prior work evaluates strategies in isolation without explaining why they work. The authors aim to systematically compare multiple perturbation strategies across languages and uncover the distinct mechanisms underlying their effectiveness.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled study comparing six training conditions (including character-level, orthographic, and lexical perturbations applied during continued pre-training) across nine dialect tasks spanning German, Italian, and Arabic. Evaluation covers zero-shot dialect robustness and standard variety performance. Mechanistic analysis examines language model adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair patterns to explain why different methods succeed.

Result: Character-noised CPT consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while largely maintaining standard variety performance. Critically, methods that achieve similar downstream performance exhibit distinct internal mechanisms: different patterns of LM adaptation, representational alignment across varieties, and prediction repair behaviour, indicating that surface-level perturbation type fundamentally shapes how robustness is acquired.

Conclusion: Perturbation-based CPT is effective for multilingual dialect robustness, but the choice of perturbation strategy matters not just for performance but for the type of robustness induced. The findings offer both a deeper understanding of synthetic surface variation and practical guidance for selecting CPT strategies in dialectal settings.

Abstract: Dialectal variation remains a major challenge for multilingual language models. Perturbation-based continued pre-training (CPT) has emerged as a promising approach to improving robustness, yet existing work largely evaluates individual perturbation strategies in isolation and provides limited insight into why they work. We present a systematic study of perturbation-based CPT for multilingual dialect robustness in LLMs, comparing six training conditions across nine German, Italian, and Arabic dialect tasks. Perturbation-based CPT, especially character-noised CPT, consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while largely preserving standard variety performance. More importantly, we show that methods with similar downstream performance induce distinct mechanisms of robustness, exhibiting different patterns of language model adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair. Our results provide a more complete understanding of how synthetic surface variation improves robustness and offer practical guidance for selecting CPT strategies in multilingual and dialectal settings.

</details>


### [29] [Where Models Converge and Humans Diverge: A Coverage Framework for Distributional Pluralism in Open-Ended Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05576)
*Zini Yang,Emily Wenger,Richard So*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a framework with two metrics (LLM Coverage and In-Boundary Rate) to systematically measure the distributional breadth of LLM-generated content relative to human writing, finding that LLMs produce plausible but narrowly concentrated content near the center of the human response distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work has qualitatively observed a "gap" where LLMs produce "average" writing while humans generate more stylistically diverse, irregular, and broadly distributed content, but no systematic method exists to measure this distributional breadth gap quantitatively.

Method: The authors propose a human-grounded framework that uses the empirical distribution of human writing on a topic as a reference. They introduce two metrics: LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov), which measures how much of the human response space the LLM covers, and In-Boundary Rate (IBR), which separates content plausibility from distributional breadth. The framework is applied across ideation and narrative tasks.

Result: Current LLMs generate content that is plausible (high IBR) but distributionally narrow (low LLM-Cov), concentrating near the center of the human response space rather than spanning the full breadth of human-written content.

Conclusion: The framework enables researchers to systematically assess the distributional breadth — termed "cultural reach" — of LLM-authored content, providing a quantitative lens for evaluating how well models capture the full diversity of human expression on a given topic.

Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) writes Harry Potter fanfiction, it reliably produces fundamental elements of the Hogwarts universe, such as recognizable places and characters. Human-written Harry Potter fanfictions, however, typically include these fundamentals and much more, incorporating stylistically irregular content and relationship-diverse plotlines. This gap between LLM and human writing has been noted across a variety of domains. LLMs tend to produce "average" writing, while human writing contains more diverse content that covers a broader distribution. Existing work has shown the existence of this distributional "gap", but no work has proposed a systematic way to measure it. Our paper proposes a human-grounded framework that uses the empirical distribution of human writing on a topic to measure the distributional breadth of LLM-generated content on that same topic. We propose two metrics, LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov) and In-Boundary Rate (IBR), that separate the plausibility of LLM content from its distributional breadth. Across ideation and narrative tasks, we find that current LLMs produce plausible but narrow content that concentrates near the center of the human response space. Our framework can enable researchers to better assess the distributional breadth of LLM-authored content, which we term its "cultural reach".

</details>


### [30] [SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05604)
*Xingyu Tan,Xiaoyang Wang,Qing Liu,Xiwei Xu,Xin Yuan,Liming Zhu,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SkillZip proposes an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework that compresses agent skill libraries by rewriting recurring, contract-valid motifs into reversible macros at the sub-skill (section-graph) level, achieving a 3.46× compression ratio while outperforming baselines by up to 12.2 points on agent benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skill libraries, existing systems face a unit mismatch: skills are retrieved as whole packages, compressed as unstructured text, and converted to execution graphs only after retrieval. This prevents reliable sub-skill reuse, breaks procedural contracts during compression, and hinders incremental library updates.

Method: SkillZip introduces contract-preserving compression over section-level execution graphs. It identifies recurring contract-valid motifs and rewrites them into reversible, ported macros while preserving boundary signatures, dependency closure, verifier reachability, and source-level expandability. At inference, a compact dependency-closed context is hydrated and macros are expanded on demand. ReZip handles incremental integration of new skills and evidence-based revision of risky macros.

Result: On technical and embodied agent benchmarks, SkillZip outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 12.2 points, achieves a 3.46× compression ratio with 99.2% dependency preservation and 98.7% verifier reachability, and demonstrates robust retrieval scaling from 200 to 100K skills.

Conclusion: SkillZip resolves the unit mismatch in LLM agent skill reuse by operating on a contract-bearing procedural unit (the section graph), enabling reliable sub-skill compression, preservation of procedural contracts, and incremental library evolution with strong empirical performance.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents whose procedural knowledge is stored in reusable skill packages and loaded at inference time. As skill libraries grow, a central challenge is to expose the smallest sufficient executable context under a limited context budget. Existing systems struggle to reuse routines below the whole-skill level, preserve procedural contracts during compression, keep compressed routines executable and expandable, and update the compressed library as skills evolve. These challenges reveal a unit mismatch: skills are retrieved as packages, compressed as text, and converted into execution graphs only after retrieval, whereas reliable reuse requires a contract-bearing procedural unit. We propose SkillZip, an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework that performs contract-preserving compression over section-level graphs. SkillZip rewrites recurring contract-valid motifs into reversible ported macros while preserving boundary signatures, dependency closure, verifier reachability, and source-level expansion. At inference time, it hydrates a compact, dependency-closed context and expands macros only when required. ReZip further integrates new skills and revises risky macros using execution evidence. Comprehensive experiments1 on technical and embodied agent benchmarks show SkillZip consistently outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 12.2 points, while achieving a 3.46x compression ratio with 99.2% dependency preservation and 98.7% verifier reachability. Scaling analyses further confirm robust retrieval across skill libraries ranging from 200 to 100K skills.

</details>


### [31] [FOCUS: Decoupling Expert Personas in LLMs to Enhance Domain Expert Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05611)
*Guanyu Wang,Zidi Zhang,Xu Chu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FOCUS fine-tunes LLMs with orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific personas and uses an expert gating module for adaptive, context-aware persona activation, improving task accuracy in financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing persona control methods exhibit cross-domain coupling, causing inappropriate behavior — overly aggressive in cautious domains (e.g., healthcare) or overly conservative in risk-tolerant domains (e.g., financial trading). The motivation is to decouple domain-specific personas so that LLMs can activate the right expert persona for the right context without interference.

Method: FOCUS operates in three stages: (1) automatic extraction of expert persona vectors from LLMs; (2) orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific expert personas, ensuring they are independent; (3) an expert gating module that adaptively controls persona activation based on task context. A two-stage training strategy with a gated selection regularizer is employed to learn appropriate persona activation for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks.

Result: Experiments on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks demonstrate that FOCUS improves task accuracy and outperforms existing persona control methods.

Conclusion: FOCUS effectively addresses cross-domain coupling in persona-controlled LLMs through orthogonal decomposition and adaptive gating, enabling safer and more accurate deployment of expert personas across diverse and sensitive domains.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can exhibit diverse personas, and activating expert personas has been shown to improve domain expertise and task accuracy. However, existing persona control methods often suffer from cross-domain coupling, which may lead to overly aggressive behavior in high-caution domains such as healthcare, or excessive conservatism in risk-sensitive domains such as financial trading. To address this issue, we propose FOCUS (\textbf{\underline{F}}ine-tuning with \textbf{\underline{O}}rthogonal \textbf{\underline{C}}ontrol for \textbf{\underline{U}}ncoupled persona\textbf{\underline{S}}). FOCUS first automatically extracts expert persona vectors from LLMs, then applies orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific expert personas, and finally introduces an expert gating module to adaptively control persona activation according to task contexts. With a two-stage training strategy and a gated selection regularizer, the model learns to activate appropriate personas for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks. Experiments on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks show that FOCUS improves task accuracy and outperforms existing persona control methods. Our code is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/openpersona-48F4}{this url}.

</details>


### [32] [Human-Like Anaphor Resolution in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05630)
*Keane Zhang,Varshini Chinta,Raj Sanjay Shah,Sashank Varma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study tests whether five open-weight LLMs (GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, Mistral-24B) mirror human cognitive biases in anaphor resolution. Using surprisal as a proxy for reading time and accuracy on comprehension questions, results reveal selective alignment: LLMs are sensitive to discourse prominence and distance effects but show weak sensitivity to semantic interference, partially delimiting the conditions for human-like processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human anaphor resolution is known to be influenced by discourse structure, situation-model properties, and semantic factors. The authors aim to determine whether these same factors govern anaphor resolution in LLMs, thereby probing the cognitive plausibility of these models' language processing mechanisms.

Method: The authors evaluate five open-weight LLMs (GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, Mistral-24B) on anaphor resolution tasks. They operationalize processing difficulty via two behavioral measures: (1) surprisal at the anaphor, under the linking hypothesis that surprisal correlates with human reading times, and (2) model accuracy compared to human accuracy on comprehension questions probing antecedent identification. The stimulus materials manipulate discourse prominence, distance between anaphor and antecedent, and semantic interference.

Result: LLMs display selective cognitive alignment with humans. Specifically, they show human-like sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance-based factors — increased surprisal and reduced accuracy when antecedents are less prominent or more distant. However, sensitivity to semantic interference effects is either weak or absent across models. This pattern holds across multiple model sizes and architectures.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs partially approximate human anaphor resolution, capturing structural and distance-based constraints but not semantic interference. This selective alignment delimits the boundary conditions under which LLM processing mirrors human cognition and points to architectural or training-data limitations in modeling semantically driven anaphor resolution.

Abstract: Anaphors are expressions that refer to other expressions, called antecedents. The process of connecting the two is called resolution. Cognitive science has identified multiple factors that affect the speed and success of anaphor resolution, including discourse structure, situation-model properties, and semantic factors. Here, we investigate whether these factors also affect anaphor resolution in five Large Language Models (LLMs) with open weights: GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, and Mistral-24B. To model processing difficulty, we adopt the standard linking hypothesis that relates human reading times to model surprisal at the anaphor. As a second behavioral measure, we compare model accuracy to human accuracy on comprehension questions probing the antecedents of anaphors. The results show selective cognitive alignment: some LLMs exhibit human-like sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance-based factors in anaphor resolution, while showing weaker or absent sensitivity to semantic interference effects. These findings delimit the conditions under which LLMs approximate human anaphor resolution.

</details>


### [33] [Relay, Don't Route: Adaptive Population Handoff for Cost-Efficient LLM-Driven Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05651)
*Sichun Luo,Yi Huang,Guanzhi Deng,Haibo Wang,Haochen Luo,Lei Li,Zefa Hu,Junlan Feng,Qi Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM-driven evolutionary search is front-loaded, with cheap models recovering much early progress. The authors propose a training-free framework that uses adaptive population handoff from cheap to strong models, guided by a bandit scheduler and a "Relay Gain" reward, outperforming baselines across benchmarks and budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Using strong LLMs throughout evolutionary search is costly. Existing budget allocation strategies operate at the individual query/mutation level, ignoring the stateful nature of evolution where each candidate changes the population for subsequent mutations. The work explores whether budget should instead be allocated at the population level via handoff from cheap to strong models.

Method: A training-free framework with three components: (1) a cheap model explores multiple evolutionary trajectories in short blocks allocated by a bandit scheduler; (2) Relay Gain — the marginal improvement of a compact, quality-diverse candidate bank — serves as the scheduler reward and determines handoff timing; (3) curated candidates initialize a shared strong model population for refinement.

Result: Across four benchmarks and three budgets (12 total settings), the proposed method achieves the highest mean score in 11 of 12 settings, outperforming competitive baselines.

Conclusion: In stateful evolutionary search, budget allocation should be organized around the population rather than individual calls. Adaptive population handoff between cheap and strong models is an effective strategy.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven evolution has shown promise for program search and algorithm discovery, but relying on strong models throughout long evolutionary runs is costly. A natural alternative is to combine cheap and strong models under a fixed inference budget. However, existing approaches typically allocate models at the level of individual queries or mutation steps, overlooking that evolutionary search is \textit{stateful}: each generated candidate changes the population from which subsequent mutations are produced.
  We empirically analyze LLM-driven evolutionary trajectories and find that search progress is strongly front-loaded, early trajectory performance is informative but noisy, and cheap models recover much of the early progress achieved by strong models at lower cost. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{\model}, a training-free framework that shifts budget allocation from individual calls to evolving populations through adaptive \textit{population handoff}. A cheap model explores multiple trajectories in short blocks allocated by a bandit scheduler. Relay Gain, defined as the marginal improvement of a compact, quality-diverse candidate bank constructed for handoff, serves as the scheduler reward and determines when to hand off. The curated candidates initialize a shared strong model population for refinement. Across four benchmarks and three budgets, \model achieves the highest mean score in 11 of 12 settings, outperforming competitive baselines. Our results suggest that in stateful search, budget allocation should be organized around the population, not the individual call.

</details>


### [34] [Answer First, Reason Later: Commitment Order in Diffusion LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05687)
*Jewon Yeom,Jaewon Sok,Seonghyeon Park,Jeongjae Park,Hwiyeong Lee,Taesup Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Masked diffusion LMs fail on reasoning tasks because unconstrained token commitment causes premature final-answer collapse; a frontier-gated commitment intervention causally recovers performance while preserving parallelism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) are marketed as superior to autoregressive models due to their ability to commit tokens in any order. However, the authors hypothesize that this very freedom causes systematic failure on reasoning tasks, and seek to diagnose and fix the underlying mechanism.

Method: The authors instrument LLaDA-8B on GSM8K, logging every commitment during decoding to characterize the "collapse" phenomenon where models emit final answers prematurely. They design a 2×2 prompt-decoder factorial experiment (with/without chain-of-thought × ordered/unconstrained commitment) to decompose the effect, then propose "frontier-gated commitment" — a single-knob intervention that restricts which positions can be committed based on a frontier that advances monotonically — and validate it on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across GSM8K and MATH-500.

Result: Unconstrained decoding commits the final answer at only 15–24% of the trajectory with half the reasoning region still masked, collapsing to answer-only outputs on up to 90% of problems as canvas size grows. Chain-of-thought helps only under ordered commitment (+34.8 pp interaction; 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]). Frontier-gated commitment recovers the full performance gap (0.528 → 0.852 accuracy) while preserving up to 4× parallel decoding. The optimal frontier window flips from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step.

Conclusion: The freedom to commit tokens arbitrarily is not an advantage but the root cause of reasoning failure in dLLMs. Frontier-gated commitment provides a minimal, causal fix, reframing existing window-style samplers (previously motivated by efficiency) as necessary remedies for a fundamental reasoning pathology.

Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) can commit tokens in any order -- a freedom marketed as their core advantage over autoregressive decoding. We show that on reasoning tasks this freedom is instead the axis of failure. Logging every commitment during decoding of LLaDA-8B on GSM8K, we find that unconstrained (pure) decoding commits the final answer at 15-24% of the trajectory while half the reasoning region is still masked, and collapses to answer-only outputs on up to 90% of problems as the canvas grows. The cause is not the model's termination beliefs -- EOS "pressure" is nearly identical across decoders -- but reachability: whether the sampler may act on those beliefs at distant positions. A 2x2 prompt-decoder design shows that chain-of-thought helps only under ordered commitment (interaction +34.8 percentage points, 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]; without reasoning text the decoders are indistinguishable), an interaction we decompose into a collapse channel and an order channel and replicate on Dream-7B and MATH-500. A single-knob intervention -- frontier-gated commitment -- causally recovers the full gap (0.528 to 0.852) while preserving up to 4x parallel decoding, along a measured frontier whose optimal window flips from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step. Our results reframe existing window-style samplers, previously motivated by efficiency, as the minimal fix for a reasoning pathology they were never designed to address.

</details>


### [35] [Sparse Mutual Information Graph Averaging for Improving Random Indexing Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05724)
*Sriram Loganathan,Gokul Anand,Aung Bo Bo,Yourui Shao,William B. Andreopoulos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Analyzes Random Indexing (RI) vectors refined via sparse PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning. On a fairytales corpus, PPMI top-K graph averaging improves RI accuracy on Google family-category analogies from ~19.4% to ~30.7%, though this method degrades performance for neural baselines (CBOW, Skip-gram, SVD variants) and yields near-zero similarity correlation on SimLex-999.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explore whether sparse word embedding pipelines — specifically Random Indexing refined by sparse PPMI graph-based weighted averaging — can serve as a viable, non-gradient alternative to dense factorization and neural embedding methods, avoiding costly co-occurrence matrix materialization and gradient training.

Method: Random Indexing (RI) vectors are initialized and then refined by weighted averaging over a sparse Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) graph with top-K pruning (e.g., K=50). Evaluated on a fairytales corpus using the Google family-category analogy subset (272 questions). Compared against PPMI+SVD, Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram baselines, with additional evaluation on text8 and SimLex-999.

Result: PPMI top-K=50 graph averaging repairs weak RI initialization on the fairytales corpus, improving family-subset analogy accuracy from 19.4±0.7% to 30.7±2.9% (best seed: 34.6%). However, the same averaging degrades analogy accuracy for PPMI+SVD, Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram. The method is not competitive with neural baselines on text8 and yields near-zero strict similarity correlation on SimLex-999. Bloom filter sketches underperform RI in the tested configuration.

Conclusion: PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning is a useful non-gradient repair mechanism specifically for weak RI embeddings, but it does not generalize as an improvement for stronger neural or SVD-based embeddings and falls short on broader semantic similarity benchmarks.

Abstract: Sparse word embedding pipelines can avoid dense co-occurrence matrix materialization, dense factorization, and gradient training while still relying on sparse global corpus statistics. This paper studies Random Indexing (RI) vectors refined by weighted averaging on a sparse Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) graph. On a fairytales corpus, the covered semantic analogy set consists of 272 Google family- category questions. On this family subset, PPMI top-K graph averaging repairs a weak RI initialization, improving accuracy from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9% across five seeds. Under the single tested runs, the same neighborhood averaging reduces family- subset analogy accuracy for PPMI+SVD (singular value decom- position), Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram. Thus the method is not competitive with neural baselines on text8 and gives near- zero strict similarity correlation on SimLex-999. While Bloom filter sketches underperform RI in the tested configuration, we find that PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning is a useful non-gradient repair for weak RI embeddings. On the fairytales dataset, PPMI top-K=50 graph averaging improves RI with accuracy going from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9%, and performing best with a seed42 of 34.6%.

</details>


### [36] [Mitigating Scoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge via Random Number Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05726)
*Yuma Asato,Kiyoaki Shirai,Natthawut Kertkeidkachorn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a method to mitigate scoring bias in LLM-as-a-Judge by first measuring an LLM's latent numerical bias through random number generation, then rectifying token probabilities during evaluation. The method outperforms baselines across four tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM evaluators (LLM-as-a-Judge) suffer from scoring bias — the tendency to generate particular scores regardless of the actual text quality — which undermines their reliability as automatic evaluation metrics. Existing calibration methods are insufficient, necessitating a more principled approach to identify and correct this bias.

Method: The method has two stages: (1) Bias measurement: The LLM is prompted to randomly generate number tokens, and the deviation of the observed distribution from a uniform distribution is measured to identify latent numerical bias. A downstream task definition is incorporated into the prompt to capture task-specific bias. (2) Bias rectification: During actual evaluation, the token generation probabilities for a given input are adjusted by accounting for the measured latent number bias, effectively debiasing the final score.

Result: The proposed method outperforms baselines — including an unmodified LLM evaluator and previous calibration methods — across four tasks: evaluation of LLM alignment, evaluation of summarization, Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), and Semantic Textual Relatedness (STR). The study also finds that scoring bias varies across different LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, underscoring the need for case-specific bias measurement.

Conclusion: Measuring and rectifying latent number bias is an effective strategy for improving LLM-as-a-Judge reliability. The variability of bias across LLMs, tasks, and score ranges highlights that debiasing must be context-dependent rather than one-size-fits-all.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are often used as evaluators of text quality, known as LLM-as-a-Judge, which can outperform conventional automatic evaluation metrics that rely on reference texts. However, LLM evaluators tend to generate particular scores regardless of the context of the evaluated text, which is known as scoring bias. This study proposes a novel method to mitigate this scoring bias. An LLM is instructed to randomly generate number tokens, and the latent numerical bias of the LLM is identified by measuring the deviation of the observed distribution of numbers from the uniform distribution. A definition of a downstream task, for which an LLM evaluator is used, is added to the prompts for random number generation to measure task-specific latent number bias. In the evaluation by an LLM, the token generation probabilities for a given input are rectified considering the LLM's latent number bias. Results of the experiment on four different tasks, evaluation of LLM alignment, evaluation of summarization, Semantic Textual Similarity, and Semantic Textual Relatedness, demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the baselines, including an LLM without debiasing and previous calibration methods. In addition, it is confirmed that scoring bias varies across LLMs, tasks, and score ranges, indicating the importance of measuring latent number bias as the case may be.

</details>


### [37] [Once a Response, Always a Response: Detecting LLM-generated Text via Latent Prompt Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741)
*Hongrui Bao,Yubing Ren,Yanan Cao,Jinhan You,Fang Fang,Shi Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EchoPrompt is a training-free, zero-shot detector for machine-generated text that identifies LLM outputs by measuring latent prompt dependency — the hidden statistical link between generated text and the upstream prompt that conditioned it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing zero-shot detectors rely on surface-level probability statistics without modeling the fundamental generation mechanism of LLMs — namely, that text is produced conditioned on a prompt. This gap limits detection robustness, especially as LLMs become more fluent and convincing.

Method: EchoPrompt restores a generic assistant-response context by prepending a unified prefix to candidate text. It then measures the likelihood gain using an instruction-tuned model, calibrates this gain against a corresponding base model, and aggregates the differences into a score quantifying latent prompt dependency.

Result: EchoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot detectors and maintains strong robustness across diverse and challenging evaluation settings.

Conclusion: By explicitly modeling the prompt-conditioned generation mechanism of LLMs, EchoPrompt provides a more robust and effective zero-shot detection approach, advancing the field of machine-generated text detection.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent and convincing text at scale, creating growing risks for misinformation dissemination, educational misuse, and platform governance. These concerns make robust detection of machine-generated text increasingly necessary. Recent zero-shot detectors mainly exploit probability-based statistical discrepancies, but they do not explicitly account for the training process of LLMs, which leaves a distinct generation mechanism insufficiently modeled and limits detection robustness. To address this issue, we propose EchoPrompt, a training-free detector based on latent prompt restoration. Our key intuition is that machine-generated text is typically produced conditioned on an upstream prompt, and this hidden dependency can be partially reactivated by prepending a unified generic prefix. Specifically, EchoPrompt restores a generic assistant-response context, measures the induced likelihood gain with an instruction-tuned model, calibrates it against the corresponding base model, and aggregates the resulting differences into a score that quantifies latent prompt dependency. Extensive experiments show that EchoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot detectors while maintaining strong robustness across challenging evaluation settings.

</details>


### [38] [How to Recognize New Words: A Comparison Between Context Biasing Methods and Speech LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05759)
*Christian Huber,Alexander Waibel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Compares context biasing and speech LLM prompting for recognizing rare words in ASR; context biasing reduces biased WER by up to 88% with minimal side effects, while speech LLMs perform well on read speech but struggle with non-read speech and are sensitive to distractors and word order.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rare and new words (named entities, acronyms, domain-specific terms) remain a major challenge for ASR systems because they are scarce in training data, motivating a systematic comparison of two emerging mitigation strategies.

Method: Two context biasing methods built on Whisper are compared against three speech large language models (LLMs). Evaluation is conducted on both read and non-read speech, measuring biased WER, unbiased WER, and overall WER. Sensitivity to distractor count and prompt word order is also assessed.

Result: Context biasing methods reduce biased WER by up to 88% relative, with negligible impact on unbiased words. Speech LLMs achieve strong results on read speech but generalize poorly to non-read speech and show sensitivity to distractors and prompt word order.

Conclusion: Context biasing offers robust, targeted improvement for rare-word recognition across speech types, while speech LLMs show promise but require further work on generalization and robustness. Trade-offs between the two approaches are characterized to inform practical method selection.

Abstract: Recognizing new and rare words - named entities, acronyms, domain specific special words, and other items scarce in training data - remains a key challenge for automatic speech recognition (ASR). We compare two strategies for this: context biasing methods, where an ASR model is extended such that during inference a word list can be supplied, and speech large language models (LLMs) prompted with context directly. We evaluate two context biasing methods based on Whisper against three speech LLMs across read and non-read speech, reporting biased, unbiased, and overall word error rate (WER). The context biasing methods cut biased WER by up to 88% relative while leaving other words largely unaffected. Speech LLMs excel on read speech but generalize less well to non-read speech, and prove sensitive to distractor count and prompt word order. We characterize the resulting trade-offs to guide method selection.

</details>


### [39] [Task-Conditional Flow Matching for Balanced Multilingual Text Embedding Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05785)
*Tirth Bhatt,Naren Kumar S,Mayank Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TCFM is a multilingual embedding adaptation framework that applies Flow Matching selectively to translation tasks while using task-aligned objectives for retrieval, classification, and pair-classification, combined with teacher-guided representation preservation and a three-stage curriculum, achieving SOTA on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multilingual text embedding models typically use a single training objective across all tasks, ignoring that different tasks (translation, retrieval, classification, pair-classification) have fundamentally different optimization dynamics and thus require distinct training strategies.

Method: TCFM selectively applies Flow Matching to translation tasks while optimizing retrieval, classification, and pair-classification tasks with objectives better aligned to their learning dynamics. It incorporates teacher-guided representation preservation and a three-stage curriculum for stable adaptation. The framework is model-agnostic, generalizing across embedding model families.

Result: On the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, TCFM establishes a new state-of-the-art, consistently improving embedding quality across diverse multilingual tasks.

Conclusion: Task-conditional optimization with Flow Matching for translation and tailored objectives for other tasks, coupled with teacher guidance and curriculum learning, yields superior multilingual embedding adaptation. Code and datasets will be publicly released.

Abstract: Multilingual text embedding models are commonly adapted using a single training objective across diverse tasks, despite different tasks requiring fundamentally different optimization strategies. We introduce Task-Conditional Flow Matching (TCFM), a multilingual embedding adaptation framework that selectively applies Flow Matching to translation tasks while optimizing retrieval, classification, and pair-classification tasks with objectives better aligned to their learning dynamics. TCFM further combines teacher-guided representation preservation with a three-stage curriculum to enable stable adaptation. Evaluated on the Indic Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, TCFM establishes a new state-of-the-art, consistently improving embedding quality across a diverse set of multilingual tasks and generalizing across embedding model families. We will publicly release the codebase and datasets upon acceptance of the paper.

</details>


### [40] [On-Policy Delta Distillation for Multilingual Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05802)
*Byeongho Heo,Jaehui Hwang,Sangdoo Yun,Dongyoon Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates On-Policy Distillation (OPD) and its variant OPD² for multilingual mathematical reasoning, finding OPD² consistently outperforms OPD, especially in Korean and Japanese, and that multilingual data is crucial for preserving target-language responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-Policy Distillation is a promising alternative to RL for LLM post-training, but its effectiveness in multilingual settings has not been studied. The authors aim to fill this gap by evaluating OPD and OPD² across English, Korean, and Japanese for mathematical reasoning.

Method: The authors study OPD and On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), where OPD² uses the probability gap between a post-trained teacher and its base model as the learning signal. Experiments are conducted using Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks in English, Korean, and Japanese. They also test whether English-only OPD transfers to other languages.

Result: OPD² consistently outperforms the original OPD, with particularly strong improvements in Korean and Japanese, and generally narrows the English-Korean performance gap. English-only OPD can improve performance in Korean and Japanese but tends to shift responses toward English, underscoring the need for multilingual data to maintain target-language generation.

Conclusion: OPD² is a robust distillation method for multilingual mathematical reasoning that improves performance across languages and reduces cross-lingual gaps. Multilingual training data is essential to prevent language shift toward English.

Abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) is emerging as a promising alternative to reinforcement learning for LLM post-training, yet its effectiveness in multilingual settings remains underexplored. We study OPD and its advanced variant, On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$), for mathematical reasoning in English, Korean, and Japanese. OPD$^2$ improves OPD by using the probability gap between a post-trained teacher and its base model as the learning signal. Experiments with Qwen3 show that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms the original OPD, with particularly strong improvements in Korean and Japanese, and generally narrows the English-Korean performance gap. We further find that English-only OPD can also increase performance for Korean and Japanese, but often shifts the responses toward English, highlighting the importance of multilingual data to preserving target-language responses.

</details>


### [41] [Hierarchical Latent Prediction for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05806)
*Chang Shi,Tim Pearce,Manan Tomar,Siddhartha Sen,John Langford*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HiLP introduces a hierarchical auxiliary latent prediction objective that reduces error accumulation in latent-space rollouts, improving long-horizon reasoning, coding benchmarks, and speculative decoding efficiency compared to standard NTP, MTP, and NextLat.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Next-Token Prediction (NTP) uses teacher forcing, which is suboptimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning. Existing alternatives like Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) have limited horizon, while Next-Latent prediction (NextLat) suffers from compounding errors during multi-step latent rollouts. There is a need for an objective that enables longer-horizon coherent representations without error accumulation.

Method: The authors propose Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP), an auxiliary training objective that introduces a higher-level abstract latent representation. This hierarchical latent is designed to mitigate error accumulation during latent-space autoregressive rollouts, enabling more coherent long-horizon belief state representations.

Result: HiLP produces longer-horizon coherent belief state representations and demonstrates improved performance on coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks. It also offers enhanced efficiency for speculative decoding.

Conclusion: HiLP effectively addresses the limitations of both MTP and NextLat by using hierarchical abstraction in latent space, yielding better long-horizon reasoning and practical decoding speedups.

Abstract: While standard Next-Token Prediction (NTP) lays the foundation of language model pre- training, its teacher-forced training paradigm may not be optimal for long-horizon reasoning and planning. Recent works such as Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) and Next-Latent prediction (NextLat) try to mitigate the problem through predicting multiple future tokens and self-supervised prediction in the latent space. However, those auxiliary objectives either have a limited horizon or suffer from compounding error from multi-step rollout. We introduce Hierarchical Latent Prediction (HiLP), which introduces an auxiliary higher-level abstract latent to help reduce the error accumulation effect in latent-space rollouts. Experiments show that HiLP can lead to longer-horizon coherent belief state representation and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across coding and multi-step reasoning benchmarks, and offers more speculative decoding efficiency.

</details>


### [42] [M$^3$R-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Metaphor Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05817)
*Hong Jiang,Junnan Zhu,Jingwang Huang,Xiao Sun,Yuming Yang,Jiang Zhong,Ruirui Chen,Jingman Shi,Hao Wu,Nayu Liu,Xinyi Jiang,Kaiwen Wei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: M³R-Bench is a unified, evidence-grounded benchmark for multimodal metaphor understanding with 1,000 image-text instances. It evaluates metaphor occurrence, Target-Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations. The authors identify a cross-modal evidence-mapping mismatch in existing models and propose M³R-Reasoner, which uses curriculum-based reasoning supervision and task-aware RL to align model reasoning with metaphor interpretation, outperforming larger proprietary MLLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing metaphor understanding benchmarks suffer from two major limitations: (1) they evaluate through isolated subtasks rather than unified, holistic assessment, and (2) they lack evidence-grounded explanations, making it impossible to determine whether models genuinely ground their Target-Source mappings in visual and textual cues. This prevents rigorous assessment of cross-modal reasoning in metaphor comprehension.

Method: The authors introduce M³R-Bench, a benchmark with 1,000 image-text instances annotated for metaphor occurrence, Target-Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations (evidence identification → mapping establishment → sentiment inference), grounded in Conceptual Metaphor Theory. They then propose M³R-Reasoner, an 8B-parameter model combining curriculum-based reasoning supervision with task-aware reinforcement learning to align reasoning with the metaphor interpretation pipeline.

Result: Existing models exhibit a cross-modal evidence-mapping mismatch: they overlook visual evidence, rely on superficial textual cues, and produce inaccurate Target-Source mappings. M³R-Reasoner outperforms larger proprietary MLLMs across four unified-task metrics, improves Visual Evidence and Sentiment Justification scores over GPT-5.5 by 28.45 and 30.11 points, and surpasses Claude-Sonnet-4.6 by 8.00 points in mean rubric score.

Conclusion: The cross-modal evidence-mapping mismatch is a fundamental limitation in current multimodal models for metaphor understanding. M³R-Reasoner demonstrates that explicitly aligning reasoning with the stages of metaphor interpretation via curriculum learning and RL enables smaller models to surpass much larger proprietary systems, underscoring the importance of evidence-grounded reasoning in multimodal metaphor comprehension.

Abstract: Metaphor enables the understanding of abstract concepts through cross-domain mappings while conveying affective attitudes. In multimodal scenarios, visual and textual information jointly construct Target--Source mappings, requiring both conceptual understanding and cross-modal reasoning. However, existing benchmarks mainly evaluate metaphor understanding through isolated subtasks and lack evidence-grounded explanations, making it difficult to assess whether models establish mappings grounded in visual and textual cues.To address these limitations, we introduce M$^3$R-Bench, a unified and evidence-grounded benchmark containing 1,000 image--text instances with human-verified annotations. Guided by Conceptual Metaphor Theory and theories of nonliteral language understanding, M$^3$R-Bench provides joint annotations for metaphor occurrence, Target--Source mapping, sentiment, and stage-wise explanations following ``evidence identification--mapping establishment--sentiment inference.''Evaluations on M$^3$R-Bench reveal that existing models often overlook visual evidence, rely on superficial textual cues, and produce inaccurate Target--Source mappings, exposing a cross-modal evidence--mapping mismatch. To address this mismatch, we propose M$^3$R-Reasoner, which combines curriculum-based reasoning supervision with task-aware reinforcement learning to align model reasoning with metaphor interpretation. Experiments show that, with only an 8B-parameter backbone, M$^3$R-Reasoner outperforms larger proprietary MLLMs across four unified-task metrics and improves Visual Evidence and Sentiment Justification scores over GPT-5.5 by 28.45 and 30.11 points, respectively, while surpassing Claude-Sonnet-4.6 by 8.00 points in mean rubric score. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/hongshi4/M3R-Bench.

</details>


### [43] [Decomposed Entailment for Factuality Checking and Hallucination Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05823)
*Achir Oukelmoun,Nasredine Semmar,Gaël De Chalendar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HallDetect is a lightweight, reference-free, black-box hallucination detection framework that decomposes generated content into atomic claims, verifies each using a contrastive entailment model against multi-scale source chunks, and aggregates results with an asymmetric scoring mechanism, outperforming comparably resourced baselines across multiple source-grounded generation benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from factual inconsistencies and hallucinations — content unsupported by source material. Existing detection methods are often resource-intensive, require reference texts, or are evaluated narrowly on summarization. There is a need for a lightweight, reference-free, black-box approach that generalizes across diverse source-grounded generation tasks while providing interpretable audit trails.

Method: HallDetect employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) decomposition of generated text into atomic claims; (2) verification of each claim using a compact encoder-based entailment model trained with a contrastive objective, comparing claims against a multi-scale library of source chunks (spanning sentence, paragraph, and document levels); and (3) aggregation via an asymmetric score where a single confidently contradicted claim is sufficient to flag the entire response as hallucinated. The framework operates under a controlled protocol using 4-bit quantized backbones on consumer-grade hardware, ensuring fair comparison across methods.

Result: Under equalized resource constraints (4-bit quantization, consumer hardware), HallDetect outperforms comparably resourced generative and embedding-based baselines on three of four benchmarks. Performance remains stable across different backbone model families. The framework additionally produces a claim-to-span audit trail that localizes each factual error.

Conclusion: HallDetect demonstrates that a decomposition-based approach with contrastive entailment verification and asymmetric scoring provides a resource-efficient, generalizable, and interpretable solution for hallucination detection across diverse generation tasks, with the added benefit of fine-grained error localization.

Abstract: The reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) is often compromised by factual inconsistencies, including hallucinations---cases where generated content is not supported by the underlying source. We present HallDetect, a lightweight, reference-free, and black-box framework for hallucination detection that we evaluate not only on summarization but across a broader range of source-grounded generation settings. HallDetect builds on decomposition-based factuality evaluation: generated content is decomposed into atomic claims, each verified by a compact encoder-based entailment model through a contrastive formulation over a multi-scale library of source chunks, and aggregated with an asymmetric score in which a single confidently contradicted claim flags the response. Under a controlled protocol in which all methods share the same 4-bit quantized backbones and consumer-grade hardware budget, HallDetect outperforms comparably resourced generative and embedding-based baselines on three of four benchmarks while remaining stable across backbone families, and yields a claim-to-span audit trail that localizes each error.

</details>


### [44] [MoCA: Implicit Social Context Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05825)
*Wenhao Xu,Kaiwen Zhang,Hao Li,Maowei You,Yongzheng Ji,Siyuan Zuo,Jingxuan Yu,Sina A,Xinyao Tan,Bobo Li,Hao Fei,Mong-Li Lee,Wynne Hsu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MoCA (Implicit Social Context Analysis), a task for modeling implicit social communication across affection, intent, and stance dimensions. A benchmark of 3,108 multimodal instances with cognitive annotations is presented, along with CoDAR, a conflict-driven abductive reasoning framework that improves model performance on inferring hidden social meanings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human social communication frequently relies on implicit signals—indirect, culturally grounded cues conveying affection, intent, and stance—rather than explicit statements. Despite the pervasiveness of such implicit social contexts in real-world interactions, no formal, systematic framework exists for studying them, leaving a critical gap in computational social understanding.

Method: The authors first define the MoCA task, systematically modeling implicit social scenarios along three dimensions (affection, intent, stance). They construct a benchmark of 3,108 real-world multimodal instances with fine-grained cognitive annotations specifying who expresses what toward whom, plus how and why. They then propose CoDAR (Conflict-Driven Abductive Reasoning), which frames the discrepancy between observed expressions and expected truthful behavior as a cognitive conflict, using this signal to abduce hidden mental states.

Result: State-of-the-art multimodal LLMs perform poorly on MoCA due to overreliance on explicit cues and weak latent social reasoning. CoDAR yields substantial improvements, yet a large performance gap persists relative to human reasoning, underscoring the fundamental difficulty of implicit social understanding.

Conclusion: Implicit social context understanding remains a profoundly challenging problem for current AI. While CoDAR advances performance by modeling cognitive conflict for abductive reasoning, the significant gap to human-level understanding highlights the need for further research into deeper, context-sensitive social reasoning.

Abstract: Human social communication, such as affection and intent, is often conveyed in highly implicit ways, where underlying meanings are expressed through indirect, socially and culturally grounded signals rather than explicit statements. Such implicit social contexts are pervasive in real-world interactions, yet there remains a lack of a formal and systematic framework for studying them. In this paper, we introduce Implicit Social Context Analysis (MoCA), a novel task that systematically models implicit social scenarios along three key dimensions: affection, intent, and stance. We construct a high-quality benchmark containing 3,108 multimodal instances collected from real-world sources, with fine-grained cognitive annotations revealing who expresses what toward whom, as well as how and why it is conveyed. Using the MoCA dataset, we show that state-of-the-art multimodal large language models struggle significantly with this task because of their reliance on explicit cues and limited ability to reason over latent social contexts. To address this challenge, we propose Conflict-Driven Abductive Reasoning (CoDAR), a novel framework that models the discrepancy between observed expressions and expected truthful behavior as cognitive conflict, thereby enabling the inference of hidden mental states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoDAR substantially improves model performance. Nevertheless, a large gap from human reasoning remains, highlighting the fundamental difficulty of implicit social understanding.

</details>


### [45] [Enhancing Social Intelligence in LLMs with Hierarchical Reasoning and Utterance-Level Goal Rewarding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05832)
*Xiaofeng Wang,Kakam Chong,Shuai Xiao,DeXin Kong,Qingyuan Tian,Chen Ju,Xu Yan,Shuai Zhao,Fei Huang,Rui Wang,Shuguang Han,jufeng chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes the Think-Strategy-Response (TSR) framework for social dialogue, decomposing it into strategic planning and linguistic execution stages, optimized via Linearized Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Variance-Gated Rewards (LHRL-VGR). A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B agent surpasses GPT-4o by 7.32% on SOTOPIA social negotiation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with dynamic social interactions because uniform goal-based rewards applied to every utterance ignore turn-specific objectives and strategic rationale. Existing methods lack the granularity to distinguish between high-level planning and low-level execution, limiting long-term goal coordination and rapid adaptation in multi-agent dialogue.

Method: The authors propose the TSR framework (inspired by the Theory of Planned Behavior), which hierarchically decomposes social dialogue into high-level strategic planning and low-level linguistic response generation. To optimize this, they introduce LHRL-VGR, a hierarchical RL algorithm that dynamically routes rewards between goal completion and strategy adherence based on the variance of goal achievement scores, enabling turn-level credit assignment.

Result: On the SOTOPIA benchmark, a Qwen2.5-7B agent fine-tuned with TSR + LHRL-VGR surpasses the GPT-4o baseline by 7.32% in goal completion success, achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-agent social negotiation tasks.

Conclusion: Hierarchical decomposition of social dialogue into strategy and response stages, combined with variance-gated dynamic reward routing, significantly improves LLM-based agents' social negotiation capabilities, outperforming even much larger proprietary models like GPT-4o.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in structured tasks but struggle with dynamic social interactions, where success requires long-term goal coordination and rapid adaptation. Current methods often apply uniform goal-based rewards to every utterance, overlooking the specificity of objectives at each dialogue turn and failing to account for the rationale of potential strategies. Inspired by the Theory of Planned Behavior, we propose the Think-Strategy-Response (TSR) framework, which decomposes social dialogue into two hierarchical stages: high-level strategic planning and low-level linguistic execution. To optimize TSR, we introduce Linearized Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Variance-Gated Rewards (LHRL-VGR), a novel algorithm that dynamically routes rewards - balancing goal completion and strategy adherence - based on the variance of goal achievement scores. Experiments on the SOTOPIA benchmark show that our approach fine-tunes a Qwen2.5-7B agent to surpass the GPT-4o baseline by 7.32% in goal completion success, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in multi-agent social negotiation tasks.

</details>


### [46] [MameLoshnLM: Yiddish Language Model and Evaluation Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05850)
*Uri Katz,Omer Goldman,Tomasz Limisiewicz,Reut Tsarfaty,Noah A. Smith*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MameLoshnLM is the first open-source 8B-parameter language model built specifically for Yiddish. The authors introduce Oytser, a high-quality Yiddish pretraining corpus, and Kashes, a multi-task Yiddish benchmark, then continue pretraining Llama 3.1 8B to achieve state-of-the-art Yiddish performance, demonstrating that general-purpose multilingual models fail to capture key lexical and morphological patterns in low-resource languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Yiddish has a rich textual tradition but suffers from a limited digital footprint and scarce, unreliable evaluation resources. Existing multilingual corpora and benchmarks contain noisy, machine-translated, and misclassified Yiddish text, making them poor proxies for genuine Yiddish language modeling. This creates a need for dedicated high-quality resources and models tailored specifically to Yiddish.

Method: The authors construct two resources: (1) Oytser, a high-quality Yiddish pretraining corpus blending contemporary web-native sources with literary materials; and (2) Kashes, a multi-task benchmark covering translation, linguistic analysis, information extraction, and language understanding. They then continue pretraining Llama 3.1 8B on Oytser to produce MameLoshnLM. The model is evaluated against open baselines of similar scale across all Kashes tasks, with additional qualitative analysis of lexical and morphological pattern capture.

Result: MameLoshnLM outperforms open baselines of comparable scale across all tasks in the Kashes benchmark. Beyond quantitative gains, analyses reveal that general-purpose multilingual models trained on noisy web-scale data fail to adequately capture language-defining lexical and morphological patterns in Yiddish, while MameLoshnLM does so effectively.

Conclusion: The work provides both a practical foundation for Yiddish NLP and a replicable template for developing language models for other historically rich but digitally underrepresented languages. It highlights a systematic failure mode of noisy multilingual web data for low-resource languages and demonstrates the value of curated, language-specific pretraining corpora.

Abstract: We present MameLoshnLM, the first open-source 8B-parameter language model built specifically for Yiddish. Despite Yiddish's rich textual tradition, its limited digital presence and the scarcity of reliable evaluation resources have constrained progress in Yiddish language modeling. Existing multilingual corpora and benchmarks are often poor proxies for the language, containing substantial amounts of noisy, machine-translated, and misclassified text. We address these gaps by introducing Oytser, a high-quality Yiddish pretraining corpus that combines contemporary web-native sources with literary materials, and Kashes, a multi-task benchmark spanning translation, linguistic analysis, information extraction, and language understanding. Using these resources, we continue pretraining Llama 3.1 8B to obtain MameLoshnLM. Across the tasks in the benchmark, MameLoshnLM outperforms open baselines of similar scale. Our analyses show that these gains are not only quantitative: relative to general-purpose multilingual models, MameLoshnLM better captures language-defining lexical and morphological patterns, pointing to a broader failure mode of noisy web-scale multilingual data for low-resource languages. Our results provide both a foundation for Yiddish NLP and a practical template for language model development in historically rich but digitally underrepresented languages.

</details>


### [47] [Mapping Similarity Spaces across Embedding Models with Synthetic Query Probing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05857)
*Marcin Rozmus,Peter van der Putten*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Synthetic Query Probing (SQP) enables cross-model similarity score calibration by generating queries from documents, learning mappings between score distributions rather than embeddings. Isotonic regression best aligns score spaces, improving threshold portability across embedding models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Similarity scores from different embedding models are not directly comparable due to distinct geometric properties, making model migration difficult and preventing reuse of retrieval thresholds. The authors aim to address this cross-model calibration problem without requiring access to embeddings themselves.

Method: Synthetic Query Probing (SQP): queries are synthetically generated from documents to create controlled query-chunk pairs, enabling large-scale, reference-free analysis of similarity behavior across models. Authors then learn score conversion functions (linear, isotonic regression, quantile mappings) to map scores between embedding configurations.

Result: Models largely agree on rankings but exhibit systematic distortions in absolute scores. Learned mappings partially align score spaces. Isotonic regression outperforms linear and quantile mappings for improving threshold portability. Validated on SciFact and a proprietary corpus.

Conclusion: Cross-model calibration is necessary for RAG systems. SQP provides a scalable, reference-free framework for analyzing embedding comparability and enabling reliable score translation between models.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems rely on similarity scores to retrieve relevant content, yet scores are not directly comparable across embedding models due to differing geometric properties, complicating model migration and limiting threshold reuse. We study how similarity scores can be related by learning mappings between score distributions rather than embeddings. We introduce Synthetic Query Probing, generating queries from documents to create controlled query-chunk pairs, enabling large-scale, reference-free analysis of cross-model similarity behavior. We evaluate the approach on multiple embedding configurations and learn score conversion functions using linear, isotonic, and quantile mappings. Experiments on SciFact and a proprietary corpus show that while models largely agree on rankings, their absolute scores exhibit systematic distortions. Learned mappings partially align these spaces and improve threshold portability, with isotonic regression performing best. Our results highlight the need for cross-model calibration and position Synthetic Query Probing as a scalable framework for analyzing embedding comparability.

</details>


### [48] [MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05872)
*Paweł Batorski,Abtin Pourhadi,Akylgali Aitaza,Przemysław Spurek,Paul Swoboda*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MACRO learns task-specific layer execution paths for LLMs via a Markov decision process, without modifying model weights. It supports skip, repeat, and residual operations, achieving +5.0% accuracy over baselines and outperforming prior routing methods by 7.2% while being 9.4× faster to search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLMs execute layers sequentially, but dynamic routing (skipping, repeating layers) can improve performance. Existing routing methods are limited: they require weight updates, expensive per-instance search, or ground-truth labels at inference time. A more efficient, label-free, parameter-static approach is needed.

Method: MACRO frames layer routing as a context-dependent Markov policy conditioned on layer index, budget phase, directional displacement, and operator context. It supports skip, repeat, and residual hidden-state addition. The Markov route distribution is trained via feedback on training data and decoded using a top-k Viterbi algorithm to extract high-probability candidate programs. No model weights are modified.

Result: MACRO achieves +5.0% average accuracy over unrouted baselines (largest gains on small models) and outperforms Dr. LLM by +7.2% while reducing route-search time from 14.8 to 1.6 hours (9.4× speedup), evaluated across diverse reasoning and knowledge benchmarks on multiple open-weight LLMs.

Conclusion: MACRO demonstrates that task-specific, parameter-free Markov chain routing over frozen LLM layers is both effective and efficient, offering substantial accuracy gains with dramatically reduced search cost compared to prior dynamic routing approaches.

Abstract: Standard Large Language Models (LLMs) execute layers sequentially.
