Dynamic layer routing, i.e. search for a different execution path through layers involving layer repetitions, skips and other moves, can improve performance. Existing routing approaches often require updating model weights, running expensive search loops per test instance, or demand ground-truth labels during inference. In this work, we propose Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers (MACRO), a framework that learns task-specific routes over LLM architectures without modifying underlying parameters. MACRO models layer routing as a context-dependent Markov policy conditioned on layer indices, computation budget phases, directional displacements, and operator context, supporting skip, repeat, and residual hidden-state addition operations. The Markov route distribution is updated via feedback on training data and decoded using a top-k Viterbi algorithm to isolate high-probability candidate programs. We evaluate MACRO across diverse reasoning and knowledge benchmarks on multiple open-weight LLMs. MACRO achieves a +5.0% average accuracy improvement over the unrouted baselines, with largest gains on small models. We outperform the best dynamic routing approach Dr. LLM by +7.2%, while reducing route-search time 9.4x (from 14.8 to 1.6 hours). Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/MACRO.

</details>


### [49] [Causal Episodic Memory for Feedback-Driven Agent Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05906)
*Khang Nhat Hoang Vo,Tam Minh Chu,Anh Trac Duc Dinh,Thuyen Vinh Ha Bui,Tho Quan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MERIT is a training-free framework that uses dual-polarity memory (successful fixes and failed directions) with hybrid retrieval to improve iterative Text-to-SQL repair across episodes, showing modest accuracy gains on Spider and BIRD benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents that iteratively repair Text-to-SQL failures discard corrections after each episode, forcing repeated rediscovery of similar solutions. The authors investigate whether storing and retrieving finalized repair outcomes from earlier episodes can improve subsequent repair attempts without any parameter updates.

Method: MERIT maintains an online dual-polarity memory: positive entries store oracle-verified corrections, negative entries record unsuccessful repair directions. A deterministic classifier assigns coarse failure types to each episode, which condition a hybrid lexical-dense retriever. During repair, the frozen LLM (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) receives retrieved memories as context for generating revisions, using only memories from earlier finalized episodes under oracle-assisted benchmark feedback.

Result: On Spider, execution accuracy improves from 66.34% to 69.79%; on BIRD, from 47.35% to 48.44%. Paired analyses show clear evidence for gains on Spider but weaker evidence on BIRD. MERIT is not reliably separable from untyped dynamic retrieval on either benchmark. Reflexion-style memory reaches 51.24% on BIRD but at substantially higher inference cost. Ablations reveal negative memory contributes modestly, type conditioning and lexical-dense ranking benefits are dataset-dependent, and schema-local experience provides the most consistent benefit.

Conclusion: Causal cross-query memory can improve iterative Text-to-SQL repair, but gains are modest and dataset-dependent. Schema-local experience is the most consistently beneficial memory source. Broader memory representations (e.g., Reflexion-style) may remain preferable in some settings despite higher inference cost.

Abstract: LLM agents that repair failures often discard successful corrections, forcing later episodes to rediscover similar solutions. We study whether finalized repair outcomes can improve subsequent Text-to-SQL episodes without parameter updates. We introduce MERIT, a training-free agent that maintains an online dual-polarity memory of oracle-verified corrections and observed unsuccessful directions. Under oracle-assisted benchmark feedback, only memories from earlier finalized episodes are eligible for retrieval. A deterministic classifier assigns a coarse failure type, which conditions a hybrid lexical-dense retriever before the frozen model generates each revision. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with identical initial predictions and repair budgets, MERIT improves execution accuracy over stateless iterative repair from \(66.34\%\) to \(69.79\%\) on Spider and from \(47.35\%\) to \(48.44\%\) on BIRD. Paired analyses provide clear evidence for the Spider gain but weaker evidence on BIRD. MERIT is not reliably separated from untyped dynamic retrieval on either benchmark, while Reflexion-style memory reaches \(51.24\%\) on BIRD at substantially higher inference cost. Ablations show that negative memory contributes modestly, the value of type conditioning and lexical--dense ranking is dataset dependent, and schema-local experience provides the most consistent benefit. These results clarify when causal cross-query memory improves repair and when broader memory representations remain preferable.

</details>


### [50] [Clinical Communication Processing with Models Trained on LLM-Generated Synthetic Data: A Structured Survey and Novel Application Case Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05993)
*Alexander Apartsin,Yehudit Aperstein*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Clinical communication conveys critical information through language rather than structured records, but annotated corpora are scarce. This paper surveys synthetic clinical communication generation using LLMs, presenting 13 case studies showing that synthetic data can bootstrap NLP systems for diverse clinical channels, with fine-tuned encoders proving competitive and degraded communication aiding robustness. The key limitation is limited train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Much clinical value is transmitted through communication (patient descriptions, handoffs, shift changes) rather than structured records. Such language differs fundamentally from tabular data because meaning depends on speaker role, intent, causality, uncertainty, omission, and channel noise. Well-annotated corpora for healthcare NLP are scarce because authentic clinical exchanges are private, fragmented, and costly to annotate. Large language models offer a way to transform structured clinical sources into synthetic communication for downstream model training.

Method: The authors present a structured narrative survey organized along four dimensions: (1) source representation (records, diagnostic labels, symptom lists, care plans), (2) communication form and participants, (3) generation method, and (4) downstream task. This is complemented by thirteen novel case studies building clinical NLP systems without labeled real-world data, covering EMS pre-arrival reports, field-radio casualty documentation, nurse handoffs, patient-portal triage, and low-resource discharge communication. Both zero-shot LLM baselines and fine-tuned encoder models are evaluated.

Result: Synthetic clinical communication can successfully bootstrap NLP systems across diverse channels and languages. Fine-tuned encoder models proved competitive against zero-shot LLM baselines. Deliberately degraded communication improved model robustness. However, most studies evaluated only on held-out synthetic data; train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic evidence remains limited.

Conclusion: Synthetic clinical communication is becoming a practical research resource. To establish it as reusable clinical infrastructure, future work must address authentic-data transfer, safety validation, and external validation.

Abstract: Much clinical value is conveyed not through structured records but through communication: exchanges in which patients describe symptoms, clinicians reason and give instructions, ambulances hand over to emergency departments, and nurses pass on a shift. Such language differs from tabular data because meaning depends on speaker role, intent, causality, uncertainty, omission, and channel noise. Healthcare natural language processing must therefore interpret information as conveyed rather than coded. This requires well-annotated corpora, which are scarce because authentic exchanges are private, fragmented, and costly to annotate. Large language models offer a way forward by transforming clinical sources, such as records, diagnostic labels, symptom lists, or care plans, into written and transcribed communication for downstream models. We present a structured narrative survey organized by source representation, communication form and participants, generation method, and downstream task, complemented by thirteen novel case studies. These build clinical NLP systems for communication channels and languages without labeled real-world data, including EMS pre-arrival reports, field-radio casualty documentation, nurse handoffs, patient-portal triage, and low-resource discharge communication. They show that synthetic communication can bootstrap such systems. Findings include the competitiveness of fine-tuned encoder models over evaluated zero-shot baselines and the value of deliberately degraded communication for robustness. The main limitation is that most studies evaluate on held-out synthetic communication, while train-on-synthetic, test-on-authentic evidence remains limited. We conclude that syn-thetic clinical communication is becoming a practical research resource; establishing it as reusable clinical infrastructure will require authentic-data transfer, safety and external validation.

</details>


### [51] [EpiBench: Can LLMs Understand Epitopes for Antibody Drug Discovery?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06022)
*Zirui Wang,Jiaqi Wang,Qinghan Wang,Yuzhi Xu,Gang Du,Tingjun Hou,Odin Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EpiBench is a sequence-based benchmark with 1,609 curated samples for evaluating how well large language models (LLMs) reason about antibody-antigen epitopes across five tasks. Current LLMs show partial epitope awareness but struggle with antibody-specific grounding, long-context localization, and biological reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Epitope understanding is central to antibody drug discovery, yet no benchmark exists to evaluate whether LLMs can infer epitope information directly from antigen and antibody sequences. Existing resources focus on isolated prediction or structural settings, leaving a gap in assessing epitope-centered reasoning across the antibody development workflow.

Method: The authors introduce EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, automatically scorable benchmark with 1,609 samples grounded in structural antibody-antigen contacts, functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape data. It spans five tasks: targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment, with controlled sampling to mitigate shortcut-based artifacts. Nine general-purpose LLMs are evaluated with task-specific baselines, antigen-length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode analysis.

Result: Current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but exhibit significant limitations in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning. Performance varies across tasks and models, with systematic failure modes identified.

Conclusion: EpiBench serves as a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs, highlighting concrete gaps that must be addressed for reliable LLM-assisted antibody discovery.

Abstract: Epitopes determine where antibodies bind antigens and shape downstream therapeutic properties such as functional blockade and escape resistance, making epitope understanding central to antibody drug discovery. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong biomedical reasoning ability, it remains unclear whether they can infer epitope information directly from antigen and antibody sequences. Existing epitope resources typically focus on isolated prediction tasks or rely on specialized structural settings, while general protein benchmarks do not evaluate epitope-centered decisions across the antibody development workflow. To address this gap, we introduce EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, and automatically scorable benchmark for evaluating epitope reasoning in LLMs. EpiBench contains 1,609 curated samples grounded in structural antibody--antigen contacts, curated functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape measurements. It covers five connected tasks: targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment, with controlled sampling to reduce shortcut-based evaluation artifacts. We evaluate nine general-purpose LLMs and analyze their behavior through task-specific baselines, antigen length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode inspection. The results show that current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but remain limited in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning. Therefore, EpiBench provides a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs toward reliable LLM-assisted antibody discovery.

</details>


### [52] [Training-Free Token-Level Steering for LLM Personalized Co-Writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06069)
*Wenhao Mao,Chengbin Hou,Weixiao Wang,Jialiang Zhu,Min Liu,Yibin Hao,Hairong Lv*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SteerWrite is a training-free framework for personalized co-writing that adapts LLMs to specialized domains without gradient updates, using token-level steering to outperform fine-tuning and RAG baselines while reducing human editing effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs lack specialized domain knowledge for personalization. Fine-tuning is computationally expensive and ill-suited for rapidly changing data; RAG cannot provide fine-grained, token-level control. Additionally, co-writing paradigms remain underexplored outside coding, with chat interfaces dominating despite their limitations for productive writing workflows.

Method: SteerWrite is a training-free framework that adapts a base LLM to specialized domains without gradient updates. It employs tailored designs for small datasets and provides token-level steering, enabling personalized co-writing by directly guiding the model's generation at inference time rather than through parameter modification or external retrieval augmentation.

Result: SteerWrite achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse datasets, evaluation metrics, and model architectures, while significantly reducing the human editing effort required in personalized co-writing tasks.

Conclusion: Training-free adaptation via token-level steering is a viable and effective alternative to fine-tuning and RAG for personalized co-writing in specialized domains, particularly when working with small datasets and when minimizing human post-editing is a priority.

Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show great promise for personalization, they often lack specialized domain knowledge. Conventional solutions like fine-tuning struggle with high computational costs and rapid data updates, while Retrieval-Augmented Generation fails to provide fine-grained, token-level steering. Furthermore, chat-based interfaces remain dominant, whereas productive co-writing paradigms have not yet been well exploited beyond the coding domain. To this end, we introduce SteerWrite, a training-free framework designed for personalized co-writing. Our method effectively adapts the base model to specialized domains without gradient updates, with specific designs tailored to small datasets. Experiments demonstrate that SteerWrite achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse datasets, metrics, and models, significantly reducing human editing effort.

</details>


### [53] [Beyond Sequence Order: Syntax-Informed Positional Embeddings for Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06111)
*Haris Riaz,Hyungji Kim,Mihai Surdeanu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SiPE introduces syntax-informed positional embeddings that inject lightweight syntactic priors from dependency parses into Transformers, improving both syntactic generalization (SyntaxGym +10.3%) and real-world language understanding (GLUE +8.2%) while reducing perplexity (9.0%), without the inference-cost overhead of existing syntactic LMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard positional embeddings encode token distance/order but remain agnostic to syntactic structure. Existing syntax-injection methods typically degrade perplexity, require marginalizing over many parses at inference, or discard syntax at runtime—creating a trade-off between syntactic supervision and inference cost. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a lightweight, parse-conditioned mechanism that improves both syntactic and general language understanding without added inference overhead.

Method: SiPE learns a syntactic prior from dependency parses during pretraining and injects it across all three dominant PE families (absolute, relative, rotary) for both encoders and decoders. The injection strategy is architecture-dependent: for autoregressive decoders with relative PE, the prior is coupled multiplicatively with the relative-position term in the attention score; for encoders, it is added directly to input embeddings, composing with the native positional mechanism. The method conditions on a single parse and leaves self-attention and the rest of the architecture unchanged.

Result: SiPE improves SyntaxGym by up to 10.3% and reduces perplexity by 9.0% over a base model with no syntactic supervision—unlike prior syntax-injection methods that degrade perplexity. GLUE scores improve by up to 8.2%. SiPE establishes a new Pareto frontier between syntactic supervision and inference cost, outperforming methods that marginalize over many parses or discard syntax at runtime.

Conclusion: SiPE demonstrates that a lightweight, single-parse-conditioned syntactic prior injected through positional embeddings can simultaneously improve syntactic generalization, language modeling perplexity, and real-world NLU benchmarks, challenging the assumption that syntax injection necessarily incurs an inference-cost or perplexity trade-off.

Abstract: Positional embeddings (PE) in Transformers encode token distance and order but are largely agnostic to \textit{syntactic structure}. We introduce \textbf{S}yntax-\textbf{i}nformed \textbf{P}ositional \textbf{E}mbeddings (\textbf{SiPE}), which learns a lightweight syntactic prior from dependency parses during pretraining and injects it across all three dominant PE families (absolute, relative, rotary), for both encoders and decoders, leaving self-attention and the rest of the architecture untouched. We isolate \emph{where} and \emph{how} the prior should enter the model, and find it depends on the architecture: for autoregressive decoders that use relative PE, the prior is strongest when coupled multiplicatively with the relative-position term of the attention score, outperforming injection into the input embeddings, into self-attention, or into the positional and attention terms jointly---while for encoders it is best added directly to the input embeddings, composing with each encoder's native positional mechanism. We find that models pre-trained with SiPE improve on the SyntaxGym benchmark by up to $10.3\%$ while simultaneously reducing perplexity by $9.0\%$ over a base model with no syntactic supervision---a metric nearly every existing syntax-injection method instead degrades. Crucially, these gains extend beyond syntactic generalization: SiPE also improves real-world language understanding, raising scores on the GLUE benchmark by up to $8.2\%$ over a model trained without it. Unlike existing syntactic language models that marginalize over many parses at inference or discard syntax at runtime, SiPE conditions on a single parse, establishing a new Pareto frontier between syntactic supervision and inference cost.

</details>


### [54] [Routing Is Least Learnable Where It Is Most Valuable: Bounds on Representation Routing for Web Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06171)
*Jiaming Wei,Zekun Wu,Adriano Koshiyama,Maria Perez-Ortiz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether dynamically choosing an agent's observation mode (text, pixels, or both) per task outperforms using a fixed mode. While an oracle mode selector promises large gains, run-to-run noise accounts for much of it. The authors find that a simple cost-minimization strategy (defaulting to cheap mode, escalating only for unsolved tasks) consistently reduces cost without sacrificing success. However, no learned routing policy robustly beats a single well-chosen fixed mode, primarily because routing supervision is scarce precisely when it's most needed — a limitation tied to current agent capability rather than routing itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Web agents typically use a fixed observation modality (text-only, vision-only, or multimodal) across all tasks. The authors question this fixed design choice and ask: what gains are possible if the observation mode is selected per task? They aim to quantify the complementarity of different modes, measure the true benefit of an oracle selector after accounting for noise, and test whether practical routing policies can realize these gains.

Method: The authors evaluate six observation modes across eight site-model combinations (cells) on VisualWebArena and WebArena benchmarks. They measure: (1) complementarity between modes via task-level agreement/disagreement, (2) run-to-run noise by re-executing identical mode-task pairs, (3) oracle routing upper bounds after noise correction, (4) a cost-bound strategy routing only unsolved tasks to the cheapest alternative mode, and (5) five practical routing policies (per-mode selector, cost-sensitive spending rule, zero-cost text-based heuristic, confidence cascade, and pooled cost tiers). They also compute the correlation between label supply and routing opportunity across cells.

Result: Key findings: (1) Modes are complementary — each solves tasks others miss, with structurally different failure modes. (2) Run-to-run noise flips 12-14% of outcomes, meaning much of the oracle's apparent gain is illusory. (3) The cost-bound strategy cuts cost by 9.5-30.6% across all 8 cells with zero success loss. (4) No routing policy robustly beats a single well-chosen fixed mode; the sole exception is fragile and occurs only in the sparsest cell. (5) Routing supervision is generated at the agent's success rate, creating a chicken-and-egg problem: weaker agents produce fewer labels exactly where routing is most needed. Label supply and routing opportunity correlate at 0.95 across cells, suggesting stronger future agents could overturn the negative result.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that per-task mode selection's theoretical promise is substantially eroded by run-to-run noise. While a simple cost-minimization heuristic works reliably, learned routing policies fail to robustly beat a fixed mode due to insufficient supervision in low-success regimes. This limitation is not inherent to routing but reflects current agent quality — as agent capability improves, label supply and routing opportunity rise together, potentially enabling effective dynamic mode selection in the future. The authors release their noise measurements and full protocol for reproducibility.

Abstract: Web agents observe a browser through text, pixels, or both, and the choice is usually fixed once for all tasks. We measure six observation modes across eight site-model combinations (cells) on VisualWebArena and WebArena and ask what choosing per task would buy. The modes are complementary: each solves tasks the others miss, they fail in structurally different ways, and the best choice reverses between task sets. The obvious prize, an oracle that picks a winning mode for every task, looks large but is inflated by run-to-run noise: rerunning the same mode on the same tasks changes 12-14% of outcomes, so a second run of a mode already in hand gains about as much as adding a new one. What survives is a cost bound: sending only the tasks no mode solves to the cheapest mode cuts cost by 9.5-30.6% in 8 of 8 cells at unchanged success. We then test five routing policies (picking the mode, deciding when to spend on the strong mode, a zero-cost rule read off the task text, a confidence cascade, and pooled cost tiers), and none robustly beats simply fixing one well-chosen mode; the one exception is a fragile result in our sparsest cell. The central obstruction is that routing supervision is produced at the agent's success rate: the weaker the agent, the fewer labels a router gets, exactly where routing would be most valuable. This limit belongs to today's agents rather than to routing itself. Label supply and routing opportunity rise together (correlation 0.95 across cells), so a stronger agent can overturn the result, and we report the rerun noise bands and the full measurement protocol.

</details>


### [55] [NeSy-RAG: Neuro-Symbolic RAG for Explainable Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06292)
*Jonas Gann,Michael Gertz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NeSy-RAG is a neuro-symbolic RAG framework that translates retrieved text into attributable Prolog modules, enabling transparent, verifiable reasoning with deterministic answers. It introduces a knowledge-gap detection mechanism for missing user context and achieves 61.1% accuracy on ShARC, substantially outperforming a standard RAG baseline (42.8%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG systems suffer from opaque reasoning processes where intermediate steps cannot be verified or attributed to specific evidence. Additionally, missing user-specific context is rarely detected systematically, leading to incomplete or incorrect outputs. There is a need for a framework that provides transparent, attributable, and auditable multi-step reasoning while proactively identifying knowledge gaps.

Method: NeSy-RAG is a modular neuro-symbolic framework that: (1) generates semantically meaningful Prolog predicates encoding Boolean claims from each retrieved text chunk; (2) uses joint natural language–code embeddings to retrieve and compose predicates into executable Prolog queries; (3) incorporates a symbolic knowledge-gap detection mechanism that identifies missing user facts affecting query outcomes and triggers follow-up interactions; and (4) executes Prolog queries to produce deterministic answers with transparent execution traces linking each reasoning step to its source.

Result: On the ShARC benchmark, without any domain-specific training, NeSy-RAG achieves 61.1% accuracy, outperforming the same-model RAG baseline by 18.3 percentage points (42.8% accuracy).

Conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach effectively addresses key limitations of standard RAG by providing transparent, attributable reasoning and systematic detection of missing user context. The significant performance gain on ShARC demonstrates that synthesizing explicit symbolic representations from retrieved evidence yields more reliable and interpretable question answering.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves question answering by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external knowledge such as text corpora. However, its reasoning process remains largely opaque: intermediate reasoning steps are difficult to verify and cannot be reliably attributed to specific evidence. Moreover, missing user-specific context is rarely detected systematically, often leading to incomplete or incorrect output.
  We propose NeSy-RAG, a modular neuro-symbolic RAG framework that synthesizes attributable Prolog modules from retrieved text chunks. For each chunk, the system generates semantically meaningful predicates that encode Boolean claims, which may depend on user facts. Using joint natural language-code embeddings, predicates are retrieved and composed into Prolog queries. To address incomplete user context, we introduce a symbolic knowledge-gap detection mechanism that identifies missing user facts whose truth values affect the query outcome and automatically triggers follow-up interactions.
  Executing the resulting Prolog queries yields deterministic answers together with transparent execution traces that link each reasoning step to its originating source. On the ShARC benchmark, without domain-specific training, NeSy-RAG achieves 61.1% accuracy, outperforming a same-model RAG baseline that achieves 42.8% accuracy.

</details>


### [56] [Benchmarking and Enhancing LLMs for Rule-Intensive Review of National Standard Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06312)
*Tao Wang,Qihao Yang,Rongjiao Liang,Lianghong Lin,Haitao Wang,Xinyu Cao,Tianyong Hao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces GB/T-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on rule-intensive review of Chinese national standard documents, featuring 7,306 traceable error instances across 25 error types. Proposes GB/T-Reviewer, a multi-agent framework that improves performance, revealing a significant gap between LLMs and human experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for complex professional tasks, but their ability to perform rule-intensive document review—particularly for highly structured standards like China's GB/T documents—remains underevaluated. Existing benchmarks focus on domain QA rather than intrinsic quality review, and human expert review is costly and hard to scale.

Method: GB/T-Bench is constructed using a hierarchical taxonomy (GB/T Review Taxonomy) with 25 error types across 5 dimensions. A controllable counterexample generation mechanism combines deterministic rules with constrained LLM rewriting to inject traceable errors into 488 documents, yielding 7,306 instances. A diagnosis-oriented evaluation protocol uses exact-match metrics (location, dimension, error type) plus document-level coverage. GB/T-Reviewer, a multi-agent framework, coordinates global inspection, targeted diagnosis, rule scanning, and result verification by converting review knowledge into specialized skills.

Result: Across 14 mainstream LLMs, the strongest achieves only 0.3280 CMCS versus 0.6640 for human experts. GB/T-Reviewer raises the best CMCS to 0.5094, substantially narrowing the gap.

Conclusion: Structured skill coordination via multi-agent frameworks significantly improves LLM performance on rule-intensive document review. The work advances trustworthy AI for standardization and high-stakes document domains, while revealing that a substantial human-LLM gap remains.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support complex professional tasks, yet their capabilities in rule-intensive document review remain insufficiently evaluated. National standard documents, such as China GB/T standards, offer a representative testbed: they are lengthy, highly structured, and governed by explicit rules for scope, terminology, normative wording, and cross-section consistency. Existing benchmarks focus on domain knowledge and question answering, largely overlooking intrinsic quality review for professional documents. Such reviews rely heavily on human experts, making them costly and difficult to scale. To bridge this gap, we introduce GB/T-Bench, the first benchmark for the structured review of national standard documents. Its GB/T Review Taxonomy is a hierarchical schema covering document structure, scope alignment, normative modality, terminology consistency, and normative references, with 25 diagnosable error types. A controllable counterexample generation mechanism combines deterministic rules and constrained LLM rewriting to process 488 documents into 7,306 traceable review error instances for evaluation. We also develop a diagnosis-oriented evaluation protocol requiring exact matches on error location, review dimension, and error type, plus document-level coverage metrics. We further propose GB/T-Reviewer, a multi-agent framework that converts review knowledge into specialized skills and coordinates global inspection, targeted diagnosis, rule scanning, and result verification. Experiments with 14 mainstream LLMs reveal a substantial human-LLM gap: the strongest model achieves only 0.3280 CMCS versus 0.6640 for experts. GB/T-Reviewer raises the best CMCS to 0.5094, showing the value of structured skill coordination for rule-intensive document review. This work paves the way for trustworthy AI in standardization and other high-stakes document domains.

</details>


### [57] [Benchmarking the Benchmarks: Evaluating Benchmarks for Conversational Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06329)
*Noam Koren,Roy Bar-Haim,Abigail Goldsteen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A reference-free framework using LLM judges to evaluate conversational agent benchmark quality across three dimensions—consistency, complexity, and policy coverage—validated against human annotations and capable of distinguishing quality levels in both synthetic and manually curated benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Task-oriented conversational agent benchmarks are widely used but rarely evaluated for quality. Poor benchmarks with inconsistent tasks, simplistic scenarios, or inadequate policy coverage produce unreliable evaluation results, undermining the validity of conversational agent assessments.

Method: A reference-free evaluation framework employing LLM judges to score benchmarks along three axes: consistency (logical coherence of tasks), complexity (richness of scenarios), and policy coverage (completeness of action/intent specifications). The framework also provides actionable diagnostics. Validation is performed through agreement with human annotations, cross-model comparisons, and controlled quality-degrading perturbations.

Result: The proposed metrics reliably distinguish between benchmark quality levels across multiple domains and judge models. The framework shows agreement with independent human annotations and successfully detects quality degradation under controlled perturbations. It proves effective on both LLM-generated and manually curated benchmarks.

Conclusion: The framework provides a practical, automated method for evaluating conversational agent benchmark quality, enabling more reliable model assessments and offering diagnostic insights for benchmark improvement.

Abstract: Task-oriented conversational agents are evaluated using curated or automatically generated benchmarks, yet benchmark quality is rarely assessed. Poor benchmarks may contain inconsistent tasks, simplistic scenarios, or limited policy coverage, leading to unreliable evaluations. We introduce a reference-free framework that uses LLM judges to assess benchmark consistency, complexity, and policy coverage, while providing actionable diagnostics of weaknesses. We validate the framework by demonstrating agreement with independent human annotations and by evaluating benchmarks generated by LLMs of varying capabilities, as well as benchmarks subjected to controlled quality-degrading perturbations. Across domains and judge models, the proposed metrics consistently distinguish between benchmark quality levels. We further demonstrate the framework's applicability to manually curated benchmarks. Our framework offers a practical approach for evaluating synthetic and manually curated conversational-agent benchmarks.

</details>


### [58] [RP-OPSD: Reasoning-Pivot-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation for Multilingual Reasoning Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06347)
*Xinye Wang,Junxiao Liu,Shujian Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RP-OPSD proposes Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, which improves multilingual reasoning transfer by concentrating privileged distillation on "reasoning pivots" — tokens that advance or redirect the reasoning process — using distributional shift between teacher views with and without English references as a guiding signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods for multilingual reasoning transfer provide dense token-level supervision but do not explicitly prioritize the reasoning signals most critical to cross-lingual transfer. The authors characterize target-language reasoning as comprising surface text generation and "reasoning pivots" (decisions that shape subsequent inference), motivating concentrated distillation around these pivots.

Method: RP-OPSD uses the distributional shift between two teacher views — one conditioned on an English reference solution and one without — as an operational proxy to identify reasoning pivots. This shift guides privileged distillation, allocating higher weight to reasoning-control and problem-conditioned state-update tokens while downweighting surface-realization tokens, combined with reference anchoring.

Result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks across 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels show RP-OPSD outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and existing OPSD variants.

Conclusion: RP-OPSD effectively improves multilingual reasoning transfer by explicitly prioritizing reasoning pivots during self-distillation, with analysis confirming the method successfully concentrates supervision on tokens that control reasoning flow and state updates.

Abstract: Multilingual reasoning transfer is crucial for extending reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) beyond high-resource languages. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and its variants have emerged as a promising paradigm, providing dense token-level supervision on student-generated rollouts, yet their objectives do not explicitly prioritize reasoning signals most critical to cross-lingual transfer. We characterize that target-language reasoning comprises the generation of both surface text and reasoning pivots, which are decisions that advance or redirect the reasoning process and shape subsequent inference. This motivates concentrating privileged distillation around such pivots. We therefore propose RP-OPSD, Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, using the distributional shift between matched teacher views with and without an English reference solution as an operational proxy to guide privileged distillation and reference anchoring. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks covering 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels show that our method outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and OPSD variants. Further analysis reveals that RP-OPSD concentrates privileged distillation on reasoning-control and problem-condistioned state-update tokens, while downweighting it for tokens that mainly support surface realization. Our code is available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/RP-OPSD.

</details>


### [59] [The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06370)
*Ishan Patel,Sahil Sen,Elias Lumer,Vamse Kumar Subbiah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper empirically compares programmatic tool calling (PTC) — where tools are Python stubs invoked via code — against native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on the BFCL v4 benchmark. PTC matches or exceeds JSON calling in 11 of 14 models, with GPT-5.6 showing a 10.6% improvement, and proves more robust under parallel fan-out and context rot conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the emergence of programmatic tool calling as a more flexible alternative to rigid JSON-based tool invocation, no systematic evaluation exists comparing PTC to JSON tool calling across model generations on an established benchmark under realistic task conditions. The authors aim to fill this gap.

Method: The authors evaluate 14 language models on BFCL v4 (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard) under two paradigms: (1) native JSON tool calling, where tools are described in JSON schema and invoked with structured JSON outputs, and (2) programmatic tool calling (PTC), where tools are exposed as typed Python stubs that the model invokes through code, with execution and results completed in a single agent turn. Evaluation covers standard calls, parallel fan-out scenarios, and context rot (long-context degradation) conditions.

Result: PTC matched or exceeded JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models on BFCL v4. The GPT-5.6 family achieved a 10.6% improvement over baseline. Under parallel fan-out, PTC matched or outperformed baseline in 13 of 14 models. Under context rot conditions, PTC remained stable while the JSON baseline degraded by an average of 2.3%. Performance of PTC tracked model capability across release generations.

Conclusion: Programmatic tool calling is a viable, robust, and often superior alternative to JSON tool calling, particularly under challenging conditions like parallelism and long contexts. Its performance scales with model capability, suggesting it is well-suited as a paradigm for future agent architectures.

Abstract: Tool use transforms LLMs into agents that act beyond their training data, and for code-capable models, programmatic tool calling extends this further by replacing rigid JSON calls with scripts that chain and parallelize naturally. However, a systematic evaluation of tools as code on an established benchmark across current and prior model generations under real-world task conditions has not been conducted. In this work, we empirically compare programmatic tool calling (PTC) to native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on BFCL v4. In the programmatic tool calling paradigm, tools are exposed as typed Python stubs that the model invokes through code, with execution and results handled in a single agent turn. Programmatic tool calling matches or exceeds native JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models on BFCL v4, with the GPT-5.6 family achieving a 10.6% improvement over the JSON tool calling baseline. Further, it matches or outperforms baseline in 13 of 14 models under parallel fan-out, and holds stable under context rot conditions where baseline degrades 2.3% on average. Our results demonstrate that programmatic tool calling is a viable and robust alternative to JSON tool calling, with performance tracking model capability across release generations.

</details>


### [60] [Learning When to Trust via Selective Context Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06377)
*Xian Sun,Wei Chow,Yingshuo Wang,Junhao Liu,Wei Gao,Qing Wu,Lingdong Kong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MIST introduces selective trust as a framework for evaluating language models' ability to use context appropriately—resisting misleading signals while still leveraging trustworthy ones. The benchmark tests models under four matched conditions, and the proposed SCOPE training method uses balanced DPO across all conditions to reduce susceptibility to misleading context without sacrificing performance on clean, correct, or irrelevant context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to making language models robust against misleading context risk overcorrecting—producing models that ignore all external signals, including trustworthy ones. The authors argue that the goal should be selective trust: knowing when to rely on context and when to resist it.

Method: The authors introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark with four matched conditions per reasoning item: clean (no context), misleading, correct-context, and irrelevant-context. They also propose SC2W, a metric measuring how often misleading context flips a correct answer to wrong. For mitigation, they introduce SCOPE, which mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failure pairs and applies Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) over balanced preference pairs across all four conditions.

Result: Susceptibility to misleading context is universal across tested models. The SCOPE training method substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-source models while preserving accuracy when context is clean, correct, or irrelevant.

Conclusion: Models should be evaluated on selective trust—the ability to appropriately leverage or resist context—rather than on resistance to misleading signals alone. The MIST benchmark and SCOPE training method together provide a framework for achieving and measuring this capability.

Abstract: Language models increasingly condition their answers on external signals, and a single misleading one can turn a correct answer wrong. The obvious remedy, training models to resist such signals, hides a failure mode: a model that ignores all context looks robust yet is useless when the context is worth trusting. We recast the problem as selective trust and introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark that renders each reasoning item under four matched conditions (clean, misleading, correct-context, and irrelevant-context), together with SC2W, a paired metric counting how often a misleading signal flips a clean-correct answer to wrong. Across a comprehensive benchmark study, we observe that such a susceptibility is universal. We then propose SCOPE, which mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failures and optimizes a standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective over matched preference pairs balanced equally across all four conditions, rather than over misleading items alone. Our approach substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-sourced models while preserving accuracy when the added context is clean, correct, or irrelevant. With this work, we argue that models should be judged on selective trust, not on resistance alone.

</details>

### [61] [Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05159)
*Xi Wang,Kun Li,Xianyao Ling,Gang Yin,Liang Zhang,Jiang Wu,Wenbo Lei,Jun Xu,Annie Wang,Fu Zhang,Weizhe Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework that encapsulates legacy enterprise applications as autonomous AI agents organized in hierarchical stewardship topologies, enabling natural-language interaction and cross-application orchestration through a central orchestrator and unified conversational interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprises suffer from severe data silos and process fragmentation due to heterogeneous business systems. Despite substantial investment in these applications, conventional integration approaches (ESB, API gateways, RPA) exhibit high architectural coupling, escalating O&M costs, and limited intelligence. A new paradigm is needed to effectively leverage and orchestrate existing enterprise applications.

Method: The Agentic Nesting framework encapsulates each legacy application as an autonomous AI agent via a digital agent proxy, enabling natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation. Agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies (not flat interconnections) that mirror enterprise ecosystem complexity. A central orchestrator handles task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, while a unified conversational interface supports cross-application querying and process orchestration.

Result: The paper introduces two novel paradigms: "Application-as-Agent" for integration and "Conversation-as-Integration" for interaction. It explores the generalization potential of this methodology across heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data application scenarios.

Conclusion: The Agentic Nesting framework offers a more intelligent, loosely coupled alternative to traditional enterprise application integration, with promising generalizability to diverse enterprise scenarios involving heterogeneous systems and large-scale data.

Abstract: Enterprise operations extensively rely on multiple heterogeneous business systems and information applications, which also result in severe data silos and process fragmentation. Enterprises have invested considerable financial and material resources in building these applications, however, effectively leveraging and orchestrating them remains a formidable challenge. Conventional approaches to enterprise application integration, encompassing middleware architectures such as Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), API gateway infrastructures, and Robotic Process Automation (RPA), suffer from inherent limitations like high architectural coupling, escalating operation and maintenance costs, and limited intelligence capabilities. This paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework in which existing enterprise applications are encapsulated as autonomous AI agents within a hierarchically nested structure. Rather than flat interconnection, agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies that mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems. The framework extracts a digital agent proxy from each legacy application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation, coordinates multiple agents through a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The main contributions of this paper are the proposition of the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, together with an exploration of the generalization potential of this methodology in scenarios encompassing heterogeneous system coordination, and large-scale data applications.

</details>


### [62] [The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05160)
*Saman Rahbar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The Ignition Index (I) is a validated scalar metric that quantifies Global Workspace Theory's all-or-none ignition phenomenon in transformer language models by fitting a sigmoid to per-layer probe accuracy vs. input strength. Tested across 11 models/5 architectures, it shows 9.6× selectivity for linguistic structure over noise, reveals feedforward transformers outperform SSMs by 89% in ignition steepness, demonstrates recurrent models exhibit ignition along recurrence rather than depth, and detects a phase transition preceding induction-head formation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global Workspace Theory (GWT) predicts all-or-none "ignition" — abrupt, thresholded global broadcast of information in cognitive systems. While influential in neuroscience and consciousness studies, GWT's dynamical predictions lacked a validated quantitative metric for testing in artificial neural networks. Existing interpretability tools could not systematically measure whether and how transformer models manifest ignition-like information propagation across layers.

Method: The authors introduce the Ignition Index (I), operationalized by fitting a four-parameter sigmoid function to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength. The key parameter, beta-hat (steepness), captures the abruptness of the transition: high values indicate ignition-like behavior, low values indicate graded accumulation. Selectivity is validated via shuffled-label controls across 11 models from five architecture families. Phase transitions are detected using PELT (Pruned Exact Linear Time) changepoint detection. Statistical comparisons use Mann-Whitney U-tests and Cohen's d.

Result: Key findings: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed state-space models (SSMs) by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, d = 0.52); Mamba shows near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12× higher ignition along its iteration axis vs. depth axis, indicating recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along recurrence. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67% change), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting saturation of available ignition mechanisms in transformers.

Conclusion: The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability. The metric enables systematic comparison of information propagation dynamics across model families, reveals fundamental differences between transformer and SSM architectures, and opens new directions for understanding how global information broadcast emerges during training.

Abstract: We introduce the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models. The metric fits a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat: high values indicate abrupt, ignition-like transitions; low values indicate graded build-up. Across 11 models spanning five architecture families, shuffled-label controls demonstrate 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test). We find: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52), with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, demonstrating that recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along the recurrence dimension. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting transformer architectures may saturate available ignition mechanisms. The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized in the scaling literature. Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/ignition-index

</details>


### [63] [Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05168)
*Dayu Wang,Jiaye Yang,Weikang Li,Jiahui Liang,Yang Li,Deguo Xia,Jizhou Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM reasoning failures often stem from localized intermediate bugs rather than global incompetence. Weak-model patches can correct these bugs, but direct fine-tuning on them fails. The authors propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong framework that contrasts successful vs. unsuccessful patches and distills the corrective distribution, improving strong-model reasoning performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs frequently fail on reasoning tasks despite having the underlying capability. The authors posit these failures are due to repairable, localized bugs in intermediate steps—not global incompetence. However, naive fine-tuning on corrected trajectories does not reliably internalize the corrective signal, because the value lies in how the intervention reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution, not in the surface-level patch text.

Method: Woodpecker Distillation is a weak-to-strong training framework that uses contrastive local interventions. For a given reasoning prefix, a weak probe model generates both successful and unsuccessful patches. The method contrasts these to construct a corrective teacher distribution based on induced future token predictions, then distills this distribution into the strong model, rather than directly imitating the patch text.

Result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines (e.g., fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories).

Conclusion: Localized reasoning bugs are repairable via weak-model interventions, but the corrective signal must be captured through contrastive distributional distillation rather than surface-level imitation. Woodpecker Distillation effectively leverages weak-to-strong training for reasoning improvement.

Abstract: Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite possessing the capability to solve them. We argue that many such failures arise from localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps rather than from global incompetence. We show that these bugs are frequently repairable: inserting a short patch generated by a weak probe model after the same strong-model reasoning prefix can redirect the trajectory toward a correct solution.
  However, this corrective effect is not reliably internalized by directly fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories, suggesting that the useful signal lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. We therefore propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. Our method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model.
  Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

</details>


### [64] [From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05203)
*Esra Zihni,Katryna Cisek,Hamzah Ziadeh,Hendrik Knoche,Robert Mikulik,John D. Kelleher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Replacing continuous predictors with clinically guideline-aligned categorical encodings in stroke outcome models yields statistically comparable performance to standard continuous models in most treatment cohorts, while better aligning with clinicians' reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite high predictive accuracy of ML models for 90-day stroke outcomes, clinical adoption is hindered because model explanations (e.g., SHAP values referencing continuous variable cut-offs) do not match how clinicians think — which is in terms of guideline-based thresholds. A prior clinician user study confirmed the need for guideline-aligned categorisation.

Method: The authors compare standard gradient-boosted models using continuous predictors against fully categorised gradient-boosted models where continuous variables are discretised into bins based on stroke clinical guideline thresholds, stratified across three treatment cohorts (multi-centre European registry). Statistical comparison of predictive performance and global feature importance rankings is conducted.

Result: Fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from continuous models in two of three treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remain consistent across both model types, indicating the core prognostic hierarchy is preserved.

Conclusion: Guideline-based discretisation of continuous predictors is a viable design choice for stroke outcome prediction models, offering clinical interpretability without meaningful loss of predictive performance in most settings.

Abstract: Machine learning models achieve strong predictive accuracy for 90-day outcome prediction in acute ischaemic stroke, yet clinical adoption is limited by the misalignment of model explanations with clinicians' reasoning. Motivated by a clinician user study calling for clinical guideline-aligned cut-offs, we ask whether continuous predictors can be replaced by clinically informed categorical encodings without sacrificing performance. On a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, we compare standard and fully categorised gradient-boosted models, the latter using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. The fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from their continuous counterparts in two of the treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in predictive accuracy in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remain consistent, suggesting that discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors across all treatment groups. Guideline-based categorisation is thus a viable design choice for stroke-outcome models.

</details>


### [65] [DoctorAgents: an agentic framework to iteratively refine AutoML pipeline for small clinical temporal data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05375)
*Ruilin Wang,Bo-Hong Wang,Elizabeth Kourbatski,Jun Bai,Hegang Chen,Ziyang Song,Gilles Boire,Marie Hudson,Yue Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DoctorAgents reformulates AutoML for small clinical datasets by replacing brute-force search with reasoning-driven refinement using LLM agents. Through textual gradient descent with natural-language feedback, it autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines, outperforming existing AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable, task-specific representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical ML deployment is hindered by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporally complex data. Existing AutoML systems rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory, making them inadequate for small clinical datasets where exhaustive search is inefficient and context-insensitive.

Method: DoctorAgents is an agentic AI framework with three specialized LLM agents: generation, validation, and refinement. These agents collaboratively construct and optimize ML pipelines. The key innovation is backpropagating natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent, enabling targeted, reasoning-driven pipeline updates without exhaustive search over the configuration space.

Result: Experiments across diverse clinical tasks demonstrate that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines. Additionally, the pipelines produced yield more interpretable, task-specific representations compared to competing methods.

Conclusion: Reasoning-driven refinement via LLM agents offers a superior alternative to brute-force AutoML for small clinical data, delivering both better predictive performance and improved interpretability. This suggests agentic AI frameworks are well-suited for domains with limited, complex data where contextual reasoning is critical.

Abstract: Clinical machine learning (ML) has the potential to support high-stakes medical decision-making, but reliable deployment is often constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporal complexity. Developing effective ML pipelines for such data remains time-consuming and error-prone, while existing automated machine learning (AutoML) systems only partially address this challenge because they largely rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory. We therefore reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. We propose DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines through specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement. DoctorAgents backpropagates natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent to perform targeted updates without exhaustive search. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.

</details>


### [66] [SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05204)
*Jialuo Chen,Minghe Wang,Lingqi Jiang,Jianan Ma,Xinhao Deng,Xiaohu Du,Ruixiao Lin,Yunhao Feng,Linkang Du,Jingyi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILLTRACE is a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for detecting LLM-agent skill reuse. It extracts three traces (Expression, Implementation, Operational), represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG), and uses deterministic comparison at audit time. On a benchmark of 820 reuse positives and 751 negatives, it achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898, and scales effectively to a 36,446-skill wild audit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing clone detection methods target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, but LLM-agent skill reuse evidence is distributed across natural-language text, code fragments, and operational structure. Partial reuse (preserving only one aspect) is missed by current detectors, motivating a multi-trace approach.

Method: SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces at ingestion: (1) Expression Trace (authored text/metadata), (2) Implementation Trace (code/tool fragments), and (3) Operational Trace, represented as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) capturing activation, procedure, and resource-flow. An LLM assists only once during Operational-trace extraction. At audit time, cached traces are compared deterministically, calibrated against same-function strict negatives, and a reuse decision with trace attribution is reported.

Result: On SKILLTRACE-BENCH (820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors, 751 negative controls), SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit demonstrates trace-attributed evidence produces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

Conclusion: Multi-trace provenance auditing substantially improves skill reuse detection over single-modality and whole-package baselines. Trace-attributed evidence enables granular, actionable review queues at scale in real-world LLM-agent skill ecosystems.

Abstract: LLM-agent ecosystems are rapidly growing around reusable skills: mixed-modality packages of metadata, natural-language instructions, code, tools, references, and operational workflows. As skills become marketplace artifacts, auditing their reuse is no longer the same problem as ordinary code clone detection. Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill. We present SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for LLM-agent skill reuse. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only the Operational-trace extraction, once at ingestion; at audit time SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports a reuse decision. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

</details>


### [67] [Adaptive Arena-based Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts for Open-Ended Care Plan Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05391)
*Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen,Hoang-Loc Cao,Phuc Ho,Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen,René Richard,Hung Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CANOE is a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework for care plan coordination that uses argumentative computation with human-in-the-loop contestability, achieving strong clinical correctness while providing faithful explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform care plan coordination—which requires synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial data across disciplines—in a manner that is both transparent and safe.

Method: CANOE employs five modules: (1) complexity assessment, (2) adaptive team recruitment, (3) role-based argumentative computation using an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), (4) human-in-the-loop contestation, and (5) care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved via arena-based clash resolution, and acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners can accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, triggering deterministic recomputation of the final plan.

Result: Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge demonstrates that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure yields faithful explanations and human contestability.

Conclusion: CANOE successfully combines the strengths of fine-tuned medical LLMs with a transparent, contestable argumentation framework, offering a safer and more explainable alternative to monolithic pipelines for multidisciplinary care plan coordination.

Abstract: Care plan coordination demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines, where monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform in a transparent or safe manner. We present CANOE (Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts), a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that addresses these limitations through five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution before acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners may accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and the framework will deterministically recompute the final plan. Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

</details>


### [68] [Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05205)
*Ziwei Zheng,Peiqiong Chen,Bang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECR), a relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that generalizes concrete cause-effect pairs into abstract causal logic. A multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system with similarity-constrained clustering distills trustworthy AECRs. An Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) injects these rules into event prediction, yielding consistent improvements, especially on rare and unseen events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instance-level causal event pairs suffer from severe generalization deficits, particularly on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. There is a need for a higher-level causal abstraction that captures generalized causal patterns rather than memorizing specific event pairs.

Method: The authors propose (1) Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR) — a relation-level abstraction transforming concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized causal logic; (2) a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy data, building two complete AECR knowledge bases; and (3) an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) that injects retrieved AECRs into the Causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion.

Result: Quantitative experiments demonstrate that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning. Consistent performance improvements are observed on event prediction tasks, with the most prominent gains on rare and unseen event samples.

Conclusion: Abstract causal rules at the relation level effectively address the generalization limitations of instance-level causal pairs, providing a robust framework for improving causal reasoning and event prediction in long-tail and zero-shot scenarios.

Abstract: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

</details>


### [69] [Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05206)
*Tarun Kumar S*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Otter is a lightweight (15.3M parameters) human chess move predictor that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (55.23% top-1) by modeling chess as a time-aware sequential process, using move history and clock pressure as conditioning signals, surpassing Maia 2 with far fewer resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior human chess models like Maia 2 treat each position in isolation, ignoring the sequential, temporal nature of human play. The authors argue that human move selection is influenced by opening repertoires, recent move context, intra-game behavioral tendencies, and time pressure — factors that position-only models cannot capture.

Method: Otter uses two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves to capture opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. The 15.3M-parameter model is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.

Result: Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing Maia 2 despite using far fewer parameters and less training data. Accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900–1999 Elo bracket across 11 brackets ranging from <1100 to ≥2000.

Conclusion: Modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, while requiring a smaller model. Code, trained models, and training logs are publicly released.

Abstract: Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

</details>


### [70] [SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05212)
*Zhixiang Liang,Yifei Liu,Yidan Huang,Haozhe Zhao,Beichen Huang,Jiaqi Wang,Nan Duan,Qiong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SearchAuditBench is a benchmark of 1,243 failed search-agent trajectories for evaluating LLM auditors on error localization, attribution, and repair. The proposed SearchAuditor framework outperforms baselines (32.3% vs. 26.6% end-to-end pass rate) and helps agents recover from failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep search agents suffer from fragile long-horizon web interactions where small reasoning errors propagate into incorrect answers. Diagnosing these failures requires manually inspecting extremely long traces, which is beyond human capacity. Automated auditing via LLMs could reduce this burden, but no benchmark exists to evaluate such auditing capabilities.

Method: The authors introduce SearchAuditBench, a curated benchmark of 1,243 failed trajectories (avg. 73.1 messages, 65.1K tokens) from 8 open-weight models across 5 deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, root cause, and reference repair with grading rubrics. They also propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that localizes, attributes, and repairs failures via evidence-grounded adjudication.

Result: The strongest baseline powered by GPT-5.5 achieves only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across frontier models, reaching a 32.3% end-to-end pass rate. Additionally, resuming failed runs with SearchAuditor's repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

Conclusion: Automated auditing of deep search agent failures remains a challenging task, with even the best systems achieving modest pass rates. The proposed SearchAuditor framework offers meaningful improvements in localizing, attributing, and repairing failures, reducing the need for human inspection of long trajectories.
