Abstract: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

</details>


### [71] [PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05218)
*Ao Fu,Yi Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PD-GS augments 3D Gaussian Splatting with time-aligned phoneme tokens via a Linguistic Fusion Module to improve lip articulation in talking-head rendering, specifically addressing over-smoothed mouth motion and bilabial closure violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3DGS-based talking-head methods produce over-smoothed lip motion and "leaky mouth" artifacts because continuous acoustic embeddings under regression objectives bias predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. Self-supervised speech encoders lack explicit, frame-aligned linguistic targets to resolve closure-level articulatory events.

Method: PD-GS integrates time-aligned phoneme tokens (via ASR and forced alignment) into a 3DGS talking-head pipeline. The Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM) uses a learned gating mechanism to adaptively fuse continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings, preserving smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. Training uses monocular video with image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision.

Result: On the HDTF dataset, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry (LMD 2.66) among compared baselines and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences.

Conclusion: Phoneme-driven augmentation of 3DGS with adaptive linguistic fusion yields more linguistically faithful neural avatars, effectively mitigating the leaky-mouth artifact while maintaining photorealistic quality.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

</details>


### [72] [From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06112)
*Manideep Dhar,Ritwik Singh,Sharat Chandra Kumar Manikonda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a compliance-first, agentic AI architecture for hospitals with multi-agent orchestration, policy-as-code governance, and privacy-preserving data fabric to move beyond siloed AI pilots toward scalable, governed enterprise deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. Most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked in departmental silos, yielding duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value despite accelerating market investment.

Method: Proposes a three-layer architecture: (1) Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent clinical/operational/financial workflows, (2) Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, DISHA, India’s DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC standards, and (3) Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric using federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves integrated with HIMS flows. Validated via a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open prototype implementation demonstrating triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging.

Result: The prototype achieved substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access across end-to-end orchestration.

Conclusion: The architecture provides hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint for transitioning from ad hoc AI tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform adaptable to on-premise, hybrid, and cloud-native deployments.

Abstract: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

</details>


### [73] [When Privileged Guidance Misaligns: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05219)
*Junzhuo Liu,Weiwei Li,Jun Ling,Peng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SMRC-SD introduces state-matched routing and contextualized self-distillation to address state–reference mismatch in privileged on-policy distillation for multi-turn agents, improving success rates significantly on ALFWorld and WebShop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-turn interactive environments, privileged distillation uses reference trajectories from a teacher to guide a student agent. However, as the student's actions diverge from the reference, the resulting execution states may not match those in the reference, creating a state–reference mismatch that makes the reference an unreliable supervision source.

Method: The proposed SMRC-SD framework consists of two key components: (1) State-Matched Routing, which at each turn verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory and applies distillation only at matched states; (2) Contextualized Self-Distillation, which constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful reference trajectory for each matched state, grounding supervision in the state actually reached.

Result: With Qwen3-1.7B, SMRC-SD improves task success from 0.746 to 0.865 on ALFWorld and from 0.574 to 0.693 on WebShop, consistently outperforming unconditional full-path distillation. Ablation studies confirm that both state-matched routing and state-compatible teacher context contribute to these gains.

Conclusion: Explicitly handling state–reference mismatch via state-matched routing and contextualized distillation is highly effective, enabling privileged on-policy distillation to provide reliable, locally compatible guidance that substantially boosts multi-turn agent performance.

Abstract: Privileged on-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multi-turn agents by allowing a synchronized teacher to re-score the student's response at every turn with access to training-only references, such as successful trajectories. In interactive environments, however, the student's preceding actions continually change the execution state. As the student takes different actions or completes subgoals in a different order, its rollout may reach states not covered by the reference, making the reference an unreliable source of guidance for the state actually reached. Applying privileged distillation indiscriminately therefore creates state--reference mismatch. This mismatch motivates a central objective: providing privileged reference guidance that remains compatible with the student's current execution state. We introduce State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD), which explicitly determines when and how a privileged trajectory should guide an on-policy student. At each turn, SMRC-SD verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Distillation is applied only at matched states, filtering out turns for which the reference lacks locally compatible guidance. For each matched state, SMRC-SD further constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory, grounding supervision in the state actually reached. Across ALFWorld and WebShop, SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from $0.746$ to $0.865$ on ALFWorld and from $0.574$ to $0.693$ on WebShop. Controlled routing and context ablations support both selecting locally supported turns and constructing state-compatible teacher context as contributors to these gains. Code is available at https://github.com/liujunzhuo/SMRC-SD.

</details>


### [74] [Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05224)
*Nick Oh,Fernand Gobet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Training 14 models (135M–14B parameters) on 10.7M trial-level choices from 160 psych experiments reveals that in-distribution performance saturates early (~0.6B–1B parameters match a 70B baseline), but out-of-distribution generalization shows steep scaling favoring larger models. Diagnostic ablation shows models rely primarily on stimuli and feedback (75.7% of learned information), not mere choice history. Small cognitively fine-tuned models can serve as noise-ceiling estimators for psych experiments, though they are bounded by training paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resolve two open questions: (1) whether scaling laws apply to cognitively fine-tuned LLMs used as cognitive proxies, and (2) whether these models genuinely process task structure or merely exploit statistical shortcuts like choice history.

Method: Fourteen models across four architecture families (135M–14B parameters) were fine-tuned on Psych-101 (10.7M trial-level choices, 160 experiments). Two diagnostics were applied: (1) progressive stripping of four prompt channels (instructions, stimuli, outcome feedback, choice history) across 27 experiments, and (2) permutation of trial order to test invariance to sequence.

Result: In-distribution: performance saturates in a narrow band; 0.6B–1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline. Out-of-distribution: steeper scaling gradient emerges, with larger models advantaged. Ablation: masking stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information, pushing models below chance, ruling out choice history as the dominant shortcut. Permutation: models are invariant on independent-trial tasks but sensitive where prior responses determine trial order.

Conclusion: Small cognitively fine-tuned models are viable as noise-ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, but their generalization is bounded by the paradigms seen during training. Scale matters primarily for out-of-distribution generalization, not for fitting known task structures.

Abstract: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

</details>


### [75] [Project2Task: Graph-Guided Project-Level Planning for Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05225)
*Huirui Xu,Runtao Xu,Shuo Ren,Jiajun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Project2Task is a graph-guided planning layer that decomposes a research project brief into a portfolio of well-defined, dependency-aware tasks (innovation atoms) organized in a directed lineage graph, using a Bernoulli block-model to select decomposition strategies. It improves coherence and executability over flat baselines, boosting portfolio quality scores and downstream task execution accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autonomous research agents treat a research project as a single oversized task or generate vague, overlapping tasks without proper boundaries, dependencies, or execution order. A research project is actually a long-horizon agenda requiring multiple bounded, related, and correctly sequenced tasks — a gap in current single-task systems that Project2Task aims to fill.

Method: Project2Task introduces a project-level planning layer that: (1) represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms in a directed lineage graph; (2) uses a lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective to select among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions; (3) generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership; (4) repairs overlaps and missing execution fields; and (5) emits dependency-aware task contracts specifying objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. These contracts are executor-agnostic.

Result: On a benchmark of 10 project briefs (~30 tasks), Project2Task achieved an average manuscript-based portfolio quality score of 7.15, outperforming the Brief Baseline (4.58) and the Topic-only Setting (5.31). When integrated with AutoResearchClaw, downstream task accuracy improved from 0.536 to 0.759.

Conclusion: Explicit project-to-task planning via Project2Task significantly improves the coherence, non-redundancy, and executability of research-task portfolios. The graph-guided decomposition and dependency-aware contracts provide a robust planning layer that enhances downstream research automation.

Abstract: Research agents can increasingly search literature, propose hypotheses, generate code, run experiments, and draft manuscripts from a single topic. However, a research project is not merely a larger task: it is a long-horizon agenda that must be advanced through multiple bounded tasks with distinct but related objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences. Existing single-task systems often treat the project as one oversized task, produce a flat set of vague or overlapping tasks, or leave task boundaries and execution order to manual coordination. We introduce Project2Task, a graph-guided project-level planning layer for autonomous research. Given a project brief, it represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms and organizes them in a directed lineage graph. A lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Project2Task then generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and emits dependency-aware task contracts that specify objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. The contracts are independent of any particular downstream research executor and support integration of task outputs into a coherent project-level result. On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding roughly 30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gives Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw increases average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759. These results demonstrate the value of explicit project-to-task planning for producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable research-task portfolios.

</details>


### [76] [TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05228)
*Jin Liu,Steffen Thoma,Achim Rettinger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TriQua introduces an adaptive fact decomposition framework that represents simple claims as standard triples and complex claims as hyperrelational facts with contextual qualifiers, enabling precise retrieval, verification, and fine-grained error annotation, with a corresponding scoring metric (TriQuaScore) that strongly aligns with human factuality judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing "decompose-then-verify" LLM factuality evaluation approaches face a trade-off: atomic facts (single-sentence, single-unit claims) lose essential context, while broader statements lack granularity for precise assessment. No prior method flexibly adapts fact representation to the complexity of each claim.

Method: TriQua models facts adaptively by complexity — simple claims become standard (subject, predicate, object) triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts where auxiliary contextual qualifiers are attached to the core triple. Verification then directly annotates errors within specific triples and qualifiers. The TriQuaScore metric quantifies factuality across these structured fact units.

Result: TriQuaScore achieves strong alignment with human-annotated factuality scores. TriQua demonstrates robust decomposition quality and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification tasks.

Conclusion: Adaptive fact representation — using hyperrelational facts with qualifiers for complex claims — resolves the atomicity-versus-context trade-off in LLM factuality evaluation, yielding both better verification accuracy and finer-grained explainability than prior decomposition-based methods.

Abstract: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment. To address this, we introduce TriQua, a framework that flexibly models facts based on their complexity. Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves the necessary context for accurate retrieval and verification without sacrificing atomicity. Furthermore, TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection. Alongside the framework, we propose TriQuaScore to quantify the factuality of these structured fact units. Empirical evaluations show that TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

</details>


### [77] [Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06305)
*Sagar Tamang,Ayush Vyas,Tabarakul Hazarika*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: READ replaces embedding-based chunked retrieval with an agentic, embedding-free search over raw documents using lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads, achieving 58.8% accuracy vs. 15.7% for dense retrieval on financial document QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG design — chunking text, embedding chunks, and retrieving top-k by similarity — is structurally unsound for financial documents where 86.8% of content lines are table rows, numbers are near-identical across contexts, and units (e.g., lakh vs. crore) are separated from figures by chunk boundaries, producing errors of two orders of magnitude.

Method: READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search) uses three deterministic operations — normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads — exposed via the Model Context Protocol. The agent reads raw documents directly, producing a replayable audit trail rather than opaque similarity scores. A table-aware chunker (steelman baseline) is also tested to isolate the structural problem.

Result: READ achieves 58.8% on 51 verified questions vs. 15.7% for dense retrieval (p_Holm = 2×10⁻⁵) and 35.3% for tuned dense retrieval (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent using top-k retrieval reaches only 27.5%, showing the gain comes from the interface, not iteration. BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, separating embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval as the key distinction, not agentic vs. lexical.

Conclusion: Embedding-based retrieval is fundamentally unreliable for table-heavy financial documents; embedding-free approaches (READ, BM25) substantially outperform dense retrieval. The READ interface — deterministic, auditable, and protocol-based — provides practical advantages, though lexical search alone accounts for much of the performance gain.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

</details>


### [78] [Coherence-Oriented Dream Scene Visualisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05233)
*Azra Açıl,Simon Colton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents DSV, a system that converts written dream descriptions into coherent four-panel image sequences using an LLM for chronological segmentation and a text-to-image model for generation, with automatic regeneration for low-quality matches. It is evaluated on 50 DreamBank dreams using CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dreams are emotionally intense experiences but inherently difficult to communicate. The authors aim to bridge this gap by creating a visual representation system that translates textual dream narratives into coherent image sequences, addressing both the communicative challenge of dreams and the technical challenge of maintaining visual coherence across generated images in a temporal sequence.

Method: The DSV system operates in three stages: (1) A large language model (LLM) is prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. (2) A text-to-image diffusion model generates four panel images, one per part, with mechanisms to maintain visual coherence across the sequence. (3) An automatic regeneration step: any image that insufficiently matches its corresponding text segment is regenerated. Evaluation uses objective metrics from CLIP (text-image alignment), DINOv2 (visual coherence), and Qwen2-VL (vision-language understanding) across 50 dream visualizations sourced from the DreamBank corpus.

Result: The authors report quality, fidelity, and coherence results for 50 dream visualizations from DreamBank. Objective measures using CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL vision-language models are presented, though specific numerical outcomes are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: The DSV system demonstrates a viable pipeline for generating temporally coherent, semantically faithful visualizations from subjective dream narratives, with the regeneration mechanism ensuring quality control. The approach shows promise for making dream experiences more communicable through visual media.

Abstract: Dreams can be emotionally intense but difficult to communicate. We describe the Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) system which turns written dream descriptions into a temporal sequence of four panel images visualising the dream. This starts with a large language model prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. Then a text-to-image model produces images for each part with visual coherence maintained across the sequence, and DSV regenerates any image not suitably matching the text. We evaluate DSV over 50 visualisations from dream descriptions in DreamBank, and report quality, fidelity and coherence results via objective measures employing the CLIP, DINOv2 and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.

</details>


### [79] [Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05245)
*Muyang Ye,Tian Lan,Feihu Jiang,Yongshi Ye,Wuyunsiqin,Bin Zhu,Qianghuai Jia,Zhao Xu,Weihua Luo,Ye Wang,Jinyang Zhang,Longyue Wang,Lingfeng Bao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Search2Skill is a framework that enables LLM agents to autonomously identify knowledge gaps, search external sources, and distill retrieved evidence into reusable skills. A rubric-based RL scheme jointly optimizes when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills, outperforming baselines across eight expert domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-evolving skill methods rely solely on the model's internal parametric knowledge or interaction trajectories, limiting them to what the model already knows. Professional domain conventions and standard procedures often lie beyond this boundary and cannot be elicited internally, necessitating external knowledge acquisition.

Method: Search2Skill automatically detects capability gaps, searches external sources to fill them, and distills retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. The framework is trained via a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly optimizes three decisions: when to initiate a search, how to formulate the search query, and how to generate the skill from retrieved evidence.

Result: On eight expert-level domains across three benchmarks, Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Gains stem from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieval, and acquired skills transfer across model scales.

Conclusion: Search2Skill demonstrates that external knowledge acquisition, combined with structured skill distillation, enables LLM agents to transcend their parametric knowledge boundaries. The rubric-based RL optimization and cross-scale skill transferability further validate the framework's effectiveness for agent self-evolution in expert domains.

Abstract: Reusable skills, which encapsulate the procedural knowledge required to solve real-world professional tasks, offer LLM-based agents a path toward self-evolution in expert domains. Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone. To address this issue, we therefore propose a novel framework, Search2Skill, that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources to address them, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Specifically, Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills. Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under both streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

</details>


### [80] [LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05246)
*Jiahao Zhang,Yongzhi Tong,Zelin Fu,Pengde Zhao,Yanmei Jiang,Jiang Feng,Min Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LUNAR is the first benchmark for evaluating cross-domain behavioral personalization in LLMs, using synthesized longitudinal app interaction histories. Experiments on 19 LLMs reveal that effective personalization depends on evidence selection and cross-domain integration rather than model size or context length, and that stronger personalization often trades off against privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks are limited to textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, failing to capture cross-domain behavioral personalization grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities across domains like clothing, food, housing, and mobility.

Method: The authors introduce LUNAR, a benchmark constructed via a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. It leverages longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains. Fidelity analyses validate alignment with real behavioral distributions. Evaluation covers 19 mainstream LLMs under varied conditions of context availability, evidence selection strategies, and integration approaches.

Result: Access to behavioral logs is necessary but insufficient for deep personalization. Neither more context nor larger models reliably improve performance. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory representations. Stronger personalization correlates with reduced privacy protection, revealing a critical trade-off.

Conclusion: Key challenges for personalized LLMs include evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control. LUNAR provides a foundation for systematically evaluating and advancing research on these fronts.

Abstract: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks primarily rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization, where responses must be grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. To address this gap, we introduce LUNAR, the first benchmark for evaluating how LLMs personalize responses from longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains, including clothing, food, housing, and mobility. To support scalable benchmark construction while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns, LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show that access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory, while stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection. These findings identify evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges for personalized LLMs.

</details>


### [81] [WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05248)
*Chunchao Guo,Jinpeng Li,Yang Li,Zilong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorldClaw is an agentic, coarse-to-fine framework that generates large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from text prompts by combining planning agents, globally coherent terrain generation, and render-based refinement to produce scenes with editable instance-level assets and consistent spatial organization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because existing approaches struggle to jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit editable assets suitable for downstream reuse.

Method: WorldClaw employs a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine pipeline: (1) planning agents convert text prompts into structured specifications of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations; (2) a globally coherent terrain foundation is built from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative/procedural materials, and a region-aware height field; (3) for detail-demanding regions, terrain-conditioned compositions are generated, editable textured meshes are reconstructed and placed; (4) render-based agents iteratively refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts.

Result: Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets, all while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

Conclusion: WorldClaw demonstrates that an agentic, coarse-to-fine approach can successfully address the multi-faceted challenge of open-world 3D scene generation, delivering both global coherence and local detail with practical, editable outputs.

Abstract: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because a system must jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse. We present WorldClaw, a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework for open-world 3D scene generation. Planning agents translate a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. WorldClaw then builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on the terrain; render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts. Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

</details>


### [82] [Posture and Sustainment Optimization Under Adversarial Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05256)
*Amelie Norris,Alyssa Lee,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CEV and RobustCEV optimizers for the military posture allocation problem, modeled as a Markov Decision Process. These scenario-weighted, adversarially robust approaches significantly outperform greedy baselines, recovering up to 158% efficiency against adaptive adversaries in simulated Indo-Pacific basing experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current military joint operational planning relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value while ignoring geographic coverage, making posture allocations structurally vulnerable to adversaries targeting high-value locations. A formally rigorous, adversarially robust solution is needed.

Method: The Posture and Sustainability Allocation (PSA) problem is modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. The Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer maximizes scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency across threat distributions. The RobustCEV extension iterates against a Bayesian adversary that adaptively updates its targeting distribution based on observed placements.

Result: Experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment (20 assets, 5 locations) show: (1) greedy baseline suffers a 25.1% permanent efficiency penalty and 57.3% readiness collapse under value-correlated threats; (2) CEV recovers up to 19.8% efficiency with 5–20 curated scenarios; (3) RobustCEV achieves up to 158% efficiency gain over naive optimizers against adaptive adversaries using deceptive priors. All results validated via paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition.

Conclusion: Performance gaps are structural properties of placement strategies, not sampling artifacts. Scenario-weighted, adversarially robust optimization provides significant and statistically validated improvements over greedy approaches for pre-commitment posture planning.

Abstract: Pre-commitment posture, the assignment of military assets to theater locations before conflict scenarios resolve, is a critical and formally unsolved problem in joint operational planning. Current practice relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value and ignore geographic coverage and are structurally vulnerable to adversaries that target high-strategic value locations. This paper presents a scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization engine for the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem, modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. We introduce the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which places assets by maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios, and the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Across three experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment with 20 assets and 5 theater locations, we demonstrate that: (1) the greedy baseline incurs a permanent 25.1% posture efficiency penalty due to geographic under-coverage and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated adversarial threat; (2) the CEV optimizer recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when the threat distribution carries a geographic signal, with a curated set of 5 to 20 scenarios sufficient to capture the majority of this gain; and (3) the RobustCEV extension recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer when an adaptive adversary employs a deceptive threat prior. All findings are validated using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, confirming that the performance gaps reported are structural properties of placement strategies rather than sampling artifacts.

</details>


### [83] [OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05263)
*Yidian Chen,Yingzi Gu,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty,Sharon Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OrchestraBench evaluates multi-agent orchestration frameworks by injecting controlled failures into templated enterprise workflows, measuring cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery. Key findings: intent-reasoning routers outperform keyword/flag routers on adversarial cases; failure recovery is tiered (tool faults recover fully, ambiguous delegation partially, latent/semantic faults never); cascade radius grows with pipeline depth; and apparent containment gains come from trusted-state signals rather than autonomous detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks for multi-agent orchestration frameworks report only task accuracy, failing to diagnose why pipelines break, where cascading failures originate, or which routing decisions trigger breakdowns. A diagnostic benchmark is needed to evaluate failure, recovery, and decomposition in a controlled, reproducible manner.

Method: OrchestraBench uses a seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces two primary metrics: cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery. The framework compares routing policies using bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. Evaluation includes: (1) a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic comparing keyword/flag routers against intent-reasoning model routers, (2) controlled mechanism probes with a Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain across five MAST failure modes, (3) blind retry experiments, (4) pipeline depth variation (depths 3–7), and (5) a trusted-state repair ablation.

Result: Key results: (1) On 26 adversarial routing cases, the keyword/flag router scored 0% while the intent-reasoning router scored 100%, matching the oracle. (2) Three failure-handling tiers emerged: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent/semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering held across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku and when reframed as a loan-approval workflow. (3) Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection. (4) Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 at depth 3 to 4.7 at depth 7). (5) Trusted-state repair ablation showed containment gains came primarily from the trusted-state signal, not autonomous detection.

Conclusion: These results are explicitly controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims. The findings demonstrate that detection and attribution are necessary for failure containment, that routing policy choice critically affects adversarial robustness, and that failure recovery capability is fundamentally tiered by failure mode type across model sizes and contexts.

Abstract: Multi-agent orchestration frameworks are moving from demos to production, yet benchmarks typically report task accuracy without diagnosing why a pipeline failed, where a cascade began, or which routing decision caused the breakdown. OrchestraBench evaluates failure, recovery, and decomposition through a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics and compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Controlled mechanism probes with a real Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted when the computation was reframed as a loan-approval workflow and across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku, although absolute rates shifted with context. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection. These results are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims.

</details>


### [84] [Epistemic Trustworthiness in Generative AI: A Normative Framework for Warranted Reliance in High-Stakes Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05602)
*Nimisha Karnatak,Max Van Kleek,Nigel Shadbolt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that responsible deployment of generative AI in professional contexts requires a framework of "epistemic trustworthiness" — not just accuracy or fairness. It proposes three jointly necessary conditions: epistemic humility (communicating limits), epistemic access (enabling user inspection and contestation), and resistance to epistemic injustice (recognizing users as legitimate epistemic agents). Case studies in law, medicine, and hiring demonstrate how failures in these conditions cause harms that standard metrics miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current responsible AI frameworks focus on accuracy, fairness, explainability, safety, and trust — but none directly addresses the distinct normative question of when users are *justified* in relying on AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning. The authors identify this gap as the problem of "epistemically warranted reliance" and argue it requires a dedicated account of what makes a system epistemically trustworthy, beyond mere output correctness.

Method: The authors draw on philosophical theories of trustworthiness — specifically accounts that ground trustworthiness in competence and audience-orientation — to develop a constitutive normative framework. They derive three necessary, non-fungible conditions for epistemic trustworthiness and then apply this framework through real-world case analyses in three high-stakes professional domains: legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring, demonstrating how violations of each condition produce distinctive harms.

Result: The case analyses reveal that failures of epistemic humility (e.g., overconfident outputs beyond competence), epistemic access (e.g., opaque systems that prevent contestation), and resistance to epistemic injustice (e.g., systems that marginalize user expertise) cause consequential harms — including flawed legal decisions, medical misdiagnoses, and discriminatory hiring outcomes — that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability fail to capture or prevent.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that GenAI systems should be designed and evaluated around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone. This entails operationalizing the three conditions — humility, access, and resistance to epistemic injustice — into concrete design requirements and evaluation criteria, shifting the normative target from "is the output correct?" to "is the user justified in relying on this output within their own reasoning process?"

Abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional contexts, where their outputs shape what users believe, how they reason, and what they treat as settled. This raises a central question for responsible AI: under what conditions is reliance on generative AI outputs epistemically warranted rather than behaviourally induced? Existing frameworks largely ask whether AI outputs are accurate, fair, explainable, safe, or trusted by users. These questions remain necessary, and each can contribute to warranted reliance. However, they do not directly specify warranted reliance as a distinct evaluative target: the conditions under which users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning. We argue that this requires an account of epistemic trustworthiness: what makes a system epistemically worthy of reliance. Drawing on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, we develop a constitutive normative framework comprising three jointly necessary and non-fungible conditions. First, epistemic humility requires systems to represent and communicate the limits of their competence. Second, epistemic access requires systems to enable users to inspect, question, and contest outputs in context. Third, resistance to epistemic injustice requires systems to recognise users as legitimate epistemic agents and avoid marginalising their knowledge and experience. Through real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring, we show how failures of epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice can produce consequential harms that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability do not address on their own. We conclude by outlining design and evaluation implications for GenAI systems organised around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone.

</details>


### [85] [Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05266)
*Nathan S Johnson,Ian Abshire*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study develops a benchmark and trace-logging framework to evaluate LLM-based agent architectures for microscope control, testing 105 configurations across 53 tasks. While benchmarks effectively compare latency, cost, and failure modes, surrogate models fail to predict generalization to unseen tasks, indicating the current test suite cannot support a task-independent global configuration model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of well-established engineering paradigms for designing LLM-based agents that control scientific instrumentation (microscopes, synchrotron beamlines). Researchers need to understand not only whether an agent performs known tasks correctly but also whether it generalizes to novel, unseen tasks. Existing evaluation approaches are insufficient for guiding architectural decisions.

Method: A benchmark and trace-logging framework was constructed encompassing 53 microscopy tasks. The framework systematically evaluated: (1) one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, (2) five different LLMs, (3) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and context parameters, and (4) operational constraints. In total, 105 agent configurations were tested across 1,949 individual runs with 49,109 RAG retrievals logged. Surrogate models were then trained on agent architecture and test results to assess whether they could predict performance on unseen tasks.

Result: Direct comparisons revealed clear differences across configurations in latency, token usage, cost, and failure modes. However, surrogate models trained on the benchmark data could not reliably predict agent performance on new, unseen microscopy tasks, revealing a fundamental limitation: the heterogeneous test suite does not support building a task-independent global configuration model.

Conclusion: The benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison of agent configurations. However, they do not enable reliable generalization to unseen tasks, highlighting a key challenge in agentic microscopy control — current evaluation suites are insufficient for deriving universal design principles that transfer across tasks.

Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

</details>


### [86] [Unified Agent: Managing Interactions across Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05729)
*Xinshuang Liu,Runfa Blark Li,Shaoxiu Wei,Xin Lin,Truong Nguyen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a stateful agent architecture (Unified Agent) that maintains a compact, action-ready state across devices and time, outperforming existing single-agent and multi-agent designs on a new cross-device, cross-time interaction benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent systems fail in cross-device, cross-time scenarios because single-agent systems treating devices as tools lack effective state management across devices over time, while multi-agent systems coordinate but do not maintain the compact carried state needed for cross-device requests. Observations are scattered across devices and moments, but mainstream designs aren't built for this.

Method: Introduces Unified Agent, a stateful agent that maintains an effectively designed state organizing engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form. Constructs a benchmark of user-agent interaction across devices and time for evaluation. Compares against adaptations of four published designs.

Result: Unified Agent significantly outperforms all four adapted published designs in the default setting. The performance advantage remains robust across different MLLM families, capability levels, and reasoning effort settings.

Conclusion: State design is a critical factor for cross-device, cross-time agent performance. The stateful approach with compact, action-ready state representation yields robust advantages over existing paradigms. Code and data will be open-sourced.

Abstract: As capabilities rapidly increase, AI agents can move from running inside one app to acting across a user's devices over time. Yet existing agent systems still fall short in this scenario. This is because observations are scattered across devices and moments, but mainstream systems are not designed around this fact: a single agent that treats devices as tools lacks effective state management for all devices across time, and multi-agent systems coordinate across agents but do not maintain the compact carried state a cross-device, cross-time request needs. We argue that the agent should maintain an effectively designed state that organizes engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form for deciding its action given the current observation. To compare state designs, we construct a benchmark of user-agent interaction across devices and time. We instantiate this principle in Unified Agent, a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments and uses it with the current observation to act. In the default setting, it significantly outperforms our adaptations of four published designs. Across changes in multimodal large language model (MLLM) family, capability, and reasoning effort, it remains ahead of all compared systems, demonstrating that the state-design advantage is robust across MLLM settings. Our code and data will be publicly available on GitHub.

</details>


### [87] [CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05359)
*Jose A. Bird*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts gene perturbation transcriptional effects from ARACNe networks. Validated against TCGA copy-number amplification data as a proxy for knockdown, it shows strong directional concordance for MYC across multiple cancer types, outperforming permutation baselines. Extension to 15 genes reveals gene-specific success (proliferation regulators work; lineage TFs fail). An LLM grounding benchmark shows 71.4–85.7% exact-match accuracy for MCP tool calls, with persistent failure on ambiguous perturbation-type queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional validation of gene-regulatory network tools checks whether predicted targets are known cancer genes (set membership). The authors argue this is insufficient: what matters is whether the predicted *direction* of transcriptional change matches real biological data. They propose using focal-gene copy-number amplification in TCGA as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown, enabling directional validation against patient tumor data.

Method: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation using precomputed ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed through MCP (Model Context Protocol). Validation uses copy-number amplification of a focal gene (e.g., MYC) in TCGA tumor samples as a dosage proxy — amplified samples approximate the opposite of knockdown. Directional concordance between predicted knockdown targets and actual expression differences (amplified vs. non-amplified) is computed. Baselines include permutation tests, PAM50 subtype controls, MSigDB gene-set comparisons via Fisher's exact test, and METABRIC independent replication. An LLM grounding benchmark tests 35 natural-language queries against MCP tool-call schema, evaluated by exact match. Extension covers 15 additional genes including proliferation regulators, lineage TFs, and cyclins.

Result: For MYC, CASCADE achieves strong concordance: BRCA 90.0%, COAD 72.0%, STAD 85.7% (all p<0.0013), with METABRIC replication at 87.2%. This survives PAM50 subtype control and outperforms permutation baselines. However, against MSigDB gene-set baselines, CASCADE does not significantly exceed existing curated knowledge of MYC/E2F biology; its advantage is in gene-specific direction-calling over naive uniform guessing. Extending to 15 genes reveals gene-specificity: proliferation-machinery regulators mostly replicate; lineage-identity TFs and CCND2 consistently fail. In LLM grounding: a local model achieves 71.4% exact match (85.7% for larger model). Schema and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side fixes, but both models confidently default to the wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure resistant to targeted patching because its trigger condition never fires.

Conclusion: CASCADE demonstrates that ARACNe-based directional predictions can be validated against real patient tumor data using copy-number amplification as a dosage proxy, but success is gene-specific rather than universal. The framework's accuracy does not surpass existing MSigDB curated knowledge for well-studied genes like MYC, though it provides gene-specific directionality. LLM-based grounding to MCP tool calls is feasible but brittle: ambiguous queries reliably elicit confident wrong answers that evade straightforward programmatic fixes. The authors frame the gene-specific failure pattern as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis warranting further investigation.

Abstract: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

</details>


### [88] [Counterfactual Analysis via Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05367)
*Zonghao Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper explores using GPT-3.5 for counterfactual ROI prediction in online lending. Prompt engineering improves GPT's R-squared from 1.97% to 2.84%, nearing gradient-boosted regression's 3.48%. GPT also generates logically coherent counterfactual ROIs under alternative interest rates, demonstrating LLMs' potential for causal decision-making tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counterfactual analysis is essential for evaluating hypothetical scenarios in decision-making, yet it is traditionally challenging due to the need for causal reasoning. The authors aim to investigate whether LLMs like GPT-3.5 can serve as effective tools for counterfactual prediction, specifically in the online lending domain where ROI under different interest rate schemes must be estimated.

Method: The study uses GPT-3.5 to predict counterfactual returns on investment (ROI) in online lending. Predictive performance is first benchmarked against advanced ML algorithms (notably gradient-boosted regression). Prompt engineering strategies are applied to enhance GPT's accuracy. Subsequently, GPT is prompted to generate counterfactual ROIs under a range of alternative interest rates, and its responses are evaluated for logical coherence and causal reasoning.

Result: Prompt engineering raises GPT's R-squared from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% of gradient-boosted regression. GPT also produces logically coherent and causally reasoned counterfactual ROI estimates across alternative interest rate scenarios.

Conclusion: LLMs, particularly GPT-3.5, show promise as tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending. The authors suggest broader applicability of LLMs in predictive and decision-making contexts that require causal reasoning.

Abstract: Counterfactual analysis aims to predict potential outcomes under hypothetical scenarios, offering valuable insights for decision-making. This paper investigates the application of large language models (LLMs), specifically the GPT-3.5 model, for counterfactual analysis. We focus on the online lending context, where the counterfactual return on investment (ROI) is crucial for evaluating different interest rate schemes. We begin by assessing the predictive performance of GPT and comparing it with advanced machine learning algorithms. The results show that prompt engineering can significantly enhance GPT's predictions, with the R-squared increasing from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. Subsequently, we utilize GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under a set of alternative interest rates. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, suggesting broader applications for LLMs in various predictive and decision-making contexts.

</details>


### [89] [C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05381)
*Swapnanil Mukherjee,Agyeya Negi,Tanuja Ganu,Ponnurangam Kumaraguru*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C³PO is a benchmark of 3,404 multimodal samples (video, audio, image, text) that diagnoses cross-modal reasoning failures in MLLMs through two tasks: information composition and counterfactual conflict resolution. It reveals that 86-95% of model failures stem from modality dominance (over-attending to text), mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness, and performance depends on modalities' structural roles rather than their combinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs exhibit brittle cross-modal reasoning due to heavy bias toward a dominant modality (typically text). There is a lack of targeted benchmarks that can diagnose when and why cross-modal reasoning fails, particularly in distinguishing between failures of information fusion versus failures of conflict resolution.

Method: The authors introduce C³PO, a benchmark with 3,404 samples constructed through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates. It features a paired Information Composition (IC) and Counterfactual Conflict (CC) structure with a four-tier design. They evaluate multiple MLLMs (including Gemini-3.1-Pro and open-source models) and conduct attention probe analyses to measure modality attention distribution and mid-layer attention entropy as predictors of reasoning success.

Result: Humans achieve 88.64% accuracy while the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%; open-source models collapse under counterfactual conflict. 86-95% of failures are attributed to modality dominance, with models concentrating 87-95% of attention on text while ignoring contradictory evidence. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness: sustained cross-modal exploration succeeds, while premature attention collapse leads to failure. A 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates shows performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not merely modality combinations.

Conclusion: Multimodal perception does not guarantee robust cross-modal reasoning. Current architectures lack mechanisms for sustained cross-modal attention, leading to premature commitment to a dominant modality. Future architectures must explicitly enable balanced, sustained cross-modal interaction to resolve conflicts and integrate dispersed evidence effectively.

Abstract: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can process diverse sensory inputs, yet their reasoning remains heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. We introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text, evaluating two abilities: information composition (fusing dispersed evidence) and counterfactual conflict (resolving deliberate contradictions). C$^3$PO's paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design enable targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails. Built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates, C$^3$PO reveals that while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. Through attention probes, we find 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. The 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates reveals that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not combinations. These findings show multimodal perception does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature

</details>


### [90] [Evaluating and Improving Pedagogical Fit in LLM-Based AI Tutors with the Pedagogical Suitability Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05411)
*Benjamin Barlog,Hudson Craig,Zedong Peng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PSI is a six-sub-score metric evaluating how well LLM tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression. Tested across four LLMs with 240 scenarios, PSI-guided feedback improved 82.3% of weak cases, showing pedagogical alignment is measurable and improvable beyond mere correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs as AI tutors produce correct answers but often lack pedagogical appropriateness — namely, alignment with a learner's current knowledge foundation, course sequencing, and timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus on answer quality while neglecting this instructional fit, creating a gap in assessing tutoring effectiveness.

Method: The authors introduce the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric comprising six theory-informed sub-scores grounded in learning science. They evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts. A PSI-guided regeneration protocol is then applied to 62 weak-performing cases, followed by focused manual evaluation to validate whether PSI-identified weaknesses and improvements correspond to human judgment.

Result: Baseline PSI scores across models were modestly differentiated (0.557–0.638), with no clear separation between open-weight and closed models. Prompt perturbations caused minimal overall PSI change (Δ = −0.002) but revealed sub-score trade-offs. Critically, PSI-guided regeneration improved 51 of 62 weak cases (82.3%), and manual evaluation confirmed that PSI-identified weaknesses were instructionally meaningful and regenerations aligned with human-judged improvement.

Conclusion: Learner- and curriculum-aware alignment matters more for effective LLM tutoring than model category alone, and such pedagogical alignment is both measurable via PSI and improvable through structured feedback-driven regeneration.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as AI tutors, but a correct answer is not always a pedagogically appropriate one. In classroom learning, effective help depends not only on correctness, but also on whether a response matches the learner's current foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus mainly on answer quality, leaving this instructional fit under-measured. We present the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores that evaluates how well LLM-generated tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and we further use PSI as a structured feedback signal for response improvement. We evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, and Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts, then apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol to 62 weak-performing cases. Baseline differences across the four tested models were modest overall (PSI range: 0.557 to 0.638), and open-weight and closed models did not exhibit a clear separation in pedagogical fit. Under the tested prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained largely stable (Delta = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. More importantly, PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak-performing cases: 51 of 62 cases improved (82.3%). Focused manual evaluation of the 62 PSI-selected weak cases provides initial evidence that the identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many PSI-guided regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement. These results suggest that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and that such alignment is both measurable and improvable.

</details>


### [91] [Negotiating Risk Boundaries in AI for Policing Through Mixed-Stakeholder Deliberation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05418)
*Mackenzie Jorgensen,Jo Reilly,Alex Sutherland,Miri Zilka*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A deliberation workshop with community members, police, and academics on AI in policing found participants broadly open to AI adoption but rejected recidivism risk assessment. Discussions centered on functionality, genuine benefit, and universal benefit, showing that a racial equity lens enriches rather than narrows risk-benefit analysis — analogous to the curb-cut effect in inclusive design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite known racial bias risks in AI policing tools, affected community representatives are rarely included in adoption decisions. The study aims to fill this participatory gap by bringing diverse stakeholders together to assess AI use cases through an explicit racial bias lens.

Method: A mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop with 30 participants — community representatives, police officers, and academics — who collaboratively assessed the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with racial bias as an explicit focal point.

Result: Participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only 3 of 13 use cases outright. Recidivism risk assessment was the most notable rejection, with objections directed at its premise rather than implementation. Rather than narrowing the deliberation, foregrounding racial equity led discussions toward three core questions: does the tool work, does it deliver genuine benefit, and does that benefit extend to everyone?

Conclusion: Integrating a racial bias lens from the outset produces integrated reasoning akin to the curb-cut effect — improving analysis for all, not just marginalized groups. This approach strengthens risk-benefit assessment and should inform participatory governance of AI in policing.

Abstract: AI tools are being increasingly adopted in policing in the UK and worldwide. Racial bias is a known and well-documented risk, yet representatives of affected communities are rarely included in decisions about AI adoption. We present results from a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop bringing together 30 community representatives, police officers, and academics to assess the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with an explicit focus on racial bias. We found that participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright, most notably recidivism risk assessment, where objections targeted the premise rather than the implementation.
