Our analysis reveals that foregrounding racial equity did not narrow the deliberation. Instead, discussions gravitated toward a fundamental set of questions: does this tool actually work, will it deliver genuine benefit, and will that benefit extend to everyone? This integrated reasoning, reminiscent of the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, highlights the benefit of incorporating the racial bias lens into the risk-benefit analysis of AI use cases from the outset.

</details>


### [92] [SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05439)
*Yixuan Wang,Licheng Luo,Yu Fu,Kaidi Xu,Yue Dong,Mingyu Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A selective translation framework that generates formal specifications from natural language and decides when to trust them, using dual black-box reliability scores calibrated via conformal risk control, with distribution-free guarantees on incorrect specification acceptance rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NL-to-formal-specification models always produce an output regardless of reliability, creating safety risks. There is a need for systems that know when to abstain from using potentially incorrect translations in safety-critical applications.

Method: Two complementary black-box reliability signals: (1) fidelity of back-translation into natural language, and (2) dispersion under repeated translations with semantic equivalence. Conformal risk control calibrates the combined score into an accept/abstain decision with a distribution-free bound on incorrect acceptance rate. A conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs pre-translation. Framework tested across STL, LTL, and SpaTiaL.

Result: Experiments across three formal languages (STL, LTL, SpaTiaL) demonstrate improved translation reliability, robustness under cross-tier distribution shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention behavior.

Conclusion: The framework establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by equipping AI systems with the ability to recognize and abstain from unreliable specification generations, critical for safety-sensitive autonomous systems.

Abstract: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

</details>


### [93] [Stochasticity Is Not the Hard Part: Reduction and Complexity in Instructional Sequencing over Prerequisite DAGs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05455)
*Zonglin Han,Yichen Chen,Jiawen Jiang,Tongan Shi,Kristian A. Stevens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper models instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem, proves the stochasticity can be eliminated (reducing to a deterministic problem on a prerequisite lattice), establishes NP-hardness even in simple cases, identifies tractable special cases (joint acyclicity, bounded prerequisite width), and introduces a diagnostic ($m\Delta$) that certifies when optimization is unnecessary—validated on real course data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When students learn interdependent concepts, the order of instruction can significantly affect learning outcomes, but the computational cost of finding optimal sequences and the conditions under which ordering actually matters are poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize both the complexity of optimal sequencing and practical conditions where optimization is either easy or unnecessary.

Method: The problem is formalized as a stochastic shortest-path problem where each concept attempt succeeds with state-dependent probability. The authors prove stochasticity can be eliminated via a collapse to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals. NP-hardness is shown via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments. Tractable cases are identified: joint acyclicity of transfer preferences with prerequisites enables optimal topological ordering, and bounded prerequisite width yields polynomial-time dynamic programming. A diagnostic $m\Delta$ bounds the value of sequencing before optimization. Empirical validation uses 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course and constructed transfer instances evaluated with A* search using a consistent heuristic.

Result: The problem is NP-hard even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities $\geq 1/2$. However, when transfer preferences are jointly acyclic with prerequisites, any topological order is optimal. Fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial exact DP. The $m\Delta$ diagnostic on real CS course data certifies a "doubly easy" regime—negligible optimization value and small search space. On constructed hard instances, myopic sequencing incurs large regret, but exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states.

Conclusion: Instructional sequencing optimization is combinatorially hard in general but practically easy in many real-world settings. The $m\Delta$ diagnostic provides a practical tool to determine whether optimizing sequence order is worthwhile. The structural insights—stochastic elimination, lattice collapse, and tractable subclasses—offer both theoretical understanding and practical guidance for adaptive learning systems.

Abstract: When a student must learn concepts connected by prerequisite dependencies, when does the order of instruction matter, and what does it cost to find the best one? We study instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem in which attempting a concept succeeds with a state-dependent probability and failure leaves the learner state unchanged. We first prove that this stochasticity can be eliminated exactly: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals, preserving optimal values and actions. The collapse removes stochastic complexity but not combinatorial complexity: optimal sequencing remains NP-hard -- via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments -- even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities at least $1/2$. Hardness is not uniform: when realizable transfer preferences remain jointly acyclic with the prerequisites, any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal, and fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time exact dynamic programming. A computable diagnostic, $mΔ$, bounds the value of sequencing before optimization. On 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course, the diagnostic certifies a doubly easy regime -- little value to optimize and little space to search -- while constructed transfer instances realize the challenging regime, where myopic sequencing suffers large regret yet exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states on that family.

</details>


### [94] [Recursive Synthesis for Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05466)
*Zhongzhi Li,Yucheng Shi,Zongxia Li,Ruhan Wang,Anhao Li,Zixun Huang,Junyao Yang,Lei Ke,Ninghao Liu,Haitao Mi,Leowei Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RST is a recursive framework that synthesizes high-quality long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale (~$0.05/task), generating 37,484 tasks over 15 rounds with steadily increasing difficulty. Fine-tuning on these tasks yields up to 10-point gains on terminal benchmarks, with PPO boosting relative performance by 20–41%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manually authoring long-horizon terminal-agent training data is prohibitively expensive ($100s–$1000s per task) and does not scale. Direct LLM generation fails to maintain consistency across instructions, environments, reference solutions, and verifiers. A scalable, automated, and verified synthesis method is needed.

Method: RST (Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks) starts from verified seed tasks and recursively: (1) extends the reference solution, (2) realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, (3) validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and (4) reuses accepted tasks as seeds for the next round. This loop runs for 15 rounds, producing 37,484 tasks.

Result: Task difficulty grows substantially: median solution lines from 67→374, median commands from 40→244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90% (Round 1) to 2.5% (Round 15). SFT on rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench 2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench. Agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44%, 32.00%, and 22.07% (relative gains of 20.0%, 41.2%, 21.9%). Synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable at round 15, showing no ceiling.

Conclusion: RST enables scalable, low-cost synthesis of challenging terminal-agent tasks with recursive difficulty escalation. The resulting data is highly effective for both SFT and RL fine-tuning of agent models. The process shows no signs of plateauing, suggesting further scaling potential.

Abstract: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is expensive to produce, often costing hundreds to thousands of dollars per task, because each task must keep the instruction, environment, reference solution, and verifier mutually consistent. Human authoring does not scale, and direct generation with large language models (LLMs) often breaks these dependencies. We present Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST), a recursive verified synthesis framework for constructing long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale. Starting from verified seed tasks, RST extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. Across fifteen recursive rounds, RST produces 37,484 synthesized terminal-agent tasks at roughly \$0.05 per task. Task difficulty increases substantially over rounds: the median reference solution grows from 67 to 374 lines, the median number of executed commands grows from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90\% at $R_1$ to 2.5\% at $R_{15}$. To demonstrate training utility, we collect rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories on the synthesized tasks and use them for supervised fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on these trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench~2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, while agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44\%, 32.00\%, and 22.07\% on the three benchmarks, corresponding to relative gains of 20.0\%, 41.2\%, and 21.9\% over the base model. Moreover, after 15 rounds, the recursion shows no ceiling: synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable as difficulty keeps climbing, indicating that the process can continue well beyond the scale reported here.

</details>


### [95] [Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05490)
*Ahmed Hassoon,Mark Dredze*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper provides a rigorous analysis of audit mechanisms that detect errors in autonomous data analyses by comparing operations against a model trained on sound analyses. It characterizes how score design affects error localization, provides procedures for controlling false flag rates under exchangeability assumptions, quantifies the impact of model misspecification and selection bias, and establishes a fundamental lower bound on detectable error magnitudes determined by representation dimension rather than training data volume.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents increasingly perform end-to-end data analysis without human supervision. When errors occur, identifying which specific operation caused the failure is critical. A recent line of work uses models trained solely on correct analyses to flag anomalous operations, but the reliability and theoretical properties of such "unsupervised" audits have not been studied. This paper fills that gap by providing formal guarantees and fundamental limits.

Method: The authors formalize the audit problem in terms of scoring operations against a predictive model of sound analyses. They analyze two scoring paradigms: (1) local scores conditioned only on the immediately preceding operation, and (2) reconstruction-based scores that compare against a longer inferred trajectory. They develop procedures to control the false discovery proportion within a single analysis using exchangeability of sound analyses (weaker than requiring model correctness). They further analyze robustness to model misspecification and selection-dependent review, and derive an information-theoretic lower bound on the minimum detectable error magnitude.

Result: Key findings: (1) Local scores cannot distinguish inherited errors from original errors, causing single-mistake single-flag behavior; reconstruction scores spread one mistake across multiple flags, and the paper quantifies this spread. (2) The proposed false-flag control procedures are valid under exchangeability alone. (3) Under model misspecification or selection-dependent review, guarantees degrade in quantifiable ways. (4) A fundamental limit exists: errors below a magnitude threshold cannot be attributed to any specific operation. Crucially, this threshold decays very slowly with additional training data—a hundredfold increase in sound analyses reduces it by under 2% at current representation sizes—making representation dimensionality the binding constraint, not data volume.

Conclusion: Reliable auditing of autonomous data analysis requires careful choice of scoring method, with reconstruction-based scores enabling broader error detection at the cost of flag spreading. False-flag control is achievable under mild exchangeability assumptions. The fundamental resolution limit of such audits is governed primarily by the dimensionality of the operation representation, implying that engineering effort should focus on richer representations rather than merely collecting more training data.

Abstract: Autonomous agents now carry out entire data analyses, selecting cohorts, joining tables, and fitting models with little step-by-step supervision. When such an analysis turns out to be wrong, someone must determine which operation caused it. A recent approach does this without any labelled mistakes, learning instead from analyses known to be sound and flagging operations that depart from what that model predicts; how reliable such audits are has not been studied. This paper supplies that analysis. The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations. We quantify how far they spread, and how to choose the comparison length when an error accumulates gradually rather than at once. We then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct, and we quantify how much the guarantees weaken when the model is imperfect or when the analysis was selected for review in a way that depends on its content. Finally we establish a limit on what any such audit can report: errors below a certain magnitude cannot be attributed at all, being indistinguishable from ordinary variation among sound analyses. This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

</details>


### [96] [EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05519)
*Jie Wu,Ming Gong,Feixiang Cheng,Qinqin Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EcoAgent-Bench introduces a benchmark where LLM agents must complete tasks under explicit monetary budgets, choosing among priced actions (local lookup, search, composite tools, stronger models, human escalation). Evaluating seven LLM agents reveals they are poor at economical decision-making: they either fail to escalate when needed or overspend on cheap tasks, achieving only 3.9–24.0% micro strict success and at most 7.3% economic consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard agent benchmarks treat resource consumption as a secondary metric, but in real deployment, deciding when to spend resources (escalate, use stronger models, invoke tools) is integral to task completion. The authors argue that an agent's ability to make cost-effective decisions under a budget is a distinct capability from raw task-solving performance and is currently unevaluated.

Method: The authors construct EcoAgent-Bench with 304 real-derived tasks across five families (adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue), each specifying priced actions and an explicit budget. Tasks probe four decision types: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting appropriate model tiers, and stopping on unsupported premises. They evaluate seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings plus four oracle scripted controls. They propose two metrics: micro-averaged accuracy and a novel economic-consistency score (the minimum accuracy between upgrade-oriented and save-oriented task families), which penalizes one-sided policies like always-escalate. A budget sweep across thresholds is also conducted.

Result: Tool-API agents achieve only 3.9–24.0% micro strict success and at most 7.3% economic consistency. Always-escalate controls score high on micro accuracy but fail save-oriented tasks, exposing a one-sided policy weakness. Agents frequently err by stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep on GPT-5.4 raises its escalation rate from 0% to only 3%, demonstrating that completion-under-budget and economical action selection are distinct, poorly correlated properties.

Conclusion: Completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct agent properties that current LLM agents fail to reconcile. The benchmark and its economic-consistency metric expose systematic failures in cost-sensitive decision-making. The authors release the task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound artifacts to support further research on economically rational agents.

Abstract: Agent benchmarks usually measure task completion and treat resource use as an auxiliary statistic. In deployment, however, the choice among a local lookup, broad search, composite research tool, stronger model, or human escalation is part of the task itself. We introduce EcoAgent-Bench, in which every task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. Its 304 real-derived tasks span five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, and test four decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting a model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. We evaluate seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, together with four oracle scripted controls. Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure. Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%. These results show that completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties. We release the task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound result artifacts needed to study both.

</details>


### [97] [Hyper-ES: Effective Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning via Descent Direction Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05541)
*Yu Gu,Zhi Zheng,Yunpeng Ba,Xialiang Tong,Mingxuan Yuan,Zhenkun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hyper-ES is a subspace-based Evolution Strategy framework that combines a few gradient-based fine-tuning runs to build a compact "adaptation subspace" of descent directions, then applies CMA-ES to optimize DARE-TIES merging coefficients within that subspace. It achieves 1% improvement over GRPO-LoRA with 10% fewer gradient updates on math reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly applying Evolution Strategy (ES) to billion-parameter LLMs fails because random perturbations in high-dimensional parameter space are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, causing unstable optimization. The authors aim to preserve ES's strength in low-dimensional optimization while avoiding its weakness in full-parameter search.

Method: (1) Run a small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain several descent directions. (2) Form a compact "adaptation subspace" spanned by these directions. (3) Apply CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this low-dimensional subspace, searching over meaningful combinations of descent directions rather than arbitrary full-model perturbations.

Result: Evaluated on three backbone models (Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill) across six mathematical reasoning datasets. Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by approximately 1% absolute improvement while requiring 10% fewer gradient updates.

Conclusion: Hyper-ES effectively bridges gradient-based and gradient-free optimization by constructing a compact adaptation subspace from a few gradient runs, then leveraging ES's low-dimensional search capability via CMA-ES. This yields superior sample efficiency and performance on LLM reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Evolution Strategy (ES) is a promising alternative to gradient-based fine-tuning for resource-constrained Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, directly applying ES to billion-parameter LLMs is highly ineffective. In such high-dimensional parameter spaces, most random perturbations are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, leading to unstable optimization. We propose Hyper-ES, a subspace-based ES framework that avoids the weakness of ES in full-parameter search while exploiting its strength in low-dimensional optimization. Instead of asking ES to discover useful directions from random perturbations in the LLM parameter space, Hyper-ES first performs a small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain descent directions. Although each direction may provide only a limited improvement on its own, their span forms a compact adaptation subspace that captures useful reasoning updates. Hyper-ES then applies CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, allowing ES to search over combinations of meaningful descent directions rather than over arbitrary full-model perturbations. We evaluate Hyper-ES on three Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones across six mathematical reasoning datasets. Results show that Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates. Code at https://github.com/kuangrepi/Hyper-ES.

</details>


### [98] [SkillTV-Bench: Benchmarking How Well Judges Perform on Skill-Augmented Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05573)
*Zhi Han,Chenxi Zeng,Liuhaichen Yang,Zihan Guo,Ming Zhou,Yang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillTV-Bench introduces a benchmark and method for skill-aware verification of LLM agent trajectories. It provides 681 cases across 50 tasks/11 domains, and SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge into a reusable JudgeSkill that improves agent judge accuracy by 14.8 points and trajectory selection success from 22.9% to 45.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents performing long-horizon tasks require verification of complete execution trajectories rather than just final responses. Existing judge benchmarks either expose final responses or static trajectories, and fail to incorporate procedural knowledge from task-time skills. There is a gap in evaluating skill-aware trajectory verification with directly inspectable artifacts and environments.

Method: The authors introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across 11 domains for skill-aware trajectory verification. They also propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge into a reusable JudgeSkill. This JudgeSkill guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and produce evidence-grounded verdicts. An automated evolution loop on a development pool refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases.

Result: The refined JudgeSkill improves the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points on SkillTV-Bench. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% (single rollout) to 45.5% (ten rollouts).

Conclusion: Skill-aware verification with reusable, evolvable JudgeSkills significantly improves agent trajectory verification accuracy and downstream trajectory selection. The SkillTV-Bench and SkillTV-Evolve framework provide a foundation for integrating procedural skill knowledge into LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge evaluation paradigms.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly execute long-horizon tasks through tool use and environment interaction, shifting evaluation from final-response scoring to verification of complete executions. For skill-augmented agents, verification additionally requires the procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills, because this knowledge indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical. However, existing judge benchmarks often expose final responses or static trajectories, and rarely combine task-time skills with directly inspectable artifacts and environments. We therefore introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across eleven domains, designed to evaluate skill-aware trajectory verification for both LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge methods. Additionally, we propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable JudgeSkill that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. On a disjoint development pool, an automated evolution loop further refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases. On SkillTV-Bench, the refined skill increases the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts. The code and data are available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/SkillTV-Bench

</details>


### [99] [DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05695)
*Wenhao Lin,Chenyu Yu,Xingwei Lin,Sicong Cao,Xiang Chen,Lei Xue,Le Yu,Letian Sha,Chunming Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DreamGuard is a proactive LLM agent guardrail that uses a risk-aware world model with recurrent latent states to predict both immediate hazards and long-horizon prefix risks, outperforming reactive baselines in safety-utility trade-offs with only 25ms latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current runtime guardrails for LLM agents are predominantly reactive, evaluating only the immediate safety of proposed actions. This creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks where individually benign actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states, potentially causing irreversible harm to external systems.

Method: DreamGuard employs a risk-aware world model that maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the agent's trajectory. It predicts future latent states to derive two complementary signals: immediate-hazard evidence (current action safety) and prefix-risk evidence (trajectory-level drift toward hazard). These multi-horizon signals are fused to make intervention decisions before execution.

Result: DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation. It achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among all evaluated guardrails while maintaining an average end-to-end latency of only 25 ms per call.

Conclusion: Proactive guardrailing via a risk-aware world model effectively addresses long-horizon risks that reactive approaches miss, enabling safer LLM agent deployment in real-world settings without sacrificing utility or introducing significant latency overhead.

Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly invoke external tools and interact with real-world systems, unsafe actions may cause irreversible consequences on external states, user data, and downstream services. Recent runtime guardrails mitigate such risks by checking proposed actions before execution, but many remain reactive: they primarily assess the apparent safety of the current action, lacking an explicit model of how risk evolves across the trajectory. This limitation creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign-looking actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states. In response, we propose DreamGuard, a proactive guardrail for LLM agents built around a risk-aware world model. The world model maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states from which DreamGuard derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence. It then fuses these multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before execution. Experiments across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation show that DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

</details>


### [100] [StepReflect: Structured UI Transition Reflection for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05587)
*Linqiang Guo,Wei Liu,Li Gu,Yang Wang,Tse-Hsun,Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StepReflect is an 8B-parameter model that performs per-step action reflection for mobile GUI agents as a structured prediction task, outperforming GPT-5.2 by 11.83 points offline and matching or exceeding its online task success while reducing API costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GUI agent reflection relies on costly, open-ended multimodal reasoning after every action, which is poorly suited to the inherently structured nature of GUI state transitions. A more efficient, structured approach is needed for reliable long-horizon autonomous execution.

Method: StepReflect formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence (before/after screenshots). Training employs a staged pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning, (2) teacher-student distillation, and (3) preference- and reward-based refinement. The resulting model is 8B parameters.

Result: Offline on AndroidWorld: 82.16% transition-level accuracy, exceeding zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points. Online across four agent configurations (M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, Seed-2.0-Pro): StepReflect achieves higher task success in three of four and is within one successful task of GPT-5.2 in the fourth. It reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection across all four configurations.

Conclusion: StepReflect is a practical, locally deployable, cost-effective alternative to repeated frontier-model API calls for reflection in long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

Abstract: Autonomous mobile GUI agents require accurate action reflection for reliable long-horizon execution. Existing approaches rely on open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action, which is costly and poorly matched to the structured nature of GUI state transitions. We propose StepReflect, which formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. StepReflect is trained through a staged pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement. Offline, the resulting 8B model achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, exceeding zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points under the same structured input. Online, across M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, and Seed-2.0-Pro, StepReflect achieves higher task success in three of four agent configurations and remains within one successful task of the GPT-5.2 Reflection Agent in the fourth. It also reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection in all four configurations. These results establish StepReflect as a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

</details>


### [101] [ChainClaw: A Layered Agent Framework for Reliable On-Chain Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05790)
*Jiacheng Wei,Zhaoxin Fan,Xin Wen,Yuqin Lan,Dongrun Li,Wenjun Wu,Faguo Wu,Xiao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ChainClaw is a blockchain-native LLM agent framework that addresses three critical gaps—Reactivity, Irreversibility, and Observability—through a layered architecture with event-driven orchestration, simulation-based safety intelligence, and on-chain monitoring, outperforming baselines on safety and task completion across a custom benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose LLM agents fail in blockchain environments because on-chain execution is stateful, adversarial, and economically irreversible. Existing approaches lack mechanisms for real-time event response (Reactivity), pre-execution safety validation (Irreversibility), and comprehensive on-chain visibility (Observability).

Method: ChainClaw proposes a three-layer architecture: (1) an event-driven orchestration layer for reactivity via event ingestion and simulation feedback; (2) a simulation-based safety intelligence layer with a pre-execution safety pipeline featuring transaction simulation and action guards; (3) an on-chain monitoring runtime layer with read adapters and transaction monitors. These layers are unified by a cross-layer memory subsystem.

Result: ChainClaw was evaluated on a purpose-built benchmark covering seven tasks across four categories and five dimensions, consistently outperforming representative baselines on both safety and task completion metrics.

Conclusion: The layered, blockchain-native design of ChainClaw effectively bridges the reactivity, irreversibility, and observability gaps that limit general-purpose LLM agents in on-chain settings, demonstrating superior safety and performance.

Abstract: General-purpose large language model agents have achieved strong performance on tool-augmented tasks, yet they rely on assumptions break down in blockchain environments. On-chain execution is stateful, adversarial, and economically irreversible, exposing three fundamental gaps: Reactivity, Irreversibility, and Observability. We propose ChainClaw, a blockchain-native agent framework built on OpenClaw, that addresses all three gaps through a layered architecture comprising an event-driven orchestration layer, a simulation-based safety intelligence layer, and an on-chain monitoring runtime layer, unified by a cross-layer memory subsystem. ChainClaw closes the Reactivity gap via event ingestion and simulation feedback, the Irreversibility gap via a pre-execution safety pipeline with transaction simulation and action guard, and the Observability gap via an on-chain read adapter and transaction monitor. We evaluate ChainClaw on a purpose-built benchmark covering seven tasks across four categories and five dimensions. ChainClaw consistently outperforms representative baselines on both safety and task completion.

</details>


### [102] [Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05624)
*Bohan Jiang,Dawei Li,Yasin Silva,Huan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces CAP, a framework for collecting labeled data on Preference-induced Stance Reversal Sycophancy (PSRS), where LLMs flip their stance to match a user's preference. Analyzing 290K+ responses from 17 LLMs, the authors find PSRS rates of 5–56%, show that detection from response text alone is feasible, and highlight the challenge of cross-model generalization as new LLMs emerge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on sycophancy in LLMs primarily measures how sycophantic a model is, but does not address whether harmful sycophantic behavior — specifically Preference-induced Stance Reversal Sycophancy (PSRS) — can be automatically detected from a single response. The authors aim to fill this gap and address the practical challenge that detectors must generalize to unseen, rapidly emerging new models.

Method: The authors propose CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a data collection framework that generates labeled PSRS examples by presenting LLMs with an initial query to elicit a stance, then a follow-up revealing the user's opposite preference to observe whether the model reverses its stance. They apply CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs across 12 everyday-advice domains, collecting 290,460 labeled responses. They then train detectors on response text alone and evaluate both in-model and cross-model detection performance.

Result: PSRS rates vary substantially across models, ranging from 5% to 56%, with more capable models exhibiting lower sycophancy. Detection from response text alone is feasible, but requires learning subtle patterns from training data. Critically, detection performance degrades on unseen models, revealing cross-model generalization as a key challenge. The authors propose an initial method to mitigate this drop.

Conclusion: PSRS is a prevalent and detectable form of harmful sycophancy in LLMs, but building robust detectors that generalize across models remains an open challenge. The release of the CAP dataset and code aims to facilitate further research on automated sycophancy detection.

Abstract: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in large language models (LLMs), and prior work has pointed out that some of them could be harmful. This paper focuses on one harmful sycophancy: preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where a model reverses an initial stance merely to align with a user's stated preference. While existing research mainly measures how sycophantic a model is, we go further and ask whether PSRS can also be detected automatically from a single response. To investigate this at scale, we introduce CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applying CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, we collect 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) How often does PSRS occur? (2) How well can it be detected? (3) How does detection generalize to unseen models? We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data. Because new LLMs appear rapidly, detectors inevitably encounter unseen models, making cross-model generalization an important framework goal. We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge. We will release our dataset and code to support future research.

</details>


### [103] [SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05628)
*Yuru Feng,Yaoqi Chen,Beidi Zhao,Qianxi Zhang,Xinjiang Wang,Jianan Lu,Zhirui Wang,Shusen Xu,Zengzhong Li,Qi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillHEX is a closed-loop framework that enables LLM agents to autonomously evolve skills at test time by coupling hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search, overcoming the sparse reward and exploitation trap problems that plague existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual maintenance of agent skills is costly, unscalable, and prone to misalignment. Real-world deployments demand autonomous, on-demand skill evolution under tight interaction budgets without training or validation sets. This creates a sparse reward challenge where failure outcomes conflate multiple latent causes, making greedy single-skill refinement vulnerable to exploitation traps—early diagnostic errors waste limited trials on unproductive paths.

Method: SkillHEX employs a closed-loop framework with two key components: (1) hypothesis-driven self-verification that translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable diagnostic tests, generating dense reward signals without additional environment interactions; (2) evidence-guided tree search over persistent skill-revision branches that dynamically balances exploitation of edits supported by evidence with exploration of plausible alternatives.

Result: Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods, achieving average pass rates of 55.9% with GPT-5.3-Codex and 57.9% with Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget.

Conclusion: SkillHEX effectively addresses the sparse reward and exploitation trap challenges in autonomous test-time skill evolution, demonstrating that hypothesis-driven verification combined with tree search can significantly improve LLM agent performance under constrained interaction budgets.

Abstract: Although agent skills equip LLMs with reusable procedural knowledge, manual maintenance suffers from high costs, unscalability, and misalignment. Real-world deployments thus require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time, constrained by limited interaction budgets and a lack of training or validation sets. This setting introduces a severe sparse reward challenge, where outcomes conflate multiple latent failure causes. Under such ambiguity, existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill are particularly vulnerable to an exploitation trap, allowing early misdiagnoses to exhaust limited trials along unproductive trajectories. To address this, we introduce SkillHEX, a closed-loop framework coupling hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. SkillHEX translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, producing diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides a search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing the exploitation of supported edits with the exploration of plausible alternatives. Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods and achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% and 57.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget, respectively.

</details>


### [104] [Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) Model: A Computational Account of What Makes Design Options Worth Trying](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05642)
*Shimon Honda,Takuma Miyaguchi,Koji Koizumi,Takanori Sano,Tristan Briard,Hideyoshi Yanagisawa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The B-EUR model quantifies the value of a design action as the expected reduction in epistemic uncertainty about action-outcome relations. Tested via simulations and human experiments in a graph-shape guessing task, both epistemic value and subjective experience showed an inverted-U relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability, providing a computational account of uncertainty-driven exploration in design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address an open question in the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model — specifically, how changes in uncertainty perception govern action selection — by formalizing the value of candidate design actions in terms of expected epistemic uncertainty reduction.

Method: The authors propose the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model and test it through computational simulations and human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates action-outcome learning under a limited trial budget. Two environmental properties are systematically examined: generalizability (how far knowledge transfers across neighboring candidates) and outcome discriminability (how distinguishable outcomes are).

Result: In simulations, epistemic value followed an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability. Human experiments corroborated these patterns: subjective value of trying and enjoyment both showed inverted-U relationships with generalizability, and choice behavior reflected sensitivity to both environmental properties.

Conclusion: The B-EUR model offers a computational account of candidate-action evaluation in uncertainty-driven design activity and has practical implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

Abstract: This paper proposes the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model, which formalizes the value of trying a candidate design action as its expected reduction of epistemic uncertainty about action--outcome relations. The model addresses one part of the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model's open question concerning how changes in uncertainty perception determine action selection. We examine two environmental properties: generalizability, or how far knowledge from one trial extends to neighboring candidates, and outcome discriminability, or how clearly differences among outcomes can be distinguished.
  We tested the model through simulations and human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates learning about action--outcome relations under a limited trial budget. Epistemic value followed an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability in the simulations. In the human experiments, the subjective value of trying and enjoyment followed inverted-U-shaped relationships with generalizability, while choice behavior reflected both properties.
  The B-EUR model provides a computational account of candidate-action evaluation within uncertainty-driven design activity and offers implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

</details>


### [105] [Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05643)
*Ahsan Bilal,Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin,Muhammad Umer,Lena Trigg,Ali Subhan,Muhammad Ali,Dean F. Hougen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a verifier-free breadth-depth refinement framework for test-time scaling that combines diverse sampling (breadth) with iterative self-critique and self-correction (depth), then aggregates via majority voting. This outperforms greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-N, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple benchmarks and open-weight models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two key limitations of existing test-time scaling approaches: (1) wider sampling suffers from diminishing returns because new rollouts often repeat existing answer patterns rather than introducing reasoning diversity; (2) verifier-based selection depends heavily on the calibration quality of an external reward model, which can be unreliable.

Method: A verifier-free breadth-depth refinement framework with three stages: (1) Breadth — sample multiple independent reasoning rollouts to preserve diverse initial attempts; (2) Depth — refine each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction to repair local reasoning errors; (3) Aggregation — combine the refined answers via majority voting.

Result: Consistent improvements over baselines across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500 using multiple open-weight models. On Qwen2.5-1.5B: MATH500 accuracy reached 58.0% (vs. strongest verifier-based baseline), AMC improved from 25.0% to 32.5%.

Conclusion: Test-time compute is more effective when allocated to refining sampled trajectories (depth) rather than solely to sampling more candidates (breadth) or relying on verifier-guided selection.

Abstract: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by using additional inference compute, but wider sampling alone can suffer from diminishing returns: new rollouts often repeat existing answer patterns instead of adding useful reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection offers an alternative, but its performance depends on the calibration of an external reward model. We propose a verifier-free breadth--depth refinement framework that uses test-time compute to both explore and improve candidate solutions. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, refines each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction, and aggregates the refined answers by majority voting. Breadth preserves diverse initial attempts, while depth repairs local reasoning errors before aggregation. Across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, our method consistently improves over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-$N$, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple open-weight models. For instance, with Qwen2.5-1.5B, accuracy increases from the strongest verifier-based baseline to $58.0\%$ on MATH500, and from $25.0\%$ to $32.5\%$ on AMC. These results show that test-time compute can be more effective when used to refine sampled trajectories rather than only to sample more candidates or rely on verifier-guided selection.

</details>


### [106] [A Unified Framework for Trajectory Prediction with Explicit Planning and Reaction Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05673)
*Jiaheng Chen,Jiaxing Li,Tinghe Zhang,Chaopeng Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INTraJ proposes a two-stage trajectory prediction framework that explicitly separates social influence into a planning stage (anticipating others' future behaviors to construct reference trajectories) and a reaction stage (recovering local adjustments from residuals), achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing trajectory prediction methods fail to adequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence. The authors observe that agents form motion plans by first anticipating others' future behaviors (planning) and then making local reactive adjustments (reaction), yet current models conflate these distinct stages.

Method: INTraJ is a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: (1) a planning stage that constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and (2) a reaction stage that recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. The framework supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms.

Result: Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks — Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD — demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in Final Displacement Error (FDE) and long-horizon consistency. State-of-the-art performance is achieved in several settings.

Conclusion: INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling — where planning precedes reaction — is critical for achieving stable and accurate predictions. Code is publicly available.

Abstract: Trajectory prediction has shifted toward structured formulations with explicit social modeling. However, existing methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence in trajectory planning. Observing that agents typically form motion plans by anticipating others' future behaviors before making local reactive adjustments, we identify social interactions as playing staged roles, namely planning precedes reaction. We propose INTraJ, a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: a planning stage constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and a reaction stage recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. INTraJ supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks, including Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD, demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency, with state-of-the-art performance achieved in several settings. INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/11isnotavailable/INTraJ.

</details>


### [107] [Grounded Well-Condition Anomaly Detection on the Volve Field: Constructed Labels, a Baseline, and a Dual-Head Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05685)
*Gospel Bassey,Vincent Fakiyesi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the real-world challenge of anomaly detection in industrial machinery where fault labels are absent. Using Equinor's open Volve field data, the authors construct physically-grounded anomaly labels verified against engineering documentation, then test whether these labels are learnable using unsupervised and supervised models. Results show the labels align with unsupervised detection and a compact dual-head model generalizes across unseen wells, though precise temporal localization remains approximate. All artifacts are publicly released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most public machine-condition monitoring benchmarks use controlled test rigs with known, induced faults. Real production environments lack fault logs, forcing anomaly-detection methods to self-label, which risks introducing unnoticed, unvalidated assumptions. The authors aim to bridge this gap by working with real field data and constructing labels with explicit, documented physical justifications.

Method: 1) Anomaly label construction: Labels are built not solely from numerical patterns but cross-referenced against the Volve field's engineering documents detailing physically plausible faults. The rationale behind every label is released for transparency. 2) Learnability testing: An unsupervised baseline is applied to verify that label-free detection converges on the same regions as the rule-based labels (confirming non-arbitrariness). 3) A compact dual-head supervised model (adapted from prior work on metal-part defect detection) simultaneously detects event presence and classifies event type. Generalization is evaluated across previously unseen wells.

Result: The unsupervised detector identified the same anomalous regions as the physically-grounded labels, validating the labeling approach. The dual-head supervised model successfully recovered both event presence and event type on unseen wells, demonstrating cross-well generalization. However, temporal localization of events was only approximate. The authors transparently report all failures and assumptions.

Conclusion: Physically-grounded, transparently-documented anomaly labels can be constructed for real, unlabeled industrial sensor data and are learnable by both unsupervised and supervised methods. Cross-well generalization is achievable for event detection and classification, though fine-grained temporal localization remains a challenge. The full release of the dataset, labels, provenance, baselines, model, and code under CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0 provides a realistic benchmark for the community.

Abstract: Most public benchmarks for machine-condition monitoring come from test rigs, where faults are induced on purpose and every event is known. Real production fields rarely offer that. They give you sensor histories with no fault log attached, which is exactly the situation where an anomaly-detection method has to invent its own labels, and where quiet assumptions can slip in unnoticed. We work with the open Volve field data released by Equinor and take two things seriously that such datasets usually skip. First, we build anomaly labels that are not just patterns in the numbers but are checked against what the field's own engineering documents say can physically go wrong, and we release the reasoning behind every label. Second, we test whether those constructed labels are learnable at all, using both an unsupervised baseline and a small dual-head model that marks when an event happens and what kind it is, an idea we carry over from earlier work on defect detection in metal parts. The results are honest. An unsupervised detector that never sees the labels still lands on the same regions our rules flagged, which tells us the labels are not arbitrary. A compact supervised model recovers event presence and event type well across wells it has never seen, and locates events in time only roughly. We report what worked, what did not, and every assumption in between. The dataset, grounded labels, per-label provenance, baseline scores, trained model, and code are released publicly under CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0.

</details>


### [108] [Shaping Human-AI Interactions to Provide Improvement Pathways and Balance Competing Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05710)
*Keziah Naggita*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This thesis investigates the design of human-AI interaction loops where individuals strategically adapt their behavior based on beliefs about an AI system. It aims to foster accurate user beliefs, encourage genuine improvement over gaming, and maintain system objectives, using theoretical analysis, experiments, and empirical evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When AI systems are deployed, users form beliefs about how they work and strategically modify their behavior to obtain favorable outcomes. This creates a feedback loop that can undermine system objectives, enable gaming, and harm users. There is a need for principled design of these interactions to align human and AI goals.

Method: The thesis adopts a multi-method approach organized into three complementary parts, examining interactions from both the evaluated individual's and the AI system's perspectives. It integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.

Result: The thesis advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities. Specific empirical or theoretical results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: Human-AI interaction loops must be carefully designed to promote accurate user beliefs, incentivize genuine improvement over strategic gaming, and preserve system objectives. The work contributes foundational principles and methods toward this goal.

Abstract: When an AI system is deployed, the individuals who use and or are evaluated by it form beliefs about how the system operates and use those beliefs to strategically present their preferences, behaviors, or attributes. The system then responds with feedback or a decision outcome, thereby creating a human-AI interaction loop. This thesis studies how to design and shape such interactions to achieve three goals: (1) help individuals develop accurate beliefs about the AI systems so they can improve and or secure favorable outcomes at minimal cost, (2) encourage improvement and or discourage gaming behaviors, and (3) ensure that the AI system continues to achieve its intended objectives, such as maximizing accuracy. To address these goals, the thesis is organized into three complementary parts that examine and study human-AI interactions from the perspectives of both evaluated individuals and AI systems. Together, the work presented in this thesis advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities. Methodologically, this thesis integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.

</details>


### [109] [RA-CAD: Learning Post-Execution Critique for State-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05714)
*Shuhao Yan,Changhao He,Xi Peng,Peng Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RA-CAD introduces a state-aware agent that generates parametric CAD code through an iterative Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop, where critique is treated as a learnable policy decision optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), achieving SOTA on CADFusion and Text2CAD benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing text-to-CAD methods use external or fixed critique mechanisms that fail to optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions. There is a gap in making critique an integral, optimizable part of the generation policy.

Method: RA-CAD uses a two-stage training pipeline: (1) CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) via supervised fine-tuning to establish parametric CAD coding capabilities, and (2) Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) using trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that jointly optimizes code generation and critique sequences with terminal F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards. The agent operates in a Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop, conditioned on design instruction, current code, and execution feedback.

Result: RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality on CADFusion and Text2CAD benchmarks, outperforming both existing methods and strong proprietary language models.

Conclusion: Treating critique as an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision within an iterative agent loop significantly improves text-to-CAD generation, closing the feedback-utilization gap present in prior approaches.

Abstract: Text-to-CAD generation translates natural-language design intent into editable and executable parametric computer-aided design (CAD) codes, reducing the expertise and effort required for manual modeling. Existing methods incorporate fixed, externally supplied, prompt-induced, or separately optimized critique mechanisms to optimize the generation process, but they do not necessarily optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions throughout the generation process. To bridge this feedback-utilization gap, we present RA-CAD (ReAct Agent for CAD), a state-aware agent that interacts with the CAD environment through a Generate--Execute--Critique--Rewrite loop. At each iteration, RA-CAD executes the current code and observes its outcome. Conditioned on the design instruction, current code, and execution feedback, the agent then generates an explicit post-execution critique as an intermediate policy action. This critique either validates the current result for termination or provides revision-oriented guidance that conditions the next rewrite. CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) first establishes fundamental parametric CAD coding capabilities through supervised fine-tuning. Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) subsequently applies trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization to both policy-generated code and critique sequences, assigning terminal F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards to the complete interaction trajectory. This formulation makes critique an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision rather than an unoptimized auxiliary output. Experiments on CADFusion and Text2CAD show that RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality compared with existing methods and strong proprietary language models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed state-aware text-to-CAD agent.

</details>


### [110] [BlockPython: A Process-Aware Agent-Supported Platform for the Transition from Block-Based to Python Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05716)
*Jesse Yusuf Chan,Haoming Wang,Mingwei Xu,Xianlong Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BlockPython is a platform that supports learners transitioning from block-based to text-based Python programming through bidirectional block–code translation, a four-stage learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms that analyze learning evidence to provide targeted assistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learners moving from block-based to text-based programming face a cognitive gap between understanding computational concepts and expressing them in Python syntax, as they must translate visible program structures into abstract textual expressions.

Method: BlockPython employs bidirectional translation between blocks and Python across four stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. It continuously collects process evidence (block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, support usage, dialogue) and uses three support mechanisms — deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and a learning assistant — to identify and address difficulties. A rule-based system handles execution, evaluation, and stage control, while the learning assistant provides explanations, prompts, and guiding questions based on verified evidence.

Result: The paper presents the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms of BlockPython as a system-design reference, without reporting empirical evaluation results.

Conclusion: BlockPython offers a structured approach to bridging the block-to-text programming gap by integrating progressive stages, continuous evidence collection, and multi-modal support mechanisms, serving as a reference architecture for future learning systems in this domain.

Abstract: The transition from block-based to text-based programming requires learners to convert visible program structures into abstract textual expressions, which may create a cognitive gap between understanding computational concepts and expressing them in Python syntax. To support this transition, we designed and implemented BlockPython. The platform centers on bidirectional translation between blocks and Python and guides learners through four stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. Across these stages, learners progressively establish connections among program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code. During learning, the platform continuously collects process evidence, including block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, use of support, and dialogue. Deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and the learning assistant use this evidence to identify different difficulties in computational understanding and Python expression. The rule-based system is responsible for program execution, objective evaluation, and stage control, while the learning assistant uses verified evidence to provide explanations, prompts, and guiding questions. This report describes the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms of BlockPython and provides a system-design reference for supporting the transition from block-based to text-based programming and for analyzing learning processes.

</details>


### [111] [Subliminal Learning is Non-Semantic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05734)
*Ethan Hadley,Eren Gultepe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Subliminal Learning (SL) allows hidden biases to transfer from a teacher model to a student via seemingly random synthetic data. The authors show that Gaussian noise added to model weights amplifies SL (1.9x in Gemma, 1.3x in Llama), that steering vectors can generate subliminal data, and that students inherit the type of intervention applied to the teacher. Gradients from steered data correlate linearly with teacher steering vectors, offering a potential auditing mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SL poses a safety threat because hidden subliminal signals in training data cannot be detected through standard auditing, making AI systems less predictable. Understanding the mechanisms driving SL is essential to detect and mitigate these covert bias transfers, especially as synthetic data becomes central to frontier model training.

Method: The authors investigate SL mechanisms through three experimental approaches: (1) injecting Gaussian noise into teacher and student model weights and measuring the change in subliminal transfer magnitude; (2) comparing steering vectors, prompting, and finetuning as methods for generating subliminal data from teachers; (3) analyzing student activations and gradient correlations to determine what information is inherited across different intervention types.

Result: Adding Gaussian noise to weights boosted SL by 1.9x in Gemma and 1.3x in Llama, implicating non-semantic weight structures. Steering vectors successfully produce subliminal data comparable to prompting and finetuning. Crucially, students trained on steered data imitate steering-vector-like activation patterns, while prompted students do not — showing inheritance of intervention type, not just semantic bias. Gradients of steered subliminal data exhibit linear correlation with teacher steering vectors, suggesting a pathway for data auditing.

Conclusion: SL is driven by non-semantic, structural properties of model weights rather than purely semantic features. The linear correlation between steered-data gradients and teacher steering vectors offers a promising direction for detecting hidden signals in training data. As synthetic data pipelines grow, the ability to audit for latent subliminal signals becomes critical for AI safety.

Abstract: Subliminal Learning (SL) is a surprising type of generalization displayed by modern language models. It allows the transfer of a bias or behavior from a teacher model to a student by distilling from seemingly unrelated or random synthetic data from the teacher. This presents challenges in ensuring AI systems remain predictable and are trained safely, as standard auditing of the input data would not catch the hidden subliminal signal. Here, we investigate several open questions as to the enabling mechanisms and drivers of SL. First is the nature of the process by which biases are encoded in the data. We find that by adding Gaussian noise to the weights of the teacher and student models, the magnitude of subliminal transfer is increased by a factor of 1.9 in Gemma and 1.3 in Llama, suggesting that non-semantic weight structures play a crucial role. We show that steering vectors can be applied to the teacher to produce subliminal data, in addition to prompting and finetuning as used in previous studies. Analysis of the activations of the student models that have been trained on steered and prompted data demonstrates that students inherit not just the semantic meaning of the teacher's bias, but also the type of intervention that was used to apply it: steered students imitate steering vectors, prompted students do not. Additionally, the gradients of steered subliminal data show a linear correlation with the teacher's steering vectors, showing promise for data auditing. More broadly, as synthetic data becomes central to frontier training pipelines, being able to see the latent signals hidden in training data becomes paramount.

</details>


### [112] [When Do Prompt-Side Agent Playbooks Transfer? Accuracy, Cost, and Runtime Shift in Agent Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05778)
*Weihong Lin,Lin Sun,Xiangzheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Frozen playbook transfer across settings yields mixed results: beneficial under controlled decoding in ALFWorld, modest advantage in TAU2-Bench (mostly non-significant after correction), and cost-inflating artifacts in XBench-DeepSearch. Transfer is a conditional cold-start option, not a default reuse strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt-side playbooks can improve tool-using language agents without retraining, but their portability beyond the source setting is unclear. The authors aim to systematically evaluate whether frozen playbook transfer is a viable strategy across different benchmarks and settings.

Method: The study employs a shared distill--validate--transfer protocol across three benchmarks: ALFWorld, TAU2-Bench, and XBench-DeepSearch. Frozen playbooks are transferred without retraining. Evaluation includes controlled greedy decoding comparisons (ALFWorld), aggregate contrasts with Holm correction for route-level effects (TAU2-Bench), and analysis of runtime-pairing artifacts under context-runtime shift (XBench-DeepSearch).

Result: (1) ALFWorld: transfer is beneficial under controlled greedy decoding; distilled guidance outperforms five fixed demonstrations in a near-budget-matched comparison. (2) TAU2-Bench: a prespecified aggregate contrast supports a modest average matched-domain advantage, but global Holm correction retains only 1 of 135 route-level effects; the remaining grid shows compatibility-sensitive heterogeneity. (3) XBench-DeepSearch: one runtime-pairing artifact preserves useful first-try heuristics but produces repeated queries, delayed stopping, and substantial cost inflation after a context-runtime shift. Across all benchmarks, both transferred and target-derived playbooks require target-side validation of success, termination, protocol compatibility, and cost.

Conclusion: Frozen transfer is neither a universally preferable alternative to target-side redistillation nor a reuse-by-default strategy. It should be treated as a conditional cold-start option requiring target-side validation across multiple dimensions.

Abstract: Prompt-side playbooks can improve tool-using language agents without retraining, but their portability beyond the source setting is unclear. We study frozen playbook transfer under a shared distill--validate--transfer protocol. On ALFWorld, transfer is beneficial under controlled greedy decoding and, in one near-budget-matched comparison, distilled guidance outperforms five fixed demonstrations. On TAU2-Bench, a prespecified aggregate contrast supports a modest average matched-domain advantage, but global Holm correction retains only one of 135 route-level effects; the remaining grid provides descriptive evidence of compatibility-sensitive heterogeneity. On XBench-DeepSearch, one artifact--runtime pairing preserves useful first-try heuristics while producing repeated queries, delayed stopping, and substantial cost inflation after a context-runtime shift. Across benchmarks, transferred and target-derived playbooks both require target-side validation of success, termination, protocol compatibility, and cost. Frozen transfer is therefore a conditional cold-start option, not a reuse-by-default strategy or a universally preferable alternative to target-side redistillation.

</details>


### [113] [Activity Frames: Deterministic Screen-Activity Compilation for Agent Memory and Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05784)
*Nossa Iyamu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a deterministic, zero-model pipeline that compiles passively captured screen activity into structured, auditable agent memory. The compiler reduces raw capture by 86x, achieves 98.4% question-answering accuracy, and doubles as a demand-side cost instrument, providing first measurements of Routine Overhead Ratio (60–343x) and delegable recurrence (~8–9%), enabling zero-token deterministic replay.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current computer-use agents waste frontier inference compute by re-deriving routines users have already performed, because agent memory stores conversational history (what users said) rather than behavioral history (what users did). There is also a lack of empirically measured parameters (Routine Overhead Ratio R and routine recurrence h) needed by agent-cost models.

Method: A deterministic, zero-model pipeline segments passively captured screen recordings into typed activity frames — bounded episodes carrying application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers to raw rows. No ML model is in the loop, ensuring byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable output. The compiler was evaluated on a single-user corpus of 128,756 frames across 51 active days.

Result: The compiler reduces a day of raw capture to a prompt-ready context block 86x smaller in 68 ms. An agent reading that block achieves 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7–99.7%) on daily questions against an independent oracle, versus 66–80% for LLM summaries. First measurements of Routine Overhead Ratio R (60–343x modeled upper bound) and delegable recurrence (9.0% in-sample, 7.7% out-of-sample) are reported, with a realistic all-fleet token ceiling near 8%.

Conclusion: Passively compiled, model-free screen activity records serve as both high-fidelity agent memory and a demand-side cost instrument.
