The approach enables deterministic replay at zero model tokens and supplies the first empirical values for key parameters in agent-cost modeling. Schema, compiler, and evaluation harness are released openly.

Abstract: Computer-use agents pay full frontier inference to re-derive routines their user has already performed, because an agent's memory today records what the user said, not what the user did. We compile passively captured screen activity into agent memory with a deterministic, zero-model pipeline: it segments a local capture stream into typed activity frames, bounded episodes carrying application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers back to the raw rows, with no model in the loop, so the output is byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable. On one professional's single-user corpus of 128,756 frames over 51 active days, the compiler reduces a day of raw capture to a prompt-ready context block 86x smaller in 68 ms, and an agent reading that block answers questions about the day at 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7-99.7%) against an independent oracle, versus 66-80% for an LLM summary of the same capture, a mid-tier model reading the block matching a frontier one.
  The same compiler doubles as a demand-side cost instrument. Read off passive, pre-delegation human activity rather than agent rollouts, it supplies two parameters that agent-cost models assume but, to our knowledge, have not measured: the Routine Overhead Ratio R and the routine recurrence h. We report first values of R, a modeled upper bound, at 60-343x, and a delegable recurrence of 9.0% in-sample and 7.7% out-of-sample, for a realistic all-fleet token ceiling near 8%; a compiled routine replays deterministically with the model out of the loop, demonstrated live at zero model tokens on a guard-matched hit. Schema, compiler, and evaluation harness are open.

</details>


### [114] [When Agentic AI Meets Integrated Sensing and Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05792)
*Kai Li,Conggai Li,Sarah Ali Siddiqui,Syed Sohail Ahmed,Xin Yuan,Shenghong Li,Wei Ni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey proposes AISAC, a paradigm reframing ISAC as a goal-driven, closed-loop intelligent system. It unifies disparate research areas within a six-stage closed-loop framework and five agentic maturity levels, audits existing studies against nine agentic criteria to reveal a maturity gap, and identifies open challenges for fully agentic ISAC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research on learning-based sensing, resource allocation, RIS, edge intelligence, multi-agent coordination, and resilient networking in ISAC has developed in isolation. There is no unified framework that captures how these components can operate together as a goal-driven, closed-loop intelligent system — hence the need to define and structure the emerging AISAC paradigm.

Method: The paper constructs a six-stage closed-loop framework (observation, contextualization, reasoning and prediction, planning and orchestration, execution and collaboration, feedback and resilience) and defines five levels of agentic maturity (from physical-layer primitives to fully closed-loop agentic ISAC). It then reviews advances across multimodal intelligence, LLMs, RL, federated learning, RIS-assisted control, UAV/vehicular networks, and AI-native network management through this lens. An audit of representative studies is performed against nine agentic-specific evaluation criteria.

Result: The audit reveals that no existing system reports more than one or two of the nine agentic evaluation criteria, exposing a significant gap between claimed and demonstrated agentic maturity. Cross-cutting requirements — privacy, security, resilience, and sustainability — are identified as underexplored dimensions of the full perception-reasoning-action loop.

Conclusion: The field of AISAC is nascent and fragmented. Key open challenges include physical-to-semantic grounding, predictive world models, real-time agent-PHY interaction, safe tool use, heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration, benchmarking, and resource-efficient autonomy. Addressing these is essential for realizing fully closed-loop agentic ISAC systems.

Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) from a function-oriented physical-layer technology into a goal-driven, closed-loop intelligent system, a paradigm we term AISAC. Existing work on learning-based sensing, resource allocation, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), edge intelligence, multi-agent coordination, and resilient networking has developed largely in isolation. This survey unifies the literature within a six-stage closed-loop framework comprising observation, contextualization, reasoning and prediction, planning and orchestration, execution and collaboration, and feedback and resilience. It also introduces five levels of agentic maturity, ranging from physical-layer primitives to fully closed-loop agentic ISAC. We use this framework to review advances in multimodal intelligence, large language models, reinforcement learning, federated learning, RIS-assisted control, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) and vehicular networks, and AI-native network management, and analyze privacy, security, resilience, and sustainability as cross-cutting requirements of the full perception-reasoning-action loop. An audit of representative studies against nine agentic-specific evaluation criteria shows that no system reports more than one or two of them, exposing a gap between claimed and demonstrated agentic maturity. We identify open challenges in physical-to-semantic grounding, predictive world models, real-time agent-PHY interaction, safe tool use, heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration, benchmarking, and resource-efficient autonomy.

</details>


### [115] [When Self-Evolution Backfires: Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05810)
*Linfang Shang,Ming Xu,Yiding Sun,Tianle Xia,Lingxiang Hu,Lan Xu,Ning Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-evolving agents suffer a capability-contamination phase transition where accumulating skills beyond a critical pool size causes irreversible performance degradation. The authors propose Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG), a three-critic filtering system with marginal-gain selection, achieving monotonic improvement at 72% pass@1 with a 5x smaller skill pool.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core motivation is the observation that self-evolving agent systems do not improve monotonically — past a critical skill pool size, newly added skills degrade rather than improve performance. This "capability-contamination phase transition" is both problematic and structurally irreversible via post-hoc fixes, demanding a pre-admission solution.

Method: Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG) employs a progressive trust hierarchy with three heterogeneous critics: (1) structural validity, (2) behavioral harmlessness, and (3) semantic consistency — each filtering skills individually before admission. At the top tier, a marginal-gain subset selection removes combinatorial contamination, ensuring only beneficial skills enter the runtime context. This is framed as a pre-commit gatekeeping mechanism rather than post-hoc rollback.

Result: On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation peaks then degrades as the pool grows, with post-hoc culprit removal recovering only a small fraction of lost performance (empirical irreversibility signature). VaG improves every round, reaching 72% pass@1 with a ~5x smaller pool, and its frozen skill pool transfers positively to four other backbones and a second benchmark without re-evolution. Ablations confirm the three critics are complementary and non-substitutable, each intercepting largely disjoint harmful skills.

Conclusion: Skill admission must be treated as a pre-commit necessity, not a post-hoc fix, due to the structural irreversibility of cross-round contamination chains. VaG demonstrates that rigorous, multi-critic gatekeeping with marginal-gain selection enables monotonic, transferable capability accumulation with significantly smaller skill pools.

Abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate capability by distilling reusable skills from their execution trajectories, but we find this process is not monotonic: past a critical pool size, newly added skills degrade performance instead of improving it. We formalize this capability-contamination phase transition and trace it to a structural cause: once a defective skill enters the decision context, it becomes reference material for distilling later skills, forming cross-round contamination chains. We further show the contamination is structurally irreversible: removing a source skill after the fact cannot erase the flawed reasoning its descendants have already inherited, so post-hoc rollback recovers only a small fraction of the lost performance. This makes skill admission a pre-commit necessity rather than a post-hoc fix, and motivates Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG): a progressive trust hierarchy whose three heterogeneous critics - structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency - filter each skill individually, coupled with a marginal-gain subset selection that removes combinatorial contamination at the top tier before skills reach the runtime context. On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation rises to a peak and then degrades, giving back most of its gains as the pool keeps growing, and post-hoc removal of the culprit skills recovers only a small part of the drop - the empirical signature of irreversibility. In contrast, VaG improves every round, reaching 72% pass@1 with a pool roughly 5x smaller, and its frozen skill pool transfers positively to four other backbones and a second benchmark without re-evolution. Ablations confirm the three critics are complementary and mutually non-substitutable, each intercepting a largely disjoint class of harmful skills.

</details>


### [116] [Cautious Context Steering for Language Model Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05813)
*Gihoon Kim,Jeyoung Lee,Suhan Woo,Sekwon Oh,Minsu Jeon,Hyounsoo Han,Euntai Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Cautious Context Steering (CCS) uses a lightweight adapter on a frozen LM to dynamically decide per-token whether and how strongly user context should influence generation, improving personalization and generalization while reducing inference cost compared to existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LM personalization methods either train per-user adapters (suffering from data sparsity and poor generalization) or use context-based approaches like ICL and Context Steering (CoS) that have fixed, uncontrolled context influence. CoS also requires two forward passes per token, increasing inference cost. There is a need for a method that dynamically modulates context influence without per-user training and with lower computational overhead.

Method: CCS trains a lightweight adapter on a frozen backbone LM that learns, at each decoding step, whether and how strongly to steer generation based on user context. The adapter is trained using an oracle context-conditioned LM as supervision, learning when context is helpful versus when to default to the base LM behavior. Only a single adapter is trained on one dataset, with no per-user fine-tuning required.

Result: A single CCS adapter trained on one dataset improves generation quality both in-domain and across four out-of-distribution personalization benchmarks, demonstrating robust generalization to unseen users and domains. CCS also eliminates the extra context-conditioned forward pass required by CoS, substantially reducing inference cost.

Conclusion: CCS offers an effective and efficient approach to LM personalization by dynamically controlling context influence per token via a single lightweight adapter, achieving strong generalization without per-user training and with lower inference costs than prior context-based methods.

Abstract: Personalizing language models (LMs) to individual user preferences is essential for aligning responses with diverse goals and backgrounds. Existing methods typically train a separate adapter for each user or learn a reward model whose scores depend on the user. Despite explicitly optimizing for each user, these methods must learn from limited observations and therefore suffer from data sparsity and poor generalization to unseen users and domains. In-context learning (ICL) and Context Steering (CoS) can instead provide more effective personalization by conditioning the base LM directly on user context and leveraging its pretrained capabilities without per-user training. Yet neither adapts the influence of that context across decoding steps: ICL leaves it uncontrolled, whereas CoS applies a fixed steering coefficient and requires two LM forward passes per step. We propose Cautious Context Steering (CCS), which adds a lightweight adapter to a frozen backbone LM to decide at each token whether and how strongly user context should affect generation. The adapter learns this behavior from an oracle context-conditioned LM and preserves the base LM when the context is not helpful. A single CCS adapter trained on only one dataset improves generation quality both in-domain and across four out-of-distribution personalization benchmarks, demonstrating robust generalization to new users and domains. CCS also avoids per-user fine-tuning and the additional context-conditioned forward pass required by CoS, substantially reducing inference cost.

</details>


### [117] [ViSR-KGC: Visual Subgraph Reasoning with Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05833)
*Jiafan Li,Mengxue Yang,Jiaqi Zhu,Liang Chang,Ying Li,Hongan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ViSR-KGC proposes a visual subgraph reasoning framework that converts multimodal knowledge graph subgraphs into visual renderings for VLM-based inference, combining representation learning for topology, VLMs for local multimodal evidence, and pretrained commonsense knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KGC methods fall into two camps: embedding-based approaches struggle with limited relation-specific evidence, while LLM-based methods linearize graphs into text, losing structural topology and visual information. VLMs excel at multimodal reasoning but cannot natively interpret structured graph topology with complex node/edge semantics. A method bridging these gaps is needed.

Method: ViSR-KGC operates in three stages: (1) multimodal representation learning to capture global topology dependencies and produce embeddings; (2) extraction of a compact, query-aware subgraph from the MMKG; (3) transformation of the subgraph into a visual layout (selected via empirical comparison) and combination with entity images, textual descriptions, and candidates into a unified VLM prompt for inference.

Result: The paper reports empirical comparisons of subgraph layout strategies and demonstrates that the visual subgraph rendering approach enables VLMs to perform MMKGC effectively by integrating topological, multimodal, and commonsense signals.

Conclusion: ViSR-KGC successfully bridges representation learning and VLM-based reasoning for MMKGC by encoding graph topology into visually interpretable subgraph images, enabling VLMs to leverage structural, visual, textual, and commonsense information jointly for knowledge graph completion.

Abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to infer missing entities or relations from incomplete graph structures, and has evolved into multimodal knowledge graph completion (MMKGC), where entities are associated with multiple modalities such as text and images. Traditional representation learning approaches follow the embedding-based paradigm and may struggle when relation-specific evidence is limited. Meanwhile, LLM-based reasoning methods typically linearize graph structures into textual prompts, which obscures structural topology and neglects vital visual information. While vision-language models (VLMs) excel at multimodal reasoning, they cannot natively interpret structured graph topology, particularly when it comes to knowledge graphs where nodes and edges carry complex semantics. To bridge this gap, we propose ViSR-KGC, a visual subgraph reasoning approach for KGC. It integrates three complementary capabilities to capture semantic correlations: identifying global topology dependencies via representation learning, analyzing local multimodal evidence using VLMs, and providing necessary commonsense knowledge inherent in pre-trained models. Based on learned multimodal embeddings, our framework first extracts a compact and query-aware subgraph from the MMKG. Then, this subgraph is transformed into a visually interpretable image using a layout strategy selected through empirical comparison.Finally, the visualized subgraph, entity images, textual descriptions, and candidate answers are combined into a unified prompt, enabling the VLM to infer the missing entity.

</details>


### [118] [Runtime Observability for Heterogeneous Attention Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05863)
*Fanzhe Wei,Li Liu,Ziyang Wang,Chenyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a runtime observability framework for modern attention memory architectures (KV caches, latent caches, learned sparse selectors, recurrent states) using three operators that compose per-stage bounds into a request-level risk ledger. The system enforces metric-type consistency through formal bridges, automatically degrades unverifiable claims to empirical tier, and was validated on 12.4M entry reads across six model configurations, successfully localizing a silent corruption in a served DeepSeek-V4 stack.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLM serving systems employ diverse memory classes (plain KV caches, latent caches, learned sparse selectors, recurrent states) that fail differently under compression. There is no unified runtime observability framework that can compose safety/performance bounds across these heterogeneous memory types into an end-to-end request-level risk guarantee, nor any mechanism to formally certify or empirically validate such composed bounds.

Method: The authors define a runtime observability contract covering all four memory classes using three primitive operators. Per-stage bounds are composed into a request-level risk ledger. Contracts carry their error metric as a type, and composition is only permitted when metrics match — this is enforced through two formally proved bridges. Claims that cannot be formally certified are automatically degraded to the empirical tier. The system runs under CUDA graphs with a fused always-on probe observing a declared one-layer subset. A machine-adjudicated discrimination campaign is used to isolate failures, with the calculus rejecting confounded inferences automatically. The entire artifact pipeline is reproducible via a single command.

Result: The framework was instantiated on six model configurations across five architecture families. Under 12.4M entry reads with eight-way concurrency and per-request budgets, the risk ledger held its budget with zero violations. On a served DeepSeek-V4 stack with packed compressed-KV prototype, the machinery localized a silent corruption to a precise structural boundary — exact in the eviction-free, identity-isolated regime, with all observed failures occurring in eviction or slot-reuse regimes. The type-checking mechanism rejected the authors' own first composed chain, and the discrimination campaign's calculus rejected two of their own confounded inferences.

Conclusion: The proposed observability contract and risk ledger provide a principled, machine-enforceable framework for composing heterogeneous attention memory guarantees into end-to-end request-level risk bounds, distinguishing formally certified, partially certified, and empirical claims with automatic tier inheritance. All artifacts are open-sourced with full reproducibility.

Abstract: Modern models no longer keep a plain KV cache: latent caches, learned sparse selectors and recurrent states each carry the model's memory in a different form, and each fails differently under compression. We give a runtime observability contract that covers all four memory classes with three operators, instantiate it on six model configurations across five architecture families, and compose the per-stage bounds into an executable request-level risk ledger. Contracts carry their error metric as a type -- composition is only defined when metrics match, and this check rejected our own first composed chain; the repaired chain crosses metrics through two proved bridges, and whatever no formal system can certify is measured instead, dropping the composed tier to empirical automatically: every claim is certified, partially certified, or empirical, composition inherits the weakest tier, and the tier is decided by the machine. Replayed over $12.4$M entry reads and run under eight-way concurrency with per-request budgets and fail-closed identity attribution, the ledger quantifies the honest trade-off on today's witness and holds its risk budget with zero violations. A fused always-on probe observes a declared one-layer subset under CUDA graphs inside the serving noise floor. Applied to a served DeepSeek-V4 stack with a packed compressed-KV prototype, the same machinery localizes a silent corruption to a precise structural boundary -- exact in the eviction-free, identity-isolated regime, with every observed failure in an eviction or slot-reuse regime -- through a machine-adjudicated discrimination campaign whose calculus rejected two of our own confounded inferences along the way. All artifacts, guards, and the Lean development are released at https://github.com/metask-ai/witprobe-attention-memory; every number in this paper regenerates from the shipped artifacts by one command.

</details>


### [119] [Seeing Is Not Deciding: Can Multimodal LLMs Act as Effective CEOs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05864)
*Yuyang Dai,Xueqing Peng,Yuxia Wang,Preslav Nakov,Zhuohan Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C-SUITEBENCH is a multimodal benchmark testing LLMs as executive decision-makers across 50 scenarios. While visual inputs improve evidence reasoning and risk forecasting, they paradoxically degrade resource allocation due to signal crowding, revealing that visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based autonomous agents in business decision-making are text-only, leaving unclear whether models can effectively perceive and integrate visual business evidence (charts, dashboards, financial graphics) to improve high-stakes executive decisions.

Method: The authors introduce C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled multimodal benchmark with five decision tasks across 50 scenarios, each presented in paired text-only and multimodal conditions. Nine frontier models are evaluated in the role of CEO. Ablation experiments isolate the effects of individual vs. combined visual channels on decision quality.

Result: Multimodal inputs consistently improve evidence-centric reasoning, with largest gains in risk forecasting and board-facing justification. However, a "multimodal integration paradox" emerges: visual information degrades constrained resource allocation across all nine models. Ablations attribute this to signal crowding — individual visual channels help, but their combination disrupts constraint satisfaction during decoding.

Conclusion: Visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents. Indiscriminate visual augmentation can harm high-stakes decisions, motivating the need for selective grounding strategies in future executive AI systems rather than naive multimodal enrichment.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly applied as autonomous decision-making agents. However, in executive business decisions, existing benchmarks are limited to textonly settings. This makes it unclear whether models can perceive visual business evidence and effectively integrate it to improve decision quality. We introduce C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled multimodal benchmark that includes five decision tasks under paired text-only and multimodal conditions across 50 scenarios. We place nine frontier models in the role of a chief executive officer and evaluate their decision-making ability. Multimodal inputs consistently improve evidence-centric reasoning, with the largest and most reliable gains appearing in risk forecasting and board-facing justification. However, we uncover a multimodal integration paradox: adding visual business information degrades constrained resource allocation for all nine models, even as visual grounding itself improves. Ablation experiments reveal that this failure emerges from signal crowding, although each visual channel helps individually, their combination disrupts constraint satisfaction during decoding. These findings demonstrate that visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents, and that indiscriminate visual augmentation can harm high-stakes decision making, motivating selective grounding strategies for future executive AI systems.

</details>


### [120] [Improving Interoperability among Defence and National Security Ontologies: Analysis and Evaluation Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05867)
*Jonathon Dilworth,Pedro Giesteira Cotovio,David Herron,Paul Cripps,Nigel Dewdney,Catia Pesquita,Ernesto Jiménez-Ruiz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper surveys over 60 publicly available defence and national security ontologies, identifies interoperability as a major challenge, and introduces a new Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI) track with eight matching tasks, consensus alignments, and manually-curated silver-standard mappings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The growing number of ontologies in defence and national security, developed across academia, industry, and government, has created a significant interoperability problem. The domain's breadth and specialization make it difficult to align these ontologies, yet no standardized evaluation benchmark exists to systematically assess ontology matching systems in this domain.

Method: The authors analyze and document over 60 publicly available defence/national security ontologies. They construct a new OAEI track comprising eight matching tasks. Consensus alignments are generated by aggregating outputs from multiple state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. A silver-standard is then produced through manual validation of the consensus alignment combined with a subset of unique mappings (those suggested by only one system).

Result: The work delivers a curated collection of 60+ defence ontologies, a new OAEI evaluation track with eight matching tasks, consensus reference alignments from aggregated system outputs, and a manually-validated silver-standard alignment combining consensus and uniquely-suggested mappings.

Conclusion: The new OAEI track provides a much-needed benchmark for evaluating ontology alignment systems in the defence and national security domain, facilitating progress toward semantic interoperability across the fragmented landscape of defence ontologies.

Abstract: The use of ontologies and knowledge graphs is becoming increasingly widespread in the defence and national security domain. Numerous ontologies have been developed through initiatives led by academia, industry, and government. Achieving interoperability across diverse defence and national security ontologies remains a major challenge due to the domain's breadth and specialisation. In this work, we analyse and document over 60 publicly available ontologies and introduce a new track for the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI). This track comprises eight matching tasks, consensus alignments and manually-curated (silver-standard) mappings. The consensus alignments are derived by aggregating the outputs of several state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. The silver-standard is obtained from the manual validation of the consensus alignment together with a subset of the unique mappings (i.e., mappings suggested by only one system).

</details>


### [121] [Personalized Deep Research Query Refinement with Graph-Scaffolded Evidence Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05876)
*Soojin Yoon,Dongha Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: G-STEER refines user requests into personalized research specifications for deep research agents by learning a clarification policy that decides which framing factors to elicit, whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop — balancing coverage against evidence acquisition costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized deep research requires research specifications that reflect user goals, constraints, preferences, and evaluation criteria. Existing approaches either embed personalization into the agent pipeline or provide it via the input specification. The authors argue that refining the user request into a personalized specification before passing it to an unchanged deep research agent is underexplored, particularly the challenge of deciding what contextual information to elicit and how to obtain it efficiently.

Method: G-STEER models framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories covering diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions. The policy decides among three coupled actions: (1) which framing factors are relevant, (2) whether available user context sufficiently supports them, and (3) whether to retrieve from user memory, ask the user directly, or stop and refine the query. The policy optimizes a trade-off between target coverage and evidence acquisition costs.

Result: G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across two evaluated deep research agents (DRAs), while asking roughly one-third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

Conclusion: Learning a clarification policy over an Intent Elicitation Graph enables efficient and effective personalization of research specifications, yielding better personalized reports with significantly fewer user interactions compared to clarification-based baselines.

Abstract: User requests serve as research specifications for deep research agents, shaping what evidence to seek and how to synthesize it. In personalized deep research, these specifications must additionally reflect user goals, constraints, preferences, and evaluation criteria. User context can be incorporated either within the deep research pipeline or into the research specification provided as its input. We focus on the latter, refining the user request into a personalized research specification before passing it to an unchanged deep research agent. This requires resolving three coupled decisions: which framing factors are relevant, whether the available user context sufficiently supports them, and whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine the query. For training, G-STEER organizes framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories spanning diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions. The policy produces a refined query while balancing target coverage against the costs of evidence acquisition. Experiments show that G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across both evaluated DRAs, while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

</details>


### [122] [AppDeltaWorld: Transition-Grounded Delta Code World Model for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05891)
*Weikai Xu,Yunren Feng,Haoxiang Lei,Kun Huang,Yuxuan Liu,Kang Zhao,Xiaolin Hu,Shuo Shang,Bo An*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AppDeltaWorld is a world model for mobile GUI agents that predicts next-screen states as executable HTML code updates (deltas), constrained by action-transition logic. It retrieves app-specific HTML references, generates updated HTML conditioned on the current screen and action, and renders via browser. This approach achieves state-of-the-art fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 and enables filtered SFT data construction and test-time RL, yielding SOTA results on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym/MobileWorld.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real mobile interaction trajectories are hard to obtain for sensitive apps due to privacy concerns. Existing simulated environments are expensive to scale, and current GUI world models suffer from unstable generation, limited modality coverage, and inconsistent action-transition logic. A better world model is needed for training and improving long-horizon mobile interaction policies.

Method: AppDeltaWorld uses a transition-grounded delta code approach: (1) retrieves app-specific Level-1 HTML references under action-transition constraints, (2) generates Level-2 executable HTML conditioned on the current screen, action, predicted next-screen text, and retrieved structure, (3) inserts generated visual assets into image slots, and (4) renders the result via browser. This replaces unconstrained image/text generation with constrained, reachable code updates. The model is used for filtered closed-loop SFT data construction and test-time RL.

Result: AppDeltaWorld achieves highest fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 under Code2World evaluation, with clear gains in structural layout and UI element reconstruction over image-only and code-only baselines. AppDeltaAgent (trained with AppDeltaWorld-generated SFT data + public supervision) achieves SOTA on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Test-time RL further improves policy performance without additional real-app interactions.

Conclusion: A transition-grounded delta code world model that predicts executable HTML updates offers a scalable, privacy-preserving alternative for mobile GUI agent training, achieving high-fidelity simulation and enabling SOTA policy performance with the added benefit of test-time RL adaptation.

Abstract: Mobile GUI agents can operate apps through pixel perception and touch actions, making them a promising interface for collecting and improving long-horizon mobile interaction policies. However, real trajectories are difficult to obtain for sensitive apps and privacy-critical operations. At the same time, existing simulated environments are costly to scale up, and GUI world models still suffer from unstable generation, limited modality coverage, and inconsistent action-transition logic. To address these limitations, we propose AppDeltaWorld, a transition-grounded delta code world model that predicts the next GUI as a reachable code update rather than as an unconstrained image or text description. AppDeltaWorld retrieves app-specific Level-1 HTML references under an action-transition constraint, generates Level-2 executable HTML conditioned on the current screen, action, predicted next-screen text, and retrieved structure, and inserts generated visual assets into image slots before browser rendering. As a world model, AppDeltaWorld achieves the highest fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 under Code2World evaluation, with clear gains in structural layout and UI element reconstruction over image-only and code-only baselines. As a training environment, AppDeltaWorld supports filtered closed-loop SFT data construction that, when combined with public supervision, enables AppDeltaAgent to achieve state-of-the-art performance on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Moreover, world-model-based test-time reinforcement learning enables policy adaptation and shows further improvements without additional interaction with real apps.

</details>


### [123] [ECG-LENS: Lead-Aware Clinical Context Enriched ECG Report Generation and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05893)
*Akanta Das,Tasinul Islam Ahon,Ahmed Mahir Sultan Rumi,Md Mahbubur Rahman,Tausif Amim Shadly,Tanzima Hashem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ECG-LENS is an end-to-end framework for automated ECG report generation that integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on PTB-XL and MIMIC-IV-ECG datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automating ECG report generation is challenging due to the need for analyzing subtle temporal morphologies and producing coherent diagnostic reasoning in dense clinical terminology. Existing systems focus mainly on classification, and current report-generation methods produce outputs insufficient for practical clinical use.

Method: ECG-LENS uses lead-wise encoders for localized waveform morphology and a global encoder for inter-lead dependencies. Signal representations are fused with clinically enriched textual prompts to condition a GPT-2 decoder. An ECG-specific report-preprocessing strategy focuses the model on clinically meaningful findings. A new evaluation metric, F1-ECGBERT, measures agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports.

Result: ECG-LENS achieves absolute gains of 4.0% in METEOR, 6.3% in ROUGE-L, and 11.5% in F1-ECGBERT over the strongest baselines on PTB-XL (in-domain) and MIMIC-IV-ECG (cross-domain).

Conclusion: ECG-LENS advances automated ECG report generation by jointly modeling multi-lead signals with clinically grounded text generation, supported by a domain-specific evaluation metric (F1-ECGBERT), demonstrating strong performance and cross-domain generalizability.

Abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is one of the most widely used non-invasive tools for diagnosing cardiovascular disease, but transforming multi-lead ECG recordings into reliable clinical reports remains challenging. Automating ECG report generation could reduce clinicians' interpretive workload, improve diagnostic efficiency, and expand access to cardiac assessment in underserved communities. Unlike image-based report-generation tasks, ECG interpretation requires the analysis of subtle temporal morphologies, followed by coherent diagnostic reasoning expressed in dense clinical terminology. Existing systems predominantly focus on classification, while current report-generation methods often produce outputs that remain inadequate for practical clinical use. To address these challenges, we propose ECG-LENS, an end-to-end ECG report-generation framework that jointly integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation. ECG-LENS combines lead-wise encoders that preserve localized waveform morphology with a global encoder that captures inter-lead dependencies. To guide report generation, we fuse signal representations with clinically enriched textual prompts that condition a GPT-2 decoder. We further introduce an ECG-specific report-preprocessing strategy that helps the model focus on clinically meaningful findings. Finally, because lexical metrics may under- or overestimate report quality, we propose F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based, ECG-specific metric that measures agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports. In-domain experiments on PTB-XL and cross-domain evaluation on MIMIC-IV-ECG show that ECG-LENS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with absolute gains of 4.0%, 6.3%, and 11.5% in METEOR, ROUGE-L, and F1-ECGBERT, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

</details>


### [124] [GSBF: Gaussian Splatting for Environment-Aware Beamforming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05896)
*Yijie Bian,Wei Guo,Zixin Wang,Shenghui Song,Jun Zhang,Khaled B. Letaief*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GSBF uses 3D Gaussian splatting with multi-modal data to synthesize environment-aware beamformers directly from AP pose and user position, eliminating the need for instantaneous CSI and iterative optimization while outperforming exhaustive beam alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional MIMO beamforming requires accurate instantaneous CSI and iterative optimization, incurring heavy pilot overhead and computational complexity. Since radio propagation is physically governed by geometry, a persistent environment representation can bypass these limitations.

Method: The GSBF pipeline represents the environment using 3D Gaussians. It models scattering responses with reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels, performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map, aggregates this via an over-complete array-manifold dictionary, and projects to constant-modulus beamformers — synthesizing beams from AP pose and user position alone.

Result: Simulations show GSBF consistently outperforms baselines such as exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) while achieving lower latency.

Conclusion: Environment-aware beamforming via 3D Gaussian splatting effectively replaces online CSI acquisition, delivering superior performance and reduced latency in MIMO systems.

Abstract: Beamforming plays a key role in multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) communication systems. However, conventional beamforming design normally requires accurate instantaneous channel state information (CSI) and iterative optimization, which incur substantial pilot overhead and computational complexity. Recognizing that radio propagation is intrinsically governed by the physical geometry, we develop a 3D Gaussian splatting for environment-aware beamforming (GSBF) pipeline based on multi-modal data, which characterizes the environment through a persistent 3D Gaussian representation. Specifically, GSBF models the environmental scattering response with reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels and performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map. The rendered map is then aggregated through an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projected to the constant-modulus beamformers, thereby synthesizing beams directly from the access point (AP) pose and user position without online instantaneous CSI. Simulations demonstrate that GSBF consistently outperforms baselines such as exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) with lower latency.

</details>


### [125] [CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910)
*Arthur Nijdam,Paul Stankovski Wagner,Sara Ramezanian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CourseGraph automates detection of course overlap between home and abroad curricula using BERT-based semantic representations and a Random Forest classifier, validated on datasets from TU Eindhoven and Lund University.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Student mobility programs like Erasmus+ create a practical challenge: ensuring external courses do not substantially overlap with courses already in a student's home curriculum. Manual review by curriculum administrators is time-consuming and lacks scalability.

Method: CourseGraph extracts course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from webpages, encodes them semantically using a BERT-based language model to compute pairwise course similarity, then feeds these similarity features into a Random Forest classifier to predict whether a candidate course overlaps with an existing curriculum course.

Result: Experimental evaluation on two datasets — the Computer Science program at TU Eindhoven (courses with known substantial overlap) and six approved international programs from Lund University (with administrator decisions) — shows CourseGraph effectively identifies overlapping courses.

Conclusion: CourseGraph provides an effective, automated approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities, reducing the manual workload of curriculum administrators in student mobility contexts.

Abstract: Student mobility programs such as Erasmus+ enable students to take courses at other universities, broadening their academic and cultural horizons. However, this flexibility also leads to a practical challenge: ensuring that students do not take courses elsewhere that substantially overlap with courses in their home curriculum. In this work, we propose CourseGraph, a methodology that automates the evaluation of external courses based on insights obtained from the process followed by curriculum administrators when assessing courses for inclusion in a degree program. Course- Graph extracts information such as course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from the course webpage. Then, this information is represented semantically using a BERT-based language model, after which the pair-wise similarity between courses can be computed. This information is then used by a Random Forest classifier to determine whether a candidate course abroad overlaps with a course already contained in the student's curriculum. We evaluate CourseGraph using (1) the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, which contains information about courses with substantial overlap, and (2) six approved international programs from students enrolled in the Computer Science program at Lund University, including the corresponding decisions made by a curriculum administrator. The experimental results indicate that CourseGraph provides an effective approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities.

</details>


### [126] [GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05948)
*Shuai Wang,Yaxin Feng,Xuekun Jiang,Shihan Tian,Ningyu Yan,Xing Shen,Chaoyang Lyu,Hui Wang,Yunsong Zhou,Hanqing Wang,Jiangmiao Pang,Yang Xiang,Xing Gao,Chunhua Shen,Weinan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAUGE is a real-world-grounded benchmark with 22 task families for jointly evaluating physics engines and generative video world models on physical fidelity. It benchmarks 3 simulators and 6 image-to-video models, revealing no uniformly faithful simulator and exposing specific failure modes in both paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of physical fidelity in simulators and world models rely on perceptual similarity or human judgments, conducted in isolation, and fail to identify which specific physical principles or parameters are violated. There is no unified, real-world-grounded benchmark for systematically diagnosing where and how these systems deviate from true physics.

Method: The authors construct GAUGE: a diagnostic benchmark with 22 controlled task families spanning rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformables. All tasks are grounded in real-world trajectories with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables. They benchmark three physics engines (Isaac Sim, Genesis, Newton) on 14 task families using generalized trajectory errors, and evaluate 6 image-to-video generative models on 5 rigid-body tasks by testing physical-law consistency and temporal stability of inferred physical parameters.

Result: No physics engine is uniformly faithful across all tasks. The largest discrepancies occur in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. Video world models can generate trajectories matching expected equation forms but recover incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing, indicating superficial rather than physically grounded fidelity.

Conclusion: GAUGE provides a systematic foundation for diagnosing physical failures in both numerical simulators and generative world models, highlighting that current systems fail in complementary ways that perceptual metrics alone cannot capture. The benchmark lays groundwork for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence.

Abstract: Physics engines facilitate large-scale training and evaluation for embodied intelligence, while generative video world models are emerging as implicit simulators of future states and interactions. However, existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated. We introduce GAUGE, a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark for jointly evaluating how numerical simulators and generative video world models reproduce or deviate from real-world physics. It comprises 22 controlled task families covering rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects. Grounded in real-world trajectories and paired with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables, these tasks cover fundamental physical processes including collision, friction, momentum transfer, oscillation, self-contact, and deformation across diverse materials and conditions. We benchmark Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families using generalized trajectory errors, and evaluate 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks by testing physical-law consistency and the temporal stability of inferred parameters. Our results reveal no uniformly faithful physics engine, with the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. We further find that video world models can produce trajectories with the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing. GAUGE lays the groundwork for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence.

</details>


### [127] [VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05949)
*Katrin Schmid,Iuri Frosio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates using Vision Language Models (VLMs) to annotate video game frames with reward signals, revealing that VLMs struggle with basic game understanding tasks. The authors analyze factors affecting annotation quality—including input sequence length, resolution, and question batching—and propose countermeasures like output mixing and prompt optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs and AI agents have transformed engineering problem-solving, but their adoption in video games remains limited due to the high variability of synthetic scenarios and poor compliance with real-world physics. The authors aim to explore whether VLMs can reliably annotate game frame sequences with reward signals for applications such as conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning.

Method: The authors empirically evaluate VLM performance on question-answering tasks over racing video game frame sequences (with observations extended to other genres). They systematically examine how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect both annotation quality and token consumption. They propose and test two countermeasures: VLM output mixing and prompt optimization.

Result: VLMs frequently fail to answer basic questions about racing video games, exhibiting poor compliance with game-world understanding. The study quantifies how sequence length, resolution, and batching affect both annotation accuracy and token efficiency. Output mixing and prompt optimization are shown to mitigate some of these failures.

Conclusion: Current VLMs are not yet reliable for automated reward annotation in video game domains due to fundamental difficulties with synthetic scenarios. The proposed countermeasures offer partial remedies, but significant challenges remain before VLMs can be practically deployed for game-based reinforcement learning applications.

Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have revolutionized how engineers approach complex problems in real-world applications. Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics. Here we investigate the use of VLMs for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals, a task with several potential applications including, among others, conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning. We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

</details>


### [128] [Training a Conditioned Video Game Agent on a VLM Annotated Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05954)
*Katrin Schmid,Iuri Frosio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes using Vision Language Models to annotate video game datasets with human-defined rewards, enabling offline RL to train conditioned agents that respond to desired returns, while discussing early limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL for video games requires engine access for reward collection, involves tedious trial-and-error reward engineering, and suffers from sparse rewards that are difficult to interpret. The authors seek to simplify this pipeline by leveraging VLMs for automatic reward annotation.

Method: A Vision Language Model is instructed to extract human-defined rewards from video game footage, producing annotated datasets. Offline RL is then applied to train a return-conditioned agent that can modulate its behavior based on desired return values, without requiring direct environment interaction.

Result: The approach enables offline RL training using VLM-annotated rewards. However, early experiments revealed difficulties and limitations, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: VLM-based reward annotation combined with offline RL shows promise for simplifying video game policy learning, but challenges remain that warrant further investigation.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful but far from easy-to-use technique for policy learning. In the specific case of video games, access to the game engine is required to get rewards for training (e.g. to collect rewards from the environment). Furthermore, the proper identification and weighting of the rewards generally requires a difficult trial-and-error approach. Lastly, rewards are often sparse and understanding how they eventually affect the learned policy is a non-trivial exercise. To ease these issues we propose annotating a video game dataset with Vision Language Models (VLMs) instructed to extract human defined rewards. We show that offline RL can then be used to train a conditioned agent that responds accordingly to the desired returns and we discuss the difficulties and limitations that emerged in our early experiments.

</details>


### [129] [Stability of Ranking-dependent Pair-wise Comparison Patterns in the Analytic Hierarchy Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05958)
*Vitaliy Tsyganok,Sergii Kadenko,Oleh Andriichuk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper compares three pairwise comparison methods (Best-Worst, Top 2, and Maximum Difference) used in AHP, evaluating their stability to expert errors to identify the most reliable incomplete ranking-dependent pattern that reduces comparisons without sacrificing credibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expert elicitation in multi-criteria decision analysis is cognitively burdensome when many pairwise comparisons are required. Ordinal ranking information can reduce the number of comparisons needed, but it is unclear which incomplete comparison pattern offers the best stability against expert judgment errors.

Method: The authors compare three pairwise comparison patterns: (1) Best-Worst method, (2) Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and (3) the original Maximum Difference method. They analytically determine conditions under which these methods can be compared for error stability, and conduct simulation experiments to empirically evaluate their relative performance.

Result: The study identifies the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pairwise comparison pattern among the three examined. The findings demonstrate that it is possible to substantially reduce the number of required comparisons without compromising the credibility of expert session outcomes.

Conclusion: The research advances algorithmic, cognitive, and applied dimensions of decision support under uncertainty by establishing which incomplete comparison method best balances efficiency (fewer comparisons) with robustness to expert errors.

Abstract: The paper addresses several ranking-dependent decision support methods. Ordinal information on compared objects can be used to improve the quality of expert data during estimation and help reduce the number of comparisons that the experts need to perform. In the paper we compare three incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison patterns which can be used in the Analytic Hierarchy Process - Best-worst method, Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and the original maximum difference method. The first two comparison patterns (and respective methods) are incomplete, while the third can be a complete one. We determine conditions under which these three methods can be compared in terms of stability to expert errors. We also present the results of a simulation-type experiment, in which the three methods are compared. The research allows us to define the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison pattern and reduce the number of comparisons without loss of credibility of expert session results. The research contributes to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments.

</details>


### [130] [Temporal Bridges for Spatial Resolution: Enhancing Climate Data Super-Resolution with Bidirectional Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05981)
*Yichen Zhang,Yixiong Xiao,Congxi Xiao,Jingbo Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment for climate data super-resolution, addressing the neglect of temporal correlations and the ineffectiveness of optical flow methods on stochastic climate data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning methods for climate data super-resolution rely solely on single-frame spatial information, ignoring temporal correlations across frames. Standard temporal alignment techniques like optical flow fail on climate data due to its inherent stochasticity and noise.

Method: A three-component Temporal-Enhanced framework: (1) Paired Latent Mapping unifies latent spaces for spatial alignment and noise reduction; (2) Bidirectional Temporal Alignment captures temporal correlations via forward and backward networks trained on consecutive latent frames; (3) Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution jointly optimizes the entire framework for final SR output.

Result: Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrate superior performance compared to existing approaches.

Conclusion: The proposed bidirectional temporal alignment framework effectively bridges temporal information to enhance spatial resolution in climate data SR, overcoming limitations of prior single-frame methods.

Abstract: High-resolution climate data is crucial for meteorological predictions and for informing decision support across diverse domains. However, the acquisition of such high-resolution climate information is often prohibitively costly, necessitating the development of data-driven meteorological prediction models. These models aim to generate fine-grained climate data from low-resolution inputs, a process termed climate data super-resolution (SR). Nevertheless, recent advancements in deep learning for climate data SR have primarily focused on leveraging single-frame spatial information, largely neglecting the temporal correlations between different time frames that could enhance SR outcomes. Furthermore, climate data are inherently stochastic and noisy, rendering widely used temporal alignment methods, such as optical flow models, ineffective in this context. Consequently, the development of a framework tailored for climate data SR that effectively captures implicit temporal correlations remains an unresolved challenge. To this end, we propose a novel Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment. In essence, our framework establishes a temporal bridge to enhance spatial resolution in climate data SR through bidirectional alignment, leading to improved SR performance. Within this framework, Paired Latent Mapping achieves spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces. Then a Bidirectional Temporal Alignment captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames. Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution then optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated the superior performance of our framework.

</details>


### [131] [AgentOPSD: Recursive Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05987)
*Zi-Han Wang,Zhengxi Lu,Zhiyuan Yao,Jinyang Wu,Jie Wu,Zhengzhou Cai,Yueqing Sun,Ziang Ye,Linji Hao,Qi Gu,Xunliang Cai,Yongliang Shen,Yujiu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentOPSD is a critic-free, recursive Bayesian method that converts sparse trajectory-level rewards into turn-level credit signals for agentic RL, outperforming GRPO and self-distillation baselines on multi-turn benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL with verifiable rewards uses trajectory-level advantage estimates, which fail to properly credit the few pivotal decisions in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. While privileged self-distillation offers denser supervision, it lacks a principled mechanism for representing sequential credit across turns.

Method: AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This produces a reweighting scheme that transforms sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals, with pivotal turns identified via marginal belief revisions between consecutive states. The method is critic-free, requires no extra rollouts, and integrates with standard policy optimization.

Result: AgentOPSD achieves 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B, outperforming GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at 3B and 7B scales. Ablations confirm gains stem from turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

Conclusion: AgentOPSD provides a principled, lightweight approach to turn-level credit assignment in agentic RL, effectively bridging sparse outcome signals and fine-grained decision attribution without additional model components or rollouts.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards constructs trajectory-level advantage estimates, yet it often fails to credit the few pivotal decisions that determine outcomes in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. Recent work introduces privileged self-distillation for credit assignment, providing denser supervision, but it remains unclear how such local signals should represent sequential credit. We propose AgentOPSD, a critic-free, recursive method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning. AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This yields a principled reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals and identifies pivotal turns through the marginal belief revision between consecutive states. The method is fully compatible with standard policy optimization and requires neither an additional critic nor extra rollouts. We evaluate AgentOPSD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at two scales (3B and 7B). AgentOPSD outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies attribute the gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

</details>


### [132] [OPERA: Operator-residual feedback for reliable autonomous optical experiments with language-model agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05990)
*Ning Xu,Xiang Zheng,Fuqiang Zhong,Huadong Wang,Xiaolong Wu,Zhiyuan Liu,Hui Ning*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPERA is an operator-residual framework for autonomous optical experiments that uses physically interpretable feedback (operators representing actions, residuals measuring departures from physical conditions) instead of abstract scores, reducing non-physical "score-hacking" from 23.6–39.0% to 0.9–1.9% across three tasks and improving experimental efficiency when transferred to real instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents in experimental settings typically rely on abstract scores to select actions, but these scores may not correlate with genuine physical improvement—agents can "hack" the scoring function without achieving better experimental outcomes. A feedback mechanism grounded in physical interpretability is needed to ensure autonomous decisions correspond to measurable physical progress.

Method: The authors propose OPERA, a framework where experimental actions are represented as optical operators (executable changes to measurement, control, or reconstruction) and outcomes are evaluated via physically interpretable residuals (departures from specified physical conditions). The agent selects, combines, or generates operators based on operator-residual feedback. Physical performance is independently validated against a withheld reference. The framework was tested in digital twins across three optical tasks and then transferred to three physical optical instruments for real-world validation.

Result: Score-only feedback produced score increases without corresponding physical improvement in 23.6–39.0% of decisions, whereas operator-residual feedback reduced this to only 0.9–1.9%. OPERA increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets while reducing experimental budgets. Protocols selected in digital twins successfully transferred to three optical instruments, with repeated experiments demonstrating a lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction.

Conclusion: Operators and residuals together provide a physically grounded decision-making framework that guides autonomous agents using measurable physical evidence rather than abstract scores, yielding more reliable, efficient, and transferable experimental protocols.

Abstract: Autonomous agents choose actions using scores that may not reflect experimental success. We developed OPERA, an operator-residual framework for optical experiments. It represents experimental actions as optical operators and evaluates their outcomes using physically interpretable residuals. Operators specify executable changes to measurement, control or reconstruction, while residuals report departures from specified physical conditions. The agent uses both to select, combine or generate operators, and physical performance is evaluated independently against a withheld reference. Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback produced score increases without physical improvement in 23.6--39.0\% of decisions, compared with 0.9--1.9\% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. Protocols selected in digital twins were transferred to three optical instruments, and repeated experiments showed a lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction. Together, operators and residuals guide autonomous decisions using measurable physical evidence.

</details>


### [133] [Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Herd-Level Cattle Growth Pattern and Weight Gain Forecasting in Grazing-Based Production Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06001)
*Muhammad Riaz Hasib Hossain,Rafiqul Islam,Shawn R. McGrath,Md Zahidul Islam,David W. Lamb*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hybrid machine learning framework for cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing data was developed. The cascade GB→RF→NN architecture achieved the best performance (R²=0.889, RMSE=21.319 kg), outperforming ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU baselines, with age, rainfall, and temperature as key predictors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial grazing systems produce irregular livestock observations, making cattle growth forecasting challenging. Reliable weight prediction is needed to support feed allocation, grazing management, and marketing decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.

Method: The study integrated weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors (2022–2024, southeastern Australia) into structured forecasting datasets. Herd-level trajectories were generated via temporal aggregation of animal-level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families (residual, stacked, cascade, ensemble-assisted) were evaluated against ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU baselines across multiple forecasting horizons.

Result: The cascade GB→RF→NN architecture achieved the best performance: test R² of 0.889, RMSE of 21.319 kg, and MAE of 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures showed greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively with extended prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors.

Conclusion: The proposed hybrid ML framework delivers accurate herd-level cattle weight forecasts under irregular sensing conditions, outperforming conventional sequential models. It offers practical value for feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions.

Abstract: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular livestock observations, which challenge cattle growth forecasting. This study developed a hybrid machine learning framework for herd level cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing observations collected between 2022 and 2024 in southeastern Australia. Weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were integrated into structured forecasting datasets. Herd level forecasting trajectories were generated through temporal aggregation of animal level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families were evaluated, including residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble assisted frameworks. ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU models were used as comparative baselines. Independent testing demonstrated strong predictive agreement across multiple forecasting horizons. The cascade GB to RF to NN architecture achieved the best performance, with a test R^2 of 0.889, RMSE of 21.319 kg, and MAE of 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures maintained greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively across extended prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors influencing herd level growth forecasting. The proposed framework may support feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.

</details>


### [134] [HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06012)
*Zhuowen Liu,Bohan Cui,YinShang Guo,Yuting Wang,Hao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HERALD is an offline audit framework that detects vulnerabilities in search-agent reward functions by applying exact same-question interventions. It identifies a citation-laundering attack that bypasses existing defenses, and isolates an inclusion-minimal repair (R[L]) that eliminates the attack while preserving model performance across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current search-agent reward functions conflate multiple signals (answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, anti-hacking), making high scores unreliable indicators of faithful evidence retrieval. Existing penalties can be circumvented, and there is no systematic method to audit reward robustness before policy optimization.

Method: HERALD performs offline audits using exact same-question interventions, separating candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerating detector contracts prior to RL. The authors test on three QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue) using Qwen3-8B pools. A 2^3 ablation identifies vulnerability to citation laundering—citing a corpus passage absent from retrieved evidence. The repair R[L] (targeted strengthening of L) is evaluated under strict 5M-token matched training with 256 paired questions per benchmark.

Result: Base reward R0 rejects search deletion and fake IDs but fails against label-free citation-laundering. R[L] achieves 0% empirical ASR with 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models. R[L] meets EM non-inferiority on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Citation precision improves by 2.02 points, support recall by 1.46, unsupported citations drop by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural L is not reduced; the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories.

Conclusion: HERALD demonstrates that robust scoring, sparse learning signals, and policy transfer can be cleanly separated. The minimal repair R[L] provides a principled defense against citation laundering without degrading natural model behavior, suggesting that targeted reward hardening is both feasible and sample-efficient.

Abstract: Search-agent rewards mix answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, and anti-hacking terms; a high score therefore need not imply that cited evidence was retrieved, and added penalties can cancel. We introduce HERALD, an offline audit that applies exact same-question interventions, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization. On four Qwen3-8B pools from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, $R_0$ rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds. A complete $2^3$ ablation identifies targeted strengthening of $L$---citing a corpus passage absent from the retrieved evidence---as the observed inclusion-minimal repair: $R[L]$ has zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models; broader hardening remains vulnerable when the attack removes an oracle support-ID penalty. Under strict 5M-token matched training evaluated on 256 paired questions per benchmark, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve by 2.02 and 1.46 points, unsupported citations fall by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced, and the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories. HERALD thus separates robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

</details>


### [135] [From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06020)
*Jiale Han,Xiang Li,Jing Qian,Wenyuan Gu,Pin Gao,Ye Luo,Hongyuan Zha,Dacheng Tao,Benyou Wang,Lin William Cong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a six-level capability ladder for building Economic World Models (EWMs) — generative simulations where heterogeneous agents, institutions, and markets co-evolve — and surveys existing work, finding most research stuck at lower levels while higher-level systems (self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, sim-to-real alignment) remain rare.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current economic simulations lack integration across agent adaptivity, institutional evolution, and empirical alignment. There is no unified roadmap for building high-fidelity EWMs that can serve as sandboxes for human decision-makers and AI training/evaluation.

Method: The authors define EWMs as inside-out generative economic models and organize them into a six-level capability ladder: (1) fixed rule-based agents, (2) adaptive agents, (3) LLM-based agents, (4) self-evolving agents, (5) evolving institutional worlds, and (6) sim-to-real economic twins. They conduct a systematic literature survey mapping existing work to these levels.

Result: Existing research is concentrated at lower levels (rules-based and adaptive agents), while systems featuring self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare and underdeveloped.

Conclusion: The EWM roadmap provides an implementation blueprint to accelerate next-generation economic simulators. The authors release a curated paper list and resources to catalyze future research toward high-fidelity, empirically grounded economic world models.

Abstract: Economic World Models (EWMs) are generative economic models that simulate how economies evolve from within by modeling heterogeneous agents, their beliefs and actions, and the market and institutional mechanisms through which their interactions produce aggregate outcomes. This paper develops an implementation roadmap for building economic world models as generative engines in which heterogeneous agents act, interact, adapt, and co-evolve with markets and institutions, thereby producing economic dynamics from the inside. We organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds to adaptive and LLM-based agent worlds, self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey across these levels reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. By translating the EWM agenda into an implementation blueprint, this paper aims to accelerate the development of the next generation of economic simulation environments that can serve as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents. We release a curated paper list and related resources to support future research.

</details>
