### [136] [Integrating Implicit and Explicit Relational Biases through Graph-Based Multiple Instance Learning: A Case Study in Skin Lesion Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06037)
*Rafał Buler,Jakub Buler,Maciej Bobowicz,Michał Grochowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a dual-level relational framework that combines implicit inter-patch relationship learning via a convolutional masked autoencoder with explicit graph-based message passing (using grid, random, and k-NN topologies). Applied to skin lesion classification on ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019, the combined approach improves balanced accuracy over the EfficientNetB3 baseline — e.g., from 76.17% to 79.27% on ISIC-2018.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard CNNs rely on local convolutional inductive biases, which limit their ability to capture long-range structural dependencies among image patches. The authors aim to bridge the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural/relational modeling to better exploit inter-patch relationships for image classification.

Method: A dual-level framework: (1) Implicit level — a convolutional masked autoencoder (MAE) operating on image patches learns inter-patch relationships via self-supervised reconstruction, initialized with an EfficientNetB3 backbone. (2) Explicit level — learned patch embeddings are organized into graph topologies (grid-based, random, k-nearest neighbour) and processed through a Graph Attention Network (GAT) for message passing. The two levels are combined for final classification. Evaluated on ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion datasets.

Result: On ISIC-2018: Baseline EfficientNetB3 achieves 76.17% balanced accuracy; adding implicit patch-based relational modeling improves to 77.12%; the full grid-structured GAT reaches 79.27%. On ISIC-2019: implicit-only achieves 59.84%, while the combined implicit+explicit model yields 60.67% balanced accuracy.

Conclusion: Combining implicit inter-patch relational learning with explicit graph-based message passing yields superior performance over either approach alone or the CNN baseline. Grid-structured graph topologies prove particularly effective, and the dual-level relational framework demonstrates consistent gains across both skin lesion benchmarks.

Abstract: Relational inductive biases are essential for capturing structural dependencies among data. This study investigates a dual-level relational framework for image classification, bridging the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling. We begin by establishing a baseline using an EfficientNetB3 architecture. To move beyond standard convolutional biases, we adopt a patch-based strategy, employing a convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relationships through self-supervised reconstruction. We then extend this approach by incorporating explicit relational modelling, organizing the learned embeddings into various graph topologies, including grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbour structures. Experimental results on the ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks show that combining implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based message passing yields the best performance. On the ISIC-2018 test set, the baseline model achieves a balanced accuracy of 76.17%, which improves to 77.12% with implicit patch-based relational modelling. The fully integrated grid-structured Graph Attention Network further increases performance to 79.27%. Similarly, on ISIC-2019, the implicit approach reaches 59.84% balanced accuracy, while the combination of implicit and explicit modelling yields 60.67%.

</details>


### [137] [When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06057)
*Xiaoqing Wu,Xingyu Fan,Feifei Li,Wenhui Que*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Historical tool-calling traces can become outdated yet remain structurally valid, causing models to make incorrect decisions by reusing stale entities or conventions. The authors introduce a paired benchmark to isolate these failures and propose a teacher-student distillation method that transfers oracle-conditioned policy to a student observing only polluted history, achieving significant accuracy gains and demonstrating scalability and cross-domain transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In persistent tool-use interactions, accumulated dialogue and tool traces may remain structurally well-formed and semantically plausible even after they are no longer authoritative for the current request. This "history pollution" can mislead tool-calling agents into reusing corrupted entities, stale interface conventions, or outdated decision logic — a distinct failure mode not addressed by existing benchmarks or training methods.

Method: The authors first construct a paired benchmark with three synchronized views per example: Original (clean), Polluted (with outdated history), and Oracle State (ground-truth context). Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures across decision state, entity binding, and interface execution. They then propose a teacher-student transfer method: an Oracle-conditioned teacher (with access to clean state) provides soft supervision over prefixes generated by a student that only observes polluted history. This is compared against baselines including Gold-SFT, Oracle sequence distillation, and off-policy token distillation.

Result: On Qwen3-1.7B, history pollution flips 32.1% of previously correct decisions. The proposed method achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). Scaling from a 1.7B to an 8B teacher raises the 1.7B student to 91.9%; an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The policies also transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop QA.

Conclusion: History reliability is a distinct and critical bottleneck in tool-use systems. The proposed reliable-state policy transfer method effectively mitigates this vulnerability in a scalable, transferable manner, establishing a new paradigm for training agents robust to stale or misleading interaction histories.

Abstract: Tool-calling agents infer task state from accumulated dialogue and tool traces. In persistent interactions, however, historical traces may remain structurally valid and semantically plausible after they cease to be authoritative for the current request. We show that such history can hijack a policy the model already possesses: on Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of decisions that are correct under the original trajectory and frequently induces reuse of corrupted entities or interface conventions. We introduce bench, a paired benchmark with synchronized Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views that preserve the system policy, current tools, latest request, and gold next action. Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures in decision state, entity binding, and interface execution across complete calls and non-call decisions. We further propose ours, which transfers an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy to a student observing only polluted history through soft supervision on student-generated prefixes. On Qwen3-1.7B, ours achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). The method scales consistently: an 8B teacher raises the same compact 1.7B student to 91.9%, while an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The resulting policies further transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, independently regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop question answering. These results establish history reliability as a distinct tool-use bottleneck and demonstrate reliable-state policy transfer as an effective and scalable solution.

</details>


### [138] [Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06085)
*Yifan Lyu,Xinran Li,Jiaqi Qiao,Xiujuan Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Disclosing that a country label was assigned at random does not reliably reduce its influence on LLM forecasts, even though verified (genuine) country metadata consistently improves forecast accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can exploit survey-country metadata to improve individual response prediction, but they may also be redirected by the same cue when assigned arbitrarily. This creates a risk of spurious reliance on non-informative metadata. The study investigates whether simply disclosing the random, record-independent origin of a label can attenuate this undesired uptake.

Method: A within-record audit design across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. The primary panel comprises 72 post-review records. Each record receives both opaque and disclosed-random country labels, with independent population anchors and recorded human answers serving as ground truth. Key metrics: (1) country-direction shift magnitude, (2) paired attenuation between opaque and disclosed conditions, (3) change in held-out Brier loss for verified vs. random labels. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel replicates the design.

Result: Both opaque and disclosed-random labels produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was negligible at 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]), confirming no reliable reduction. Verified country metadata reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), a significant improvement. Random-label regret (the cost of using random labels) included zero. The consistency panel replicated positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. Disclosure thus does not reliably counteract spurious metadata uptake, even though verified metadata is robustly useful.

Conclusion: Verified survey-country metadata is useful for improving LLM forecast accuracy, but disclosing a label's random origin does not reliably prevent models from being influenced by it. This suggests transparency alone is insufficient to debias LLM reliance on spurious cues; alternative mitigation strategies are needed. The PROV-FORECAST dataset provides 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions for further research.

Abstract: Survey-country metadata can improve an LLM's forecast of an individual response when informative, yet the same cue may redirect the forecast when assigned at random. A within-record audit tests whether disclosing a random label's uniform, record-independent origin reduces its country-directed uptake, and whether verified survey country lowers held-out Brier loss. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers measure direction and consequence across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. In the primary post-review 72-record panel, opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. On the selected targets, verified metadata was useful in both panels, but disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake. PROV-FORECAST contains 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

</details>


### [139] [Evaluating Investment Logic in Large Language Models: A Real-World Benchmark Towards Personalzied Financial Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06108)
*Yuanhong Jiang,Jingjie Zou,Zhenghong Lin,Xusheng Yu,Qiqi Huang,Shuai Jia,Shijie Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InvestLogicBench introduces a process-native benchmark with 201K+ real investor decisions, evaluated via a P→E→R→D→O trace (Profile, Events, Reasoning, Decision, Outcome). It reveals that LLMs produce polished but weakly grounded reasoning, which terminal profit/loss evaluation alone conceals, and argues for a data-system interface standard for personalized, consequential agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investment competence is inherently personalized—different investors warrant different actions from the same evidence. Existing financial LLM evaluation methods are flawed: static QA omits investor agency, while terminal P&L cannot distinguish grounded, profile-consistent decisions from luck. The authors argue the community is using the wrong evaluation paradigm for consequential, personalized agents.

Method: The authors construct InvestLogicBench, comprising 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode is structured as a P→E→R→D→O trace: investor Profile → observable market Events → investment Reasoning → executable Decision → delayed Outcome. The benchmark includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, and post-mortems. It supports three evaluation modes: comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Four leading LLMs are evaluated on logical plausibility and event grounding.

Result: Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility scores are near 4/5, while event grounding scores are only 0.8–2.8/5. Return-based metrics and process quality metrics disagree, exposing polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides.

Conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation is insufficient for personalized financial agents. P→E→R→D→O should serve as a data-system interface standard, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance serves as a stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential AI agents.

Abstract: Investment competence is inherently personalized: the same market evidence can justify different actions for investors with different goals, horizons, portfolios, and risk boundaries. Yet financial LLMs are evaluated either by static question answering or by terminal profit and loss. The former omits agency; the latter cannot reveal whether a profitable action was grounded, profile-consistent, or merely lucky. We ask whether the community is using the wrong ruler for consequential agents.
  We introduce \textsc{InvestLogicBench}, a process-native benchmark containing 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode instantiates a \textbf{P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O} trace: investor \textit{Profile}, observable market \textit{Events}, investment \textit{Reasoning}, executable \textit{Decision}, and delayed \textit{Outcome}. The release includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, and post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility remains near 4/5 while event grounding is only 0.8--2.8/5; return and process quality also disagree. These results expose polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides. We further argue that P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O should be a data-system interface, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance is our stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential agents.

</details>


### [140] [ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06110)
*Abdulkadir Külçe,Alihan Esen,Cağla Fikir,Berke Kurt,Kuzey Arar,Gökhan Ercan,Faik Boray Tek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ECHO is a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for chronic care management, combining an agentic chatbot with temporal knowledge graph memory (94.9% tool-execution pass rate), a hybrid safety layer with a signed GNN (88.8% accuracy), and a multimodal speech assessment module (macro F1 0.652), all running on consumer hardware with full data privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term chronic care management requires persistent, context-aware conversational support with robust safety guarantees, yet existing solutions often rely on cloud services, lack cross-session memory, and have inadequate clinical safety filtering — motivating a fully local, privacy-compliant integrated system.

Method: ECHO integrates three modules: (1) an agentic chatbot using a LangGraph-orchestrated ReAct loop with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent memory, (2) a two-stage hybrid safety layer combining a rule-based filter (<1ms) for explicit crises/jailbreaks and a signed GNN with APPNP-style propagation for boundary-case classification, and (3) a multimodal speech assessment module using Whisper + BERT with cross-attention fusion for emotion, depression, and pain estimation. The system runs as a local web app with no external data transmission.

Result: The agentic chatbot achieves a 94.9% tool-execution pass rate on a 59-scenario benchmark (GPT-5 Mini). The safety GNN attains 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query Turkish health dataset, outperforming zero-shot Llama 3.3 70B. The multimodal speech module reaches a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system operates entirely on consumer hardware.

Conclusion: ECHO demonstrates that a capable, safe, and privacy-preserving conversational health assistant can be deployed entirely locally on consumer hardware, meeting GDPR/KVKK compliance requirements while delivering competitive performance across clinical tool use, safety filtering, and multimodal assessment.

Abstract: This paper presents ECHO (Enhanced Care \& Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. ECHO integrates three complementary software modules developed under shared supervision as a unified system. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; it achieves a 94.9\% tool-execution pass rate across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini. A two-stage hybrid safety layer intercepts all incoming queries: a rule-based layer handles explicit crisis signals and jailbreak attempts in under 1ms, while a signed graph neural network (GNN) with APPNP-style propagation classifies boundary cases by clinical intent, achieving 88.8\% accuracy and 90.6\% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query annotated Turkish health dataset while outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. A multimodal speech assessment module combining Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion estimates emotion, depression, and pain, reaching a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system is implemented as a web application that can run entirely on consumer hardware, with no patient data transmitted to external services, supporting compliance with GDPR and KVKK.

</details>


### [141] [Mind the Gaps: Mixture-of-Minds for Human Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06115)
*Pranav Dahiya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Anacreon is an audience simulation model that achieves state-of-the-art individual-level prediction accuracy (0.775 ordinal alignment) on survey responses by learning per-cluster adapters on a Gemma 12B base, using authorship embeddings, chain-of-emotion augmentation, and debiasing techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Statistical methods and LLM simulators capture population-level central tendencies but fail at individual-level heterogeneity, introduce social biases, and suffer from prompt brittleness. There is a need for faithful individual-level simulation within narrow domains.

Method: Anacreon learns authorship embeddings to separate individuals, clusters a qualitative corpus around seed people, and trains a dedicated LoRA adapter per cluster ("mixture of minds") on a Gemma 4 12B base. It harvests demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, augments records with chain-of-emotion, shuffles response options to reduce prompt brittleness, and balances the training distribution to mitigate positive bias.

Result: On a large externally sourced survey, Anacreon achieves state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775 with small residual bias.

Conclusion: The work represents progress toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals, bridging the gap between population-level and individual-level prediction.

Abstract: Predicting how a population will answer a new question is a long-standing goal. Statistical methods succeed at the level of the mass but falter at the level of the individual. Large language model simulators inherit this gap. They recover a population's central tendencies while flattening its heterogeneity, and they carry social biases and prompt brittleness that distort individual predictions. This paper introduces Anacreon, an audience simulation model that targets the individual level within a narrow, well-specified domain. Anacreon learns an authorship embedding that separates individuals, clusters a real qualitative corpus around seed people, and trains a dedicated adapter for each cluster, a mixture of minds, on a Gemma~4 12B base. It harvests demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, and augments each record with a chain-of-emotion. It reduces prompt brittleness by shuffling response options and reduces positive bias by balancing the training distribution. On a large, externally sourced survey, Anacreon reaches a state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775, the individual-level accuracy measure on which the field has converged, with a small residual bias. The work is a step toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals.

</details>


### [142] [Poli-Bias: Understanding and Measuring Large Language Model Biases in International Political Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06123)
*Massi-Nissa Abboud,Aladin Djuhera,Elena Cabrio,Holger Boche*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Poli-Bias is a counterfactual framework that measures political bias in LLMs by swapping country identities in legally equivalent conflict scenarios and analyzing response disparities across five interpretable dimensions, revealing systematic unequal treatment across 13 models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Measuring political bias in LLMs is difficult because bias manifests through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning rather than overt judgments. Existing single-metric approaches fail to capture these nuanced disparities, motivating a multidimensional, counterfactual framework.

Method: Poli-Bias uses paired prompts where country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than a single bias score, the framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, enabling fine-grained analysis of how and where unequal treatment occurs.

Result: Across 13 contemporary LLMs of varying families and sizes, country identities and user affiliations systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law.

Conclusion: Poli-Bias provides a fine-grained auditing framework for assessing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs, moving beyond simplistic bias metrics to reveal multidimensional patterns of unequal treatment.

Abstract: Measuring political bias in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as it can manifest through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that are difficult to capture with a single metric. In this work, we introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework for measuring whether LLMs treat legally equivalent conflict scenarios differently depending on the countries involved. Poli-Bias compares responses to paired prompts in which country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than reducing bias to a single judgment, our framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, revealing how and where unequal treatment manifests. Across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes, we find that country identities and user affiliations can systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Our results thus establish Poli-Bias as a fine-grained framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs.

</details>


### [143] [Contextual Information Policy Optimization for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06128)
*Xingyu Guo,Wei Chen,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CIPO is an evidence-oriented RL framework that assigns turn-level credit to reasoning actions grounded in retrieved evidence, reducing prior-driven reasoning (confirmation bias) in search agents without needing human annotations or reward models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL for search agents rewards only final-answer correctness or intermediate progress, failing to assess whether post-retrieval actions are grounded in retrieved evidence. This misalignment promotes prior-driven reasoning — agents use retrieval mainly to confirm internal beliefs rather than inform reasoning, causing confirmation bias and inefficient evidence use.

Method: CIPO (Contextual Information Policy Optimization) introduces dense, turn-level credit assigned to reasoning actions that are influenced by retrieved information. This evidence-use signal is combined with a global outcome reward to preserve answer correctness. The framework explicitly aligns policy optimization with external evidence use, discouraging evidence-detached guesses and promoting trajectories where retrieved facts guide or revise subsequent reasoning.

Result: Extensive experiments on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CIPO reduces the prevalence of prior-driven reasoning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.

Conclusion: CIPO effectively addresses the evidence-grounding gap in search agent training by providing turn-level credit for evidence-informed reasoning, yielding more reliable and evidence-grounded multi-step reasoning without requiring costly human process supervision.

Abstract: Search agents extend large language models beyond static parametric memory by enabling them to acquire and use ex ternal evidence during multi-step reasoning. For knowledge intensive tasks involving complex or evolving information, their reliability depends not only on retrieving relevant ev idence but also on using it to guide subsequent reasoning. However, existing methods primarily reward final-answer cor rectness or intermediate progress, without directly assessing whether post-retrieval actions are grounded in the retrieved evidence. This misalignment encourages prior-driven reason ing: agents form conclusions based on internal knowledge and use retrieval mainly to confirm them, resulting in confirma tion bias and inefficient evidenceuse.Toaddressthisissue, we propose Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO), an evidence-oriented reinforcement learning framework that explicitly aligns policy optimization with external evidence use. CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning ac tions influenced by retrieved information, while combining this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward to pre serveanswercorrectness.Withthismanner,CIPOdiscourages evidence-detached guesses and promotes reasoning trajecto ries in which retrieved facts can guide or revise subsequent reasoning. Importantly, CIPO requires neither human process annotations nor an additional reward model. Extensive exper iments on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show that CIPO reduces the prevalence of prior-driven rea soning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.

</details>


### [144] [FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06144)
*Bo Deng,Kang Zhou,Lifan Guo,Chongyang Tao,Xuanren Chen,Chenggang Xie,Renzhao Liang,Feng Chen,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FinEvo-Bench is a longitudinal benchmark for evaluating AI agents' self-evolution in professional financial workflows. Using 120 tasks across 6 financial domains with 20 business scenes (each containing 6 related cases), it measures how agents improve from prior experience. Testing four self-evolving scaffolds with Qwen3.7-Max, Letta achieved the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues, while Codex showed the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Rubric feedback outperformed reference-answer feedback across all scaffolds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and fail to measure cross-task learning (self-evolution). Current self-evolution benchmarks also lack joint coverage of professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a benchmark that assesses both professional task performance and an agent's ability to improve from accumulated experience.

Method: FinEvo-Bench comprises 120 real-case-grounded tasks organized into 20 business scenes across 6 financial domains. Each scene contains 6 related but distinct cases sharing a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric covering task quality and financial compliance. Institutional procedures and publicly documented cases ensure realism. Four self-evolving agent scaffolds (Letta, Codex, and two others) were compared using Qwen3.7-Max as the backbone, processing three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimated self-evolution gains. An independent Claude Code scoring agent (backed by Claude Opus 4.6) evaluated all outputs. The study also compared skill-only, memory-only, and combined memory-skill evolution, as well as rubric versus reference-answer feedback.

Result: Letta achieved the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task). Codex showed the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37 points). Across all scaffolds, the evolving condition raised scores by 9.33–19.37 points and reduced compliance issues by 0.12–0.44 per task. Within-scene rank analysis showed that paired score gains at ranks 4–6 exceeded those at ranks 1–3 by 6.10–8.70 points, demonstrating cumulative learning. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution outperformed memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution on both quality and compliance. Rubric feedback consistently yielded higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback across all four scaffolds.

Conclusion: FinEvo-Bench successfully measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability in financial AI agents. The results demonstrate that agents can meaningfully improve from retained experience, with evolution gains varying by scaffold design. Skill-only evolution and rubric-based feedback emerge as particularly effective design choices for self-evolving agent systems.

Abstract: Most agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task helps with later tasks. Existing self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. We introduce FinEvo-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark with 120 real-case-grounded tasks, 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Institution-provided professional procedures define the required operations and constraints. Eligible institution-provided and publicly documented cases supply the task facts. Each scene contains six related but substantively distinct cases that share a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for task quality and financial compliance. We compare four self-evolving agent scaffolds using the same Qwen3.7-Max backbone and three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate each scaffold's self-evolution gain from retained experience, while an independent Claude Code scoring agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 evaluates all outputs. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task); Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task. Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution. Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively an agent turns prior experience into later improvement.

</details>


### [145] [Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06167)
*Modhurita Mitra,Jan-Willem Versteeg,Maarten D. Schermer,Shiva Nadi Najafabadi,Marie L. De Bruin,Lourens T. Bloem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A schema-based framework using generative AI (Claude Opus 3) extracts complex, hierarchical, nested information from unstructured text in a single zero-shot call, followed by a path-based semantic matching algorithm for automated evaluation. Achieved >90% F1 on 12/14 attributes from NICE documents, ~30× faster than human experts, with demonstrated generalisability across models, HTA organisations, and languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual extraction of complex, structured information from unstructured documents (e.g., health technology assessment reports) is time-consuming, inconsistent, and requires domain expertise. There is a need for an automated, systematic framework that handles hierarchical, nested attributes with variable cardinality and provides rigorous, domain-aware evaluation of extraction quality against a gold standard.

Method: A schema serves as a unified information model encoding domain knowledge, defining hierarchical nested attributes with variable cardinality. Information extraction is performed via a single zero-shot call to a generative AI model (Claude Opus 3). Automated evaluation uses a novel path-based semantic matching algorithm to align nested, variable-cardinality extracted attributes with gold-standard attributes. Generative AI performs semantic comparison of attribute values, classified into four rubric categories: exact match, semantic match, useful match, or non-match.

Result: 12 out of 14 attributes were extracted with F1 >90% from NICE HTA documents. Extraction was ~30× faster than human domain experts. The framework demonstrated generalisability across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

Conclusion: The proposed schema-based framework, combining zero-shot generative AI extraction with path-based semantic matching evaluation, is a highly efficient and accurate method for extracting complex structured information from unstructured text, with strong potential for cross-model, cross-organisation, and cross-lingual deployment in the HTA domain.

Abstract: We present a schema-based framework for extracting complex, structured information from unstructured text documents using generative AI, followed by automated semantic evaluation of the extracted information against a gold standard. The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.
  In the evaluation step, we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard. We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.
  We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of $>$90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was $\sim$30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert. We further demonstrate generalisability of this framework across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

</details>


### [146] [PaDoc: Layout-Grounded Parallel Decoding for Document Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06146)
*Hao Yu,Jiabo Zhan,Kang Liu,Linnan Zhao,Dongxu Yue,Rui Chen,Jinglin Wang,Chong Sun,Chen Li,Jing Lyu,Chun Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PaDoc is a layout-grounded document parser that factorizes page parsing into concurrent layout and content branches over a shared representation, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on OmniDocBench and significantly faster throughput/latency compared to sequential baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing end-to-end document parsers serialize layout and content into one long autoregressive sequence, forcing independent regions into a sequential decoding path that grows with total content. Two-stage crop-based parsers offer region-level parallelism but incur repeated visual prefills and lose full-page context. The authors aim to retain full-page context while eliminating inter-region decoding dependencies.

Method: PaDoc treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, it derives a prefix-conditioned factorization where layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. This is realized within a single MLLM using: (1) packed variable-length ancestor attention preserving visibility under standard next-token training, and (2) masked parallel decoding that creates branches served as concurrent requests by a vLLM backend with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse.

Result: On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc achieves Overall Layout F1 of 91.1 and Overall score of 94.24 (top-tier among end-to-end parsers), with best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset with one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4–118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2–54.9% versus a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline.

Conclusion: PaDoc demonstrates that layout-grounded branching factorization within a single MLLM can simultaneously improve both parsing accuracy and inference efficiency, outperforming both sequential end-to-end and parallel two-stage approaches.

Abstract: End-to-end document parsers provide a unified interface, but serialize page layouts and regional contents into one autoregressive sequence. This formulation forces independent regions onto a decoding path whose length grows with the total content, whereas crop-based two-stage parsers expose region-level parallelism at the cost of repeated visual prefills and fragmented page context. To retain full-page context while removing dependencies, we propose PaDoc, a layout-grounded parser that treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, we derive a prefix-conditioned factorization in which the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing the decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. We realize this factorization within a single MLLM: packed variable-length ancestor attention preserves the visibility under standard next-token training, while masked parallel decoding creates branches that the evaluated vLLM backend serves as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse. On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc attains an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, a top-tier Overall score of 94.24 together with the best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset and one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4-118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2-54.9% relative to a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Longin-Yu/Padoc

</details>


### [147] [HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06301)
*Varun Ursekar,Apaar Shanker,Yash Maurya,Shehab Yasser,Vijay S. Kalmath,Veronica Chatrath,Yuan Xue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HarnessOpt-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating how well frontier LLMs optimize agentic system harnesses (prompts, tools, control flow, memory, orchestration code) under expensive, stochastic evaluation with a fixed budget. Testing 5 LLMs across 4 tasks over 111 scored runs, the authors find that optimizer models matter more than coding harnesses, native harnesses aren't consistently better, and there is substantial room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in agentic systems, their real-world performance depends heavily on the surrounding "harness" (prompts, tools, control flow, memory, orchestration code), not just model weights. Automated harness optimization is a critical capability, yet the community lacks a standardized protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task.

Method: The authors introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, an end-to-end benchmark for harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer (an LLM paired with a coding harness) receives a seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It iteratively edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, scored by normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. Five frontier LLMs are evaluated under both shared and native coding harnesses across four downstream tasks.

Result: Optimizer model identity separates performance more than the coding harness they operate through. Native harnesses are not consistently superior to a shared harness. Gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes, indicating that harness optimization is a measurable, discriminative capability with significant headroom for improvement.

Conclusion: Harness optimization is established as a measurable and discriminative capability for frontier LLMs. The benchmark reveals that optimizer quality matters more than the harness framework used, and there remains large space for improvement, making automated harness optimization a promising direction for advancing agentic AI systems.

Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed within agentic systems, their capabilities depend not only on the model weights but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code surrounding them. This makes automated harness optimization -- the iterative and evaluation-guided improvement of a harness by an AI system -- both an important route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability for AI systems themselves. Yet the community lacks a common protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task. We introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer, an LLM paired with a coding harness, receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by its normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition that remains inaccessible throughout search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters target-agent resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. We evaluate 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers both under a shared coding harness and under their native harnesses across 4 downstream tasks, over 111 scored runs. Experiment results show that optimizer models separate more than the coding harnesses they act through, native harnesses are not consistently superior, and gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes. These results establish harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with large space for improvement.

</details>


### [148] [CogVis: Must Open-Vocabulary Change Detection Perceive the Scene Anew for Every Query?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06150)
*Zijie Wang,Chen Zhong,Wei He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CogVis is a cognitive-inspired framework for open-vocabulary change detection that decouples temporal perception from semantic discrimination using a perception-memory-verification paradigm, achieving SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks while improving inference efficiency by 28.50%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OVCD methods entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, leading to unstable results and redundant computation. The authors draw inspiration from human visual change perception to design a more efficient, decoupled architecture.

Method: CogVis reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm with three components: (1) Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) extracts a category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features; (2) Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) dynamically estimates image-query-specific decision thresholds to compensate for category-dependent score shifts; (3) Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability scores.

Result: CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven benchmarks spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment. Additionally, by sharing scene-level change perception across queries, it avoids redundant temporal computation and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

Conclusion: The perception-memory-verification paradigm effectively decouples temporal, semantic, and spatial reasoning in OVCD, yielding both superior accuracy and computational efficiency. CogVis demonstrates that category-agnostic change priors can be shared across queries without sacrificing semantic discrimination capability.

Abstract: Earth-surface monitoring requires change detection models capable of recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) addresses this need. However, existing methods often entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, causing unstable results and redundant computation. Inspired by human visual change perception, we propose CogVis, a cognitive memory-guided framework that reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm. CogVis first employs a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) to extract a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features, thereby decoupling temporal evidence from semantic category decisions. A Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) then compensates for category-dependent score shifts by dynamically estimating an image-query-specific decision threshold. Finally, an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability. Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment show that CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated datasets. By sharing scene-level change perception, CogVis further avoids repeating category-agnostic temporal perception across queries and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

</details>


### [149] [iARCS: Iterative Agentic RL for Controllable 3D Scene Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06161)
*Saugat Adhikari,Ashok Prasad Neupane,Pramish Paudel,Ajad Chhatkuli,Danda Pani Paudel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: iARCS is an iterative agentic RL framework that adapts pretrained 3D scene generators to satisfy natural-language task constraints (e.g., walkability, reachability, clearance) while maintaining scene diversity, using LLM-generated reward programs refined through training feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D scene generators prioritize perceptual realism but fail to satisfy functional constraints (accessibility, traversability, spatial rule compliance) essential for downstream embodied AI and computer vision training. This renders much synthetic data impractical for task-specific applications.

Method: A two-stage iterative agentic RL framework: (1) universal-reward pretraining for physical plausibility and layout quality, then (2) task-specific fine-tuning where LLMs generate reward programs that are iteratively refined using training feedback. The framework adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements.

Result: Improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks; effective task-specific constraint optimization; competitive scene diversity. Data generated by iARCS also improves the base generator, demonstrating utility beyond controllable editing.

Conclusion: iARCS demonstrates that agentic RL with LLM-generated, iteratively refined reward functions can bridge the gap between perceptual realism and functional correctness in synthetic 3D scene generation, yielding a practical data generation tool for embodied AI training.

Abstract: Synthetic 3D scene generation is increasingly used as a data source for computer vision and embodied AI, but existing generators often optimize perceptual realism without reliably satisfying task-critical functional constraints. This mismatch limits the usefulness of synthetic data for downstream training, where accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance are often essential. We present iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework that adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements. iARCS uses a two-stage strategy: universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, followed by task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined from training feedback. Experiments show improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity. We further show that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, supporting its value as a practical synthetic data generation tool rather than only a controllable scene editing method.

</details>


### [150] [MicroEvo: Knowledge-Guided LLM Sampling for Efficient Microarchitecture Design Space Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06183)
*Jia Xiong,Runkai Li,Chenxu Niu,Guangyuan Gao,Changwen Xing,Yifan Zhang,Xinlai Wan,Jieran Cui,Chen Bai,Yusheng Hua,Ying Wang,Ming Ling,Xi Wang,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MicroEvo is a framework combining LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. It uses LLM-driven evolutionary operators, Pareto-aware tree policies, knowledge accumulation, and state-aware directives to achieve up to 36.2% better Pareto-front quality over NSGA-II and 10.6x higher search efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Microarchitecture design space exploration faces two core challenges: (1) the search space is vast and PPA (Power, Performance, Area) evaluation is expensive, severely limiting simulation budgets; (2) existing methods conduct blind search without leveraging microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn iteratively, resulting in wasted evaluations and poor Pareto convergence.

Method: MicroEvo integrates off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). The framework consists of four key components: (1) LLM-driven evolutionary operators that generate and mutate design candidates informed by architectural knowledge; (2) a Pareto-aware tree policy that balances Pareto contribution and diversity during node selection; (3) an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights across iterations; and (4) state-aware directives that adapt search behavior online based on current search progress.

Result: MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% compared to NSGA-II and achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency. The framework also demonstrates strong scalability when applied to a complex industrial-scale core design.

Conclusion: LLMs combined with MCTS provide an effective knowledge-guided approach to microarchitecture optimization, substantially outperforming traditional evolutionary methods in both Pareto-front quality and search efficiency, with scalability to industrial-scale designs.

Abstract: Microarchitecture design space exploration suffers from expansive search spaces and expensive PPA evaluation, leaving only a small simulation budget for design decision-making. Existing methods perform blind search without considering microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn from the iterative search effectively, leading to wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence. In this paper, we propose MicroEvo, a knowledge-guided framework that couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. MicroEvo combines LLM-driven evolutionary operators, a Pareto-aware tree policy that balances Pareto contribution and diversity, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt the search behavior online. Experiments show that MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency, and also demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/GEAR-SEU/MicroEvo-ICCAD-26.

</details>


### [151] [Comparative Approaches to Agent Retrieval over Large Skill Libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06196)
*Indivara Kolluru,Nathan Sportsman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hybrid ranker (lexical + dense retrieval) retrieves the correct skill within top-5 for 73.5% of queries. Adding a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations does not improve retrieval and significantly degrades performance (-11.2 points). The graph cannot extend retrieval reach because 98.6% of its edges connect skills the ranker already surfaces together. Author-written queries inflate hit@5 by up to 44 points, masking this failure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents with large skill libraries need efficient, structured mechanisms to select and sequence skills. Loading all skills into context is expensive, and autonomous sequencing lacks structure. The paper investigates whether adding a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations (prerequisites, data flow, ordering) improves retrieval over a strong hybrid ranker alone.

Method: Two systems are compared on a corpus of 690 skills with 117 realistic, non-echoing queries: (1) a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading, and (2) the same ranker augmented with a typed knowledge graph whose edges encode workflow relations. Graph neighbours substitute additional ranked results at matched token budget. The graph's edges are LLM-generated and compared against neighbours from local embedding. Evaluation contrasts author-written vs. realistic queries.

Result: The hybrid ranker achieves 73.5% ± 8.0 hit@5. The knowledge graph significantly underperforms (-11.2 points, p=0.0007). The LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over embedding-derived neighbours. 73% of queries the ranker misses are unreachable through the graph. 98.6% of typed edges connect skills already co-surfaced by the ranker, revealing a pre-filter topology bound: the graph enriches relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. Author-written queries inflate hit@5 by up to 44 points.

Conclusion: Adding structural interdependence via a knowledge graph does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker when graph edges are drawn from the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches. The graph can enrich semantics but cannot extend reach. The paper identifies conditions under which structural augmentation is optimal and warns that author-written evaluation queries dramatically overstate performance.

Abstract: Agents backed by large skill libraries must decide which skills to load and in what order. Loading the entire library into context is expensive and provides no structure for autonomous sequencing. We study two systems for this problem over a corpus of 690 skills: a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading, and a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations such as prerequisites, data flow, and ordering. On a set of 117 realistic, non-echoing queries, the hybrid ranker retrieves the correct skill within the top five in 73.5% +/- 8.0 of cases, leaving roughly a quarter of queries unserved. When used as the design intended (substituting graph neighbours for additional ranked results at matched token budget), the graph is significantly worse (-11.2 points, p = 0.0007). Its LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over neighbours obtained free from a local embedding pass, and 73% of the queries the ranker misses are not reachable through the graph at all. We attribute this to a pre-filter topology bound. Because the graph's candidate edges are drawn from the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches, 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker had already surfaced together. The graph can enrich relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. We further show that evaluating on author-written queries overstates hit@5 by up to 44 points, which would have hidden these results entirely. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of why added structure does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker, and identify the conditions under which adding structural interdependence into the retrieval is optimal.

</details>


### [152] [EnvACE: Internalizing Environment Dynamics via World Rehearsal for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06197)
*Zishan Xu,Zhiyuan Yao,Yuxin Chen,Yifu Guo,Zhengxi Lu,Yuquan Lu,Jinyang Huang,Yan Xu,Yasheng Wang,Weinan Zhang,Xingshan Zeng,Weiwen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EnvACE introduces world rehearsal, where an LLM agent alternates between acting and simulating environment responses during training, jointly optimizing both roles end-to-end with task rewards. This internalizes an agent world model, removing the need for costly external environments, and achieves strong performance across multiple benchmarks while enabling test-time private rehearsal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training LLM agents for long-horizon tool use requires interaction with executable environments (real or synthesized), which are expensive to construct, verify, and ground. External simulators are also difficult to align with real-world dynamics. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency by having the agent learn to internally model environment responses.

Method: EnvACE is an agentic reinforcement learning method based on world rehearsal. The policy alternates between two roles: (1) acting — generating a tool call, and (2) rehearsing — playing the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action. Subsequent decisions are conditioned on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards, internalizing the action–response relationship as a world model within the policy parameters. At test time, the model can optionally perform private rehearsal before committed execution for further gains.

Result: EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance across BFCL-v4, tau²-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, outperforming environment-scaling baselines. Controlled studies show consistent improvement in policy learning across model scales. Test-time private rehearsal yields further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction.

Conclusion: World rehearsal is a viable new paradigm for scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments, enabling efficient policy learning through internalized world models.

Abstract: Training large language model agents for long-horizon tool use typically relies on interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, whose construction and verification are costly, or on external simulators that are difficult to ground. We introduce EnvACE, an agentic reinforcement learning method that replaces external environment interaction during training with world rehearsal. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it first generates a tool call, then plays the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. Through world rehearsal, the policy internalizes the relationship between actions and their environment responses in its parameters, yielding an agent world model that directly supports decision making. Across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in the overall evaluation. Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction. Our findings establish world rehearsal as a new path toward scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Within-yao/EnvACE.

</details>


### [153] [TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06223)
*Yixiong Xiao,Congxi Xiao,Jingbo Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TS-RAG introduces retrieval-augmented generation to time series forecasting by using specially designed reference tokens to fuse retrieved similar sequences with input data, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While RAG has proven effective in NLP, its application to time series forecasting remains underexplored. Time series models typically have limited data, smaller scale, and lack the generative capabilities of LLMs, meaning naive concatenation of reference sequences is ineffective. A specialized fusion mechanism is needed to leverage retrieved similar sequences for improved forecasting.

Method: TS-RAG proposes a framework that retrieves similar time series sequences and integrates them via specially designed reference tokens. These tokens fuse information from the input sequence with retrieved references, enabling the model to capture complex temporal dynamics more robustly than simple concatenation approaches.

Result: TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world time series forecasting benchmarks.

Conclusion: Retrieval-augmented generation can be effectively adapted to time series forecasting through a dedicated fusion mechanism (reference tokens), overcoming the limitations of directly applying LLM-style RAG to smaller time series models.

Abstract: While deep learning models, particularly transformer-based architectures, have shown impressive performance in time series forecasting, the application of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this domain remains limited. Since RAG has proven effective in enhancing the capabilities of large language models by incorporating relevant external information, retrieving similar time series sequences as references might also improve accuracy in time series forecasting tasks. However, most time series models are constrained by limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and a lack of the extensive generative capabilities found in large language models. Simply concatenating reference sequences into the prompt, as done in language models, may not yield the expected results. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, TS-RAG, which leverages RAG to enhance forecasting performance. The framework introduces specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from the input sequence with that from retrieved similar sequences, enabling a more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

</details>


### [154] [DASH: Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons for On-Policy Self-Distillation of Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243)
*ZhiYan Hou,Xinyu Tang,Hongyan An,Jianjin Zhang,Weizhen Wang,Yunyun Han,Gengsheng Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Haiyun Guo,Wenbin Hu,Jinqiao Wang,Yafeng Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DASH improves on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) for RLVR by making token-level supervision weights adaptive to the temporal evolution of teacher-student divergence during autoregressive generation, achieving gains without extra computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard OPSD assigns uniform weights to all local divergences, ignoring the temporal context in which they occur. Since the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories during autoregressive generation, a scalar alone cannot distinguish these contexts, leading to suboptimal supervision.

Method: DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean into an adaptive propagation gate, which controls backward multi-step aggregation. This allows token-level supervision weights to adjust according to how local divergences evolve over the generation trajectory.

Result: Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show DASH outperforms matched vanilla OPSD reruns at every scale and benchmark.

Conclusion: DASH effectively exploits temporal structure in teacher-student divergence sequences, yielding consistent improvements over standard OPSD without requiring additional forward passes, as it reuses already-computed teacher and student distributions.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models using automatically verifiable outcome signals, but these signals are typically sparse and at the sequence-level. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mitigates this sparsity by querying a privileged teacher at student-visited prefixes and providing dense token-level distributional supervision. Although this dense supervision alleviates signal sparsity, we find that standard OPSD still underexploits the temporal structure of the rollout. It assigns every local divergence the same coefficient, regardless of its position or the divergence sequence in which it occurs. In on-policy autoregressive generation, the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories, reflecting different evolutions of the mismatch between the teacher and student. Since the local scalar alone cannot distinguish these temporal contexts, standard OPSD cannot adapt its token-level weights to the realized discrepancy sequence. To address this limitation, we propose Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons (DASH). DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean to an adaptive propagation gate and then uses these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation. By doing so, DASH adjusts token-level supervision weights according to how local divergences evolve during generation. Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show that DASH improves over our matched vanilla OPSD reruns on every benchmark at all three scales. DASH reuses the teacher and student distributions that OPSD already computes, so the gains require no additional teacher or student forward pass.
  Code: https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD

</details>


### [155] [Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06265)
*Omid Bazgir,Md Nasir,Jacob Hoffman,Yang Yang,Manu Agrawal,Anusua Trivedi,Vinay Rao Dandin,Chris Gibbons,Christine Swisher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Synthetic clinical benchmarks can pass utility checks yet remain structurally unrealistic. The authors formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement, showing that deterministic revisions improve realism metrics (missingness, actionability, concentration) while maintaining the utility floor, and argue that utility alone is insufficient evidence of benchmark realism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise healthcare AI agents often pass existing utility checks but remain structurally unrealistic. This is particularly problematic in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where access to real operational data is restricted. The authors aim to improve benchmark realism without breaking downstream utility checks already used in practice.

Method: The authors formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes must increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. They instantiate this on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients, exercised through demonstration EHR workflows, and processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured across four dimensions: missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment. Two deterministic revision strategies are compared against a naive densification control.

Result: The baseline benchmark exhibits extreme thinness: 79.44% sampled-pair missingness, only 12.75% actionable rows, 38.94% of patients with zero actionable measures, and 100.0% top-three token concentration. Both deterministic revisions improve realism across these panels while remaining above the utility floor, whereas the naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. Internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are shown to be related but distinct objectives.

Conclusion: Synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as a constraint rather than sufficient evidence of realism. Improving structural realism is feasible without compromising downstream utility checks.

Abstract: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents can pass existing utility checks and still remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are hard to access. We study how to improve such benchmarks without breaking the downstream utility checks already used in practice.
  We formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes should increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. We instantiate this idea on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients exercised through demonstration electronic health record workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured through missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment.
  The baseline benchmark is extremely thin: sampled-pair missingness is 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while remaining above the current utility floor, whereas a naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. We further show that internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives. These results suggest that synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as one constraint rather than as sufficient evidence of realism.

</details>


### [156] [The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06270)
*Zhiheng Wang,Bo Peng,Lai Wei,Chaochao Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper reveals that vision-capable LLMs using tool-use operations (like crop-and-zoom) often exhibit an "illusion of visual tool-use," where aggregate accuracy gains mask causal ineffectiveness in most rollouts. Through a causal audit framework across policy, trajectory, and step levels, it identifies two failure modes: Calling Without Looking (observations have no causal effect) and Looking Without Planning (informative but incoherent scheduling).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the promise of active visual operations (crop, zoom) for multimodal LLMs, these methods often yield only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at higher token cost, and they can fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. The authors aim to determine whether returned visual evidence causally affects answers, rather than providing spurious correlations.

Method: The authors formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph separating observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. They audit via three levels of intervention: (1) policy-level: comparing tool-use accuracy with direct inference; (2) trajectory-level: corrupting all observations during rollout; (3) step-level: counterfactually replacing individual observations under a fixed prefix, yielding the "Visual Evidence Gain" estimand. Six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks are evaluated.

Result: Two failure modes are uncovered: "Calling Without Looking" (returned observations have no causal effect on the answer) and "Looking Without Planning" (observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent). A trajectory-level diagnostic shows that policy-level accuracy gains are concentrated in a small "Calibrated" minority, while most rollouts exhibit no causal benefit, creating an illusion of effective visual tool-use.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that visual tool-use in multimodal LLMs is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts despite aggregate accuracy improvements. The proposed causal audit framework (CauAudit) can diagnose and decompose policy miscalibration, revealing the discrepancy between surface-level gains and genuine causal contribution of visual observations.

Abstract: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm equips multimodal LLMs with active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom. However, models using these operations often achieve only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at substantially higher token cost. They may also repeatedly crop irrelevant regions and fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. We ask whether the returned visual evidence causally affects the answer. To answer this question, we formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. We then audit it through interventions at the three levels: policy (comparing tool-use with direct inference), trajectory (corrupting all observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix). Our step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates the contribution of each returned observation. Across six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks, we uncover policy miscalibration with two failure modes. In Calling Without Looking, returned observations have no causal effect on the answer. In Looking Without Planning, observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes the policy-level accuracy gain and shows that the gain is concentrated in a Calibrated minority. We term this discrepancy the illusion of visual tool-use: despite aggregate accuracy gains, visual tool-use is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauAudit.

</details>


### [157] [QuanTiMedAI: Quantum-Enhanced Time-Series Model guided by Agentic AI for Cardiac Arrest Mortality Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06294)
*Mutasim Fuad Sarker,Adiba Rahman Namira,Wafa Binte Alam,Md Adnan Arefeen,Mahzabeen Emu,Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuanTiMedAI is a quantum-agentic framework for cardiac arrest mortality prediction that combines an agentic LLM for feature selection with a compact quantum recurrent network (605 parameters), achieving an AUROC of 0.852 on MIMIC-IV data — a ~2.9% improvement over the state-of-the-art baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cardiac arrest mortality prediction models rely on static, early-admission summaries of EHR data and fail to capture the temporal dynamics of physiological deterioration and recovery throughout the ICU stay. This temporal blindness limits prognostic accuracy.

Method: The QuanTiMedAI framework integrates two components: (1) an agentic LLM that performs clinically informed feature discovery and selection, and (2) a compact quantum recurrent network that models temporal dependencies with nonlinear feature enhancement. The architecture is evaluated via extensive experimentation on a MIMIC-IV cardiac arrest cohort, with a structured ablation study validating each design choice.

Result: Agentic LLM-guided feature selection consistently outperforms conventional feature selection methods. The quantum recurrent architecture achieves an AUROC of 0.852 using only 605 parameters, representing a ~2.9% improvement over the state-of-the-art baseline.
