The ablation study confirms that each architectural component contributes meaningfully to overall performance.

Conclusion: Quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can surpass classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters, demonstrating a promising direction for temporally aware mortality prediction in critical care settings.

Abstract: Cardiac arrest remains one of the most lethal conditions encountered in intensive care units. Despite the growing availability of electronic health record data, existing mortality prediction studies in this population largely depend on static summaries derived from early admission. Such approaches ignore the temporal progression of physiological deterioration and recovery that unfolds throughout a patient's ICU stay. To address this limitation, we introduce QuanTiMedAI, a quantum-agentic framework developed for cardiac arrest mortality prediction using agentic AI guided quantum enhancement time series model. The proposed system combines an agentic large language model (LLM) for clinically informed feature discovery with a compact quantum recurrent network for temporality aware mortality prediction. Our findings demonstrate that agentic LLM-guided feature selection consistently outperforms conventional feature selection approaches, and the proposed quantum architecture achieves competitive predictive performance through nonlinear feature enhancement while keeping the number of parameters very low. Through extensive experimentation on a MIMIC-IV cohort of cardiac arrest patients, QuanTiMedAI's quantum-enhanced architecture attains an AUROC of 0.852 using only 605 parameters, an improvement of approximately 2.9\% over a current state-of-the-art baseline for this task. A structured ablation study systematically validates the contribution of each architectural design choice. These results show that quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can exceed classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters.

</details>


### [158] [Bias Analysis of L2 Speaking Assessment Systems Using Concept Activation Vectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06300)
*Arya Labroo,Mengjie Qian,Kate Knill*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper extends Concept Activation Vector (CAV) analysis to neural L2 speaking assessment systems (BERT and Whisper-based graders) to audit bias, and investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) improve concept detection. Key finding: concept recoverability and sensitivity are architecture-dependent, and SAEs improve linear recoverability but attenuate original sensitivity, highlighting the need to distinguish concept encoding from concept influence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatic speaking assessment systems are increasingly used in high-stakes L2 testing, making fairness critical — scores must reflect speaking proficiency, not irrelevant attributes like L1 or age. Transformer-based graders achieve high accuracy but are black-boxes, complicating fairness and interpretability analysis. Prior CAV-based bias detection methods for feature-based graders need extension to these neural architectures.

Method: The authors extend CAV-based analysis to two neural speaking graders: (1) a text-based BERT grader and (2) a speech-and-text multimodal Whisper grader. CAVs represent human-interpretable concepts as directions in activation space. The authors distinguish between concept encoding (whether a concept is linearly recoverable from representations) and concept influence (gradient-based sensitivity of predicted scores to the concept direction). They further investigate sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by learning CAVs in a sparse latent space and mapping them back to activation space, testing whether SAEs yield cleaner concept directions.

Result: Concept recoverability depends strongly on the representation and architecture probed, not solely on the concept itself. Sensitivity to concepts is also architecture-dependent. SAEs make concepts more linearly recoverable but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers.

Conclusion: The findings highlight the critical need to distinguish between concept recoverability (whether a concept is encoded) and concept influence (whether it affects predictions) when auditing bias in speaking assessment systems, as these two properties can diverge, particularly when SAEs are employed.

Abstract: Automatic speaking assessment systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings to mark second language (L2) learners' speaking tests, making it critical to show that their scores depend on speaking proficiency rather than irrelevant speaker attributes such as first language (L1) or age. Transformer-based foundation models have improved the accuracy of these L2 speaking graders, but their black-box representations make fairness and interpretability analysis more difficult. Building on prior work that used Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to detect bias towards unwanted attributes (`concepts') in feature-based graders, we extend CAV-based analysis to two neural speaking assessment systems: a text-based BERT grader and a speech-and-text multimodal grader based on Whisper. CAVs represent human-interpretable concepts as directions in a model's activation space, allowing us to distinguish between whether a concept is encoded in a model's internal representations and whether it influences the predicted score, the latter quantified using a gradient-based sensitivity metric. Since CAVs rely on linear separability, which is less likely in complex neural embedding spaces, we also investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide cleaner concept directions by learning CAVs in a sparse latent space and mapping them back to activation space. Our analysis shows that concept recoverability depends strongly on the representation and architecture being probed, rather than on the concept alone. Sensitivity to concepts is also architecture-dependent. SAEs make concepts more linearly recoverable, but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers. These findings highlight the need to distinguish concept recoverability from concept influence when auditing bias in speaking assessment systems.

</details>


### [159] [TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06346)
*Yunjia Qi,Zehua Yin,Xintong Shi,Hao Peng,Songyuanyi Lu,Yixian Liu,Richeng Xuan,Yuhong Liu,Zhichao Hu,Xiaozhi Wang,Lei Hou,Bin Xu,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrajDebug is a framework for detecting the earliest critical error in failed LLM agent trajectories by compressing long histories and tracing error lifecycles. Paired with TrajErrBench (486 manually annotated failed trajectories), it outperforms baselines and provides actionable feedback for improving agent success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agentic systems suffer from cascading errors that are hard to debug. Existing critical error detection faces two key challenges: (1) long trajectories scatter evidence across distant steps, making individual error identification difficult; (2) failed trajectories often contain multiple local errors, but only some are causally responsible for the final failure. No existing method adequately addresses both challenges simultaneously.

Method: TrajDebug introduces an error-lifecycle tracing framework with two core components: (1) multi-granularity history compression to condense long trajectories while preserving key evidence, and (2) evidence-based error identification that traces each error's resolution status and terminal impact to support critical attribution. The framework is evaluated on TrajErrBench, a newly constructed benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories drawn from Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro, spanning tool-use and coding domains.

Result: TrajDebug achieves the best overall performance compared to existing baselines across diverse agent benchmarks. Application studies demonstrate that its error diagnoses provide actionable feedback that improves downstream agent success rates.

Conclusion: TrajDebug effectively addresses the dual challenges of long-trajectory error discovery and critical error attribution in failed LLM agent trajectories. By combining history compression with error-lifecycle tracing, it not only outperforms prior methods but also yields practical, actionable insights for improving agent systems.

Abstract: LLM-based agentic systems have shown remarkable capabilities in complex domains, while suffering from cascading errors and difficulty in debugging. Critical error detection aims to locate the earliest error step in a failed trajectory that is responsible for the final failure. However, progress faces two main challenges. First, long trajectories make it difficult to identify individual errors, since the evidence for judging a step may be scattered across distant instructions, observations, and prior context. Second, failed trajectories often contain multiple local errors with different downstream effects, only some of which remain responsible for the final failure. In this work, we propose TrajDebug, an error-lifecycle tracing framework that addresses long-trajectory error discovery with multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification, and supports critical attribution by tracing each error's resolution status and terminal impact. We further construct TrajErrBench, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories from Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro, covering realistic tool-use and coding scenarios. Experiments across diverse agent benchmarks show that TrajDebug achieves the best overall performance over existing baselines, and application studies further demonstrate that its diagnoses provide actionable feedback for improving downstream agent success. We will release the codes and data to facilitate further research.

</details>


### [160] [Challenges in Evaluating Explanation Methods for Static and Evolving Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06351)
*Jerzy Stefanowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper critiques insufficient evaluation in XAI, illustrates issues via a bias-detection system (DetoxAI), presents a human-grounded evaluation of image classification explanations, and explores adapting explanations (counterfactuals) to evolving data streams with concept drift, linking this to the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: XAI methods suffer from insufficient rigorous evaluation, limiting their practical reliability. The paper aims to highlight this gap and explore solutions, particularly in dynamic environments where data distributions shift over time (concept drift), which existing explanation methods rarely address.

Method: The paper employs a multi-pronged approach: (1) a case study using the DetoxAI system for bias detection and concept unlearning to illustrate evaluation shortcomings; (2) a human-grounded evaluation study for image classification explanation methods; and (3) exploration of adapting counterfactual explanations to evolving data streams with concept drift, discussing practical experiences and relating findings to the broader challenge of tracking co-evolution among data, models, and explanations.

Result: The DetoxAI case study concretely demonstrates XAI evaluation deficiencies in bias detection contexts. The human-grounded evaluation provides empirical insights into explanation method effectiveness for image classification. Experiences with counterfactual adaptation reveal challenges in maintaining explanation fidelity under concept drift, underscoring the need for frameworks that track the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.

Conclusion: Rigorous, human-grounded evaluation of XAI methods is essential and currently insufficient. Explanation methods must be designed to adapt to evolving data streams, and future XAI systems should account for the dynamic co-evolution of data, models, and explanations to remain reliable in real-world, non-stationary environments.

Abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) with respect to insufficient evaluation. They are illustrated through the DetoxAI image recognition system for bias detection and concept unlearning. Then, an example of a human-grounded evaluation of methods for explaining image classification is presented. The paper further explores methods for adapting explanations to evolving data streams with concept drift. Experiences with adapting counterfactuals for this problem are discussed. Finally it is related to the challenges of tracking the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.\footnote{This paper has been accepted for a publication in J.Nalepa (ed) Explainable AI in Space. Proceedings of EASi 2026 Workshop at IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Bremen, Springer CCIS vol 3107 (2016).}

</details>


### [161] [The Low Frequency Trap: Video Language Models Fail at Simple Event Bookkeeping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06361)
*Sarvesh Baskar,Zikui Cai,Shayan Shabihi,Anirudh Satheesh,Muhammad R. Islam,Udari Madhushani Sehwag,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces trace-grounded parametric profiling for evaluating video understanding models on event counting tasks. By using controlled synthetic videos with executable ground-truth event traces, the authors reveal that model performance exhibits a "staged temporal failure" — reliability depends heavily on event representation (persistent vs. transient), event count, and frequency, with near-total failure in high-count, high-frequency regimes. Increasing sampling rate boosts aggregate accuracy but not faithful event recovery, highlighting the gap between final-answer scoring and true temporal reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world video benchmarks have fixed clips that conflate multiple variables (event count, rate, duration, visual complexity), making it impossible to isolate specific failure modes. Existing programmatic benchmarks offer control but only score final answers, lacking the ability to audit whether models correctly identify individual events against executable ground truth. The authors aim to decompose video temporal reasoning into controllable axes and evaluate models at timestamp-level granularity.

Method: The authors design three parametric video tasks — bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, and categorical state transitions — producing 2,190 controlled videos. They independently vary event count N and frequency F while holding rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace enabling both capability-surface estimation (identifying the N-F region where models achieve ≥80% reliability) and timestamp-level evaluation of reported events against ground truth. They also test the effect of increased sampling rate and different prompting strategies, and validate findings on real-world videos.

Result: Results reveal a staged temporal failure: (1) At 80% reliability, Gemini 3.6 Flash counts persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5–1.0 Hz but has no reliable region for transient blinking events. (2) In high-count, high-frequency regimes, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and only 18.1% of true events are recovered. (3) Increasing sampling rate boosts Bounce Ball accuracy from 19.6% to 29.3%, but the reported sequence matches ground truth only 3.7% of the time — aggregate scores inflate without faithful recovery. (4) Different prompting strategies yield similarly limited gains, and real-world evaluations confirm that success concentrates at low event counts.

Conclusion: Trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy metrics toward detailed diagnostics of temporal reasoning failures. Event representation fundamentally governs whether a model can initially access visual evidence, and this limitation compounds with increasing count and frequency. Aggregate metrics can mask failure modes, since extra frames can inflate scores without improving faithful event recovery. The approach enables fine-grained capability mapping that reveals precisely where and how temporal reasoning breaks down.

Abstract: Real-world video benchmarks provide broad coverage, but their fixed clips entangle event count, rate, duration, and visual complexity, making failure modes hard to isolate. While existing programmatic benchmarks offer better control, they score only the final answer rather than auditing reported events against executable ground truth. To bridge this gap, we introduce trace-grounded parametric profiling for event counting in three controlled video tasks: bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, and categorical state transitions. Across 2,190 videos, we vary event count N and frequency F while holding rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace for capability-surface estimation and timestamp-level evaluation. Our results reveal a staged temporal failure. At an 80% reliability threshold, Gemini 3.6 Flash reliably counts persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5 and 1.0 Hz, yet demonstrates no reliable positive-count region for transient blinking events. Thus, event representation dictates whether a model initially accesses evidence -- a limitation that compounds as count and frequency increase. In the high-count, high-frequency regime, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and the model recovers just 18.1% of true events. To test if visual access is the primary bottleneck, we increase sampling rate. Although this boosts Bounce Ball accuracy from 19.6% to 29.3%, the reported sequence agrees with ground truth only 3.7% of the time. Extra frames can therefore inflate final scores without producing faithful event recovery. Different prompting strategies yield similarly limited gains, and real-world video evaluations show the same concentration of success at low event counts. Ultimately, trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy metrics to a detailed diagnostic of where temporal reasoning fails.

</details>


### [162] [Tracing the Heart: An Evidence-Linked Pipeline for Heart-Failure Feature Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06366)
*Soorya Ram Shimgekar,Michelle Hu,Dorisa Shehi,Daniel Kang,Roy Ka-Wei Lee,Koustuv Saha,Christian Poellabauer,Christopher Lee,Sajeev Singh,Piyum Zonooz,Navin Kumar,Zeeshan Ahmed,Priyadarshini Kachroo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS) automates evidence-linked, auditable EHR feature engineering for heart failure phenotyping. Tested on 500 dummy records, nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 aggregated features, improving AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 (HFrEF) and 0.870 to 0.910 (HFpEF), with 81.5% rubric-assessed methodological soundness. The system addresses the 39-45% workload bottleneck of manual feature engineering while ensuring provenance and guideline compliance, though external validation remains needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EHR feature engineering consumes 39-45% of data scientists' time in clinical research and AI, creating a major bottleneck. Heart failure (affecting ~6.7M U.S. adults) is especially challenging due to fragmented EHR data requiring disease-specific, guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and LLM-based approaches offer only partial automation and suffer from limited maintainability and evidence traceability.

Method: The authors developed nMAS, a multi-agent system with evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipelines for heart failure feature engineering. It ingests data from nine EHR source tables, generates structured and aggregated features, and verifies them for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance using a restricted LLM audit. The system was evaluated on 500 dummy patient records, with downstream phenotyping tasks (HFrEF and HFpEF classification) measured by held-out AUROC and an independent LLM-based rubric assessment of evidence support and methodological soundness.

Result: nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features. Adding aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and from 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping. An independent LLM-based rubric assessment scored features at 81.5% of maximum points for evidence support and methodological soundness.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data. However, evaluation was limited to a single-institution dummy cohort, and external validation on real-world data is needed to confirm generalizability.

Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI, accounting for 39-45% of data scientists' workload. This is especially pronounced in heart failure, which affects an estimated 6.7 million U.S. adults and requires integrating fragmented EHR data with disease-specific, guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and large language model (LLM)-based approaches offer only partial automation with limited maintainability and evidence traceability. We developed the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering, and evaluated it on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM. Adding the aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping, and an independent LLM-based rubric assessment of evidence support and methodological soundness scored the features at 81.5% of maximum points. These results demonstrate the feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data, though evaluation was limited to a single-institution cohort and external validation is needed.

</details>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [163] [BioMedJImpact: A Comprehensive Dataset and LLM Pipeline for AI Engagement and Scientific Impact Analysis of Biomedical Journals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05227)
*Ruiyu Wang,Yuzhang Xie,Xiao Hu,Carl Yang,Jiaying Lu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: BioMedJImpact is a large-scale biomedical dataset (1.74M articles, 2,744 journals) that combines bibliometrics, collaboration features, and an LLM-derived AI engagement rate to analyze how team size and AI research jointly influence journal prestige, revealing that larger teams correlate with higher citations while AI engagement positively associates with Impact Factor only in the 2019 subset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing resources for assessing journal impact rarely capture how collaboration patterns and AI research jointly shape venue prestige in biomedicine. There is a need for a comprehensive, content-aware dataset that integrates both dimensions at scale.

Method: The authors construct BioMedJImpact from 1.74 million PubMed Central articles across 2,744 journals. They integrate bibliometric indicators, collaboration features, and a novel AI engagement rate — defined as the proportion of AI-related articles per journal-year — extracted via a reproducible three-stage LLM pipeline. They analyze how collaboration intensity and AI engagement rate jointly influence scientific impact across two temporal subsets (2016–2019, 2020–2023). Human evaluation validates the LLM pipeline for AI relevance detection and subfield classification.

Result: Two main patterns emerge: (1) journals with larger author teams tend to have higher citation impact, and (2) AI engagement rate is positively associated with Impact Factor only in the 2019 subset. Human evaluation confirms substantial agreement in AI relevance detection and consistent subfield classification.

Conclusion: BioMedJImpact provides a validated, scalable framework for content-aware scientometric analysis at the intersection of biomedicine and AI, along with a comprehensive dataset and reproducible LLM pipeline, all publicly available.

Abstract: Assessing journal impact is central to scholarly communication, yet existing resources rarely capture how collaboration and artificial intelligence (AI) research jointly shape venue prestige in biomedicine. We present BioMedJImpact, a large-scale, biomedical-oriented dataset built from 1.74 million PubMed Central articles across 2,744 journals. BioMedJImpact integrates bibliometric indicators, collaboration features, and an LLM-derived AI engagement rate, defined as the proportion of AI-related articles within each journal-year. Specifically, AI engagement rate is extracted through a reproducible three-stage LLM pipeline. We analyze how collaboration intensity and AI engagement rate jointly influence scientific impact across two temporal subsets (2016-2019, 2020-2023). Two main patterns emerge: journals with larger author teams tend to have higher citation impact, while AI engagement rate is positively associated with Impact Factor only in the 2019 subset. To validate the LLM pipeline for deriving the AI engagement rate, we conduct human evaluation, confirming substantial agreement in AI relevance detection and consistent subfield classification. Together, BioMedJImpact provides both a comprehensive dataset at the interface of biomedicine and AI and a validated framework for scalable, content-aware scientometric analysis. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/JonathanWry/BioMedJImpact.

</details>


### [164] [From Trajectories to Evidence: Auditable Experimental Records for Industrial Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05235)
*Zijie Zhuang,Changxin Lao,Pengbo Xu,Hanwen Xu,Ruochen Yang,Yingzhi He,Peng Zhang,Jiangxia Cao,Yusheng Huang,Guohong Mu,Jian Liang,Ruiming Tang,Shuang Yang,Zhaojie Liu,Wenwu Ou,Kun Gai*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper formalizes "trajectory-to-evidence conversion" for multi-round ML experiments in recommendation systems, introducing a framework with bounded artifact verification, post-execution claim qualification, and hybrid LLM-assisted control to ensure research trajectories yield auditable, qualified evidence rather than unverified outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In industrial recommendation settings, research agents conduct multi-round experiments and retain trajectories for future decisions. However, completed trajectories are not automatically valid evidence: generated artifacts may be unsupported or incomplete, executed rounds may be invalid or confounded, and later modifications can obscure earlier findings. There is a need for systematic methods to determine what a completed research process has actually established.

Method: The authors propose an evidence-grounded framework with three core components: (1) a context-isolated generate-verify-repair process that checks artifacts for evidence violations and missing downstream requirements before release; (2) post-execution validity and attribution checks that consolidate evidence across rounds, qualify intervention-level claims as actionable repairs, diagnostic guards, or withheld findings, and preserve admitted claims as auditable records with explicit provenance and applicability boundaries; (3) a hybrid LLM-assisted controller that applies, defers, or rejects records based on available target evidence. Record audits and downstream diagnostics are used to evaluate claim survival and identify bottlenecks.

Result: Record audits characterize which claims survive qualification. Downstream diagnostics identify affirmative applicability judgment as a bottleneck for the tested controller. Across paper-to-target adaptations, later rounds often improve on the first, while final rounds frequently underperform an earlier best, exposing non-monotonic trajectory evolution. Candidates produced through the complete workflow yielded positive online lifts relative to deployed baselines.

Conclusion: Trajectory-to-evidence conversion is a critical but underexamined problem in agent-driven research. The proposed framework demonstrates that systematic verification, claim qualification, and auditable provenance can transform raw experimental trajectories into reliable evidence. Non-monotonic trajectory evolution highlights the importance of retaining and auditing intermediate rounds rather than relying solely on final outcomes.

Abstract: Research agents increasingly conduct multi-round machine-learning experiments in industrial recommendation settings and retain the resulting trajectories to guide later decisions. Yet a completed trajectory is not automatically evidence: generated artifacts may be unsupported or incomplete, executed rounds may be invalid or confounded, and later modifications may obscure earlier findings. We study \textbf{trajectory-to-evidence conversion}, asking what a completed research process has actually established. We introduce an evidence-grounded framework that couples bounded verification of consequential artifacts with post-execution claim qualification. A context-isolated generate--verify--repair process checks artifacts for evidence violations and missing downstream requirements before release. After execution, validity and attribution checks consolidate evidence across rounds, qualify intervention-level claims as actionable repairs, diagnostic guards, or withheld findings, and preserve admitted claims as auditable records with explicit provenance and applicability boundaries. A hybrid LLM-assisted controller subsequently applies, defers, or rejects records based on available target evidence. Record audits characterize which claims survive qualification, while downstream diagnostics identify affirmative applicability judgment as a bottleneck for the tested controller. Across paper-to-target adaptations, later rounds often improve on the first, while final rounds frequently underperform an earlier best, exposing non-monotonic trajectory evolution. Candidates produced through the complete workflow also yielded positive online lifts relative to deployed baselines.

</details>


### [165] [Cross-platform epistemic verification for improving factual reliability in AI-generated news summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05302)
*Zhuo Xie,Haoze Ni*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MECV is a post-hoc hallucination correction framework for AI-generated news summaries that aggregates evidence from multiple heterogeneous sources (source document, Wikipedia, open web) and uses a multi-LLM jury with contradiction-aware consensus scoring to identify and iteratively revise unsupported claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-generated news summaries often contain factual hallucinations. Single-source retrieval for verification is unreliable; a multi-source, consensus-driven approach can better identify factual uncertainty and improve correction quality, especially in information-sensitive domains like financial news.

Method: MECV aggregates evidence from three heterogeneous sources: the source document, Wikipedia, and open-web retrieval. A multi-LLM jury (GPT-4o-mini and DeepSeek-Chat) performs contradiction-aware consensus scoring to estimate factual reliability. Claims flagged as unsupported undergo iterative minimal-edit refinement, orchestrated by Qwen-Plus. Evaluated on the SummEdits benchmark.

Result: MECV improved factual consistency while preserving the semantic structure of original summaries. Agreement across heterogeneous evidence sources proved useful as a signal for identifying factual uncertainty, including in financial news aggregation scenarios.

Conclusion: Multi-source evidence consensus verification with a multi-LLM jury effectively corrects hallucinations in AI-generated news summarization. The framework advances trustworthy AI and automated journalism by demonstrating that consensus-based verification enhances factual reliability.

Abstract: This study proposes Multi-source Evidence Consen- sus Verification (MECV), a post-hoc hallucination cor- rection framework for AI-generated news summariza- tion. Instead of depending on a single retrieval channel, MECV aggregates evidence from multiple heterogeneous sources, including the source document, Wikipedia, and open-web retrieval. The framework further incorporates a multi-LLM jury mechanism that estimates factual reliabil- ity through contradiction-aware consensus scoring across verifier models. Claims identified as potentially unsup- ported are revised through iterative minimal-edit refine- ment. The proposed framework is evaluated on the SummEd- its benchmark using GPT-4o-mini and DeepSeek-Chat as the verifier jury, with Qwen-Plus as the orchestra- tor. Experimental results show that MECV improves fac- tual consistency while preserving the semantic structure of the original summaries. The findings further suggest that agreement across heterogeneous evidence sources can serve as a useful signal for identifying factual uncertainty in AI-generated summaries, including in information- sensitive domains such as financial news aggregation. This study contributes to research on trustworthy AI and automated journalism by introducing a multi-source verification framework for hallucination correction and demonstrating the value of consensus-based verification for improving factual reliability in AI-generated news summarization.

</details>


### [166] [Robustness and User-Perceived Value of Popularity Calibration in Music Recommendation: A User Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05402)
*Oleg Lesota,Gustavo Escobedo,Bruce Ferwerda,Simone Kopeinik,Dominik Kowald,Elisabeth Lex,Markus Schedl*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper investigates the perceived value and measurement reliability of popularity calibration in music recommendation. Through a user study, it finds that while users perceive differences in popularity composition of recommendation lists, they do not clearly prefer calibrated lists; the relationship between JSD-based calibration metrics and perceived popularity depends heavily on item familiarity, list composition, and available user history, and computational popularity labels only weakly align with users' own judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on popularity calibration relies primarily on offline metrics and assumes users prefer lists matching their historical consumption. However, user studies are limited, findings on calibration's effect on user experience are mixed, and the robustness of calibration metrics under varying item familiarity and incomplete user history remains unclear. This motivates a deeper, user-centered investigation into whether calibration truly matters to users and how reliably it can be measured.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled user study in music recommendation. They construct personalized track lists from users' recent listening histories and use a naive recommender to generate lists with three popularity compositions: highpop-heavy, lowpop-heavy, and calibrated. They then investigate: (1) whether users perceive differences between these lists, (2) whether calibrated lists are preferred, (3) how robust JSD-based popularity calibration is under varying familiarity and history-availability conditions, and (4) how computational popularity labels align with users' own popularity judgments.

Result: Users can perceive differences in popularity composition across recommendation lists, but they do not clearly prefer calibrated lists over highpop-heavy or lowpop-heavy ones. The relation between JSD-based calibration metrics and perceived popularity is not robust — it depends on item familiarity, list composition, and the availability of user history. Additionally, computational popularity labels and user-judged popularity labels exhibit only weak alignment.

Conclusion: Popularity calibration as an offline metric does not straightforwardly translate into user-perceived value, and its measurement via JSD is sensitive to contextual factors. The weak alignment between computational and user-perceived popularity further complicates its use as a reliable user-facing construct. These findings call for a more critical and nuanced approach to popularity calibration in recommender systems research and practice.

Abstract: Popularity calibration in recommender systems has been studied both as a form of user-centered personalization and as an indicator of popularity bias. Most existing work evaluates calibration through offline metrics, often assuming that users prefer recommendation lists whose popularity distribution matches their historical consumption profile. However, user studies on calibration remain limited, and existing findings suggest that calibrated recommendations do not necessarily have a strong effect on user experience. Moreover, although prior work has shown that calibration metrics can correlate with users' perceptions of recommendation lists, the robustness of this relation remains unclear under different levels of item familiarity and incomplete user-history information. In this work, we study the perceived value and measurement reliability of popularity calibration in music recommendation. We construct personalized track lists from users' recent listening histories and use a controlled naive recommender to create lists with different popularity compositions: highpop-heavy, lowpop-heavy, and calibrated. We investigate whether users perceive differences between these lists, whether calibrated lists are preferred, how robust JSD-based popularity calibration is under different familiarity and history-availability conditions, and how computational popularity labels align with users' own popularity judgments. Our results show that users perceive differences in popularity composition, but do not clearly prefer calibrated lists. We further find that the relation between JSD and perceived popularity depends on item familiarity, list composition, and available user history, while computational and user-judged popularity labels only weakly align. These findings contribute to a more critical understanding of popularity calibration as both an offline metric and a user-facing construct.

</details>


### [167] [A Mechanistic Analysis of Gender Sensitivity in Dense Retrieval Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05467)
*Catherine Chen,Maarten de Rijke,Carsten Eickhoff*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper investigates the internal mechanisms behind gender bias in bi-encoder dense retrieval models, identifying that bias originates in input embeddings and propagates through specific late-layer attention heads. Steering at these two loci produces distinct effects: embedding steering non-specifically neutralizes score differences, while attention steering yields directional shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While gender bias in dense retrieval models is well documented (male-gendered documents scored higher), the internal mechanistic pathways producing these disparities remain poorly understood. The authors seek to fill this gap by conducting a mechanistic interpretability analysis to localize where and how gender sensitivity arises in bi-encoder architectures.

Method: The authors perform a mechanistic analysis of bi-encoder retrieval models, localizing gender sensitivity to two key points: (1) input embeddings, where the bias signal originates, and (2) a small set of late-layer attention heads that jointly encode both gender and term-matching (relevance) signals. They then test steering interventions at both the embedding and attention-head levels to compare their effects on retrieval score disparities.

Result: Embedding-level steering non-specifically neutralizes score differences between male, female, and neutral documents, while attention-level steering produces directional shifts in scoring. The overlap of gender and relevance signals in shared attention heads highlights the difficulty of cleanly disentangling bias from genuine relevance matching.

Conclusion: The study provides a mechanistic foundation for targeted debiasing interventions in dense retrieval models and underscores the challenge that gender and relevance signals are entangled within shared model components, complicating efforts to remove bias without degrading retrieval quality.

Abstract: While gender bias in dense retrieval models is well documented, with prior work showing that models often score male-gendered documents higher than female or neutral variants, the internal mechanisms producing these disparities are poorly understood. In this paper, we mechanistically analyze bi-encoder models to localize gender sensitivity, finding that the signal originates in input embeddings and propagates through a small set of late-layer attention heads that carry both gender and term-matching signals. Guided by these findings, we test steering interventions at both identified points and find distinct effects: embedding-level steering non-specifically neutralizes score differences, while attention-level steering produces directional shifts. Our findings provide a mechanistic basis for targeted debiasing and highlight the challenge of disentangling gender from relevance signals in shared model components.

</details>


### [168] [An Ontology-Based Framework for Student Profiling and Content Personalization in Higher Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05489)
*José Luiz M. Morais,Arlindo F. da Conceição,Cacilda Encarnação Augusto Alvarenga,Daniela Musa*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This qualitative study explores how to improve self-paced e-learning in higher education by rethinking pedagogical models. It emphasizes automated monitoring of student learning, profile management, and proposes an ontology-based computational architecture to store educational process information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of digital technologies and distance education in virtual learning environments demands that students become more autonomous protagonists. Existing pedagogical models for distance courses often fail to fully achieve their learning objectives, necessitating a systematic re-examination of key implementation and improvement factors.

Method: Qualitative, bibliographic research discussing techniques for electronic and automatic monitoring and recording of learning process outcomes. The paper proposes using ontologies to store educational process information and presents a computational architecture designed for this purpose.

Result: The study identifies critical aspects for implementing self-paced and e-learning courses, highlights the importance of processes that store and manage student profiles (both in terms of content and access patterns), and delivers a proposal for an ontology-based computational architecture to manage educational data.

Conclusion: Effective self-paced e-learning requires robust, ontology-driven systems for automatically tracking learning outcomes and managing student profiles. Integrating such architectures into pedagogical models can help distance education courses better achieve their learning objectives.

Abstract: The expansion of access to Digital Information and Communication Technologies and the offer of distance or semi-distance education courses that make use of virtual learning environments brought changes in the teaching and learning processes, requiring that the student be even more protagonist in this process. The present study aimed to identify important aspects to be considered in the implementation and improvement of self-paced learning and e-learning in higher education courses, with the purpose of rethinking pedagogical models of courses offered at a distance so that they reach even more of your learning objectives. The research is characterized as qualitative, of bibliographic nature, and discusses techniques to monitor and record, electronically and automatically, the results of the process and learning. The importance of processes that store and manage the student's profile is highlighted, both in terms of content and forms of access. The article proposes the use of ontologies to store information about the educational process and presents a computational architecture for this purpose.

</details>


### [169] [EXCISE: Query-Side Exclusion for Late-Interaction Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05497)
*Mohammed Ali,Abdelrahman Abdallah,Adam Jatowt*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: EXCISE is a query-time module that fixes late-interaction retrievers' inability to handle exclusion queries (e.g., "X but not Z") by identifying the excluded topic and re-ranking a shortlist, achieving near-perfect Boolean NOT accuracy without sacrificing standard retrieval quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Late-interaction retrievers like ColBERT suffer from "exclusion inversion": when users query for X but not Z, the additive MaxSim scoring mechanism inadvertently boosts documents containing Z. The authors prove this is a fundamental limitation — no readout of frozen document vectors can recover the exclusion constraint because the excluded topic depends solely on the query, not the document representations.

Method: EXCISE operates entirely at query time, leaving the document index frozen. It consists of three components: (1) two lightweight query-side modules (totaling 1.5M parameters) that identify the excluded topic from the query and re-embed a 100-document shortlist; (2) a parameter-free rule that demotes candidates matching the identified excluded topic. The authors also introduce X-BENCH, a tiered benchmark covering explicit, implicit, and compound exclusions with no-harm and Boolean controls.

Result: Across six collections and three backbones, EXCISE outperforms all frozen and fine-tuned baselines in all 18 backbone-collection cells. It raises exclusion success@10 on ExcluIR from 0.058 to 0.691 and Boolean NOT accuracy from 0.25–0.29 to 0.90–0.92. Over 1,860 pooled queries, EXCISE surpasses every fine-tuned cross-encoder, all of which lose no-harm nDCG@10, while EXCISE matches its frozen baseline on its strongest backbone.

Conclusion: EXCISE demonstrates that exclusion handling in late-interaction retrieval can be effectively addressed through lightweight query-side intervention without re-indexing. The approach is practical, backbone-agnostic, and preserves standard retrieval quality while dramatically improving exclusion accuracy.

Abstract: Late-interaction retrievers handle exclusion queries poorly. When a user asks for X but not Z, the additive MaxSim score promotes documents covering Z, a problem we call exclusion inversion. We show that no readout of the frozen vectors recovers the constraint, because the difficulty lies in identifying the excluded topic, which depends on the query alone. EXCISE operates at query time and corrects the inversion while leaving the index frozen. Two query-side modules totalling 1.5M parameters identify the topic and re-embed a 100-document shortlist, and a parameter-free rule demotes candidates matching that topic. Across six collections and three backbones, EXCISE is the strongest system in all eighteen backbone-collection cells against that backbone's own frozen and fine-tuned baselines. It raises exclusion success@10 on ExcluIR from 0.058 to 0.691 and raises Boolean NOT accuracy from 0.25-0.29 to 0.90-0.92. Pooled over 1,860 queries, it outperforms every fine-tuned cross-encoder, each of which loses no-harm nDCG@10, whereas EXCISE matches its frozen baseline on its strongest backbone. We release X-BENCH, a tiered benchmark of explicit, implicit, and compound exclusions with no-harm and Boolean controls.

</details>


### [170] [omni-macos: On-Device Omni-Modal Search on Apple Silicon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05543)
*Han Xiao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A local-first multimodal search engine, omni-macos, runs entirely on a Mac—indexing, encoding, and querying text, code, documents, images, audio, and video—without any data leaving the device, using a user-defined memory budget with incremental re-encoding, GPU-aware query scheduling, and quantized retrieval with exact rescoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal search engines assume a server-based architecture, requiring files, queries, and vector embeddings to leave the user's machine. This poses privacy risks and adds latency. The authors aim to build a fully local, privacy-preserving search engine that operates within user-defined resource constraints on consumer hardware.

Method: The system, omni-macos, co-locates the encoder, vector index, and blob store on the user's Mac. Key techniques include: (1) a background indexer that only re-encodes chunks affected by file edits; (2) GPU scheduling that processes smaller units during interactive typing to maintain responsiveness; (3) a quantized vector replica for fast approximate search followed by exact rescoring of top candidates; (4) unified memory budget propagation across all allocators (encoder, index, store). Evaluation spans five Macs varying 8× in accelerator width and 32× in memory.

Result: The paper measures the performance of each mechanism across five Mac configurations with an eightfold range in GPU width and a thirty-twofold range in memory, each indexing its own local files. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract but are characterized as measured across this hardware diversity.)

Conclusion: A fully local, resource-adaptive multimodal search engine is feasible on consumer Mac hardware, eliminating the need for server-side infrastructure while preserving privacy and maintaining interactive query responsiveness through careful memory budgeting and incremental processing strategies.

Abstract: A search engine that embeds text, code, documents, images, audio and video into the same representation space has to run its encoder and keep its index somewhere, and almost every component built for the purpose assumes a server. We present omni-macos, which runs that whole engine, encoder, index and store, on the Mac the files are already on, so no file, query or vector ever leaves the machine. It keeps a background indexer and an interactive search box inside one memory budget the user sets: it re-encodes only the chunks an edit changes, hands the GPU smaller units while the user is typing, answers queries from a quantized replica with exact rescoring, and propagates that budget to the allocators that draw on unified memory. We measure every mechanism on five Macs spanning an eightfold range of accelerator width and a thirty-twofold range of memory, each one indexing its own local files.

</details>


### [171] [Is Personalized Modality Weighting Actually Personalized? A Controlled Audit of Per-User Weighting Claims in Multimodal Recommenders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05655)
*Jingyuan Zheng,Xin Zhang,Yang Gu,Dongjing Wang,Yuxiang Wang,Xudong Shen,Haiping Zhang,Youhuizi Li,Dongjin Yu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper audits per-user modality weighting in multimodal recommenders and finds that a single global modality weight captures nearly all performance gains, with user-specific weights adding negligible and inconsistent value. The authors propose a two-contrast audit (real-GM and real-shuf) as a minimum standard for validating personalization claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on per-user modality weighting in multimodal recommenders claims ranking gains from user-specific modality preferences, but none rigorously isolate whether the observed gains stem from genuine user-specific signal versus merely adding model capacity with a global modality weight. The authors seek to close this evaluation gap.

Method: The authors propose a two-contrast audit framework: (1) real-GM — comparing per-user weighting implementations against a single global modality weight to measure utility gain; (2) real-shuf — permuting the user-weight binding at evaluation time to test identifiability. Six per-user implementations (user modality-strength vectors, attention gates, meta-weight hypernetworks, low-rank guided weights) are reduced onto one shared collaborative backbone. Evaluations span three short-video corpora with a replication on an e-commerce dataset, plus a monotone signal-implant dose-response experiment to verify the harness can detect user-specific structure when present.

Result: A single global weight delivers nearly all content gain (+1.9/+3.6/+3.5 pp over no-modality baseline, p<.001). Per-user weighting adds no consistent utility: no implementation wins across all corpora/metrics, and positive gaps are small (≤0.9 pp) and flip signs. The real-shuf control reaches up to +128% of content gain for heads that simultaneously lose to the global weight. Decoupling gate inputs from the shared collaborative embedding collapses inflated real-shuf to near zero. The dose-response experiment confirms the harness detects user-specific structure when present (capture AUROC rising from 0.57→0.89 and 0.64→1.00).

Conclusion: Per-user modality weighting in current multimodal recommenders fails to demonstrate genuine user-specific signal beyond a global weight. The authors recommend reporting real-GM and real-shuf together as a minimum evidentiary standard for personalization claims, and caution that shuffle controls alone are insufficient without utility comparisons against a global weight baseline.

Abstract: Per-user modality weighting is deployed at billion-user scale in multimodal recommenders, through user modality-strength vectors, attention gates, meta-weight hypernetworks, and low-rank guided weights, each claiming a ranking gain from user-specific modality preference. Yet, to our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate a genuinely user-specific signal from a global modality weight plus model capacity. We audit this family with a two-contrast audit principle, reducing six implementations onto one shared collaborative backbone and measuring a utility gap (real-GM) against a single global modality weight and an identifiability gap (real-shuf) against an eval-time permutation of the user-weight binding. Across three independent short-video corpora, a single global weight already delivers nearly all of the content gain (+1.9/+3.6/+3.5pp over a no-modality baseline, p < .001). Making the weight per-user adds no consistent utility: no implementation wins on all corpora and metrics, and the few positive gaps are small (<=0.9pp) and flip. The shuffle control is necessary but not sufficient, since real-shuf reaches +128% of the content gain for heads that simultaneously lose to the global weight. We trace this dissociation to gates reading the shared collaborative embedding: decoupling the gate input collapses the inflated real-shuf to near zero while the utility conclusion stands. A monotone signal-implant dose-response (capture AUROC rising from 0.57 to 0.89 and from 0.64 to 1.00) verifies the harness would detect user-specific structure if present, and every finding replicates on a fourth, cross-domain e-commerce corpus. We propose reporting real-GM alongside real-shuf as a minimum evidentiary standard for personalization claims.

</details>


### [172] [Gryphon-v2: One Model in Place of a Cascade - Generate-and-Rank Recommender with Rollout Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06213)
*Anna Lipkina,Daria Tikhonovich,Viktor Yanush,Mariia Ulianova,Oleg Sorokin,Vladislav Dodonov,Ilya Murzin,Denis Burshtein,Nikolay Savushkin*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Gryphon-v2 is a unified generate-and-rank architecture that replaces multi-stage industrial recommendation cascades with a single end-to-end model. It uses an autoregressive decoder to generate Semantic-ID candidates and a shared-encoder Ranking Module distilled from a training-only Teacher Ranker via Rollout Distillation, achieving a 1.41% increase in active users when deployed at Yandex Music.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional multi-stage recommendation cascades (candidate generation → pre-ranking → final ranking) are effective but involve repeated user-history processing, complex feature pipelines, and multiple serving stages. Semantic-ID-based generative retrieval simplifies this, but next-item prediction alone fails to capture the fine-grained preferences that production ranking objectives encode. The authors aim to unify generation and ranking into one model without adding a costly second model to the serving path.

Method: Gryphon-v2 employs a shared encoder that processes user history once, an autoregressive decoder that generates Semantic-ID candidates, and an item-level Ranking Module that reuses encoder states to score resolved catalogue items. A high-capacity Teacher Ranker (training-only) is distilled into the Ranking Module using Rollout Distillation: teacher scores serve as the sole ranking supervision and are collected over two complementary candidate distributions — decoder rollouts (matching the serving-time generation mechanism) and logged impressions (items users were actually shown).

Result: In an online A/B experiment at Yandex Music, a single Gryphon-v2 model replaced a production cascade of 15+ candidate generators, pre-ranking, and final ranking. The deployment yielded a 1.41% increase in active users while maintaining serving latency comparable to the original cascade.

Conclusion: A generative retriever augmented with a Ranking Module distilled from a Teacher Ranker via Rollout Distillation is a practically viable end-to-end replacement for multi-stage production recommendation cascades, delivering both simplified architecture and improved user engagement.

Abstract: Industrial recommender systems are commonly deployed as multi-stage cascades with separate candidate generators, pre-rankers, and final rankers. Although effective, these cascades require repeated user-history processing, complex feature pipelines, and multiple serving stages. Semantic-ID-based generative retrieval offers a path toward simpler end-to-end systems, but next-item prediction alone does not capture the fine-grained preferences encoded by production ranking objectives. We present Gryphon-v2, a unified generate-and-rank architecture for end-to-end recommendation. The model encodes a user history once, generates Semantic-ID candidates with an autoregressive decoder, resolves them to catalogue items, and ranks them with an item-level Ranking Module that reuses the shared encoder states. To transfer fine-grained production ranking preferences without adding an expensive second model to the serving path, we distill a high-capacity, training-only Teacher Ranker into the Ranking Module. Gryphon-v2 is trained with Rollout Distillation: teacher scores are the only ranking supervision, and they are collected over two complementary candidate distributions. Rollouts from the current decoder expose the Ranking Module to candidates produced by the same generation mechanism used at serving time, while logged impressions cover items users were actually shown. In an online A/B experiment on a large-scale recommendation surface at Yandex Music, a single Gryphon-v2 model replaces a production cascade comprising more than 15 candidate generators, pre-ranking, and final ranking. The deployment increases the number of active users by 1.41% at serving latency comparable to the production cascade. These results support the practical viability of a generative retriever with a Ranking Module distilled from the Teacher Ranker as an end-to-end alternative to a production cascade.

</details>
