### [173] [Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05223)
*Rui Yang,Michael Fu,Kla Tantithamthavorn,Chetan Arora,Joey Chua*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper exposes a critical vulnerability in autonomous coding agents: malicious shell commands can be disguised within natural-language skill files. The authors created a benchmark of 2,826 adversarial skills spanning 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics and tested two enterprise agents, finding exploitation rates of 95.5-96.1% (Gemini CLI) and 71.6-74.0% (Qwen Code), with explicit safety recognition in only 1.99% of runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As autonomous coding agents are increasingly deployed in enterprise settings with delegated access to systems, the skill interface—folders of instructions and scripts that agents dynamically load—becomes a dangerously expanded attack surface. The authors aim to systematically characterize and quantify how easily malicious commands can be concealed within benign-appearing natural-language skill files, since current safety mechanisms appear largely blind to this vector.

Method: The authors developed an adversarial skill-synthesis pipeline using six LLMs (across four model families) to transform 471 real-world shell commands into natural-language skill files that appear benign. They constructed a reproducible evaluation pipeline featuring run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, a deterministic declared-intent override, and a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel validated against a blind human gold standard (Cohen's κ = 0.85). Two enterprise-grade agents (Gemini CLI and Qwen Code) were tested across 5,629 completed runs, with results reported from raw majority vote through to declared-intent-corrected estimates.

Result: Gemini CLI was successfully exploited in 95.5–96.1% of runs and Qwen Code in 71.6–74.0% (range spanning raw majority vote to declared-intent-corrected estimates, both within the human gold standard). These exploitation rates were nearly invariant to which LLM generated the adversarial skill. Explicit safety recognition occurred in only 1.99% of all runs, indicating that current guardrails are effectively absent against this attack vector.

Conclusion: The skill interface represents a severe and underappreciated attack surface in agentic enterprise systems. Enterprises must rigorously assess and mitigate skill-interface risks before adopting autonomous coding agents. The authors release their benchmark (2,826 skills across 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics) and code to facilitate further research and defense development.

Abstract: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly embedded in enterprise software workflows with delegated authority over connected systems. Central to this architecture is the agent skills interface: folders of instructions and scripts that agents load dynamically to specialize their behavior. This interface also widens the attack surface, letting malicious shell commands hide within natural-language skill files. We make three contributions. First, an adversarial skill-synthesis method using six LLMs across four families to transform 471 real-world shell commands into benign-appearing skills, released as a benchmark of 2,826 skills mapped to 11 MITRE ATT&CK tactics. Second, a reproducible evaluation pipeline coupling run stratification, evidence anchoring, a refusal veto, and a deterministic declared-intent override with a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel, validated against a blind human gold standard (Cohen's kappa = 0.85). Third, a large-scale characterization of two enterprise-grade agents across 5,629 completed runs. Gemini CLI is exploited in 95.5-96.1% of runs and Qwen Code in 71.6-74.0% (raw majority vote to declared-intent-corrected estimate, both within the human gold standard), nearly invariant to the generating model. Explicit safety recognition occurs in only 1.99% of runs. Enterprises must assess and mitigate skill-interface risk before adopting coding agents. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/awsm-research/AgentJailbreak

</details>


### [174] [Improving Debugging in Verification-Aware Languages Through Automated Fault Localization: A Case Study in Dafny](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05399)
*Álvaro Silva,Isabel Amaral,João Pascoal Faria,Alexandra Mendes*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper compares state-based and counterexample-based fault localization techniques for Dafny, finding that structured single-trace ranking and multi-trace aggregation of counterexamples significantly outperform state-based methods like AutoFix's snapshot approach. The study uses a mutant dataset (MutDafny) and EXAM score for evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When Dafny verification fails, feedback is limited to the specific violated condition (e.g., a failed postcondition) rather than the root cause. While counterexample traces exist, they expose only a single failing path per assertion, forcing developers to manually inspect entire traces. This motivates automated fault localization that pinpoints the actual error location.

Method: Two paradigms are compared: (1) state-based localization, replicating AutoFix's snapshot methodology via inferred invariants and predicates to flag suspicious program states; (2) counterexample-based localization, a family of techniques progressing from raw counterexample extraction to structured single-trace ranking and multi-trace aggregation. Evaluation uses MutDafny to generate mutants from DafnyBench, with effectiveness measured by the EXAM score.

Result: Counterexample-based approaches substantially outperform state-based localization. Structured single-trace ranking yields the largest improvement over raw counterexamples. Multi-trace aggregation further improves robustness and debugging utility by increasing coverage and reducing solver-induced path bias.

Conclusion: Effective fault localization in verification-aware languages depends on leveraging counterexample information, and critically on how that information is structured and diversified across multiple traces.

Abstract: Verification-aware languages, like Dafny, integrate formal specifications directly into source code to enable static correctness checks. However, when verification fails, the feedback provided is often limited to the specific condition of the error, such as a violated postcondition, rather than the root cause of the fault. While Dafny's counterexample features provide concrete execution traces, these typically expose a single failing path per assertion failure, leaving the developer to manually look through the entire trace to locate the error.
  This paper investigates automated fault localization for verification-aware languages by comparing two paradigms: state-based and counterexample-based localization. Our state-based localization strategy replicates the ``snapshot'' methodology of AutoFix by inferring invariants and predicates to identify suspicious program states. The counterexample-based strategy consists of a family of techniques that progressively enrich the use of verifier output: from raw counterexample extraction, to structured single-trace ranking, and to multi-trace aggregation.
  To validate these methods, we present an evaluation framework using MutDafny to generate a diverse mutant dataset from DafnyBench and measure localization effectiveness using the EXAM score. Our results show that counterexample-based approaches substantially outperform state-based localization in this setting. Structured ranking over a single trace yields the largest improvement over raw counterexample output, while multi-trace aggregation provides additional gains in robustness and debugging utility by increasing coverage and reducing path bias introduced by the solver. These findings demonstrate that effective fault localization in verification-aware languages depends both on using counterexample information, and how that information is structured and diversified.

</details>


### [175] [Reasoning from Traces: Divergence-Guided Agentic Repair of WebAssembly Discrepancies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05521)
*Liyan Huang,Kaicheng Wang,Weihang Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: WasmMend is an automated system that repairs functional discrepancies between WebAssembly and native binaries compiled from the same C/C++ source code. It combines differential trace analysis to localize divergent functions with LLM-based reasoning to generate patches, achieving a 70.0% fix rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-compiling C/C++ to WebAssembly often produces binaries that behave differently from native builds due to library implementation differences or compiler bugs. These discrepancies are hard to detect and fix because root causes lie in platform-level runtime behavior hidden beneath source code, and even state-of-the-art LLM-based repair agents struggle with them.

Method: WasmMend operates in two stages: (1) differential trace analysis that localizes the specific function where Wasm and native executions first diverge, converting undirected exploration into a focused task; (2) LLM agents then reason about root causes using this localization and generate targeted patches to eliminate the divergent behavior.

Result: On real-world C/C++ projects, WasmMend achieves a 70.0% fix rate, outperforming the agentic baseline (50.2%) and an approach augmented with repair-time LLM-based instrumentation (54.5%).

Conclusion: Divergence-guided reasoning, enabled by differential trace analysis, significantly improves cross-platform repair of Native-Wasm functional discrepancies compared to undirected LLM-based approaches.

Abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) promises seamless reuse of C/C++ codebases as portable, fast, sandboxed binaries. In practice, however, this promise often falls short: recent studies show that cross-compiling the same C/C++ source to Wasm and native binaries frequently leads to runtime discrepancies, owing to library implementation differences or compiler bugs. Since the root causes lie in the platform-level runtime and are hidden beneath the source code, even state-of-the-art LLM-based repair agents often fail to fix these discrepancies. In this paper, we present WasmMend, the first system to automatically repair Native-Wasm functional discrepancies. WasmMend converts the undirected exploration to a focused reasoning task in two stages: First, a novel differential trace analysis approach localizes the function where Wasm and native executions initially diverge; guided by this localization, LLM agents then reason about the root causes and generate patches that eliminate the divergent behavior. Experiments on real-world C/C++ projects show that WasmMend achieves a fix rate of 70.0%, compared to 50.2% for the agentic baseline and 54.5\% for the approach augmented with repair-time LLM-based instrumentation, demonstrating the value of divergence-guided reasoning for cross-platform repair.

</details>


### [176] [Exploring Dependence, Overreliance, and Addiction Related Behaviors Associated with Large Language Model Use Among Software Engineers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05561)
*Ronnie de Souza Santos,Italo Santos,Matheus de Moraes Leça,Cleyton Magalhaes,Mairieli Wessel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An exploratory survey of 119 software practitioners reveals that LLM use in professional development is characterized primarily by functional dependence and overreliance patterns (e.g., prioritizing LLMs over documentation/peers), while addiction-related behaviors are rare and mostly involve emotional attachment rather than impaired control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly integrated into software engineering workflows, raising concerns about developers' dependence, overreliance, and potential addiction-related behaviors. The authors aim to empirically characterize how these behavioral patterns manifest in professional practice.

Method: An exploratory survey was administered to 119 software practitioners. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended responses to identify patterns of functional dependence, overreliance, and addiction-related behaviors.

Result: Functional dependence was dominant: LLMs are routinely used for productivity and efficiency. Overreliance patterns emerged, notably prioritizing LLMs over documentation and peer consultation while still verifying outputs. Addiction-related behaviors were uncommon, manifesting mainly as difficulty moderating use or emotional attachment rather than loss of control.

Conclusion: LLMs are becoming a habitual component of software engineering practice. While most use is functional, the findings highlight the need to promote appropriate reliance through trust calibration, professional judgment, and sustained verification practices.

Abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has changed how software engineers perform everyday development activities. While these systems provide substantial support for tasks such as code generation, debugging, and documentation, their increasing integration into professional workflows has also raised questions regarding developers' reliance on these tools and the emergence of dependence, overreliance, and addiction-related behaviors. This study investigates how software engineers experience the use of LLMs during professional software development, with attention to behavioral patterns associated with dependence, overreliance, and addiction-related behaviors. An exploratory survey was conducted with 119 software practitioners. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and qualitative thematic analysis of participants' open-ended responses. Participants primarily described functional dependence, with LLMs becoming integrated into routine software engineering activities because of the productivity and efficiency they provide. Responses also suggested patterns consistent with overreliance, particularly through prioritizing LLMs over documentation or peer consultation while continuing to verify generated outputs. Reports associated with addiction-related behaviors were less common and primarily reflected difficulty moderating use or emotional attachment to the technology rather than impaired control. The findings suggest that LLMs are becoming a habitual component of professional software engineering practice. While most reported use appears functional, the results indicate the importance of promoting appropriate reliance by supporting trust calibration, professional judgment, and verification throughout software development.

</details>


### [177] [JTA: Joint Testability Architecture for Scenario-Based Validation of Safety-Critical Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05594)
*Wenyao Xue,Jiandi Wang,Yichen Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: JTA is an architectural framework that models scenario-based validation as a tripartite system (scenario, test system, SUT), assessing capability through controllability, observability, and isolability dimensions, supported by scenario contracts and bridge-oriented design actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing testability research is artifact-centric and lacks architectural support for reasoning about the combined validation capability of scenarios, test systems, and the system under test together — a critical gap for safety-critical software where validation adequacy requires more than just focusing on the SUT.

Method: JTA treats scenario, test system, and SUT as a unified object of analysis. It characterizes validation capability along three dimensions (controllability, observability, isolability), organized through three domains, three bridges, and an iterative analysis-design-evaluation-refinement loop. It introduces scenario contracts, joint capability assessment, blind-spot identification, and bridge-oriented design actions that map gaps to concrete improvements.

Result: An illustrative application to ArduPilot failsafe validation demonstrated that link-loss scenarios are comparatively mature in validation capability, while state-estimation anomaly scenarios remain harder to validate due to weaker evidence alignment and attribution semantics.

Conclusion: JTA is not a replacement for existing testing or safety-analysis techniques but provides a foundational architectural basis for modeling, designing, and assessing scenario-based validation in safety-critical software systems.

Abstract: Validation adequacy in safety-critical software depends on more than the system under test. Critical scenarios must be constructed under controlled conditions, execution evidence must be aligned into verdict-ready form, and abnormal outcomes must be attributable to actionable causes. Existing testability research remains largely artifact-centric and offers little architectural support for reasoning about the combined capability of the scenario, the test system, and the system under test. Joint Testability Architecture (JTA) addresses this gap by treating those three elements as a single object of analysis and design. It characterizes validation capability along three dimensions--controllability, observability, and isolability--and organizes them through three domains, three bridges, and an analysis-design-evaluation-refinement loop. JTA also introduces scenario contracts, joint capability assessment, validation blind-spot identification, and bridge-oriented design actions that map capability gaps to concrete improvements in control points, evidence organization, and attribution boundaries. An illustrative analysis of ArduPilot failsafe validation shows that link-loss scenarios are comparatively mature, whereas state-estimation anomaly scenarios remain harder to validate because evidence alignment and attribution semantics are weaker. JTA is not a replacement for existing testing or safety-analysis techniques; it provides an architectural basis for modeling, designing, and assessing scenario-based validation in safety-critical software.

</details>


### [178] [Towards Competence-Based Management for Open Source Software Projects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05599)
*Sabahat Younas,Márcia Moraes,Fabio Santos*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a competence assessment model for OSS contributors using code metrics from their contributions to predict competence levels required for tasks, aiming to identify and train replacements for disengaging core contributors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OSS projects face a growing risk of core contributor disengagement, threatening project survival. Replacing these contributors is difficult and time-consuming due to insufficient knowledge about potential candidates' actual competence levels, which current approaches fail to capture in depth.

Method: The authors collect code metrics from contributors' source code submissions and propose a competence model that predicts the competence level required to solve specific tasks. This enables systematic assessment of contributor capabilities.

Result: A replication package containing code, data, and documentation is provided, indicating empirical validation was conducted, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: Properly assessing contributor competences through code metrics enables identification and targeted training of candidates to replace disengaging core contributors, helping sustain OSS project health.

Abstract: Contributors to Open Source Software (OSS) projects are vital to maintaining the health of both communities and projects. However, the number of projects experiencing core contributors' disengagement has increased to the point that it risks the projects' survival. Finding new contributors to replace the workforce is challenging and time-intensive due to several factors, including a lack of precise knowledge about potential candidates' competences, which may need to be confirmed through interviews and exams. Previous studies provided indications of the contributor's competences, although they lack depth in understanding competence levels, which can result in poor knowledge about the contributor's capabilities. To address this gap, we assess contributors' competence by collecting code metrics related to source code from contributions. We also propose a competence model able to predict the competence level required to solve tasks. By properly assessing contributors' competences, we can identify and train candidates to replace core contributors. Our replication package, including code, data, and documentation, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21605122

</details>


### [179] [Keeping Models and Code in Sync: Roundtrip Engineering for Tactical Domain-Driven Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05612)
*Weixing Zhang,Mario Herb,Wai Chung Dorothy Cheng,Michael Wagner,Bowen Jiang,Tianhai Liu,Anne Koziolek*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: JDomInO is a bidirectional synchronization toolchain that keeps Java code and domain models aligned in Domain-Driven Design by generating code from models (forward) and reconstructing models from code (reverse), with full forward validation on a Hotel Management scenario and ongoing reverse validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In Domain-Driven Design (DDD), the shared vocabulary embodied in the domain model must stay aligned with the actual codebase. In practice, model-code drift is common — code evolves faster than model updates, or model revisions fail to propagate to code — undermining the utility of the ubiquitous language.

Method: JDomInO implements a bidirectional synchronization toolchain for tactical DDD based on a shared metamodel. The forward path deterministically generates Java code structure from a domain model. The reverse path reconstructs a domain model from existing Java code through mapping logic. The metamodel covers 12 building block types.

Result: The forward path was fully validated on a Hotel Management scenario encompassing all 12 building block types. The reverse path's mapping logic passed unit testing; end-to-end validation is still in progress.

Conclusion: JDomInO demonstrates a viable round-trip engineering approach for tactical DDD. The structured domain model it produces could also function as a precision context layer for AI code assistants, enabling them to respect aggregate boundaries and DDD semantics invisible in raw source code.

Abstract: Domain-Driven Design gives teams a shared vocabulary for complex business logic, but that vocabulary only stays useful as long as the model and the code agree with each other. In practice, they drift apart: code changes outpace the model, or model revisions never make it into the codebase. This paper presents JDomInO, a bidirectional synchronization toolchain for tactical DDD that keeps a Java codebase and its domain model connected through a shared metamodel, with the goal of keeping the two in sync as the system evolves. JDomInO generates Java code structure deterministically from a domain model (forward path) and reconstructs a domain model from existing Java code (reverse path). The forward path has been fully validated on a Hotel Management scenario covering all 12 building block types in the metamodel; the reverse path's mapping logic has passed unit testing, with end-to-end validation underway. We also outline how the structured domain model produced by JDomInO could serve as a precision context layer for AI code assistants, helping them respect aggregate boundaries and DDD semantics that raw source code alone does not convey.

</details>


### [180] [Agent-Based Test Assertion Generation via Diverse Perspective Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05822)
*Dong Wang,Qiaoyu Han,Lin Yang,Jianyi Zhou,Guangtai Liang,Junjie Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AssertMate is an agent-based framework that improves LLM-driven test assertion generation through three components: static analysis for actual values, multi-perspective expected value prediction (code generation, RAG, CoT), and an LLM-as-a-Judge selector. It significantly outperforms existing methods on Defects4J and integrates effectively with EvoSuite.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based assertion generation (e.g., ChatAssert) suffers from modest accuracy, heavy reliance on oversampling, and vulnerability to model randomness due to one-shot prompting. These limitations motivate the need for a more robust, multi-perspective approach.

Method: AssertMate uses a three-component agent-based framework: (1) actual value construction via static analysis and type-aware heuristics to identify assertion targets; (2) multi-perspective expected value prediction using three agents — code generation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning; and (3) an LLM-as-a-Judge collaboration mechanism to select the best assertion from candidates.

Result: On the Defects4J benchmark, AssertMate significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in compilation success, pass rates, and bug detection. Integration with EvoSuite yields superior mutation coverage and kill counts. Ablation studies confirm each component contributes significantly and complementarily.

Conclusion: Aggregating diverse perspectives through a multi-agent collaboration framework substantially enhances LLM-based assertion generation, validating the approach's effectiveness and practical utility in automated test generation pipelines.

Abstract: Test assertions are critical elements of unit tests, serving as checkpoints to validate expected behavior and ensure software correctness. Numerous techniques have been proposed to automate assertion generation, with recent progress notably driven by large language models (LLMs). Despite the promise, existing approaches such as ChatAssert suffer from modest accuracy, heavy reliance on oversampling, and vulnerability to model randomness due to one-shot prompting. To address these limitations, we propose AssertMate, a novel agent-based assertion generation framework that enhances the quality and reliability of LLM-generated assertions through three key components: (1) actual value construction that identifies assertion targets via static analysis and type-aware heuristics; (2) multi-perspective expected value prediction using code generation, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning agents; and (3) an LLM-as-a-Judge collaboration mechanism to select the most appropriate assertion. Evaluation on the Defects4J benchmark demonstrates that AssertMate significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in compilation success and pass rates, along with substantially higher bug detection capabilities. Integration with EvoSuite further validates AssertMate's practicality, yielding superior mutation coverage and kill counts. Ablation studies reveal that each of the three components makes a significant and complementary contribution to the overall performance. This work affirms the great potential of aggregating diverse perspectives to enhance the effectiveness of LLM-based assertion generation.

</details>


### [181] [CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05886)
*Wuya Chen,Yihao yang,Yang Cao,Yue Lin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CodeGrep is a 14B retrieval agent trained with GRPO that performs multi-turn parallel repository search (grep, glob, read) to find relevant files for downstream coding agents. It improves efficiency on SWE-Bench Verified by reducing rounds (-15%) and tokens (-19%) while maintaining resolve rate, demonstrating that retrieval quality must cross a precision threshold (~0.677) to benefit agent efficiency rather than degrade it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLM coding agents waste substantial token budgets on repository exploration (grep, glob, view_file) rather than actual patching. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per issue, with exploration dominating costs. The authors aim to offload this expensive file-finding process to a specialized, efficient retrieval agent that can reduce downstream costs without sacrificing resolve rate.

Method: The authors introduce CodeGrep, a 14B retrieval model trained end-to-end using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It performs multi-turn parallel tool calls (grep, glob, read) and returns candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent. Training supervision is mined from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM, and a custom Git-worktree environment is built for multi-turn RL. A key design choice: the efficiency signal is applied at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer, which reduces KL drift and improves downstream efficiency translation.

Result: On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep achieves 27.0% resolve rate versus 25.8% baseline (no retrieval), with 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances. A precision threshold phenomenon is observed: BM25 (precision 0.375) degrades the agent, Jina (0.445) is neutral, and CodeGrep (0.677) crosses the threshold where retrieval begins reducing rollout cost.

Conclusion: Specialized retrieval agents like CodeGrep can offload repository exploration from coding agents, improving token and round efficiency while maintaining solve rates. Retrieval quality must exceed a minimum precision threshold to be beneficial. Applying efficiency signals at the advantage layer rather than reward layer proves critical for stable RL training and downstream performance.

Abstract: Modern LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenHands share a common inefficiency: they spend much of their token budget finding the file to patch, rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with many calls spent on grep, glob, and view_file during repository exploration. We introduce CodeGrep, a 14B retrieval agent trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep, glob, and read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent.
  On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep preserves resolve rate while substantially improving efficiency: 27.0% versus 25.8% for the no-retrieval baseline, with 15% fewer rounds and 19% fewer tokens on resolved instances. Across retrievers, downstream utility follows a precision threshold: BM25 with precision 0.375 degrades the agent, Jina with precision 0.445 is neutral, and CodeGrep with precision 0.677 crosses the threshold at which retrieval begins to reduce rollout cost. To enable this study, we mine supervision from 67K open-source agent trajectories using CATM and build a Git-worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL. In our setting, applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer reduces KL drift and translates cleanly into downstream efficiency. We will release the model, training pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

</details>


### [182] [Mapping the Emerging Curriculum for AI-Assisted Software Engineering via Syllabus Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05898)
*Francis Geng,Anshul Shah,Mia Chen,Paul Denny,Juho Leinonen,Bill Griswold,Gerald Soosai Raj,Leo Porter*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study analyzes 23 publicly available syllabi of upper-division, credit-bearing university courses that explicitly address Generative AI in software engineering, using iterative qualitative coding to characterize learning objectives, assessments, topics, and AI tools, revealing commonalities and differences to guide future curriculum design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As Generative AI coding tools (e.g., GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT) increasingly reshape professional software development workflows, universities are designing new courses to prepare students for AI-assisted development. However, there is limited empirical evidence about how this emerging curricular area is being defined and structured. The study aims to fill this gap by systematically analyzing course syllabi to understand current pedagogical approaches and inform future curriculum development.

Method: The authors collected 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials from upper-division, credit-bearing courses that explicitly address Generative AI in software engineering contexts. They employed iterative qualitative coding to systematically characterize each course across four key dimensions: learning objectives, assessment methods, topics covered, and documented AI tools used or discussed.

Result: The analysis revealed both commonalities and differences across the 23 courses. Commonalities included shared learning objectives around critical evaluation of AI-generated code and ethical considerations. Differences emerged in assessment strategies (ranging from traditional exams to AI-augmented projects), topic breadth (from narrow AI-code-generation focus to broader socio-technical coverage), and the specific AI tools documented in syllabi. These findings provide an empirical foundation for understanding how AI-assisted software engineering education is currently being defined.

Conclusion: The systematic characterization of existing AI-in-SE courses provides a valuable empirical baseline for both researchers studying computing education and educators designing future curricula. The identified patterns and variations offer concrete guidance for curriculum design, highlighting key topics, assessment approaches, and tools that constitute this emerging field.

Abstract: As Generative AI coding tools reshape professional software development, universities have begun designing courses to prepare students for AI-assisted development workflows. By analyzing the syllabi of these courses, we can gather empirical evidence about these courses, reveal how this emerging curricular area is being defined, and gain guidance for future curriculum design. We analyzed 23 publicly available syllabi and course materials of upper-division, credit-bearing courses that meet specific criteria, including explicitly addressing Generative AI in software engineering. Through iterative qualitative coding, we characterized courses' learning objectives, assessments, topics, and documented AI tools. Our analysis reveals commonalities and differences among these courses that allow researchers and educators to study and develop future courses.

</details>


### [183] [Escaping the Self-Repair Trap: Improving Test Oracle Generation via Dual-Context Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05917)
*Kefan Li,Hongyue Yu,Yuan Yuan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper identifies a "Self-Repair Trap" where iterative LLM-based repair for regression oracle generation progressively degrades fault-revealing capability despite improving execution success. The authors propose DCAware, a non-iterative framework that uses structured static context and selectively retrieved dynamic states, achieving better fault detection at lower computational cost than iterative methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Iterative self-repair with execution feedback is widely used for regression-oracle completion, but optimizing for execution success is a misaligned proxy for the true goal of generating effective fault-revealing oracles. This misalignment causes feedback-driven degeneration, dubbed the Self-Repair Trap, where models converge toward trivially satisfiable assertions that fail to detect faults.

Method: DCAware is a non-iterative, computationally efficient framework that prioritizes high signal-to-noise contextual grounding. It integrates structured static context (program structure, type information) with selectively retrieved dynamic states (runtime values, execution traces) to enable precise oracle generation in a single pass, avoiding multi-round repair loops entirely.

Result: Extensive experiments using execution and mutation testing show DCAware consistently improves fault-revealing effectiveness while maintaining high execution success, outperforming prior iterative methods with substantially lower computational cost.

Conclusion: Improving contextual quality is more effective than adding iterative repair complexity for regression-oracle generation. The Self-Repair Trap demonstrates that execution-feedback loops can be counterproductive, and structured, context-rich single-pass generation offers a superior alternative.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for regression-oracle completion, where a test prefix is given and the current program version is treated as expected behavior. Recent approaches increasingly rely on iterative self-repair and execution feedback, but optimizing execution success does not necessarily yield strong fault-revealing oracles. This objective, widely adopted in repair-based methods, serves only as a proxy and may be misaligned with the true goal of oracle generation. Such misalignment biases the repair process, giving rise to a feedback-driven degeneration that we term the Self-Repair Trap, where iterative repair progressively drives models toward assertions that are easier to satisfy but less effective at detecting faults. To address this issue, we propose DCAware, a computationally efficient, non-iterative framework that prioritizes high signal-to-noise contextual grounding over multi-round repair. DCAware integrates structured static context with selectively retrieved dynamic states, enabling precise and robust oracle generation without iterative feedback loops. Extensive experiments based on execution and mutation testing show that DCAware consistently improves fault-revealing effectiveness while maintaining high execution success, outperforming prior methods with substantially lower computational cost. Our results suggest that improving contextual quality is more effective than adding iterative repair complexity in the studied regression-oracle setting.

</details>


### [184] [Expertise-Based Developer Assignment for Long-Term Software Components in Open-Source Projects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05919)
*Faheem Ullah,Babar Shah,William Shanks,Ayesha Mohsin,Abrar Ullah*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A web application that models developer expertise from Git history and automatically assigns developers to tasks in new projects, achieving 72.4% recall of target developers within the top-10 recommendations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual task assignment in open-source projects often mismatches developers to tasks outside their expertise, leading to slower completion and lower code maintainability. Existing automation focuses on specific job types but neglects long-term, expertise-aligned component assignment for new projects.

Method: A web application that extracts and models developer expertise from historical Git commits, then uses this model to match and assign developers to optimal tasks within a new project. Server-side data caching is employed to improve performance.

Result: Server-side caching improved worst-case response speeds by a factor of 9.86. In evaluation, 72.4% of tasks had their correct target developer ranked within the top 10 out of 47 possible developers.

Conclusion: The system effectively automates expertise-based developer-to-task assignment for new open-source projects, with caching substantially mitigating performance bottlenecks and recommendation accuracy proving practically useful.

Abstract: Open-source software development through GitHub has enabled countless software projects to be developed by developers from across the world. Assigning the right task to the right developer enables teams to work efficiently. Assigning a task which is not representative of a developer's expertise results in slower completion time and less maintainable code. Whilst much work has been done to automate this assignment for specific jobs, there is little work addressing the assignment of developers to expertise-specific long-term components of a new project. This paper produces a web application that models developers' expertise based on their previous Git commits and automatically assigns them to an optimal task within a new project. Testing showed that the system's speed varies depending on the back-end model used but server-side data caching improved worst-case speeds by a factor of 9.86. 72.4% of tasks had their target developer listed in the top 10, out of a possible 47.

</details>


### [185] [Sensor-Level Fault Diagnosis for Automotive Software Validation Using Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05921)
*Mohammad Abboush,Hamza Ouarrad,Andreas Rausch*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes using instruction-tuned LLMs with low-rank adaptation for fault detection and diagnosis in automotive HIL validation, achieving 81.6% accuracy on a gasoline-engine case study while providing interpretable justifications, with performance depending on convergence rather than model size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current threshold-based tools for automotive HIL validation can only flag deviations without identifying their nature or source, while data-driven classifiers require large labeled datasets and offer opaque decisions incompatible with ISO 26262 traceability demands.

Method: A two-phase framework: (1) automated requirement checking on a dSPACE real-time platform isolates violating recordings; (2) only violating recordings are inspected via sliding windows reduced to statistical, relational, and contextual descriptors, embedded in a fixed prompt, and mapped by a 4-bit low-rank-adapted (LoRA) instruction-tuned LLM to a fault location with written justification. Four model families (2B–8B parameters) were tested across six injected fault classes on a gasoline-engine case study.

Result: The smallest model matched the largest at 81.6% accuracy. A comparably sized model failed to converge, demonstrating that diagnostic competence under task-specific adaptation depends on convergence rather than parameter count. The entire adapt-and-evaluate cycle fits on a single commodity accelerator.

Conclusion: Instruction-tuned LLMs with low-rank adaptation offer a data-efficient, interpretable alternative for fault detection and diagnosis in automotive HIL validation, with practical feasibility on commodity hardware and performance governed by adaptation convergence, not model size.

Abstract: The pre-series validation of automotive software on hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) platforms produces large volumes of multivariate sensor recordings whose assessment against functional safety requirements exceeds what manual review can sustain at campaign scale. Threshold-based tooling reports that a deviation has occurred but neither identifies its nature nor locates its source, while data-driven classifiers, although accurate, rely on large labelled datasets and return opaque decisions that sit uneasily with the traceability demanded by ISO 26262. This study examines whether open-source instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), given a textual description of sensor behaviour, can serve as data-efficient and interpretable engines for fault detection and diagnosis inside the validation loop. A two-phase framework is proposed: automated requirement checking on a dSPACE real-time platform first isolates the recordings that violate a safety requirement, and only these are inspected, with sliding windows of the signals reduced to statistical, relational, and contextual descriptors, embedded in a fixed prompt, and mapped by a 4-bit low-rank-adapted LLM to a fault location accompanied by a written justification. Four model families ranging from two to eight billion parameters were adapted and tested on a gasoline-engine case study spanning six injected fault classes. The smallest model matched the largest at 81.6\% accuracy, whereas a comparably sized model failed to converge, indicating that diagnostic competence under task-specific adaptation follows convergence rather than parameter count, with the entire adapt-and-evaluate cycle fitting on a single commodity accelerator.

</details>


### [186] [AgentExecutor: Partial Code Execution via Agentic Context Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05959)
*Junkai Chen,Chengran Yang,Xing Hu,Zhenhao Li,Xin Xia,David Lo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentExecutor is a multi-agent LLM framework for partial code execution that achieves up to 94% code coverage, outperforming Treefix by 19.9%, while reducing execution time by up to 80.3% and cost by up to 56.6%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing partial code execution tools (LExecutor, Treefix) are limited by restricted action spaces, inadequate feedback, and rigid optimization strategies, which hinder both effectiveness and efficiency in executing arbitrary code snippets with missing context and dependencies.

Method: A three-phase multi-agent framework: (1) execution environment preparation, (2) dynamic exploration with iterative refinement using LLM agents that think, act, and receive feedback, and (3) prefix evolution via program synthesis. Key techniques include coverage-guided context pruning and adaptive optimization for diverse operations like creating resource files and resolving environment configurations.

Result: On Stack Overflow snippets and open-source project code datasets, AgentExecutor achieves up to 94% and 90% code coverage respectively, outperforming Treefix by 19.9% and 13.8%. It also reduces execution time by up to 80.3% and cost by up to 56.6%.

Conclusion: AgentExecutor provides an effective and efficient solution for partial code execution by leveraging autonomous LLM agents with richer action spaces and adaptive optimization strategies.

Abstract: Executing code snippets is essential for dynamic program analysis, but it remains challenging to execute an arbitrary code snippet due to issues like missing context and incomplete dependencies. Existing approaches to partial code execution, such as LExecutor and Treefix, leverage the power of language models to infer missing information and enable execution. However, they suffer from (i) limited action spaces and feedback, and (ii) rigid optimization strategies, which restrict their effectiveness and efficiency. In this paper, we propose AgentExecutor, a novel multi-agent framework for partial code execution. Our approach introduces a three-phase design: execution environment preparation, dynamic exploration with iterative refinement, and prefix evolution via program synthesis. Supported by the power of LLM agents who can think, act, and get feedback iteratively, AgentExecutor is able to autonomously explore a richer action space, enabling diverse operations such as creating resource files and resolving environment configuration. Furthermore, it adopts adaptive optimization strategies, including coverage-guided context pruning and prefix evolution via program synthesis, to systematically improve the execution quality of partial code. We evaluate AgentExecutor on two widely used datasets comprising Stack Overflow snippets and open-source project code. The results show that AgentExecutor achieves up to 94% and 90% code coverage, outperforming the state-of-the-art approach Treefix by 19.9% and 13.8%, respectively. In addition, AgentExecutor significantly reduces execution time (by up to 80.3%) and cost (by up to 56.6%). These findings demonstrate that AgentExecutor provides an effective and efficient solution for partial code execution.

</details>


### [187] [LangChoiceBench: Measuring and Explaining Programming-Language Choice in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06041)
*Lukas Twist,Twm Stone,Helen Yannakoudakis,Jie M. Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LangChoiceBench is a benchmark for measuring LLM language preferences in project-level code generation. Evaluation of 25 models reveals strong Python over-selection, low recommendation-implementation consistency, and reasoning failures including automatic Python choices and "phantom evidence" fabrication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit strong Python preferences in project-level code generation, but no systematic method exists to measure this across models. The authors aim to quantify Python preference, consistency between language recommendations and actual implementation, and overall language diversity.

Method: The authors introduce LangChoiceBench, a benchmark spanning 28 projects across 7 software domains where Python is suboptimal. They evaluate 25 diverse LLMs (varying in size and openness) and analyze 9,826 reasoning traces to understand the mechanisms behind language selection decisions.

Result: Python is heavily over-selected across models. Recommendation-implementation consistency is low. Smaller open-weight models exhibit stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. Analysis of reasoning traces shows most Python choices are automatic or ease-driven rather than requirement-driven. Two failure modes identified: "phantom evidence" (fabricating contextual support for Python) and code that contradicts the model's own stated language recommendation.

Conclusion: LLMs systematically over-select Python for project-level code generation, often without deliberate reasoning about project requirements, and the phenomenon of phantom evidence represents a concerning reliability issue in model reasoning about language choice.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit strong Python preferences when generating project-level code, but there is currently no systematic way to measure this behaviour across new models. To bridge this gap, we introduce LangChoiceBench, a project-level code-generation benchmark for measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. LangChoiceBench covers 28 projects across seven software areas where Python is often a poor default. We evaluate 25 diverse LLMs and find that Python remains heavily over-selected, recommendation-implementation consistency is low, and smaller open-weight models generally show stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. We further analyse 9,826 reasoning traces and find that most Python choices are automatic or driven primarily by ease, rather than explicit consideration of project requirements. In a smaller but important set of cases, models fabricate contextual support for choosing Python - a failure mode we call phantom evidence - or produce code that contradicts the language selected in their own reasoning.

</details>


### [188] [In Terms of Explainability: Refining Requirements for Self-Explainable Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06049)
*Arno Leue,Akhila Bairy,Maike Schwammberger*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes unified definitions and a structured taxonomy of explainability requirements for autonomous and software-intensive systems, incorporating "explanation goodness" (correctness) to support the development of formal standards, certification, and auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous and software-intensive systems are increasingly complex and responsible, yet no universally applicable definition or development guide for (self-)explainable systems exists. The EU AI Act and IEEE 7001-2021 acknowledge this gap, motivating the need for unified explainability standards.

Method: The authors analyze and synthesize existing definitions of explainability, derive structured explainability requirements, and construct a taxonomy. They then augment this taxonomy with the concept of "explanation goodness" (correctness of explanations).

Result: A set of unified definitions for explainability, a structured taxonomy of explainability requirements, and the incorporation of explanation goodness/correctness into the definitions, forming a foundation for formal standards.

Conclusion: Establishing a uniform taxonomy for explainability is a crucial step toward developing formal standards, enabling certification and auditing of (self-)explainable systems, and aligning with emerging regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act.

Abstract: Autonomous and software-intensive systems have been growing in occurrence, complexity, and assumed responsibility. Due to the high complexity of these systems, properties like transparency and explainability must be a focus of investigation. To date, no universally applicable definition and guide for the development of (self-)explainable systems exists. A need for explainability standards has already been recognized in the EU AI Act and the IEEE Transparency Standard 7001-2021. To address this need, we propose unified definitions in explainability based on an analysis and combination of existing definitions. Additionally, we present structured explainability requirements that are necessary to build (self-)explainable systems. By analysing the resulting taxonomy, we propose the incorporation of explanation goodness and thus correctness of explanations into the unified definitions. With our approach, we support the development of formal standards for (self-)explainable systems. Establishing such a uniform taxonomy also is a beneficial step towards certifying or auditing explainable systems.

</details>


### [189] [DCAS: Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding to Internalize Planning across Scaffolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06113)
*Kishanthan Thangarajah,Boyuan Chen,Ahmed E. Hassan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CLI-based software engineering agents suffer from scaffold overfitting: models fine-tuned on trajectories from one scaffold (OpenHands) perform poorly on others. The authors identify planning structure—both explicit (pre-execution plans) and implicit (loop-level conventions)—as the key scaffold-specific behavior. They introduce DCAS, a backend-substitution layer enabling cross-scaffold evaluation and planning-aware data collection, and demonstrate that planning-aware fine-tuning closes the cross-scaffold gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-source CLI-based SE agents are almost exclusively fine-tuned on OpenHands-collected trajectories, causing significant performance degradation when deployed under different scaffolds. This scaffold overfitting threatens the generalizability and real-world utility of fine-tuned models. The authors aim to diagnose the root cause and provide a remediation strategy.

Method: The authors propose DCAS (Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding), a backend-substitution interception layer that transparently routes API traffic between any CLI scaffold and any backend model without modifying either. This enables: (1) cross-scaffold evaluation to quantify the overfitting gap; (2) controlled plan-source interventions to isolate planning quality as a causal factor; and (3) collection of planning-aware trajectories that capture explicit and implicit planning as learnable model capabilities rather than fixed scaffold artifacts.

Result: Base (non-fine-tuned) models show no cross-scaffold performance divergence, confirming the gap is fine-tuning-induced. A controlled intervention shows planning quality is high-leverage, with gains exceeding the observed cross-scaffold drops. Fine-tuning on a small set of DCAS-collected planning-aware trajectories from a single scaffold yields consistent gains across non-training scaffolds. Explicit and implicit planning are empirically separable in the training data.

Conclusion: Scaffold overfitting in CLI agents is driven primarily by planning structure conventions baked into training data. Moving planning from a fixed scaffold artifact to a learned model capability—via DCAS-enabled planning-aware trajectory collection—effectively closes the cross-scaffold generalization gap, improving robustness across diverse deployment environments.

Abstract: CLI-based software-engineering agents have matured rapidly, yet the open ecosystem has converged on a single training environment: trajectory datasets used to fine-tune open models are collected almost exclusively under OpenHands. Models fine-tuned on this data score well under OpenHands but degrade substantially when deployed under any non-training scaffold. Untrained base models do not show this divergence, indicating the gap is fine-tuning-induced and tied to the conventions of the training scaffold. We argue that a load-bearing scaffold-specific behavior is planning structure, in two senses this paper distinguishes: explicit planning, a pre-execution plan produced as a first-class artifact, and implicit planning, the structural conventions that shape execution throughout the agent loop. Under this hypothesis, closing the gap requires moving planning from a fixed scaffold artifact to a learned model capability. We introduce Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding (DCAS), a backend-substitution interception layer that routes API traffic between any CLI scaffold and any backend model without modifying the scaffold, enabling cross-scaffold evaluation and planning-aware trajectory collection. Using DCAS, a controlled plan-source intervention confirms planning quality is a high-leverage component, with gains exceeding the cross-scaffold drops we observe. A model fine-tuned on a small set of DCAS-collected planning-aware trajectories under a single scaffold gains consistently across non-training scaffolds, and the two senses of planning are empirically separable in training data.

</details>


### [190] [Learning Globally Reusable Skills for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06153)
*Chen Yang,Jiashuo Tian,Ziqi Wang,Xinyin Liu,Meiru Ye,Junjie Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: GSE is a framework for evolving LLM agent skills that jointly optimizes skill compatibility via a Skill Relation Graph (SRG) and skill generalization through cluster-based consolidation and replay-driven verification, outperforming existing methods on software engineering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated skill evolution methods treat updates as isolated local changes, ignoring inter-skill relationships, which leads to overfitting and poor generalization. There is a need for a framework that considers global skill structure and prevents behavioral regression.

Method: GSE introduces: (1) a Skill Relation Graph (SRG) that explicitly models and co-evolves inter-skill relationships for consistency; (2) cluster-based skill consolidation to abstract reusable capabilities from local updates; and (3) replay-driven verification to prevent overfitting and behavioral regression.

Result: On bug-revealing test generation and false-positive bug report filtering, GSE achieved SOTA precision, recall, and F1-score across OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent. Improvements over baselines: precision +6.1%~34.1% and recall +31.8%~180.0% (test generation); precision +15.4%~96.4% and recall +13.1%~19.8% (false-positive filtering). An industrial deployment yielded +61.4% F1-score.

Conclusion: GSE demonstrates that jointly modeling skill relationships and promoting generalization significantly outperforms local-update-based evolution, proving effective and generalizable across multiple coding agents and industrial deployment.

Abstract: Automated skill evolution enables Large Language Model (LLM) agents to continuously improve without expensive retraining. However, existing approaches typically treat skill evolution as a sequence of local updates, overlooking relationships among skills and often producing overfitted skill updates that fail to generalize across tasks. We propose GSE, a globalized skill evolution framework that jointly optimizes skill compatibility and skill generalization. To preserve consistency across the skill bank, GSE maintains a Skill Relation Graph (SRG) that explicitly models and co-evolves inter-skill relationships. To improve generalization, GSE performs cluster-based skill consolidation to abstract reusable capabilities from local updates and employs replay-driven verification to prevent overfitting and behavioral regressions. We evaluate GSE on two representative software engineering tasks: bug-revealing test generation and false-positive bug report filtering. Across two state-of-the-art coding agents, OpenHands and mini-SWE-agent, GSE consistently achieves the best precision, recall, and F1-score. Compared with existing evolution techniques, GSE improves precision and recall by 6.1%~34.1% and 31.8%~180.0% for test generation, and by 15.4%~96.4% and 13.1%~19.8% for false-positive filtering. Deployment on an internal industrial agent further yields a 61.4% improvement in F1-score, demonstrating the effectiveness and generalizability of GSE for evolving effective skills.

</details>


### [191] [Predicting Agile Success: The Critical Few Factors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06228)
*Ridewaan Hanslo,Maureen Tanner*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study investigates critical success factors (CSF) for Agile software development projects using a positivist approach and PLS-SEM analysis, identifying key factors that significantly contribute to project success and developing a novel evaluation model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite Agile projects outperforming traditional approaches, overall success rates remain low, with many projects still challenged or failed. This is attributed to insufficient rigorous evaluation against Agile-specific CSFs and contemporary success criteria. The study aims to bridge this gap by identifying CSFs that Agile practitioners perceive as critical to project success.

Method: A positivist research approach was adopted. Data was collected from Agile practitioners and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS software to test hypotheses and identify statistically significant relationships between constructs and project success criteria.

Result: The research identified several critical factors that significantly contribute to Agile project success. It produced a novel model capable of evaluating and measuring project success based on these validated CSFs.

Conclusion: Agile project success can be improved through rigorous evaluation using identified CSFs. The proposed model offers a practical tool for organizations to assess and measure Agile project success more effectively.

Abstract: While Agile projects are more successful than traditional software development project management approaches, their overall success rate remains relatively low, with a high percentage of projects still deemed challenged or failed. This low project success rate is attributed to projects not being rigorously evaluated against critical success factors (CSF) of Agile projects and contemporary project success criteria. To identify the CSF that contribute to Agile software development project success as perceived by Agile practitioners, this study used a positivist approach to investigate the CSF of Agile software development projects. PLS-SEM with SmartPLS was used to analyse the data and test the hypotheses to identify significant relationships between the constructs and project success criteria. This research found that a few critical factors significantly contribute to Agile project success. The study developed a novel model that can be used to evaluate and measure project success.

</details>


### [192] [Automatic Translation of Unstructured Requirements into Linear Temporal Logic through Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06287)
*Alexandra Newcomb,Omar Ochoa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates six off-the-shelf LLMs on translating unstructured natural language requirements into Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas using few-shot prompting. Across a 15-requirement benchmark with 450 generated formulas, results show modern LLMs achieve practically significant performance without fine-tuning, suggesting viability as front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Translating unstructured natural language requirements into formal specifications (specifically LTL) is a persistent bottleneck in requirements engineering for safety- and mission-critical systems. Manual formalization is error-prone and labor-intensive, yet mathematically precise specifications are essential for verification. The authors investigate whether modern LLMs can bridge this gap without task-specific fine-tuning.

Method: Six contemporary off-the-shelf LLMs were evaluated using a few-shot prompting strategy on a heterogeneous benchmark of 15 structurally varied natural language requirements. For each requirement-model pair, five independent stochastic generations were collected, producing 450 candidate LTL formulas total. Evaluation combined three approaches: (1) manual semantic assessment of correctness, (2) pass@k metrics for k ∈ {1, 3, 5}, and (3) a self-consistency measure quantifying syntactic reproducibility across trials. Understandability was also assessed via model-generated natural language explanations of the LTL formulas and discussion of timeline-based visualization.

Result: Current general-purpose LLMs achieve practically significant performance on the unstructured NL-to-LTL task without task-specific fine-tuning. The pass@k and self-consistency metrics provide complementary insights into model reliability and output stability across stochastic generations. Pairing generated formulas with natural language explanations and timeline visualizations enhances interpretability for non-expert stakeholders.

Conclusion: Modern LLMs are becoming viable front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows, reducing the manual effort required to translate natural language requirements into formal LTL specifications. Their practical utility is further supported by explainability features that make formal artifacts more accessible to non-experts.

Abstract: Automatically translating unstructured natural language requirements into formal specifications remains a challenge in requirements engineering and formal methods, particularly for safety- and mission-critical systems whose verification depends on mathematically precise specifications. This paper evaluates whether contemporary off-the-shelf Large Language Models (LLMs) can help bridge this gap by generating Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas directly from unstructured requirements. The study examines six modern LLMs using a few-shot prompting strategy on a heterogeneous benchmark of 15 structurally varied requirements. Five independent generations were collected for each requirement-model pair, yielding 450 candidate LTL formulas in total. Performance was assessed through manual semantic evaluation, pass@k for k in {1, 3, 5}, and a self-consistency measure capturing syntactic reproducibility across stochastic trials. The results indicate that current general-purpose LLMs can achieve practically significant performance on the unstructured NL-to-LTL task without task-specific fine-tuning. The study also considers understandability for non-experts by pairing generated formulas with model-produced natural language explanations and discussing the complementary use of timeline-based LTL visualization. The findings suggest that modern LLMs are becoming viable front-end assistants for semi-automated formalization workflows.

</details>


### [193] [A Study of LLMs' Preferences for Libraries and Programming Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17181)
*Lukas Twist,Mark Harman,Don Syme,Joost Noppen,Helen Yannakoudakis,Detlef Nauck,Jie M. Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: First empirical study revealing that LLMs exhibit strong biases toward popular libraries (e.g., NumPy, used unnecessarily in up to 45% of cases) and programming languages (Python dominates even when suboptimal), prioritizing familiarity over task-specific suitability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM code generation focus narrowly on functional correctness and syntactic validity, completely overlooking the critical design choices LLMs make regarding library and programming language selection. This gap matters because suboptimal choices can impact performance, maintainability, and project suitability.

Method: The authors conduct an empirical study across eight diverse LLMs, analyzing their library and programming language preferences during code generation. They measure how often LLMs select widely-adopted libraries unnecessarily (compared to ground-truth solutions) and assess language choice patterns, including a specific focus on high-performance project initialization tasks where Python is suboptimal.

Result: LLMs overuse NumPy in up to 45% of cases where it is not required and deviates from ground truth. Python is the dominant default language across models, chosen in 58% of high-performance initialization tasks despite being suboptimal, while Rust is never selected once.

Conclusion: LLMs prioritize familiarity and popularity over task-specific optimality in library and language selection. This highlights the urgent need for targeted fine-tuning, training data diversification, and new evaluation benchmarks that explicitly measure language and library selection fidelity.

Abstract: Despite the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs) in code generation, existing evaluations focus on functional correctness or syntactic validity, overlooking how LLMs make critical design choices such as which library or programming language to use. To fill this gap, we perform the first empirical study of LLMs' preferences for libraries and programming languages when generating code, covering eight diverse LLMs. We observe a strong tendency to overuse widely adopted libraries such as NumPy; in up to 45% of cases, this usage is not required and deviates from the ground-truth solutions. The LLMs we study also show a significant preference toward Python as their default language. For high-performance project initialisation tasks where Python is not the optimal language, it remains the dominant choice in 58% of cases, and Rust is not used once. These results highlight how LLMs prioritise familiarity and popularity over suitability and task-specific optimality; underscoring the need for targeted fine-tuning, data diversification, and evaluation benchmarks that explicitly measure language and library selection fidelity.

</details>

### [194] [Post-Hoc Trajectory-Risk Certification for Modular LLM-Based Security Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05199)
*Zhenpeng Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper addresses the challenge of providing finite-sample coverage guarantees across multi-stage autonomous security pipelines. While split conformal prediction offers per-stage guarantees, these do not compose to trajectory-level guarantees. The authors show Bonferroni correction is conservative, pairwise-correlation extensions beyond two stages are invalid, and propose a valid spanning-tree alternative. They derive sample-complexity bounds, uncover a label-selection artifact inflating correlation, and demonstrate on intrusion detection that auditing trajectory failure outperforms Bonferroni only with sufficient samples. Cross-dataset deployment reveals distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous security agents deploy as staged pipelines (e.g., traffic classification → attack attribution). Split conformal prediction provides per-stage finite-sample coverage, but real-world deployment demands trajectory-level guarantees across the entire chain. These guarantees fail to compose when stages are independently trained and calibrated. Existing Bonferroni allocation is distribution-free but overly conservative under correlated errors, and no valid method existed for leveraging pairwise correlations across three or more stages.

Method: The authors (1) prove that extending pairwise-correlation bounds to ≥3 stages yields invalid lower bounds rather than upper bounds; (2) derive a valid spanning-tree alternative for multi-stage correlation; (3) distinguish statistical dependence from audit-certifiable dependence and establish matching upper and information-theoretic lower sample-complexity bounds; (4) identify and correct a coarse-to-fine label selection artifact inflating measured correlation; (5) propose a direct trajectory-failure audit and a modular certificate using per-stage certificates with pairwise overlap bounds; (6) validate on a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline across 6 open LLMs and 2 datasets, with same-model, cross-model, and permuted-pairing tests.

Result: Removing the label-selection artifact reduces measured correlation from near 1 to 0–0.78. Direct trajectory-failure audit becomes 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni once the audit sample is sufficiently large, but underperforms when undersized. The modular certificate yields a positive average gain of 0.6%. Residual dependence reflects shared sample difficulty rather than shared model representations. Average trajectory coverage across 12 configurations is 92.7% ± 2.4% at α = 0.10. Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage reaches 100% even when accuracy remains at 78%, demonstrating that distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy degrades.

Conclusion: Valid trajectory-level conformal guarantees for multi-stage pipelines require careful handling of stage dependencies. Spanning-tree bounds provide the correct multi-stage extension. The label-selection artifact is a critical confound that must be corrected. Direct auditing outperforms Bonferroni only with adequate sample sizes, and modular certificates incur a modest cost from lacking joint access. Distribution shift poses a more severe threat to calibrated confidence than to raw accuracy, with important implications for security pipeline deployment.

Abstract: Autonomous security agents operate as staged pipelines, such as classifying network traffic and then attributing attacks to a specific technique. Split conformal prediction gives each stage finite-sample coverage, but deployment requires a trajectory-level guarantee across the full chain. These guarantees do not compose automatically when stages are independently trained and calibrated. Bonferroni allocation is distribution-free but conservative under correlated errors. We show that a natural pairwise-correlation extension to three or more stages is invalid because it gives a lower rather than an upper bound, and derive a valid spanning-tree alternative. We distinguish whether stages are dependent from whether an audit sample is large enough to certify that dependence, and give matching upper and information-theoretic lower sample-complexity bounds. We also show that coarse-to-fine label selection can create near-perfect measured correlation without learned dependence.
  On a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline across 6 open LLMs and 2 datasets, removing this artifact reduces measured correlation from near 1 to 0-0.78. A direct audit of trajectory failure becomes 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni once the audit reaches the required sample size, but is worse when undersized. A modular certificate using per-stage certificates and a pairwise overlap bound yields a positive average gain of 0.6%, quantifying the cost of lacking joint access. Same-model, cross-model, and permuted-pairing tests show that residual dependence reflects shared sample difficulty, not shared model representations. Average trajectory coverage across 12 configurations is 92.7% +/- 2.4% at alpha = 0.10. Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage reaches 100% even when accuracy remains 78%, showing that distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy.

</details>


### [195] [ASTELD: A Six-Axis Classification Framework for Autonomous AI Agents - Design, Evaluation, and an OpenClaw Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05201)
*Siyuan Li,Peng Shu,Churan Yu,Peilong Wang,Ruidong Zhang,Bowen Guo,Xinliang Li,Ruiyu Yan,Arif Hassan Zidan,Yi Pan,Wei Ruan,Lifeng Chen,Junhao Chen,Zhaojun Ding,Yiwei Li,Zhengliang Liu,Haixing Dai,Lin Zhao,Yu Bao,Xiang Li,Wei Zhang,Tianming Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ASTELD is a six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agent platforms (Architecture, Security, Tool integration, Execution, Level of autonomy, Deployment). Evaluated on eight platforms with an OpenClaw case study, it discriminates all platforms, reveals cross-platform patterns (security-accessibility diagonal, execution-architecture coupling, capability convergence), identifies a gap where no system combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security, and provides a reproducible method for comparison, framework selection, and future research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous AI agent platforms vary widely in architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, yet there is no common classification scheme to systematically compare these design choices, hindering framework selection and empirical research.

Method: The authors propose ASTELD, a six-axis classification framework synthesized from prior agent taxonomies and observable platform properties with explicit category-assignment rules. The axes are: Architecture pattern, Security posture, Tool integration model, Execution paradigm, Level of autonomy and human control, and Deployment topology. Discriminative utility is evaluated by mapping eight representative agent frameworks and conducting an in-depth case study of OpenClaw (including 50+ derivatives, a vulnerability taxonomy, five institutional assessments, and adoption/governance analyses).

Result: ASTELD successfully separates all eight platforms under dominant configurations. Three cross-platform patterns emerge: (1) a security-accessibility diagonal, (2) strong execution-architecture coupling, and (3) capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation. The 50+ OpenClaw derivatives show innovation concentrated on Security, Execution, and Deployment axes. The framework also exposes an unoccupied design region: no evaluated system combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.

Conclusion: ASTELD provides a reproducible method for comparing agent platforms, identifying underexplored design regions, guiding framework selection, and organizing future empirical research. The uncovered local-first/enterprise-security gap represents a consequential opportunity for future platform development.

Abstract: Autonomous AI agent platforms differ substantially in architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, yet the field lacks a common classification scheme for comparing these design choices. We propose ASTELD, an operational six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agents: Architecture pattern, Security posture, Tool integration model, Execution paradigm, Level of autonomy and human control, and Deployment topology. ASTELD is constructed by synthesizing prior agent taxonomies with observable platform properties and explicit category-assignment rules. We evaluate its discriminative and explanatory utility by mapping eight representative frameworks and by using OpenClaw as an in-depth case study.
