The resulting profiles separate all eight platforms under their dominant configurations and reveal three cross-platform patterns: a security-accessibility diagonal, strong execution-architecture coupling, and capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation. We further classify 50+ OpenClaw derivatives and find that innovation concentrates on the Security, Execution, and Deployment axes, indicating that ASTELD can explain where ecosystem fragmentation occurs. The OpenClaw case study also supplies a six-category vulnerability taxonomy, evidence from five institutional assessments, and adoption and governance analyses that connect platform coordinates to observed risks. These results position ASTELD as a reproducible method for comparing agent platforms, identifying unoccupied design regions, guiding framework selection, and organizing future empirical research. The analysis also exposes a consequential empty region: none of the evaluated systems combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.

</details>


### [196] [A Survey of Adversarial Efficiency Degradation for Vision Transformer by Exploiting Input-adaptive Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05217)
*Anadi Goyal,Nandish Chattopadhyay,Anupam Chattopadhyay,Chandan Karfa*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey analyzes adversarial attacks that exploit input-adaptive inference mechanisms in Vision Transformers—specifically token pruning and early halting—to degrade computational efficiency rather than accuracy, comparing SlowFormer and DeSparsify across A-ViT, ATS, and AdaViT frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision Transformers increasingly use input-adaptive inference (token pruning, early halting) to meet energy/latency budgets in resource-constrained deployments (mobile, embedded). Understanding how these mechanisms create attack surfaces for efficiency degradation is critical for designing lightweight countermeasures.

Method: The survey unifies and compares two representative attacks—SlowFormer (universal adversarial patch) and DeSparsify (per-image perturbations)—across three token-pruning frameworks (A-ViT, ATS, AdaViT). Standardized reporting uses GFLOPs, accuracy loss, and an Attack Success (AS) metric quantifying the fraction of compute savings negated by the attack. Analysis is structured around three research questions examining attack surfaces, operational mechanisms/vulnerabilities, and existing defenses.

Result: Both SlowFormer and DeSparsify effectively degrade computational efficiency across all three token-pruning frameworks. The AS metric provides a standardized way to measure how much of the model's compute savings an attack eliminates. The survey identifies which input-adaptive optimizations are most vulnerable and evaluates whether current defenses meaningfully restore efficiency under attack.

Conclusion: Input-adaptive inference mechanisms in ViTs introduce exploitable attack surfaces for efficiency degradation. Current defenses remain insufficient for fully restoring computational savings under attack, highlighting a need for lightweight countermeasures suitable for low-power deployment environments.

Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) increasingly rely on input-adaptive inference, such as token pruning and early halting, to meet energy and latency budgets. This survey examines a recent class of adversarial efficiency degradation attacks that target these mechanisms to increase computation without necessarily degrading accuracy. We unify and compare two representative attacks, SlowFormer (a universal adversarial patch) and DeSparsify (per-image perturbations), across three popular token-pruning frameworks: A-ViT, ATS, and AdaViT. We standardize reporting using GFLOPs, accuracy loss, and an Attack Success (AS) metric that measures how much of the model's compute savings the attack takes away. Understanding these attacks is crucial for designing countermeasures that not only mitigate risk but also remain lightweight, since deployment often occurs in low-power settings such as mobile or embedded devices. To organize our analysis, we focus on three questions: how input-adaptive optimizations (e.g., token pruning and early halting) create attack surfaces for efficiency degradation; how such attacks operate in practice and which optimizations are most vulnerable; and which defenses exist today and whether they meaningfully restore efficiency under attack.

</details>


### [197] [CyberBridge: Bridging the Gap Between Cybersecurity Education and Industry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05231)
*Arthur Nijdam,Paul Stankovski Wagner,Sara Ramezanian*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CyberBridge is an interpretable framework that uses sentence-BERT embeddings to automatically map cybersecurity job descriptions to professional role profiles by decomposing vacancies into Knowledge, Skill, and Task (KST) statements, supporting job recommendation, market analysis, and curriculum planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Academic cybersecurity programs struggle to keep curricula aligned with rapidly evolving industry competency expectations, creating a gap between what is taught and what employers actually require.

Method: CyberBridge decomposes job vacancy descriptions into constituent Knowledge, Skill, and Task (KST) statements, embeds them using a sentence-BERT model, and performs semantic similarity matching against workforce profiles. The framework emphasizes interpretability by tracing recommendations back to specific competencies and providing human-readable justifications for each mapping.

Result: The framework enables three practical use cases: (1) job recommendation for students based on completed curricula, (2) market analysis for educators to identify in-demand roles, and (3) curriculum planning to evaluate which course programs best prepare students for target cybersecurity roles.

Conclusion: CyberBridge serves as a practical, interpretable tool for educational institutions to support career guidance and evidence-based curriculum development in cybersecurity education.

Abstract: This full research paper presents CyberBridge, a framework that automatically maps cybersecurity job descrip- tions to professional role profiles. As the cybersecurity landscape evolves rapidly, it is difficult for academic programs to align curricula with the competencies expected in practice.
  CyberBridge addresses this gap by decomposing a given vacancy description into its constituent Knowledge, Skill, and Task (KST) statements, embedding them using a sentence- BERT model, and matching them to the most semantically similar workforce profiles. A key contribution of our approach is its interpretability. Rather than functioning as a black box, CyberBridge enables users to trace recommendations back to the specific competencies driving each match, providing a human- readable justification for the resulting mappings.
  CyberBridge supports three primary use cases; (1) job recom- mendation, providing students with vacancies and closely match- ing professional roles based on their completed curriculum, (2) market analysis, enabling educators and curriculum developers to analyze which roles are currently in demand, and (3) curriculum planning, assessing which course program best prepares students for in-demand cybersecurity roles.
  As such, CyberBridge can be used by educational institutions as a practical tool for career guidance and evidence-based curriculum development in cybersecurity education.

</details>


### [198] [The Hidden Life of Public Safety Communications Signals: A Comparative Security Analysis of TETRA, TETRAPOL, and P25](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05247)
*Larry Hernandez,Sergey Bratus*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Trunked LMR systems (P25, TETRA, TETRAPOL) expose sensitive operational metadata through unencrypted signaling planes. Even with perfect content encryption, passive SDR observers can infer network topology, unit mobility, organizational structure, and key management details—turning local sniffing into nationwide mapping. For TETRAPOL, signaling metadata also enables unencrypted voice extraction via a standards-level confidentiality failure in emergency calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing security analyses of trunked LMR systems focus on the content plane (encryption key recovery, cleartext capture), but a critical gap remains: the signaling plane is almost entirely unencrypted. The authors aim to expose the depth of sensitive inference possible from this exposed signaling, even when content encryption is perfect.

Method: Passive, receive-only software-defined radio (SDR) observation of trunked LMR signaling across P25, TETRA, and TETRAPOL standards. The approach infers operational metadata through timing analysis, association patterns, and signaling-plane traffic analysis without requiring decryption of voice/data payloads.

Result: Demonstrated inference of: network topology and geography, unit presence, inter-cell mobility, group affiliations, organizational structure, special key domains, and key-epoch rotation. Local SDR observation scales to nationwide network mapping, defeating identity obfuscation mechanisms. In TETRAPOL, signaling metadata combined with an emergency-call confidentiality failure enables extraction of unencrypted voice.

Conclusion: The signaling plane in trunked LMR standards represents a severe and underappreciated confidentiality vulnerability. Countermeasures are needed to protect inter-cell, base station, and subscriber identities. The paper provides specific mitigation recommendations.

Abstract: Public-safety agencies and critical infrastructure operators rely on trunked land-mobile radio (LMR) systems, based on P25, TETRA, and TETRAPOL. These systems are expected to protect not just the content of a communication but the fact of it. Yet LMR standards leave a stark gap between confidentiality of \emph{content} and of \emph{communication}: underneath an encrypted traffic plane, their signaling plane is almost entirely in the clear. We probe the depth and impact of adversarial inference from this exposed signaling.
  Prior security analyses of these systems have concentrated on the content plane---recovering encryption keys or capturing accidental cleartext. We show that comparably sensitive information can be \emph{inferred from passively observed signaling even if the content encryption were perfect}.
  In particular, we show that across the trunked LMR standards, a passive, receive-only software-defined radio (SDR) observer can recover operationally sensitive network topology and geography details, unit presence, mobility across cells and groups, organizational structure, as well as operational security details such as special key domains and key-epoch rotation. This signaling-plane inference reaches far beyond the observer's direct area of reception, turning \emph{local} sniffing into \emph{nationwide} network mapping capabilities that degrade or defeat LMR standards' identity obfuscation through timing and association. In the case of TETRAPOL, we demonstrate how inference and tracking of such signaling metadata and a standards-level confidentiality failure in emergency call handling enable unencrypted voice extraction.
  Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and mitigations, including specific recommendations for protecting inter-cell, base station and subscriber identities.

</details>


### [199] [eMicro: Real-Time Multi-Hop Access Control for Microservices with eBPF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05300)
*Rizky Ramadhana Putra,Osama Bajaber,Saimon Amanuel Tsegai,Teryl Taylor,Frederico Araujo,Yuede Ji,Peng Gao*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: eMicro is a path-aware defense system for microservices that prevents multi-hop attacks by enforcing real-time access control over complete service invocation sequences using DFA-encoded policies, history-based access control, and eBPF-based in-kernel tracing, achieving microsecond-level policy checks and 50M policies in 100MB with negligible runtime overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern cloud applications with thousands of microservices suffer from a critical security gap: traditional inter-service access control only validates individual request hops, leaving systems vulnerable to multi-hop attacks where each pairwise interaction appears legitimate but the overall request path violates security intent, enabling unauthorized access and data exfiltration.

Method: eMicro employs three core techniques: (1) history-based access control that captures and validates full service invocation sequences rather than just individual hops; (2) security policies encoded as deterministic finite automata (DFA) for constant-time lookups and compact label propagation; (3) eBPF-based in-kernel request tracing that provides transparent, low-overhead enforcement without requiring application code modifications.

Result: Evaluated on DeathStarBench and production traces from Uber, Alibaba, and ByteDance (12 million request workflows, thousands of services), eMicro achieves policy checks in 1 microsecond, stores 50 million policies in only 100 MB, reduces propagation overhead by 90%, and imposes negligible runtime impact.

Conclusion: eMicro demonstrates that scalable, efficient protection against multi-hop attacks in large-scale microservice environments is practical and deployable, filling a critical gap left by traditional per-hop access control mechanisms.

Abstract: Modern cloud applications often comprise thousands of microservices whose interactions form complex request paths. Traditional inter-service access control restricts individual service-to-service requests, but fails to prevent multi-hop attacks, where each hop appears legitimate yet the overall path violates security intent. This gap leaves systems exposed to unauthorized access and data exfiltration. In this paper, we present eMicro, a path-aware defense system for microservices that prevents such attacks while remaining efficient and deployable. eMicro enforces real-time multi-hop access control through three key techniques: (1) history-based access control extended to capture service invocation sequences; (2) security policies encoded as efficient deterministic finite automaton (DFA), supporting constant-time lookups and compact label propagation; (3) eBPF-based in-kernel request tracing for transparent, low-overhead enforcement without code changes. Evaluations on DeathStarBench and production cloud traces from Uber, Alibaba, and ByteDance, covering 12 million request workflows and thousands of services, demonstrate the scalability of eMicro. eMicro performs policy checks in 1 microsecond, stores 50 million policies in only 100 MB, and reduces propagation overhead by 90% with negligible runtime impact. These results show that eMicro delivers scalable and efficient protection against multi-hop attacks, making it practical for deployment in large-scale microservice environments.

</details>


### [200] [The Trust-Free Aggregation Layer of the Unicity Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05316)
*Risto Laanoja,Mike Gault,Dirk Draheim,Ahto Buldas*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Unicity introduces an Aggregation Layer that uses Radix Sparse Merkle Trees and STARK-based proofs to enable off-chain token transactions with compact, trustless double-spending prevention, achieving 10,000 insertions/sec and millisecond verification on consumer hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable off-chain peer-to-peer token transactions while preventing double-spending with minimal on-chain complexity and storage, without compromising trust.

Method: The Aggregation Layer maintains an append-only key-value store using Radix Sparse Merkle Trees (RSMTs) to produce round digests r_i. It generates cryptographic proofs of append-only consistency — showing r_{i+1} derives solely from adding new (k,v) pairs — and verifies these proofs via an Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR) circuit implemented on the Plonky3 STARK toolkit.

Result: The system requires no trusted setup, achieves a throughput of 10,000 insertions per second, and provides millisecond-range verification time on a single consumer-class CPU.

Conclusion: Unicity's Aggregation Layer successfully demonstrates a practical, STARK-based layer-2 solution for trustless double-spending prevention in off-chain token transactions, combining high throughput with low-latency verification.

Abstract: Unicity is a novel blockchain infrastructure for enabling users to execute off-chain peer-to-peer token transactions while preventing parallel states of tokens (double-spending) with minimal blockchain complexity and storage. A key component of the infrastructure is the Aggregation Layer responsible for storing information about the spent states of tokens and providing compact cryptographic proofs of no double-spending for the users without making any compromises in trust. Aggregation Layer is a layer 2 style service that holds an append-only key-value repository that periodically certifies its state using a traditional blockchain that we call the Consensus Layer. Every time while certifying a changed state the Aggregation Layer provides a cryptographic proof to the Consensus Layer about the append-only consistency of the key-value store. We use the Radix Sparse Merkle Trees (RSMTs) to create the cryptographic digest r_i of the store in every round i and authentication paths of special type in order to prove that the next digest r_{i+1} was obtained while only adding some key-value pairs (k,v) to the repository. The proof verification code is implemented as an Algebraic Intermediate Representation (AIR) circuit on top of the Plonky3 STARK toolkit. Our implementation uses no trusted setup, achieves throughput of 10,000 insertions per second and and millisecond range verification time on a single consumer-class CPU.

</details>


### [201] [S12X Patch Diffing with QBinDiff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05350)
*Ben Gardiner*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Reverse engineering of a commercial vehicle Brake ECU firmware update reveals that a safety recall simultaneously patched undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing, confirming the remediation served dual safety and security purposes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether a commercial vehicle Brake ECU firmware recall addressed only safety concerns or also remediated undocumented security vulnerabilities in legacy protocol handling, thereby exposing the hidden security dimension of safety-critical automotive recalls.

Method: Reverse engineering of the updater executable to extract firmware images, followed by differential binary analysis of S12X architecture firmware to identify changes between pre-recall and post-recall versions.

Result: The analysis identified specific code changes addressing previously undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing. The patched functionality was found to contain critical flaws, confirming the recall served as both a safety and security remediation.

Conclusion: The safety recall functioned as a covert security patch, highlighting that automotive recalls may obscure security fixes and that undisclosed vulnerabilities exist in safety-critical vehicle systems.

Abstract: This paper presents a reverse engineering analysis of a firmware update for a commercial vehicle Brake ECU. We analyze the updater executable to extract firmware and perform differential binary analysis of the S12X architecture firmware images. Our research identifies specific changes in the recall that address undocumented vulnerabilities in legacy protocol processing. We demonstrate that the patched functionality contained critical flaws. The findings confirm the safety recall remediation was also a security patch.

</details>


### [202] [Robust Context-Aware Detection of Malicious Instructions in Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05430)
*Buzhao Liu,Xinhang Ma,Yevgeniy Vorobeychik*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a context- and query-aware malicious sentence classifier for defending against indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks on LLM agents, and introduces two adversarial training methods—embedding-space AT and LLM-based paraphrasing AT—to harden the classifier against adaptive evasion attacks, demonstrating superior utility-robustness tradeoffs over state-of-the-art baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing IPI detectors lack query-relative detection at the segment level and are not hardened against adaptive evasion attacks realizable in agentic LLM executions. This gap motivates the development of a robust, fine-grained malicious sentence classifier.

Method: The authors develop a context- and query-aware malicious sentence classifier. They then propose two adversarial training (AT) variants to improve robustness: (1) feature-space AT using projected-gradient-based optimization in embedding space, and (2) LLM-based paraphrasing that simulates realizable evasion attacks within the AT loop. Both AT variants are parameterized to enable smooth utility-robustness tradeoffs.

Result: The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art IPI defense baselines under static attacks. Under adaptive attacks, the AT variants provide significantly higher utility, lower attack success rates, and often both. Results also show that optimal AT parameters depend on the application domain, suggesting domain-dependent tuning is necessary in practice.

Conclusion: Combining query-aware segment-level detection with adversarial training yields robust IPI defenses that outperform existing methods. The domain-dependence of optimal AT parameters implies that practical deployment requires domain-specific tuning of malicious text detectors.

Abstract: The remarkable instruction-following ability of modern LLMs has enabled their practical use as the minds of agents that can autonomously complete increasingly complex tasks. Therein, however, also lies their vulnerability to attacks which embed malicious instructions in text, common variants of which are known as indirect prompt injection (IPI). A fundamental task in addressing this vulnerability is successful segmentation of a given text into benign and malicious sentences (if any). While a number of approaches for this task have been proposed, no detector combines query-relative detection at the segment level, and none are hardened against adaptive evasion attacks realizable in agentic executions. We address the former limitation by developing an approach for malicious sentence classification that is both context- and query-aware. Next, to harden the resulting classifier against evasion, we present two adversarial training methods. The first is directly adapted feature-space adversarial training (AT) in which evasions are approximated using projected-gradient-based optimization in the embedding space. The second simulates realizable evasion attacks in the AT loop through LLM-based paraphrasing. Crucially, we parametrize both AT variants to facilitate a smooth tradeoff between utility and attack robustness. In extensive experiments using indirect prompt injection benchmarks we show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art IPI defense baselines under static attacks, while in the case of adaptive attacks, our AT variants provide significantly higher utility, lower attack success rate, and often both. Finally, we show that the best AT parameters can depend intimately on the particular application domain. Consequently, domain-dependent tuning of malicious text detectors is likely necessary in practice. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tavia-liu/CAD.

</details>


### [203] [Quantifying Bitcoin Network Resilience Through Critical Scenario Discovery: A Dual-Layer Framework for Discovering Contentious Fork Conditions in Decentralized Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05461)
*Peter Foytik,Sachin Shetty,Ross Gore,Eranga Bandara*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Using simulation of 1,330 scenarios with real Bitcoin nodes, this paper identifies the economic and hashrate parameter thresholds that determine whether a contentious soft fork resolves cleanly or fractures into a persistent chain split, finding that economic weight distribution — not hashrate — is the primary determinant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bitcoin consensus emerges from heterogeneous nodes with divergent economic stakes, making the outcome of contentious soft forks (clean resolution vs. persistent chain split) difficult to predict analytically. Controlled experimentation is needed to map the parameter space governing these outcomes.

Method: Scenario Discovery using the Patient Rule Induction Method (PRIM), an ensemble-simulation methodology. Authors ran 1,330 valid scenarios on Warnet using real bitcoind nodes, varying economic weight, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime to identify configuration regions producing contentious fork outcomes.

Result: Three key findings: (1) an economic-support floor (0.45–0.50) and override ceiling (0.78–0.82) bound the contested space, with an Economic Self-Sustaining Point at 0.74; (2) a pool-commitment "flip-point" at 0.214 committed hashrate, where committing the largest pool to the upgrading chain paradoxically reverses the outcome; (3) fork outcomes resolve on two independent layers — hashrate and economic adoption — governed by different parameters. Individual user nodes showed no detectable influence.

Conclusion: Economic weight distribution across a partition, not hashrate majority, primarily determines contentious fork resolution under Bitcoin's operational retarget interval and moderate price divergence. The authors translate their threshold findings into three operational monitoring questions answerable from public data.

Abstract: Bitcoin's consensus depends not only on protocol rules but on the emergent behavior of a heterogeneous network of nodes with divergent economic stakes. Whether a contentious soft fork resolves cleanly or fractures into a persistent chain split is difficult to predict analytically but can be explored through controlled experimentation. This paper applies Scenario Discovery, an ensemble-simulation methodology using the Patient Rule Induction Method (PRIM), to identify the configuration regions that produce contentious fork outcomes. Using Warnet to run real bitcoind nodes across 1,330 valid scenarios spanning economic weight, mining-pool commitment, pool ideology, hashrate, and difficulty-retarget regime, we identify the parameter thresholds separating clean resolution from contested split. We show that economic weight distribution across a partition, not hashrate majority, is the primary determinant of resolution under Bitcoin's operational retarget interval and moderate price divergence. Three findings follow: an economic-support floor (0.45-0.50) and override ceiling (0.78-0.82) bound the contested space, with an Economic Self-Sustaining Point (0.74) between them; a pool-commitment "flip-point" (0.214 of committed hashrate) at which committing the largest pool to the upgrading chain paradoxically reverses the outcome; and outcomes resolve on two independent layers, hashrate and economic adoption, governed by different parameters. Individual user nodes show no detectable influence on fork outcomes under the modeled economic weightings. We close with three monitoring questions, answerable from public data, that translate these thresholds into operational guidance.

</details>


### [204] [Exploring Privacy Leakage and Data Disclosure Violations in the MacOS Application Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05474)
*Jyotirmay Chauhan,Kostas Solomos,Mir Masood Ali,Jason Polakis*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper presents the first comprehensive study of privacy mechanisms in the macOS ecosystem, developing NutriScan—a hybrid static/dynamic analysis framework—to evaluate data practices of 1K macOS apps. Findings reveal widespread undisclosed data access (85% of apps), data exfiltration to trackers (49.7%), and systemic fragmentation in Apple's privacy mechanisms, with proposed mitigations for both developers and Apple's vetting process.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior privacy research has extensively examined web, mobile, and IoT ecosystems, but desktop environments—particularly macOS—remain critically understudied despite widespread usage. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically investigating how macOS mechanisms regulate and disclose data collection, and whether those mechanisms are effective in practice.

Method: The authors adopt an app-development-centric view, analyzing macOS's data-access mediation mechanisms. They build NutriScan, a framework combining static and dynamic analysis to produce a consolidated view of data practices and disclosures. They then apply NutriScan to dynamically analyze 1,000 macOS apps, examining both API-level data access and network-level data exfiltration against stated disclosures.

Result: 85% of analyzed apps access user-data APIs without proper disclosure; 49.7% exfiltrate data to advertising entities and hosting providers, with 12.5% doing so without any corresponding disclosure. Desktop apps are actively leveraged by online trackers for user profiling and device fingerprinting. The macOS ecosystem's disjoint mechanisms and divergent data abstractions increase developer complexity and facilitate undisclosed privacy-invasive practices.

Conclusion: The macOS privacy landscape is fragmented and weakly enforced, enabling widespread undisclosed data collection. The authors propose mitigations including streamlining data disclosure processes for developers and strengthening Apple's app vetting procedures to close the gap between accessed data and disclosed practices.

Abstract: The systematic and excessive data collection practices of tech companies have rendered online privacy both a necessity and a sought-after commodity. However, while the privacy risks of the web, mobile, and IoT ecosystems have been extensively examined, desktop environments have been largely overlooked. As desktop apps continue to be widely used, they remain a critical yet understudied dimension of user privacy. In this paper, we address this gap by presenting the first, to our knowledge, comprehensive study of the mechanisms designed to regulate and disclose data collection and sharing practices in the macOS ecosystem. We adopt an app-development-centric view, and shed light on the interactions between the various macOS mechanisms that mediate apps' data access. Driven by our findings, we develop NutriScan, an analysis framework that incorporates both static and dynamic analysis techniques to create a consolidated view of macOS apps' data practices and disclosures. We use our system to dynamically analyze 1K macOS apps, and find that 85% of them access user-data APIs without disclosing it. 49.7% also exfiltrate data to advertising entities and hosting providers, 12.5% of which do so without a corresponding disclosure. We find that desktop apps are being leveraged by online trackers to enrich user profiles and device fingerprints, thus shedding new light on the true scope of the online tracking ecosystem. Our analysis reveals how the macOS app ecosystem is comprised of disjoint mechanisms with divergent data abstractions, thus increasing complexity for developers while also facilitating undisclosed privacy-invasive practices. Accordingly, we propose a series of mitigations that aim to both streamline the data disclosure process for developers and improve Apple's app vetting process.

</details>


### [205] [PromptShield Home: Ambient Multimodal Prompt Injection Defense for Smart-Home Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05495)
*He Zhang,Feilong Li,Dingning Long,Yilin Cui,Peijun Zhang,Yuewen Zhang,Qianyao Xu,Xinyi Fu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PromptShield-Home is a benchmark testing whether multimodal LLM-based smart-home assistants can distinguish genuine user commands from ambient/screen/injected speech. All MLLM configurations over-refuse (near-zero safe-completion), while traditional detectors over-trigger; their correct sets are disjoint, motivating learned routing and sensor fusion rather than full MLLM replacement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Smart-home assistants increasingly use MLLMs that perceive video and audio directly, raising a critical safety question: can the agent distinguish a genuine user command from ambient content (TV speech, on-screen text, overheard conversations) that merely resembles a command? Existing evaluations lack realistic multi-modal home scenarios addressing addressee ambiguity, screen/audio injection, health-monitor false triggers, and mixed occupancy.

Method: The authors introduce PromptShield-Home, a benchmark of realistic smart-home scenarios. They compare three abstraction layers: (L0) traditional detectors, (L1) single MLLM agents (vision-only, vision+ASR, audio-visual), and (L2) multi-agent mediation (voting, role specialists, cross-model arbitration). Given label skew toward inaction, they report unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately rather than aggregate accuracy. They also compute an oracle upper bound by combining complementary correct sets across layers.

Result: A constant always-block predictor achieves 82% accuracy due to label skew. Detectors act on everything (poor specificity), while all MLLM configurations over-refuse, completing almost no genuine commands and missing a true fall in every case. The correct sets of detectors and MLLMs are disjoint. An oracle that always picks the right layer reaches 94.1%, against 76.5% for the best single layer.

Conclusion: Home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion, not by replacing detectors with an MLLM. The complementary failure modes of detectors and MLLMs, evidenced by disjoint correct sets and the oracle gap, indicate that a hybrid architecture with intelligent layer selection can substantially outperform either paradigm alone.

Abstract: Smart-home assistants increasingly use multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that perceive video and audio directly. This raises a safety question specific to the home: can the agent tell a genuine user command from ambient or externally-sourced content, television speech, on-screen text, or an overheard conversation, that merely looks like a command? We introduce PromptShield-Home, a pilot benchmark of realistic smart-home scenarios spanning addressee ambiguity, screen/audio injection, health-monitor false triggers, mixed occupancy, and a legitimate-command floor, and use it to compare three abstraction layers: traditional detectors (L0), a single MLLM agent (L1; vision, vision+ASR, and audio-visual), and multi-agent mediation (L2; voting, role specialists, cross-model arbitration). Because the label distribution is skewed toward inaction, aggregate accuracy is misleading, a constant always-block predictor scores 82%, so we report unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately. The two paradigms fail in opposite ways: detectors act on everything, while every MLLM configuration over-refuses, completing almost no genuine command and missing a true fall in every case. Crucially, their correct sets are disjoint: an oracle that always picks the right layer reaches 94.1%, against 76.5% for the best single layer. We report this as an upper bound, not a system - no router is implemented - and argue that home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion, not by replacing detectors with an MLLM.

</details>


### [206] [Behavioral Residualization for Unsupervised Intrusion Detection in Automotive CAN Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05548)
*Chandan Hegde,Mukundh R Reddy*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A CAN-specific representation called "per-ID behavioral residualization" extracts temporal, protocol, and payload features from sliding windows, residualizing them against each arbitration ID's normal baseline. This representation — not any specific detector — drives performance gains, achieving high recall (≥0.99) on realistic attacks but failing on novel-ID flooding and cross-ID fuzzing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAN intrusion detection systems rely on presence-based features (novel IDs, frozen bytes, anomalous DLC) that work on clean datasets but fail when attackers reuse legitimate arbitration IDs — a realistic attack scenario. A representation is needed that can detect attacks even when legitimate IDs are reused.

Method: Per-ID behavioral residualization: for each arbitration ID, fourteen temporal, protocol, and payload features are extracted from sliding windows. These features are then residualized — subtracted from each ID's normal behavioral baseline — to highlight deviations. The representation is evaluated across six unsupervised detectors on two datasets (HCRL and ROAD).

Result: Residualization improved mean F1 in the majority of evaluations: 21/24 on HCRL and 30/36 on ROAD (across five seeds). On ROAD, recall ≥0.99 with high ROC-AUC on targeted signal-manipulation attacks. Limitations: novel-ID flooding (HCRL DoS, F1=0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (ROAD, F1=0.27).

Conclusion: The per-ID behavioral residualization representation is the key driver of intrusion detection performance, not the choice of detector. Its coverage boundary is clearly defined: it excels against attacks reusing legitimate IDs but cannot handle novel-ID flooding or cross-ID fuzzing.

Abstract: Modern vehicles rely on the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, whose design prioritizes low cost and real-time performance but provides no message authentication or encryption. An attacker with physical or remote access can therefore inject arbitrary frames, making intrusion detection an important defense-in-depth mechanism.
  Most published CAN intrusion detection systems rely on presence-based features, such as novel arbitration IDs, frozen payload bytes, or anomalous DLC values. These features perform well on public datasets containing easily separable attacks but fail when attackers reuse legitimate arbitration IDs. We present per-ID behavioral residualization, a CAN-specific representation that extracts fourteen temporal, protocol, and payload features from sliding windows and residualizes them against each arbitration ID's normal baseline. Our central claim is that this representation, rather than any individual detector, drives the performance gains.
  Across six unsupervised detectors and two datasets, residualization improves mean F1 in the majority of evaluations (21/24 on HCRL and 30/36 on ROAD across five seeds). On the more realistic ROAD dataset, where attacks reuse legitimate IDs, the representation achieves recall >= 0.99 with high ROC-AUC on targeted signal-manipulation attacks. Two limitations are explicitly quantified: novel-ID flooding (HCRL DoS, F1 = 0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (ROAD, F1 = 0.27), defining the measured coverage boundary of the proposed representation.

</details>


### [207] [A Self-Explainable Deep Architecture for Security Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05552)
*Ananth Shreekumar,Jyun-Jhu Syu,Muslum Ozgur Ozmen,Dongyan Xu,Z. Berkay Celik*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: XSec is a self-explainable deep architecture for security applications that uses mask-based sub-feature extraction and prototype learning to generate deterministic, interpretable explanations without post-hoc analysis, achieving 97.33% average accuracy across five security scenarios while substantially reducing explanation latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models in security applications suffer from poor interpretability. Existing explanation methods (visual, post-hoc) exhibit three key limitations: reduced faithfulness from local approximation errors, instability from randomness reliance, and computational inefficiency that prevents real-time use. Security-critical scenarios demand both high performance and transparent, trustworthy explanations.

Method: XSec is a self-explainable deep architecture. During training, it employs a novel mask-based mechanism to extract informative sub-features from input data and learns class-representative prototypes. At inference time, a dedicated similarity layer computes similarity scores between input features and learned prototypes, directly generating interpretable explanations without requiring post-hoc analysis.

Result: XSec achieved an average classification accuracy of 97.33% across five diverse security scenarios with minimal performance degradation. It produced deterministic explanations (fixed for a given trained model and input) and demonstrated substantially lower explanation latency compared to both approximation-based and perturbation-based post-hoc methods.

Conclusion: XSec successfully extends self-explainable AI to security applications, effectively bridging the gap between high deep learning performance and the critical need for explainability in security-sensitive contexts.

Abstract: Deep learning models have become integral to security applications due to their ability to model complex relationships in data and detect sophisticated threats. However, their complexity makes it difficult to understand how predictions are generated, posing significant challenges for interpretability, particularly in security applications where transparency is critical. Existing explanation methods, such as visual explanation techniques and post-hoc approaches, suffer from several limitations: reduced faithfulness due to local approximation errors, instability caused by reliance on randomness, and computational inefficiency that hinders real-time usage. To address these issues, we introduce XSec, a self-explainable deep architecture developed for security applications. During training, XSec uses a novel mask-based approach to extract informative sub-features from the data and learns prototypes, representative patterns that characterize each class. XSec then leverages the prototypes in a dedicated similarity layer at test time to compute similarity scores and generates interpretable explanations without the need for post-hoc analysis. We evaluate XSec across five diverse security scenarios, demonstrating its ability to achieve an average classification accuracy of 97.33% with minimal performance compromise. XSec produces deterministic explanations for a fixed trained model and input and substantially reduces explanation latency compared with approximation-based and perturbation-based post-hoc methods. Through this effort, we extend the applicability of self-explainable AI to security applications, bridging the gap between deep learning performance and the need for explainability in critical scenarios.

</details>


### [208] [When Experience Becomes Instruction: Trajectory Poisoning in Self-Evolving Agent Skill Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05563)
*Jialuo Chen,Lingqi Jiang,Xinhao Deng,Xiaohu Du,Jianan Ma,Yunhao Feng,Yuqi Qing,Zhihao Yuan,Linkang Du,Jingyi Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PoisonedEvolution is a trajectory-poisoning attack that exploits the evidence promotion mechanism in self-evolving skill (SES) systems, achieving 91% success rate at 10% attacker support by making poisoned behaviors appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-evolving skill systems promote untrusted agent trajectories into trusted skills, but the security of this "evidence promotion" boundary has not been systematically evaluated. The authors aim to expose vulnerabilities in the promotion pipeline that could allow adversaries to embed malicious behaviors into the skill bank.

Method: The authors design a skill-visible black-box attack where the attacker can inspect target skills and inject bounded poisoned trajectories, but cannot access private pools, evolution logic, or edit the skill bank. The attack targets three bottlenecks — Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization — with Attribution being the critical one requiring poisoned behaviors to appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable. Evaluated across four security-effect families using inert canary specifications on six LLM evolvers (SkillClaw) and the Trace2Skill pipeline, with ablations on attacker record count, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding.

Result: At 10% attacker support, PoisonedEvolution achieves 91.0% success rate (546/600 trials) on SkillClaw and 61.5% (369/600) on Trace2Skill. Three consistent attacker records in a 30-record batch suffice for reliable poisoning, while a single record is substantially weaker. Recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding are identified as the primary determinants of attack success.

Conclusion: Evidence promotion constitutes a critical security boundary in self-evolving agent systems. The attribution stage — where behaviors must demonstrate causal utility, recurrence, and generalizability before skill promotion — is the key bottleneck that PoisonedEvolution exploits, and defending this stage is essential for secure SES architectures.

Abstract: Self-evolving skill (SES) systems distill agent trajectories into persistent skills, allowing untrusted experience to become trusted instruction. We introduce PoisonedEvolution, a trajectory-poisoning attack on this promotion process. Our skill-visible black-box attacker can inspect a target skill and contribute bounded evidence, but cannot observe private pools or evolution logic or edit the skill bank. Artifact poisoning requires Inclusion, Evolution Attribution, and Realization. Attribution is the distinctive bottleneck: the target behavior must appear causally useful, recurrent, and generalizable before promotion. We evaluate four representative security-effect families using inert canary specifications. At 10% attacker support, across six mainstream LLM evolvers in SkillClaw, PoisonedEvolution embeds target behaviors in 546/600 trials (91.0% SER). On the structurally different Trace2Skill pipeline at the same ratio, it embeds target behaviors in 369/600 trials (61.5% SER), demonstrating transfer across evolution architectures. In a representative controlled study, three consistent attacker records suffice in a 30-record batch, whereas a single record is much weaker. Ablations identify recurring support, causal framing, and domain-aligned encoding as the main determinants of success. These findings expose evidence promotion as a security boundary for self-evolving agents.

</details>


### [209] [Detecting Safety Training Modification in Language Models via Activation Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05578)
*Glen Messenger*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AMS detects safety-training modifications in language models by analyzing geometric structure of safety concepts in activation space. It identifies a four-class taxonomy of modifications and achieves 71% detection accuracy across 14 model configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety training in LLMs can be modified or removed through various techniques (abliteration, uncensored fine-tuning). There is a need for a diagnostic tool that can detect whether and how safety training has been altered, without relying solely on behavioral testing, which can be gamed or is insufficient for detecting subtle modifications.

Method: AMS measures the geometric structure of safety-relevant concepts in activation space by computing sigma (separation between harmful and benign content class representations). It uses a two-tier detection approach: Tier 1 sigma-threshold detects collapsed cluster separation; Tier 2 direction-similarity verification detects rotation of refusal direction without separation collapse. The method was validated via leave-one-out cross-validation on 14 model configurations across 4 architecture families and 4 safety-modification categories.

Result: Leave-one-out cross-validation achieved 71% accuracy (10/14 correct). Bootstrap 95% CI on sigma estimates had median width 3.4 sigma. Sigma on harmful-content concept predicted behavioral compliance with Pearson r = -0.546 (p = 0.043). A four-class taxonomy emerged: training removal (collapses separation), weight-orthogonalization abliteration (collapses separation + rotates refusal direction), rotation-without-collapse abliteration (preserves separation, rotates direction), and behavioral fine-tuning (preserves both, undetectable by activation-only probing).

Conclusion: AMS provides a principled activation-space diagnostic for detecting safety-training modifications, with defined strengths (detecting structural changes) and a documented failure mode (behavioral-only modifications). The four-class taxonomy offers a framework for understanding how different modification techniques manifest in activation geometry. Open problems include threshold calibration and detecting purely behavioral safety modifications.

Abstract: We introduce AMS (Activation-based Model Scanner), a tool that detects modifications to safety training in language models by measuring the geometric structure of safety-relevant concepts in activation space. Safety training creates measurable separation between harmful and benign content classes; certain safety modifications collapse or rotate this structure, while others leave it intact. We validate AMS across 14 model configurations spanning 4 architecture families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral) and four safety-modification categories (instruction-tuned, base, abliterated, uncensored fine-tunes). Leave-one-out cross-validation of thresholds achieves 71% accuracy (10/14); bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on sigma point estimates have median width 3.4 sigma. We measure behavioral compliance on 20 stratified JailbreakBench prompts per model and find that sigma on the harmful-content concept predicts compliance with Pearson r = -0.546 (p = 0.043), directionally but with meaningful noise. Mechanistic analysis identifies a four-class taxonomy of safety-training modifications distinguished by activation-space signature: training removal collapses cluster separation; weight-orthogonalization abliteration both collapses separation and rotates the refusal direction; rotation-without-collapse abliteration preserves separation while rotating direction; and behavioral fine-tuning preserves both magnitude and direction. AMS's Tier 1 sigma-threshold detects the first two classes; Tier 2 direction-similarity verification detects the third. The fourth is undetectable by activation-only probing and represents a documented failure mode. We discuss threshold calibration, limitations of single-run measurement, and the open problem of detecting behavioral-only safety modifications.

</details>


### [210] [Enhancing Anomaly Resilience in Research Networks: A Large-Scale Forecasting Benchmark for Dynamic Security Baselining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05605)
*Mohammad Arafath Uddin Shariff,Byrav Ramamurthy*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes and benchmarks a traffic forecasting framework to establish dynamic security baselines for Research and Education Networks (RENs). Using 57 days of Internet2 backbone data (13.7B packets), six model families are evaluated across 960 configurations, with advanced architectures (especially TiDE) reducing prediction error by 30-42% over traditional methods, enabling better distinction between legitimate scientific elephant flows and genuine DDoS attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RENs face a security paradox: legitimate scientific traffic patterns (massive, bursty elephant flows) are statistically indistinguishable from volumetric DDoS attacks to conventional monitoring systems. This causes high false-positive rates in anomaly detection, blinding operators to real threats. No statistically validated framework exists to establish dynamic baselines that can separate scientific workflows from attacks.

Method: The authors leverage a 57-day dataset from Internet2 spanning 10 backbone routers (13.7 billion packets). They systematically benchmark six model families — from classical SARIMA to state-of-the-art long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST) — across 960 experimental configurations for anomaly-aware traffic forecasting. A novel anomaly-integration strategy is introduced to improve model robustness under noisy conditions.

Result: Advanced architectures, particularly TiDE, reduce baseline prediction error by 30-42% compared to traditional methods (p < 0.001), significantly improving distinction between legitimate bursts and anomalies. The proposed anomaly-integration strategy yields a 3.3% improvement in model robustness in the presence of noise.

Conclusion: This work delivers the first statistically validated framework for distinguishing scientific workflows from network attacks in REN environments, paving the way for more autonomous and resilient network security operations.

Abstract: Research and Education Networks (RENs) serve as critical infrastructure for scientific discovery, yet they face a unique security paradox: their normal traffic patterns which are characterized by massive, bursty "elephant flows" are statistically indistinguishable from volumetric attacks such as DDoS to conventional monitoring systems. This similarity leads to high false-positive rates in anomaly detection, blinding security operators to genuine threats. In this paper, we propose and evaluate a high-fidelity traffic forecasting framework designed to establish dynamic security baselines for RENs. Leveraging an exclusive 57-day Internet2 dataset spanning ten backbone routers (13.7 billion packets), we perform the first large-scale benchmark of anomaly-aware forecasting models in this domain. We systematically evaluate six model families, from SARIMA to state-of-the-art long-sequence architectures (TiDE, PatchTST), across 960 experimental configurations. Our results demonstrate that these advanced architectures, particularly TiDE, reduce baseline prediction error by 30-42% compared to traditional methods ($p < 0.001$), significantly improving the distinction between legitimate scientific bursts and potential anomalies. Furthermore, we introduce a novel anomaly-integration strategy that improves model robustness by 3.3% in the presence of noise. This work provides the first statistically validated framework for distinguishing scientific workflows from network attacks, enabling more autonomous and resilient network security operations.

</details>


### [211] [Breaking Customized LLMs for Coding: Automated Red Teaming for Instruction Backdoor Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05659)
*Yuchen Chen,Wei Cheng,Yuan Xiao,Wising Sun,Chunrong Fang,Yang Liu,Zhenyu Chen,Baowen Xu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ARIA is an automated red-teaming framework that uses an attacker LLM to iteratively generate covert and effective backdoor instructions for LLM customization platforms, achieving high attack success rates while evading detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM customization platforms are vulnerable to instruction backdoor attacks, but existing attacks rely on explicit, easily detectable trigger patterns and require substantial manual effort to craft, limiting scalability and stealth.

Method: ARIA uses an attacker LLM in an iterative generation-refinement loop guided by structured feedback from the target LLM along three dimensions: stealthiness, clean-task utility, and backdoor effectiveness. Evaluated on three code intelligence tasks with four LLMs against three baselines.

Result: ARIA achieves a 0.945 attack success rate with the best clean-task utility, generalizes across programming languages, remains robust to generation temperature, achieves up to 1.000 false negative rate against detection, and resists existing defenses.

Conclusion: ARIA demonstrates strong generalizability and robustness as a red-teaming tool, exposing critical vulnerabilities in LLM customization platforms and underscoring the need for more effective defenses against instruction backdoor attacks.

Abstract: LLM customization platforms allow users to build task-specific models for code intelligence tasks by embedding instructions into system prompts, without modifying the underlying model parameters. While these platforms lower the barrier to developing customized LLMs, they also introduce a new attack surface: instruction backdoor attacks, in which adversaries implant hidden malicious behaviors into customized instructions. However, existing attacks suffer from two key limitations. First, they often rely on explicit trigger patterns readily detected by platform-side or user-side inspection. Second, they require substantial manual effort to craft task-specific backdoored instructions, limiting their scalability.
  In this paper, we propose ARIA, an automated red-teaming framework for crafting covert and effective backdoored instructions against customized LLMs. ARIA leverages an attacker LLM to iteratively generate and refine backdoored instructions, guided by structured feedback from the target LLM along three dimensions: stealthiness, clean-task utility, and backdoor effectiveness. We evaluate ARIA on three code intelligence tasks, using four representative LLMs, and compare it with three baseline attacks. Experimental results show that ARIA achieves the highest attack success rate of 0.945, while maintaining the best clean-task utility across all tasks. ARIA also generalizes well across programming languages and remains robust to generation temperature. Furthermore, ARIA significantly outperforms existing attacks in evading platform-side and user-side detection, achieving a false negative rate of up to 1.000, and stays effective against existing defense methods, demonstrating its strong generalizability and robustness.

</details>


### [212] [Algebraic Cryptanalytic Extraction on Hard-Label Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05736)
*Zirui Chen,Shi Tang,Zhengchao Gao,Yongjia Su,Lingyue Qin,Xiaoyang Dong*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes an Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method to drastically accelerate hard-label neural network model extraction by replacing expensive SVD-based clustering with efficient inner-product operations, and extends the attack to max-pooling CNNs for the first time via a kernel-centric clustering scheme.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Carlini et al.'s state-of-the-art hard-label model extraction attack (EUROCRYPT 2025) is theoretically polynomial-time but suffers from a practical computational bottleneck: its dual-point clustering relies on SVD with O(n²·(d^(k))³) complexity, making it infeasibly slow. The authors aim to eliminate this bottleneck and extend hard-label extraction to CNNs with max-pooling, which was previously unsolved.

Method: The authors reframe the geometric hard-label attack into an algebraic framework and introduce the Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method. ASV exploits two observations: (1) high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal, and (2) practical DNN neurons learn disentangled features. Instead of SVD-based rank checking for clustering, ASV uses simple inner-product operations, reducing average complexity to O(n·(d^(k))³). For CNNs with max-pooling, they extend ASV with a kernel-centric clustering scheme that leverages weight sharing in convolutions, enabling the first hard-label extraction attack on such architectures.

Result: Experiments on a 64-64×4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5 (CNN with max-pooling) show that the ASV method dramatically reduces clustering time and significantly improves overall model extraction efficiency compared to the SVD-based approach.

Conclusion: The ASV method successfully resolves the practical runtime bottleneck of Carlini et al.'s attack through an algebraic reformulation and efficient inner-product-based clustering. The extension to max-pooling CNNs fills a critical cryptanalysis gap, demonstrating the first viable hard-label extraction attack on convolutional architectures.

Abstract: Although the state-of-the-art neural network model extraction attack in the hard-label setting by Carlini et al. at EUROCRYPT 2025 has polynomial-time complexity in theory, its dual-point clustering relies on singular value decomposition (SVD) with a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n^2 \cdot (d^{(k)})^3)$, resulting in huge runtime in practice. To address this computational bottleneck, this work transforms Carlini et al.'s geometric-view hard-label attack into an algebraic framework, and proposes a novel Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method to achieve efficient parameter extraction on Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNNs) by leveraging two key observations: high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal, and neurons in practical DNNs tend to learn disentangled features. The proposed ASV method replaces SVD-based rank checking with simple inner-product operations, reducing the clustering complexity to $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot (d^{(k)})^3)$ on average. Furthermore, this paper presents the first model extraction attack against hard-label max-pooling Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by proposing an advanced ASV method with a kernel-centric clustering scheme instead of the neuron-centric clustering, which fully exploits the property of weight sharing in convolutions and fills the cryptanalysis gap. Experiments on a 64-64$\times$4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5 (CNN) with max pooling demonstrate that our ASV method drastically cuts clustering time, and improves the overall efficiency in the model extraction.

</details>


### [213] [ABC: Numerical Data Collection under Local Differential Privacy without Prior Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05737)
*Incheol Baek,Hyungbin Kim,Yon Dohn Chung*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes an adaptive Local Differential Privacy (LDP) framework called ABC (Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions) that dynamically estimates the data domain without prior knowledge. Users send both perturbed data and a privatized signal indicating clipping, enabling iterative domain adjustment. The method is shown theoretically to converge and empirically improves data quality across various datasets and LDP mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LDP mechanisms require a predefined data domain, which is often unknown in practice. A domain that is too narrow clips values and loses information, while one that is too wide adds excessive noise. This creates a critical need for methods that dynamically estimate the data domain to balance these trade-offs.

Method: The ABC (Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions) method: each user sends (1) their perturbed numerical data and (2) a privatized binary signal indicating whether their original value was clipped by the current domain. The data collector aggregates these signals and iteratively adjusts the domain bounds to fit the underlying data distribution. Theoretical convergence analysis is provided.

Result: The framework significantly improves numerical data collection quality across diverse datasets and underlying LDP mechanisms. The estimated range converges in practice. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate robustness to hyperparameter choices.

Conclusion: The proposed adaptive LDP framework successfully resolves the domain-specification dilemma in LDP by dynamically learning the data range. It delivers strong empirical performance, theoretical convergence guarantees, and robustness, making it a practical solution for numerical data collection under LDP without prior domain knowledge.

Abstract: Local Differential Privacy (LDP) provides strong privacy guarantees for collecting numerical data. A fundamental challenge, however, is that existing LDP mechanisms require a predefined data domain, which is often unknown in practice. This lack of prior knowledge creates a critical dilemma for the data collector: if the chosen domain is too narrow, values outside the range are clipped, leading to information loss. Conversely, if the domain is too wide, excessive noise is added during the privatization process, which degrades the quality of collected data. This highlights the need for methods that can dynamically estimate the data domain.
  In this work, we propose an adaptive LDP framework that addresses this problem. In our method, each user sends two pieces of information: their perturbed numerical data, and a privatized signal indicating if their original value was clipped by the current domain. By aggregating these signals, our proposed method, Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions (ABC) method, iteratively adjusts the domain to fit the underlying data distribution without prior knowledge. Our theoretical analysis shows that the estimated data domain converges to an appropriate range.
  In the empirical evaluation, the results demonstrate that our framework significantly improves the quality of numerical data collection across various datasets and underlying LDP mechanisms. We also show that the estimated range successfully converges in practice and our approach is robust to its hyperparameters through comprehensive ablation studies.

</details>


### [214] [On the Figures of Merit for Quantum Software Security: Toward a Benchmarking Rubric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05831)
*Badhon Rahman,Majid Haghparast,Tommi Mikkonen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Quantum software security lacks standardized quantitative metrics. The paper proposes Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs) organized by ISO/IEC 25010 sub-characteristics, mapped to the QaaS pipeline, and aggregated into a unified Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score, addressing a three-layer measurement gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While quantum computing has established mature performance benchmarks (qubit count, Quantum Volume, CLOPS) and is developing software-quality metrics, security measurement remains ad hoc. Existing indicators like TVD and DFC are technique-specific and incompatible. The authors argue quantum software security deserves explicit, standardized figures of merit comparable to performance metrics.

Method: The paper (i) characterizes a three-layer measurement gap in quantum software security, (ii) proposes a structured S-FoM framework organized along three axes: ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics, QaaS pipeline mapping, and measurement maturity levels, and (iii) defines a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates individual S-FoMs into a composite Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. An illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques demonstrates the approach.

Result: The paper delivers a structured taxonomy of Security Figures of Merit mapped to the full QaaS stack, a normalization and aggregation methodology producing a single QSSP score, and demonstrates feasibility through reanalysis of existing circuit obfuscation techniques, showing how disparate ad hoc metrics can be unified within the proposed framework.

Conclusion: The work represents a first step toward security-aware benchmarking for the Quantum Software Stack, establishing that quantum software security should be measured as rigorously as performance, through standardized, composable, and pipeline-aware metrics.

Abstract: Quantum software is increasingly provided through multi-tenant and cloud-based Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) stacks. A growing concern about the diverse attack vectors across the pipeline has been demonstrated in recent research. Yet the community has converged on three mature pillars: Scale (Qubit Count), Quality (Quantum Volume), and Speed (Circuit Layer Operations per Second (CLOPS)) for the merit performance figures. Moreover, it has also begun to define software-quality metrics. However, the security of quantum software remains largely unmeasured. A few quantitative security indicators, such as Total Variation Distance (TVD) and Degree of Functional Corruption (DFC), exist. Although they were introduced ad hoc for individual circuit obfuscation techniques, they are incompatible. We assert that the security of quantum software deserves the same attention as the performance: an explicit set of Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs). The research of this paper is threefold: (i) characterizes a three-layer measurement gap, (ii) proposes a structured S-FoM set organized by ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics, QaaS pipeline mapping, and measurement maturity, and (iii) defines a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates S-FoMs into a combined Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. Additionally, an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques has been presented. Our aim is a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the Quantum Software Stack (QSS).

</details>


### [215] [An End-to-End Threat Model for the Quantum-as-a-Service Pipeline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05836)
*Badhon Rahman,Majid Haghparast,Tommi Mikkonen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a six-stage decomposition of the QaaS workflow with STRIDE threat modeling, producing a matrix that classifies attack vectors into quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers, while identifying underexplored threat categories and cross-stage attack chains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing attacks on QaaS platforms (calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer, etc.) are siloed by their own terminology, and current STRIDE-based threat modeling for quantum systems lacks a structured, stack-oriented view of the entire QaaS pipeline.

Method: The authors decompose the hybrid quantum-classical workflow into a six-stage model (orchestration, compilation, and execution layers) and apply STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) threat modeling across each stage, producing a matrix that categorizes attack vectors into quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers.

Result: The resulting matrix systematically maps known attacks to pipeline stages and threat categories, reveals underexplored areas (particularly repudiation and elevation-of-privilege), and identifies three distinct cross-stage attack chains with higher composite impact than isolated attacks.

Conclusion: A structured, stack-aware STRIDE approach to QaaS threat modeling exposes gaps in current security research, especially in repudiation and elevation-of-privilege, and demonstrates that cross-stage attack chains pose amplified risks requiring holistic defenses.

Abstract: Cloud-based accessing of Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) platforms such as IBM Quantum, IonQ Cloud, and Amazon Braket is becoming popular day by day. Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VQE, QAOA, QML) transfer data via a long layered pipeline of orchestration, compilation, and execution. Recent works have demonstrated various critical attacks at individual stages: Calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer, and so on. However, these attacks remain separated because of their own terminology, and existing STRIDE-based threat modeling in the context of quantum lacks a structured view towards the QaaS stack itself. We address this concern by decomposing the workflow into six-stage model with STRIDE threat modeling. Our matrix demonstrated attack vectors in quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers for each of the stages. We further investigate the underexplored sections (repudiation and elevation-of-privilege) and distinguish three different cross-stage attack chains with higher impacts.

</details>


### [216] [RustGo: Fairly Directed Greybox Fuzzing for Enforcing Rust Memory Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05870)
*Dongyeon Yu,Jiun Min,Yewan Na,Mijung Kim,Taegyu Kim,Yuseok Jeon*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RustGo is a directed greybox fuzzer for Rust that focuses on memory-unsafe code regions by identifying potential bug targets via static analysis, pruning irrelevant paths, and maintaining independent per-target fuzzing states. It achieves significant speedups in reaching targets and discovered 13 previously unknown bugs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Rust fuzzers waste resources by fuzzing both safe and unsafe code indiscriminately. Since memory bugs can only occur in unsafe Rust code (which constitutes ~10% of codebases), there is a need for a fuzzer that efficiently directs efforts toward these vulnerable regions rather than the already compiler-guaranteed safe code.

Method: RustGo employs three core techniques: (1) automatic identification of potential memory bug targets using Rust-specific static analysis, (2) accurate path pruning to eliminate paths irrelevant to each target, and (3) a novel fuzzing approach that maintains independent state per target and applies dynamic pruning for balanced, focused fuzzing across multiple targets.

Result: On real-world Rust applications, RustGo prunes an average of 78.49% of irrelevant paths, reaches targets 2.09× to 5.08× faster than existing fuzzers, and discovered 13 previously unknown bugs, with six receiving RUSTSEC IDs and one assigned a CVE ID.

Conclusion: RustGo demonstrates that Rust-specific, directed fuzzing focused on unsafe code regions significantly outperforms general-purpose fuzzers in both efficiency and effectiveness, uncovering real-world vulnerabilities that had evaded prior testing.

Abstract: Rust is a popular systems programming language that provides strong memory safety and introduces low-performance overhead. While Rust guarantees memory safety through strict security policies, such as ownership, memory bugs can still occur in unsafe-related Rust codes where these policies are not fully enforced. Although such unsafe Rust code accounts for only a small portion of the entire code (e.g., 10%), existing approaches fuzz the entire code-including safe Rust, whose memory safety is already enforced by the Rust compiler-resulting in inefficient use of fuzzing resources. In this paper, we propose RustGo, the new Rust-directed greybox fuzzer that effectively and fairly focuses on code regions potentially containing memory bugs. For this, RustGo automatically identifies potential memory bug targets and accurately prunes the paths irrelevant to each target by leveraging Rust-specific static analysis. For each identified target, RustGo includes a new fuzzing approach that maintains an independent state and applies dynamic pruning to maximize balanced and focused fuzzing. We evaluate RustGo on various real-world Rust applications. On average, RustGo prunes 78.49% of irrelevant paths, reaches targets x 2.09 to x 5.08 faster than existing fuzzers, and identifies 13 unknown bugs (six assigned RUSTSEC IDs and one assigned CVE ID).

</details>


### [217] [The Vulnerability With No CVE: Managing Persistent Gaps Between Mandate and Authority in AI Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05884)
*Shayell Aharon Salomon Amir Shaked Matan Noga*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Introduces Agentic Posture Vulnerability (APV) as a persistent, task-conditioned vulnerability-management abstraction for composed agent-control exposures, operationalizing existing risks like excessive agency and authorization gaps across long-lived agent deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing risk frameworks (excessive agency, weak authorization, inadequate controls) and control models (constrain, authorize, observe, validate, respond) lack a mechanism to manage persistent, cross-component agent deployments that outlive individual events. APV fills the operational gap by providing a durable vulnerability record that ties runtime manifestations to an invariant posture.

Method: Defines APV conceptually as a task-conditioned abstraction; distinguishes it from CVEs, OWASP Excessive Agency, Agent Baseline controls, and runtime authorization-execution gaps; provides a thresholded definition, six recurring APV patterns, a vulnerability lifecycle, a minimum record schema, a control-and-closure matrix, tooling implications, and a research agenda.

Result: APV bridges the gap between static control assessments and runtime agent behavior by linking multiple task-specific manifestations to a single durable posture record, which remains open until authority is narrowed, controls are added, risk is accepted, or closure is verified.

Conclusion: APV is not a new root-cause class but an operational abstraction that makes existing agent-security weaknesses manageable and testable. The framework provides a concrete path for security programs to track, triage, and close agent-control exposures across persistent, composed deployments.

Abstract: Existing guidance identifies excessive agency, excessive permission, weak task-bound authorization, and inadequate agent controls as important risks. Control frameworks also describe capabilities for constraining, authorizing, observing, validating, and responding to agent activity. Yet security programs still need a way to manage persistent deployed instances that span components and outlive any one event.
  We propose the agentic posture vulnerability (APV) as a task-conditioned vulnerability-management abstraction: a durable record for a composed agent-control exposure. One posture may produce different runtime manifestations across tasks; APV links those manifestations to the invariant posture and remains open until authority is narrowed, a missing control is added, risk is accepted, or closure is verified. APV is not proposed as a new root-cause class of risk; it operationalizes existing excessive-agency, authorization, and control-composition weaknesses.
  We distinguish APVs from CVE-addressable product defects, OWASP Excessive Agency, Agent Baseline control outcomes, and the runtime authorization-execution gap. We then provide a field vignette, a thresholded definition, six recurring APV patterns, a vulnerability lifecycle, a minimum record, a control-and-closure matrix, tooling implications, and a testable research agenda.

</details>


### [218] [Tool Demo: Topology analysis with GPML for detection of cyberattacks in Water Distribution Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05902)
*Majed Jaber,Abdul Qadir Khan,Ankush Meshram,Julien Michel,Côme Frappé - - Vialatoux,Pierre Parrend*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A topology-driven detection method transforms network traffic into dynamic graphs and extracts community/spectral metrics via GPML to identify cyberattacks in water distribution networks, validated on HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Water distribution networks integrate physical processes with communication networks via ICS, exposing them to cyberattacks that alter traffic patterns and network behavior. Traditional detection methods relying on raw traffic or protocol information fail to capture structural changes induced by such attacks.

Method: Raw network traffic is transformed into dynamic graphs. Community metrics and spectral metrics are extracted from these graphs using a Graph Processing for Machine Learning (GPML) framework. These graph-theoretic features capture structural and communication modifications over time, which are then used for attack detection.
