Result: Spectral and community graph metrics improved model detection performance on all three industrial water distribution datasets: HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest.

Conclusion: Topology-driven, graph-based analysis effectively captures structural anomalies from cyberattacks in water distribution networks, outperforming traditional traffic-based detection methods.

Abstract: Water distribution networks depends on industrial control systems to integrate the physical process with communication network, making them vulnerable to cyberattacks that alter the traffic pattern and network behavior. Traditional detection approaches that rely on raw traffic or protocol information often oversee structural changes that are induced by such attacks. In this work, we presents a topology-driven approach for detection of cyberattacks in water distribution networks based on Graph Processing for Machine Learning (GPML) framework. The raw traffic is transformed into dynamic graphs, from which community and spectral metrics are extracted and analyzed for any structural and communication modifications with time. The proposed methodology is evaluated on three industrial water distribution datasets such as HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest. Spectral and community graph metrics improve the model performance in detection of cyber and pyhiscal attacks across the three datasets.

</details>


### [219] [MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models through Representation Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05909)
*Shenyi Zhang,Keyan Guo,Zihao Wang,Xuebin Li,Lingchen Zhao,Hongxin Hu,Chao Shen,Qian Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MLLMs refuse unsafe text but accept unsafe multimodal inputs due to representation shift. MMAligner realigns unsafe multimodal representations into the pre-existing refusal region, achieving 99% refusal rate with <2% utility loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs exhibit a safety disparity: they refuse unsafe text prompts but generate harmful responses to equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses (external guardrails, safety fine-tuning) are inefficient or degrade utility. The authors aim to identify the root cause of this disparity geometrically.

Method: The authors geometrically analyze MLLM representations, discovering a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary that persist across modalities. Unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places them outside this boundary. Based on this, they propose MMAligner, which calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the refusal region using: (1) a hard lower bound to enforce refusal, (2) a soft upper bound to limit excessive modification, and (3) a preservation objective for benign inputs.

Result: Across multiple open-source MLLMs, MMAligner achieves an average refusal rate of 99% on unsafe multimodal inputs with less than 2% utility degradation, using minimal training data. It substantially improves the safety-utility trade-off over existing baselines.

Conclusion: Multimodal safety degradation in MLLMs is caused by representation misalignment rather than absent safety capability. Realigning unsafe multimodal representations into the text-learned refusal region is an effective, data-efficient safeguarding strategy.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often refuse unsafe text prompts yet generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses either rely on external guardrails, which add inference overhead without repairing intrinsic flaws, or safety fine-tuning, which treats alignment as black-box optimization and may sacrifice utility or require large multimodal datasets. To identify the cause of this safety disparity, we analyze MLLM representations geometrically. We find that safety mechanisms learned from text persist across modalities: a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary remain effective, and representations inside this boundary consistently trigger refusals. However, unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places most of them outside the boundary, allowing them to bypass the model's intrinsic safety mechanism. This indicates that multimodal safety degradation stems from representation misalignment rather than the absence of safety capability. Based on this finding, we propose MMAligner, a safeguarding method that calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the pre-existing refusal region. MMAligner applies a hard lower bound to ensure refusal, a soft upper bound to avoid excessive modification, and a preservation objective for benign inputs. Experiments across multiple open-source MLLMs show that MMAligner raises the average refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data, substantially improving the safety-utility trade-off over existing baselines. (*Due to the notification from arXiv, "The Abstract field cannot be longer than 1,920 characters", the Abstract that appeared is shortened.)

</details>


### [220] [A Note on the Influence of a Zero Length Nonce on GCM and GMAC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06061)
*Yaobin Shen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A simple attack recovers the hash key of GCM/GMAC when a zero-length nonce is used, enabling arbitrary ciphertext/message forgery. The attack applies to the ISO/IEC version but not the NIST version, which mandates a nonce of at least one bit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To highlight a critical vulnerability in the ISO/IEC version of GCM and GMAC that arises from permitting zero-length nonces, contrasting it with the NIST specification which explicitly forbids this.

Method: The attack exploits the use of a zero-length nonce. When the nonce length is zero, the initial counter block (ICB) and the pre-counter block (J0) are constructed in a way that allows the adversary to directly recover the hash subkey H through a simple algebraic manipulation of the authenticated encryption/authentication tag computation.

Result: The hash key H can be fully recovered. With H known, the adversary can forge valid authentication tags for arbitrary ciphertexts (GCM) or messages (GMAC), completely breaking the authentication security of the scheme.

Conclusion: The ISO/IEC standard's allowance of zero-length nonces introduces a trivial but catastrophic security flaw in GCM/GMAC. The NIST version avoids this by requiring a minimum nonce length of one bit, underscoring the importance of this seemingly minor specification difference.

Abstract: In this note, we show a simple attack that can recover the hash key of GCM and GMAC by using a zero length nonce. After recovering the hash key, the adversary can forge an arbitrary ciphertext or message as she wants. We note that the ISO/IEC version of GCM and GMAC allows the nonce to be a zero length string, while the NIST version of GCM and GMAC explicitly requires the nonce to be at least one bit. Hence, our attack works for the ISO/IEC version and cannot work for the NIST version.

</details>


### [221] [dfence: Fine-Grained Speculation Barriers for Efficient and Effective Hardware-Software Protection in the Spectre Era (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06124)
*Davide Davoli,Marton Bognar,Lesly-Ann Daniel,Benjamin Grégoire,Frank Piessens,Tamara Rezk*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: dfence is a new CPU instruction that generalizes Speculative Load Hardening to mitigate both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL attacks. It allows developers to annotate sensitive registers, with hardware preventing transient leaks. Implemented in the Proteus CPU, it incurs <1% average overhead, and a companion type system statically verifies correct dfence placement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing software mitigations for speculative execution attacks have critical limitations: Speculative Load Hardening (SLH) only covers Spectre-PHT and requires error-prone, costly software-managed speculative masks; SSBD defenses against Spectre-STL incur high performance overhead and lack fine-grained control. A unified, low-overhead, hardware-assisted defense covering both attack vectors is needed.

Method: The authors introduce dfence, a new CPU instruction generalizing SLH. Developers annotate sensitive registers; the hardware ensures these values cannot leak transiently during speculative execution. The approach is implemented and evaluated on the Proteus CPU. Additionally, a static type system is designed to verify correct dfence instruction placement in code.

Result: dfence achieves less than 1% average performance overhead across evaluated benchmarks while providing protection against both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL. The type system further enables safe and correct adoption of the instruction.

Conclusion: dfence demonstrates that a single, minimal-hardware instruction can effectively and efficiently unify defenses against two major Spectre variant classes, with a type system ensuring safe deployment, offering a practical path toward secure speculative execution.

Abstract: Speculative execution attacks such as Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL remain a critical security concern in modern processors. While software-based mitigations like Speculative Load Hardening (SLH) offer effective protection against Spectre-PHT, they are limited in scope and require software-managed speculative masks, which can be error-prone and costly. Defenses against Spectre-STL, such as the Speculative Store Bypass Disable bit (SSBD), incur additional performance overhead and lack fine-grained control. In this work, we introduce dfence, a new CPU instruction that generalizes SLH to mitigate both Spectre-PHT and Spectre-STL with minimal hardware support. dfence enables developers to annotate sensitive registers, with the hardware ensuring that these values do not leak transiently. We implement dfence in the Proteus CPU and evaluate its security and performance, demonstrating less than 1% average performance overhead for our benchmarks. In addition, to support easy and secure adoption, we design a type system that statically verifies the correct placement of dfence instructions in code.

</details>


### [222] [Hardware Keystores for AI Agent Signing Workflows: A Zero-Trust MCP Enforcement Architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06130)
*Leo Sambrook,Sampo Sovio*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes replacing software-stored cryptographic keys for AI agents with hardware-confined keys accessed via PKCS#11, wrapped in a five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack. In evaluation against 12 AgentDojo injection scenarios across four LLMs (192 runs), baseline attack success rate was 19.3%, while the protected system achieved 0% ASR with zero false positives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents currently store private keys in software-accessible locations (plaintext files, environment variables, container memory), exposing raw key material to any process with read privileges. A real-world incident demonstrated keys exfiltrated via email injection in under five minutes from a widely deployed framework. The authors aim to enforce both key confidentiality and content-aware authorization for key use.

Method: The authors replace software-resident keys with hardware-confined keys accessible through a vendor-neutral PKCS#11 interface. Cryptographic operations execute on-device within a hardware keystore (HSM, TPM, smart card); the host receives only results via opaque handles. This hardware confinement is augmented by a five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack: (1) session identity (SAGA), (2) scope bounds (Smax), (3) semantic validation (RAV), (4) taint tracking, and (5) the hardware execution boundary. Evaluation uses 12 injection scenarios from AgentDojo's ImportantInstructionsAttack template across four LLM models with 192 combined runs.

Result: Baseline Attack Success Rate: 19.3% [95% CI: 14.3%–25.4%] across three models (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash). Protected ASR: 0% (Wilson 95% CI upper bound: 2.0%). Zero false positives across four benign task scenarios.

Conclusion: Hardware-confined keys combined with the five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack effectively eliminate prompt injection attacks targeting cryptographic key exfiltration in AI agents, reducing ASR from 19.3% to 0% without impairing legitimate operations.

Abstract: AI agents performing cryptographic operations (signing Git commits, authenticating API calls, issuing certificates) currently store private keys in software-accessible locations: plaintext files, environment variables, or container memory. Any process with sufficient read privileges can extract the raw key material. A recent production incident demonstrated the practical severity: private keys were exfiltrated from a widely deployed framework via email injection in under five minutes. We aim to enforce both key confidentiality and content-aware authorisation for key use. To that end, we replace software-resident keys with hardware-confined keys accessible through a vendor-neutral PKCS#11 interface. A hardware keystore (HSM, TPM, smart card) executes cryptographic operations on-device; the host receives only the result via opaque handles. Hardware confinement is the primary contribution; it is enabled by a surrounding five-layer Zero-Trust enforcement stack comprising session identity (SAGA), scope bounds (Smax), semantic validation (RAV), taint tracking, and the hardware execution boundary. We evaluate against 12 injection scenarios derived from AgentDojo's ImportantInstructionsAttack template (Debenedetti et al., arXiv:2406.13352). We run four LLM models; three follow injections in baseline mode (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, n=192 combined). Baseline Attack Success Rate (ASR): 19.3% [14.3%, 25.4%]; protected ASR: 0% (Wilson 95% CI upper bound 2.0%). Zero false positives across four benign task scenarios.

</details>


### [223] [Reversible Unlearnable Examples: Towards the Copyright Protection in Deep Learning Era](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06211)
*Binze Wang,Jinyu Tian,Xingrun Wang,Xiaochen Yuan,Jianqing Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a copyright protection mechanism that simultaneously prevents unauthorized model training (via unlearnable examples) and malicious data leakage (via watermarking), addressing the negative interaction effects that occur when naively combining the two techniques. The method generates perturbations that minimize mutual information between input and output, coupled with a dual watermark extraction strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing unlearnable example methods only address illegal model training but overlook data leakage risks. Naively combining availability attacks and watermarking fails due to negative interaction effects between the two mechanisms. A unified solution is needed for comprehensive copyright protection.

Method: The method generates unlearnable perturbations by minimizing the mutual information between model inputs and outputs, forcing models to learn uncorrelated features. For watermarking, a dual extraction strategy with two distinct watermark extractors is designed to eliminate the side impact of unlearnable perturbations on watermark extraction. This enables both preventing unauthorized training and tracing data leaks.

Result: Extensive experiments on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and Pets datasets demonstrate that the proposed method provides comprehensive copyright protection, effectively addressing both unauthorized model training and data leakage threats simultaneously.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully unifies unlearnable perturbations for training prevention with robust watermarking for leak tracing, overcoming the negative interactions that plague naive combinations. This provides holistic copyright protection for deep learning datasets.

Abstract: Significant advancements in deep learning have been made possible by the utilization of large datasets, underscoring the critical importance of copyright protection. Adding meticulously designed perturbations to examples, making them unlearnable has become a crucial approach for safeguarding data copyright. Existing methods for creating unlearnable examples overlook the risk of data leakage, which can threaten data ownership. Thus, copyright protection in deep learning faces two main threats: illegal model training and malicious data leakage. We investigate that these two threats cannot be solved by straightforwardly combining existing availability attacks and watermarking techniques as their negative interaction effects. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel copyright protection mechanism for the aforementioned security concerns. Considering that the prevention of unauthorized model training requires powerful generalizability of unlearnable perturbations, we generate perturbations to induce the model to learn uncorrelated features of input images. It works by minimizing the mutual information of the input and output of the model. On the other hand, to eliminate the side impact of unlearnable perturbations on the watermark extraction, we design a dual extraction strategy by using two distinct watermark extractors. Extensive experiments on the image datasets {ImageNet, CIFAR10, and Pets} show that our proposed method could provide comprehensive copyright protection to images. The code is available at {https://github.com/Yeah21/ReversibleUnlearnableExamples}.

</details>


### [224] [Game Hopping in Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06261)
*Stefan Dziembowski,Grzegorz Fabiański,Daniele Micciancio,Rafał Stefański*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: HOPSCOTCH is a Lean 4 framework for mechanizing game-based cryptographic proofs using a shallow embedding that integrates with Mathlib. It represents proofs as explicit objects corresponding to game-hopping steps, proves a general computational soundness theorem with concrete advantage bounds, and supports state-abstraction for observational equivalence. The framework is demonstrated on IND-CCA, ElGamal, public-key CPA, and the first mechanized proof of GGM for non-constant depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mechanizing game-based cryptographic proofs is challenging due to the need to manage stateful probabilistic oracles, reductions, and concrete advantage bounds. Existing mechanization efforts often use deep embeddings that limit integration with general mathematical libraries. The authors aim to provide a shallow-embeddable, sound, and general framework within Lean 4 that directly leverages Mathlib while making game-hopping proofs explicit, inspectable, and automatable.

Method: HOPSCOTCH employs a shallow embedding in Lean 4 where oracles and reductions are ordinary Lean definitions. Security definitions are expressed as indistinguishability between stateful probabilistic oracles. Game-hopping proofs are reified as explicit formal objects whose constructors correspond to standard game-hopping steps (e.g., transitioning between games, applying reductions). A general computational soundness theorem interprets these proof objects, constructing reductions against assumptions and deriving concrete advantage bounds. Observational equivalence is handled via a state-abstraction methodology supporting transformations such as adding/forgetting state and replacing eager sampling with lazy sampling.

Result: The framework is demonstrated on four case studies: IND-CCA security of encrypt-then-MAC, ElGamal encryption security from DDH, the implication from one-time secrecy to public-key IND-CPA security, and the GGM pseudorandom-function construction. Notably, the GGM proof is the first mechanized proof for non-constant depth, establishing a new milestone in the mechanization of cryptographic proofs.

Conclusion: HOPSCOTCH successfully bridges the gap between formal verification and game-based cryptography by providing a shallowly-embedded, sound framework in Lean 4 that integrates with Mathlib. Its explicit proof objects facilitate construction, automation, and inspection of game-hopping arguments, advancing the state of the art in mechanized cryptographic proofs.

Abstract: We present HOPSCOTCH, a Lean 4 framework for mechanizing computationally sound, game-based cryptographic proofs. Security definitions are expressed as indistinguishability between stateful probabilistic oracles, and proofs follow the standard game-hopping paradigm. HOPSCOTCH uses a shallow embedding: oracles and reductions are ordinary Lean definitions, enabling direct integration with the full Lean ecosystem, including general mathematical theories from Mathlib, such as finite-group theory. A game-hopping proof in HOPSCOTCH is represented as an explicit formal object whose constructors correspond to the standard steps of a game-hopping argument, making proofs easier to construct, automate, and inspect. We prove a general computational soundness theorem that interprets these proof objects by constructing reductions against the assumptions they use and deriving a concrete bound on the advantage of any distinguisher. Observational equivalence between oracles is established using a state-abstraction methodology: a simple yet powerful approach that supports transformations such as adding or forgetting state and replacing eager sampling with lazy sampling. We illustrate the framework with formalized proofs of the IND-CCA security of encrypt-then-MAC, the security of ElGamal encryption from DDH, the implication from one-time secrecy to public-key IND-CPA security, and the GGM pseudorandom-function construction. To the best of our knowledge, the last is the first mechanized proof of GGM for non-constant depth.

</details>


### [225] [A Sound Translation from Tamarin to ProVerif: Enabling Comparative Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06315)
*Kevin Morio,Yavor Ivanov,Robert Künnemann*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif is presented, enabling rigorous comparison. Within a faithful fragment, soundness and completeness guarantees are proven. Evaluation on 121 models shows ProVerif is faster in 92.3% of comparable cases with ~6-7x median runtime/memory advantages, and 246 of 247 non-XOR tasks agree.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tamarin and ProVerif are two leading tools for security protocol verification but differ fundamentally in formalisms (multiset rewrite rules vs. applied-pi calculus) and verification guarantees (sound-and-complete vs. fast-but-potentially-incomplete). No systematic, rigorous comparison exists due to this gap. A sound translation is needed to enable cross-tool benchmarking and to understand when ProVerif's incomplete results can be trusted relative to Tamarin's ground truth.

Method: The authors develop a formal translation from Tamarin to ProVerif featuring: (1) novel formula rewriting techniques, (2) encoding of multiset rewrite rule semantics into applied-pi calculus, and (3) handling of simultaneous events. They identify a "faithful fragment" with formal soundness (ProVerif-verified properties hold in Tamarin) and completeness (exists-trace properties without attacker knowledge are preserved). Best-effort encodings (e.g., XOR) fall outside these guarantees. The translation is evaluated on 121 Tamarin models covering 566 lemma tasks.

Result: The translation covers 562 of 566 lemma tasks. Among non-XOR tasks with definitive results from both tools, 246 of 247 agree; the sole disagreement is flagged as using an incomplete model. Of 362 tasks where Tamarin returns a Boolean result and ProVerif completes with a logical result, ProVerif is faster in 334 cases (92.3%), with median per-task runtime ratio of 6.74x and peak-memory ratio of 6.24x in favor of ProVerif.

Conclusion: The translation provides a principled foundation for comparing Tamarin and ProVerif. ProVerif delivers substantially faster verification with strong agreement (246/247) on the faithful fragment, making it a practical first-line tool when its incompleteness is acceptable. The formal soundness and completeness proofs give users clear guarantees about when ProVerif results can be relied upon. The flagged disagreement demonstrates the value of the faithful/incomplete distinction.

Abstract: Tamarin and ProVerif are two prominent tools for the formal verification of security protocols. They share the same high-level goal but differ significantly in their underlying formalisms and verification techniques, making a systematic comparison challenging: Tamarin uses multiset rewrite rules with sound and complete verification, whereas ProVerif employs an extension of the applied-pi calculus that provides fast but potentially incomplete results.
  We present a sound translation from Tamarin to ProVerif that enables a rigorous comparison of the two tools. It introduces novel techniques for formula rewriting, encoding multiset rewrite semantics, and handling simultaneous events, supporting an extensive subset of Tamarin's features, including multiset rewrite rules, lemmas, and restrictions, while precisely characterizing the cases where faithful translation is not possible. We provide formal proofs: within the faithful fragment, soundness ensures that any property verified in ProVerif also holds in the original Tamarin model, and completeness ensures that exists-trace properties not involving attacker knowledge are preserved. Best-effort encodings, in particular XOR, are reported separately and are outside these guarantees.
  Finally, we evaluate our translation on 121 Tamarin models. The translation covers 562 of 566 lemma tasks. Among non-XOR tasks with definitive results from both tools, 246 of 247 agree, with the remaining verdict explicitly flagged as using an incomplete model. Among the 362 tasks for which Tamarin returns a Boolean result and ProVerif completes with a logical result, ProVerif is faster in 334 cases (92.3%), with median per-task runtime and peak-memory ratios of 6.74x and 6.24x, respectively.

</details>

### [226] [Mixed Uncertainty in One View: Co-Visualizing Statistical Variability and Qualitative Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05487)
*Racquel Fygenson,Lace Padilla,Laura E. Matzen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how different visualization techniques for conveying qualitative confidence alongside quantitative uncertainty in line chart forecasts affect non-experts' decision making, finding that non-textual encoding methods (color, transparency, blurred stroke) can effectively signal qualitative confidence and alter judgments similarly to text-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasts involve both quantitative uncertainty (directly quantifiable) and qualitative confidence (subjective expert judgment). While prior work shows that conveying both affects decision making, little research examines how the presentation method of these dual uncertainty forms influences readers' judgments, especially in time-series visualizations.

Method: Three preregistered human-subjects studies (total n=923) testing different visualization methods for qualitative uncertainty alongside line charts with confidence intervals. Methods included separate text/icon representations and integrated encodings (color, transparency, blurred stroke). Experiment 1 replicated prior findings in the time-series context; Experiments 2 and 3 compared non-textual encoding techniques.

Result: Experiment 1 confirmed that displaying qualitative confidence alongside statistical variability changes decision-making patterns, replicating prior work. Experiments 2 and 3 demonstrated that several non-textual encoding techniques (color, transparency, blurred stroke) produce similar effects to text in incorporating qualitative confidence into judgments.

Conclusion: The findings provide actionable guidelines for visualization designers representing multiple uncertainty forms in line chart forecasts. Non-textual visual encodings can effectively convey qualitative confidence, offering flexible design alternatives beyond text-based approaches.

Abstract: Forecasting involves multiple forms of uncertainty, including both uncertainties that can be quantified directly (quantitative uncertainty) and those that must be expressed through experts' subjective judgments about the forecast and its context (qualitative confidence). Past work has established that conveying both quantitative uncertainty and qualitative confidence in forecasts can alter readers' decision making, but little research investigates the impact of how these forms of uncertainty are presented. In this work, we present three preregistered human-subjects studies (total n = 923) on how different methods of visualizing qualitative uncertainty alongside line charts' confidence intervals affects non-experts' decision making. In particular, we investigate representing qualitative uncertainty separately via text and icons, and integrated into quantitative confidence intervals via color, transparency, and a blurred stroke design. In Experiment 1, we confirm that showing qualitative confidence alongside statistical variability can change patterns of decision making, replicating findings from previous work in the new context of time-series line charts. In Experiments 2 and 3, we find several non-textual encoding techniques that produce similar effects in participants' incorporation of qualitative confidence into their judgments. Our findings suggest actionable guidelines for visualization designers who seek to represent multiple forms of uncertainty for a single line chart forecast. A free copy of this paper and all supplemental materials are available at https://osf.io/7ya2c/overview.

</details>


### [227] [Turing's Frist Imitation Game: Design Concepts and a Human-Approximates-Machine Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05558)
*Sharon Temtsin,Christoph Bartneck*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Turing's 1948 "Intelligent Machinery" report is analyzed as a foundational source for his later imitation games, identifying key design concepts (machine error, physical feature exclusion, human judge, search as intellectual activity) and arguing that constraining the human to a poor chess player amplifies the role of search, reframing the game as human-approximates-machine.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to recover Turing's 1948 report as an overlooked conceptual source for the imitation game, arguing that its design principles offer a richer understanding of Turing's vision—particularly the symmetrical question of when human cognition becomes machine-like under constraints.

Method: This is a conceptual and historical analysis. The author identifies and integrates four design concepts from Turing's 1948 chess-based imitation game, then develops a novel interpretive argument about how restricting the human player's skill level reshapes the game's epistemic function.

Result: The analysis yields two contributions: (1) an integrated framework of four design concepts undergirding the 1948 game, and (2) the argument that a poor human chess player increases reliance on search, making human behavior more machine-like and transforming the game into a human-approximates-machine test.

Conclusion: The imitation game framework is bidirectional: it can test whether machines imitate humans and also reveal conditions under which human intelligence becomes machine-like. The 1948 report is thus not merely a precursor but a conceptually distinct and philosophically significant formulation.

Abstract: This paper examines Turing's 1948 report, "Intelligent Machinery", as an important conceptual source for the later imitation games. Its first contribution is to identify and integrate the design concepts underlying the 1948 chess-based imitation game: the possibility that intelligent machines may make mistakes, the exclusion of irrelevant physical features, the role of the human judge, and Turing's claim that intellectual activity consists mainly of search. The paper's second contribution is to argue that restricting the human contestant to a rather poor chess player increases the role of intellectual search and makes human behaviour more comparable to machine behaviour. This interpretation presents the 1948 game as a human-approximates-machine game and suggests that the imitation game framework can be used not only to ask whether machines imitate humans, but also to examine when human intelligence becomes machine-like under specific task constraints.

</details>


### [228] [A Multi-Layer System for Ultra-High-Resolution Static 360-Degree Telepresence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05570)
*Jiapeng Chi,Gerd Bruder,Carsten Neumann,Carolina Cruz-Neira,Dirk Reiners*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A multi-layer system for static 360° telepresence that combines an 8K panoramic camera with a rotatable 4K PTZ camera to create ultra-high-resolution, interactively updatable panoramic representations beyond native capture resolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 360° video telepresence is limited by the resolution of capture/display hardware. Existing installations often feature fixed viewpoints and static scenes, yet optimization strategies for such setups are underexplored.

Method: A three-layer representation: (1) a tile-based ultra-high-resolution panoramic background built by offline stitching 4K PTZ scans onto an 8K panorama; (2) a dynamic update layer using real-time background matting on the 8K stream for foreground motion; (3) a region-of-interest 4K layer streaming a real-time PTZ view while updating corresponding background tiles.

Result: Evaluated via comparisons with video super-resolution approaches and a user study on perceived detail and immersion. Results show tile-based background refinement with user-guided updates effectively balances panoramic fidelity and interactivity.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-layer, tile-based approach offers a practical solution for enhancing resolution and interactivity in static 360° telepresence, outperforming naive super-resolution methods while maintaining immersive quality.

Abstract: 360-degree video telepresence offers strong immersive potential but remains constrained by the limited resolution of current capture and display hardware. Many telepresence installations feature fixed viewpoints and largely static scenes, yet optimization strategies tailored to such setups have received limited attention. We present a multi-layer, ultra-high-resolution system for static 360-degree telepresence that combines an 8K panoramic camera with a rotatable 4K pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) camera. Our approach builds a three-layer representation: (1) a tile-based ultra-high-resolution panoramic background, generated by offline stitching high-detail 4K PTZ scans onto the base 8K panorama to achieve effective resolution beyond native capture, and represented as a set of spatial tiles; (2) a dynamic update layer that composites foreground motions from the 8K stream via real-time high-resolution background matting; and (3) a region-of-interest 4K layer that streams a real-time PTZ view of the selected region and additionally updates the corresponding background tiles over time. We evaluate the proposed system through comparisons with representative video super-resolution approaches and a user study assessing perceived detail and immersive experience. Our results indicate that tile-based background refinement, together with user-guided updates, provides a practical way to balance panoramic fidelity and interactivity in static 360-degree telepresence.

</details>


### [229] [Toward Resilient Human-AI Collaboration: A Lifecycle Taxonomy of Sociotechnical Risks and Cascading Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05614)
*Md Foysal Ahmed,Isaac Kobby Anni,Md Main Uddin Rony*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A lifecycle-oriented synthesis identifying six recurring cross-domain risk clusters in human-AI collaboration — Trust Miscalibration, Cognitive Burden, Accountability Gap, Capability Erosion, Goal Misalignment, and AI Anxiety/Technostress — and proposing a conceptual model of how these sociotechnical risks interact and cascade across four stages: task allocation, interaction, feedback, and adoption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human-AI collaboration risks are typically studied in isolation within specific domains (healthcare, journalism, education, etc.), obscuring recurring failure mechanisms that cut across contexts. The authors aim to unify fragmented literature to explain why piecemeal interventions often produce unintended consequences.

Method: The paper conducts a lifecycle-oriented synthesis of human-AI collaboration risks across four stages (task allocation, interaction, feedback, and adoption), drawing evidence from diverse application domains. It identifies six cross-domain risk clusters and proposes a conceptual interaction model illustrating how these risks emerge from sociotechnical drivers, interact through cascading pathways, and affect team performance and human well-being.

Result: Six recurring cross-domain risk clusters were identified: (1) Trust Miscalibration, (2) Cognitive Burden, (3) Accountability Gap, (4) Capability Erosion, (5) Goal Misalignment, and (6) AI Anxiety and Technostress. The analysis reveals that most collaboration failures arise from interconnected sociotechnical dynamics rather than isolated technical deficiencies, explaining why isolated fixes frequently backfire.

Conclusion: The unified framework provides a foundation for future empirical research, lifecycle-oriented governance, and the design of more resilient, trustworthy, and human-centered human-AI collaboration systems, shifting focus from isolated fixes to holistic sociotechnical intervention.

Abstract: As AI systems become increasingly integrated into consequential domains such as healthcare, journalism, education, scientific research, organizational decision-making, and defense, effective human-AI collaboration has emerged as a critical challenge. However, the sociotechnical risks that undermine collaboration are often studied in isolation, obscuring the recurring failure mechanisms that cut across domains. This paper presents a lifecycle-oriented synthesis of human-AI collaboration risks spanning four stages: task allocation, interaction, feedback, and adoption. Drawing on evidence from diverse application domains, we identify six recurring cross-domain risk clusters: Trust Miscalibration, Cognitive Burden, Accountability Gap, Capability Erosion, Goal Misalignment, and AI Anxiety and Technostress. We further propose a conceptual interaction model that illustrates how these risks emerge from sociotechnical drivers, interact through cascading pathways, and ultimately affect team performance and human well-being. Our analysis shows that many collaboration failures stem not from isolated technical deficiencies but from interconnected sociotechnical dynamics, helping explain why piecemeal interventions frequently create unintended consequences. By synthesizing fragmented literature into a unified framework, this work provides a foundation for future empirical research, lifecycle-oriented governance, and the design of more resilient, trustworthy, and human-centered human-AI collaboration systems.

</details>


### [230] [CaRing: Preventing Carpal Tunnel Syndrome based on Daily Activities from Always-Available Input Device](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05619)
*Shuowei Li,Houdong Liang,Xingjian Dong*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: CaRing is an index-finger-worn ring that uses an optical flow sensor to detect the start and end of mouse usage sessions, aiming to prevent Carpal Tunnel Syndrome by sensing finger movement that software timers and wrist-worn devices miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome involves permanent median nerve damage, and existing approaches (software timers, wrist-worn devices) fail to detect subtle finger movements that indicate actual mouse use. A more precise detection method is needed for timely interventions.

Method: CaRing uses an optical flow sensor on an index-finger ring to measure finger displacement, accumulating it into a running value. A zero point is established when the hand rests on the desk at each session's start, and start/end thresholds are expressed relative to this zero point. No per-user parameter tuning is required. Evaluation involved 35 recordings and a lab study with ten users.

Result: Approximately 90% of mouse-use start and end events were detected within two seconds of the researcher's ground-truth labels across 35 recordings and a ten-user lab study.

Conclusion: CaRing demonstrates that an optical-flow-based ring sensor can accurately and automatically detect mouse usage boundaries without per-user calibration, offering a promising wearable approach for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome prevention.

Abstract: We present CaRing, a ring worn on the base knuckle of the index finger, a wearable system for detecting the start and end of mouse use to help prevent Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, in which the damage to the median nerve is permanent. CaRing senses finger movement, which neither a software timer nor a wrist-worn device detects. The displacement reported by an optical flow sensor is accumulated into a running value, then a zero point is measured while the hand rests on the desk at the start of each session. With this formulation, the start and end thresholds are expressed relative to the session's zero point. CaRing does not introduce any per-user parameter. We empirically demonstrate that approximately $90\%$ of start and end events are detected within two seconds of the researcher's label, using 35 recordings and a lab study with ten users.

</details>


### [231] [ASIDE: From Conflict Participants to Co-Observers Through Dyadic Spectator Reflection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05690)
*Xinyi Zhang,Jingting He,Zicheng Zhu,Yuxin Su*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ASIDE is a dyadic reflection system that helps couples revisit text-based conflicts by generating a pixel-art theatrical replay with AI-inferred inner states. Partners independently annotate their own and their partner's perspectives, then view divergences together through "Divergence Cards," enabling shared observation of interpretation gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People arguing over text share a record of what was said but hold divergent interpretations of what it meant. Existing reflection tools either support only one person's perspective or enable co-expression without making interpretation gaps visible and inspectable. The authors identify a need for tools that help dyads externalize independently and then encounter each other's interpretations together.

Method: The authors designed ASIDE implementing Dyadic Spectator Reflection (DSR): first externalize independently, then encounter together. ASIDE takes a past chat conflict and creates a pixel-art theatrical replay with revisable AI-generated inner-state hypotheses. Partners first confirm hypotheses about themselves, separately edit interpretations of the other, then view the co-annotated scene together. Divergence Cards pair each person's confirmed account with the partner's reading at specific conversational beats. An exploratory study was conducted with 10 couples who revisited real text-based conflicts using the system.

Result: In the exploratory study with 10 couples, participants reported that the theatrical replay helped them step out of their roles and observe the conflict together from a shared observer position. The system enabled couples to identify and inspect specific interpretation gaps in their past conversations.

Conclusion: The paper contributes Dyadic Spectator Reflection (DSR) as a reusable interaction structure for dyadic reflection tools, along with an exploratory account of how partners used this approach to revisit past text-based conflicts from a shared observer standpoint.

Abstract: When people argue over text, they share a record of what was said but may hold different accounts of what it meant. Existing AI reflection tools typically work from one person's account, while dyadic tools support co-expression without making interpretation gaps inspectable. We present ASIDE, a system for Dyadic Spectator Reflection (DSR). DSR follows the sequence externalize independently, then encounter together. From a past chat conflict, ASIDE creates a pixel-art theatrical replay with revisable AI-generated inner-state hypotheses. Partners first confirm hypotheses about themselves and separately edit their interpretations of the other. After both finish, they view the co-annotated scene together and review Divergence Cards that pair a confirmed account with the partner's reading at a specific conversational beat. In an exploratory study with 10 couples who revisited real text-based conflicts, participants described the theatrical replay as helping them step out of their roles and observe the conflict together. We contribute DSR as a reusable interaction structure for dyadic reflection and an exploratory account of how partners used it to revisit past text-based conflicts from a shared observer position.

</details>


### [232] [SpaceVLA: Spatially Grounded VLA for Robotic Manipulation with User-Authored Grasp and Place Anchors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05730)
*Daniia Zinniatullina,Iaroslav Kolomiets,Mikhail Konenkov,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Dzmitry Tsetserukou*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces Visual Intent Anchors, an XR pipeline that overlays user-specified grasp/placement regions onto RGB images for VLA models, fine-tunes OpenVLA-7B with LoRA on 200 Unity demonstrations, and achieves 91.25% grasp success with sub-centimeter spatial errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA models can follow language commands but lack explicit spatial intent for precise manipulation tasks. Users need a way to communicate where to grasp and place objects beyond natural language alone.

Method: The authors propose an XR pipeline where users specify grasp and placement regions, which are rendered as image-space visual overlays (anchors). They collect 200 pick-and-place demonstrations in Unity, temporally subsample and annotate observations, and fine-tune OpenVLA-7B using LoRA. The policy predicts tokenized 7-DoF incremental actions from marked RGB observations combined with language instructions.

Result: In closed-loop Unity evaluations, the fine-tuned policy achieves a grasp success rate of 91.25%, with mean grasp error of 0.5 cm and mean placement error of 0.7 cm.

Conclusion: Augmenting VLA models with visual intent anchors enables precise spatial manipulation by bridging the gap between high-level language commands and low-level spatial execution, yielding high success rates and low positioning errors in simulated pick-and-place tasks.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models follow language commands but often lack explicit spatial intent for manipulation. We present Visual Intent Anchors, an XR pipeline that lets users specify grasp and placement regions and renders them as image-space overlays for VLA control. We collect 200 Unity pick-and-place demonstrations and fine-tune OpenVLA-7B with LoRA on temporally subsampled annotated observations. The policy predicts tokenized 7-DoF incremental actions from marked RGB observations and language. We evaluate the policy in closed-loop Unity trials, achieving a grasp success rate of 91.25% and mean grasp and placement errors of 0.5 cm and 0.7 cm, respectively.

</details>


### [233] [Temporal Tracking of Reeb-Space Sheets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05837)
*Mohit Sharma,Petar Hristov,Talha Bin Masood,Ingrid Hotz*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A framework for tracking Reeb space sheets across timesteps in time-varying bivariate fields, using complementary similarity measures in spatial and range domains to establish temporal correspondences, demonstrated on synthetic and molecular electronic structure datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Topological methods for univariate time-varying data (e.g., merge trees) are well-established, but analogous approaches for bivariate fields remain underexplored. Reeb spaces extend topological analysis to multivariate data, yet establishing temporal correspondences between their constituent sheets is challenging due to structural complexity, noise sensitivity, and difficulty in defining meaningful similarity measures across timesteps.

Method: The authors propose a framework for tracking Reeb space sheets in time-varying bivariate fields. It establishes correspondences between sheets in consecutive timesteps by employing complementary similarity measures defined jointly in the spatial domain (how sheets map to the original domain) and the range space (how sheets relate to the bivariate scalar values).

Result: Evaluation on a synthetic torus dataset and two time-varying molecular electronic structure datasets shows that Reeb space sheet tracking effectively reveals persistent structures and highlights intervals of significant temporal change.

Conclusion: Reeb space sheets can serve as trackable topological structures, providing a foundation for visual analysis of time-varying bivariate data.

Abstract: Time-varying bivariate fields arise in many scientific applications, where the relationship between two scalar quantities evolves over time. While topological methods such as merge trees provide an effective framework for identifying and tracking features in univariate data, analogous approaches for bivariate fields remain comparatively underexplored. Reeb spaces extend topological analysis to multivariate data by representing fiber connectivity through a collection of interconnected sheets, making these sheets natural candidates for describing bivariate structures. However, establishing temporal correspondences between sheets is challenging due to the structural complexity of Reeb spaces, sensitivity to noise, and the difficulty of defining meaningful similarity measures across timesteps. We present a framework for tracking Reeb space sheets in time-varying bivariate fields. The method establishes correspondences between sheets in consecutive timesteps using complementary similarity measures defined in the spatial domain and the range space. We evaluate the method on a synthetic torus dataset and two time-varying molecular electronic structure datasets. The results show that Reeb space sheet tracking reveals persistent structures and highlights interesting intervals of temporal change. Overall, the results demonstrate that Reeb space sheets can serve as trackable topological structures and provide a foundation for the visual analysis of time-varying bivariate data.

</details>


### [234] [Topic Matters: How Linguistic Properties can Shape Reading Behaviour in Selective Exposure Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05942)
*Thomas Krämer,Dagmar Kern,Thomas Kosch,Daniel Hienert*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Researchers found that linguistic properties vary systematically across controversial topics (climate change vs. migration), which in turn affects eye-tracking measures of reading behavior — revealing a methodological confound in selective exposure research that assumes cross-topic comparability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Selective exposure research using eye tracking often assumes that texts on different controversial topics are comparable after basic controls. The authors challenge this assumption, arguing that topic-dependent linguistic properties may systematically influence reading behavior and attention allocation, introducing an unacknowledged methodological confound.

Method: The authors conducted a laboratory study with 68 participants who searched for and read news articles on two controversial topics: climate change and migration policy. They analyzed linguistic features of the texts and corresponding eye-tracking data to examine whether topic-dependent linguistic properties relate to systematic differences in reading behaviour.

Result: Systematic differences in both textual characteristics (linguistic features) and reading behaviour (eye-tracking measures) were found across the two topics, confirming that topic-dependent properties influence how users read and allocate attention.

Conclusion: The findings identify a significant methodological confound in selective exposure research: cross-topic comparisons of eye-tracking data may be invalid without accounting for topic-specific linguistic properties. This has implications for both interpreting eye-tracking measures and designing systems aimed at mitigating biased information consumption.

Abstract: Research on selective exposure frequently relies on eye tracking to study reading behaviour, often assuming that texts across different controversial topics are comparable once basic controls are applied. This assumption is problematic if topic-dependent linguistic properties systematically shape how users read and allocate attention. We therefore examine whether such properties relate to differences in reading behaviour in selective exposure contexts. We analyse linguistic features and eye-tracking data from a laboratory study in which 68 participants searched for and read news articles on climate change and migration policy. Our results reveal systematic differences in both textual characteristics and reading behaviour across topics. These findings identify an important methodological confound in selective exposure research and highlight the need to account for topic-specific linguistic properties when interpreting eye-tracking measures and designing systems intended to mitigate biased information consumption.

</details>


### [235] [A Modular Workflow for Multimodal Reading Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05966)
*Thomas Krämer,Thomas Kosch,Dagmar Kern,Daniel Hienert*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A reusable web-based workflow integrating eye tracking, EEG, and interaction data for real-time multimodal experiments in naturalistic online reading, demonstrated via a selective exposure study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge the gap between controlled lab-based reading experiments and ecologically valid online reading contexts by enabling synchronized, real-time multimodal data collection and analysis in a browser-based environment.

Method: A modular, web-based workflow that integrates eye tracking, EEG, and peripheral interaction data (mouse/keyboard), synchronized via Lab Streaming Layer (LSL). Gaze data is mapped to browser-based text at word, sentence, and AOI levels. Fixation-triggered segmentation enables post-task processing of EEG and other streams, supporting online computation of gaze-derived measures and selection of passages for post-task rating.

Result: The workflow successfully supports real-time multimodal experimentation in naturalistic reading. In the selective exposure use case, it enables online gaze metric computation and immediate post-task EEG analysis based on fixation-triggered segmentation, yielding behavioral, neural, and linguistic metrics for targeted post-task rating within a single lab session.

Conclusion: The workflow provides a generalizable foundation for multimodal reading research in ecological contexts and supports the empirical validation of constructs traditionally operationalized through self-report, enhancing ecological validity without sacrificing experimental control.

Abstract: We introduce a web-based modular workflow for real-time multimodal experiments in naturalistic online reading. The workflow integrates eye tracking, EEG, and interaction data from mouse and keyboard, synchronizes them via Lab Streaming Layer, and links gaze to browser-based text at the word, sentence, and AOI levels. It is designed as a reusable experimental procedure that can be adapted to different sensors, tasks, and analysis goals. As a use case, we apply the workflow to a study of selective exposure in online news search and reading. During the experiment, gaze-derived measures are computed online, while EEG and other synchronized streams are processed immediately after task sessions based on fixation-triggered segmentation. The resulting behavioral, neural, and linguistic metrics support selecting text passages for targeted post-task rating or labelling within the same lab session. The workflow thus provides a general basis for multimodal research on reading and related cognitive processes, and supports the empirical validation, in ecological contexts, of constructs that are typically operationalised through self-report measures.

</details>


### [236] [PoseForge: Editable Pose Analytics for AI-Assisted Sports Coaching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05971)
*Shuvam Swapnil Dash,Arpit Narechania*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: PoseForge is a visual analytics system that extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera sports videos, computes kinematic metrics, compares them against norms, and uses an AI coach to suggest and visualize corrective adjustments for cricket batting, validated with eleven domain experts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Raw sports video footage lacks tools to quantify motion or simulate valid technique corrections. Current video analysis in athletic coaching is qualitative and does not provide interpretable kinematic metrics or actionable, anatomically plausible correction suggestions.

Method: The system extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera video, computes kinematic metrics (e.g., feet gap, elbow angle), compares them against scientifically derived norms, and employs an AI coach for targeted natural-language adjustments. Users can modify poses via mouse interaction or natural-language instructions, with inverse kinematics ensuring anatomical plausibility and real-time metric updates. Design was informed by formative interviews with eleven cricket experts.

Result: Evaluation with the same eleven cricket experts (coaches, performance analysts, captains, players) found PoseForge effective for diagnosing movement issues and exploring corrective alternatives. The system was highlighted as applicable in low-resource, academy, and grassroots coaching settings.

Conclusion: PoseForge demonstrates strong potential for democratizing quantitative movement analysis in cricket coaching, with identified opportunities for enhanced sport-specific metrics and longitudinal tracking. The system is released as open-source software.

Abstract: Athletic coaching increasingly relies on video analysis, yet raw footage lacks tools to quantify motion or simulate valid technique corrections. Drawing on formative interviews with eleven cricket experts (coaches, performance analysts, captains, and players), we introduce PoseForge, a visual analytics system that extracts 3D skeletal poses from single-camera sports videos for interactive movement analysis. In a cricket batting case study, PoseForge computes interpretable kinematic metrics such as feet gap and elbow angle, compares them against scientifically derived norms, and uses an AI coach to suggest targeted adjustments, presented visually and through natural-language feedback (e.g., "increase feet gap by 10 cm"). Users can directly modify poses via mouse interaction or natural-language instructions, with inverse kinematics maintaining anatomical plausibility and real-time updates of metrics and comparisons. An evaluation with the same eleven cricket experts found PoseForge effective for diagnosing movement issues and exploring corrective alternatives, highlighting its applicability in low-resource, academy, and grassroots coaching settings, while identifying opportunities for enhanced sport-specific metrics and longitudinal tracking. PoseForge is available as open-source software at https://github.com/DataVisards/PoseForge.

</details>


### [237] [Cleo: A Transparent and Controllable Chatbot for Conversational Commerce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06068)
*Kevin Schott,Jan Lattenkamp,Daniel Hienert,Dagmar Kern*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Cleo is a transparent, controllable conversational product advisor that combines a deterministic ranking engine with a constrained LLM to enable fluid dialogue, auditable attribute-level loss explanations, and hallucination-mitigated product comparisons across 3,638 product specifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conversational commerce systems suffer from three key problems: (1) opacity of LLM decision-making, (2) unpredictability and hallucination risks in generated content, and (3) the cognitive complexity of comparing products. Traditional faceted search lacks conversational fluidity, while purely LLM-based recommenders lack algorithmic transparency.

Method: A hybrid architecture that separates deterministic ranking from language generation. The ranker applies categorical filters and numeric loss functions over 3,638 product specifications to produce auditable, per-attribute loss values. A constrained LLM generates grounded descriptions restricted to catalog evidence, preventing hallucination. Transparency is achieved by prompting the LLM to reflect on interpreted user needs and exposing the ranking rationale. Controllability comes from the decoupled design, and decision support is provided through natural-language comparisons and a highlights feature that contextualizes specifications relative to user needs.

Result: The system is presented as a live demonstration where attendees can experience: information needs elicitation and reflection, conversational refinement with real-time re-ranking, inspection of per-attribute loss explanations, and AI-generated multi-item comparisons. The system is positioned as an extensible experimental platform for IR and HCI researchers as well as practitioners.

Conclusion: Cleo advances the design of transparent and controllable conversational systems for decision support in online product search, demonstrating that fluid conversation and algorithmic transparency are not mutually exclusive through a hybrid ranker-LLM architecture.

Abstract: We demonstrate Cleo, a transparent and controllable conversational product advisor that addresses the challenges of opacity, unpredictability of LLMs, and the complexity of comparisons in conversational commerce. With our chatbot system, we make four contributions: First, we introduce transparency by prompting the LLM to reflect on interpreted user needs, while an auditable ranking mechanism reveals loss values per attribute, explaining ranking decisions. Second, we propose controllability through a hybrid architecture separating deterministic ranking from language generation. A ranker applies categorical filters and numeric loss functions over 3,638 product specifications. Meanwhile, a constrained LLM generates grounded descriptions constrained to catalog evidence, thus mitigating the risk of hallucinated or persuasive content. Third, we provide decision support in the form of natural-language comparisons and a highlights feature. These aim to reduce mental workload by contextualizing specifications relative to user needs. Fourth, we contribute an extensible experimental system for IR and HCI researchers, as well as practitioners of conversational search and recommendation. Unlike traditional faceted search or opaque LLM-only recommenders, our approach allows for fluid conversation while maintaining algorithmic transparency. In a live demonstration, attendees will experience information needs elicitation and reflection, conversational refinement with real-time re-ranking, inspection of per-attribute loss explanations, and AI-generated multi-item comparisons. The system aims to advance the design of transparent and controllable conversational systems that provide support for decision-making during online product search.

</details>


### [238] [OneEmo: A Unified Multimodal Reasoning Model for Emotion Perception, Understanding, and Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06013)
*Jiahao Huang,Zheng Lian,Jingyi Zhang,Zhide Chen,Xiaojiang Peng,Shaonan Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: OneEmo is a unified MLLM for affective computing that jointly masters emotion perception, comprehension, and interaction. It uses a curated dataset (EmoWorld-130K) with reasoning trajectories and a novel multi-task RL strategy (Emo-Chord) to achieve SOTA performance, outperforming similarly sized models and rivaling commercial systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLM research in emotional intelligence focuses on isolated task specialization, missing opportunities for inter-task synergy and underexploiting latent reasoning capabilities. This motivates a unified affective generalist that can leverage multi-task mutual benefits.

Method: (1) EmoWorld-130K: a human-in-the-loop dataset distilling specialized affective knowledge into explicit reasoning trajectories across emotion perception, comprehension, and interaction tasks. (2) Supervised fine-tuning on this corpus to unlock cross-task mutual benefits. (3) Emo-Chord: a novel reinforcement learning strategy with unified multi-task reward allocation to stabilize optimization and unlock latent reasoning.

Result: OneEmo achieves state-of-the-art performance against similarly sized baselines on most benchmarks and delivers highly competitive results against much larger commercial models despite having significantly fewer parameters.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a unified multi-task approach with structured reasoning data and stabilized multi-task RL can produce a highly capable, interpretable, and competitive affective computing model, paving the way for more reliable affective systems.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in emotional intelligence. However, prevailing research predominantly focuses on task-specific specialization, often neglecting inter-task synergy and leaving latent reasoning potential underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce OneEmo, a unified affective generalist capable of mastering emotion perception, comprehension, and interaction. For this purpose, we first construct EmoWorld-130K, a comprehensive dataset that distills specialized affective knowledge into explicit reasoning trajectories via a human-in-the-loop workflow. Supervised fine-tuning on this corpus reveals significant mutual benefits derived from multi-task learning. Second, to fully unlock the latent reasoning potential, we propose Emo-Chord, a novel reinforcement learning strategy that stabilizes optimization through unified multi-task reward allocation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneEmo achieves state-of-the-art performance against similarly sized baselines across most benchmarks. Notably, despite having significantly fewer parameters than commercial models, OneEmo delivers highly competitive results. This paper paves the way for more reliable and interpretable affective computing. The code is available at https://github.com/waHAHJIAHAO/OneEmo.

</details>


### [239] ["I don't know anything about laptops!" - User Perception of Digital Product Advisors Adapting to Their Knowledge Levels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06091)
*Kevin Schott,Andrea Papenmeier,Daniel Hienert,Dagmar Kern*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study investigates how chatbot-based product recommendations can be adapted to users with varying domain knowledge. In a laptop search experiment (n=251), novices benefited significantly from attribute explanations and performance categories, while experts were unaffected by supplementary information. The authors propose four design guidelines for inclusive conversational commerce interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conversational commerce agents need to present complex product information effectively to users with different levels of domain expertise. The key open challenge is how to adapt the presentation of technical product attributes—through explanations, performance categories, or both—to support shared understanding without alienating either novice or expert users.

Method: A between-subjects experiment (n=251) using a chatbot-assisted laptop search scenario. Participants (novices and experts) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions for product attribute recommendations: technical information only (T), technical + performance categories (TC), technical + attribute explanations (TE), or technical + categories + explanations (TCE). Perceived helpfulness, information quantity appropriateness, and perceived learning were measured and analyzed across conditions and expertise levels.

Result: Novices rated conditions with explanations (TE, TCE) as significantly more helpful and promoting greater perceived learning than those without. The combined TCE approach was rated more appropriate than T and TC for information quantity. Experts showed no significant differences across any conditions, indicating that supplementary information did not harm their experience.

Conclusion: Four design guidelines emerge: (1) use TCE (technical + categories + explanations) by default, (2) maintain a single inclusive interface rather than separate versions for different expertise levels, (3) avoid standalone performance categories without explanations, and (4) support user agency and personalize to the stated use case.

Abstract: Conversational commerce uses digital assistants to support the search process and decision-making in e-commerce. Effective communication in these interactions can be facilitated by assistants adapting their communication style to users and supporting shared understanding. An open challenge in this context is adapting the presentation of complex product information to users with varying levels of domain knowledge. To investigate strategies for such knowledge-level adaptation, we set up a chatbot-assisted laptop search scenario. In a between-subjects experiment (n = 251), we examined novice and expert perceptions of product attribute recommendations presented as technical information only (T), or augmented with performance categories (TC), attribute explanations (TE), or both (TCE). For novices, approaches with explanations (TE, TCE) were perceived as more helpful and led to higher perceived learning than those without. Novices also rated the combined approach (TCE) more appropriate than the baseline (T) and TC in terms of information quantity, indicating that explanations are crucial to understand and benefit from performance categories. Critically, experts showed no significant differences across conditions, suggesting that providing supplementary information beneficial to novices did not detract from their experience. We distill these findings into four concrete design guidelines for inclusive text-based product advisors in technical domains: use TCE by default; keep a single inclusive interface; avoid standalone categories; and support user agency and personalize to the stated use case.

</details>


### [240] [Divergent Perceptuomotor Recalibration in Virtual Reality and Video-Passthrough Mixed Reality on the Same Head-Mounted Display](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06132)
*Xiaoye Michael Wang,Grant Monahan,Timothy N. Welsh*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study compared visually guided manual pointing in virtual reality (VR) versus video-passthrough mixed reality (MR-VPT) using the same headset. Results revealed opposite initial biases (VR undershooting, MR-VPT overshooting), different adaptation rates, and persistent aftereffects, demonstrating that perceptuomotor behavior differs significantly between these modalities despite identical hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VR and MR-VPT can be delivered on the same headset, yet it remains unclear whether these two modalities produce comparable perceptuomotor behavior. Although identical hardware controls many display-level factors, the modalities differ in visual-feedback pipelines and in the action-relevant visual information available (synthetically rendered versus preserved through passthrough). Understanding these differences is critical for ensuring that interaction techniques validated in one modality transfer reliably to the other.

Method: Forty adults were assigned to either a VR or MR-VPT group. Both groups performed a visually guided manual pointing task in unmediated reality (UR) as a baseline, then completed the same task in their assigned XR modality, and finally returned to UR for a post-test. The same headset was used for both XR conditions, and pointing accuracy, bias direction, adaptation patterns, and aftereffects were measured and compared across groups.

Result: Baseline UR performance was comparable between groups. During XR exposure, the VR group undershot the target while the MR-VPT group overshot — opposite initial biases. The VR group adapted more slowly and showed stronger distance-dependent undershooting. Post-XR, both groups exhibited undershooting aftereffects, with the VR group showing persistent residual undershoot, indicating incomplete de-adaptation.

Conclusion: Perceptuomotor recalibration is shaped not only by display-level constraints but also by the action-relevant visual information available within the interaction environment. These findings underscore the necessity of validating perceptuomotor interaction techniques separately in VR and MR-VPT, even when implemented on identical hardware, as the two modalities produce meaningfully different sensorimotor outcomes.

Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and video-passthrough mixed reality (MR-VPT) can be delivered on the same headset, but it is unclear whether these two interaction modalities produce comparable perceptuomotor behavior. Although delivery through the same headset controls many display-level characteristics, VR and MR-VPT differ in both their visual-feedback pipelines and the action-relevant visual information available to guide movement, such as whether the surrounding environment and the user's body are synthetically rendered or preserved through passthrough. This study compared visually guided manual pointing in VR and MR-VPT using the same headset. Forty adults were assigned to either a VR or MR-VPT group and completed a pointing task in the physical, unmediated reality (UR) before and after performing the same task in their assigned XR modality. The analyses revealed numerous important insights. First, groups had comparable baseline performance in UR prior to XR exposure. Second, the two modalities produced opposite initial biases during XR exposure: the VR group undershot the target, whereas the MR-VPT group overshot. Third, although both groups reduced error with continued exposure to XR, there were differences in the patterns of adaptation: the VR group adapted more slowly and exhibited stronger distance-dependent undershooting than the MR-VPT group. Finally, after XR exposure, both groups showed significant undershooting aftereffects with the VR group retaining a persistent residual undershoot, suggesting incomplete de-adaptation. The results suggest that perceptuomotor recalibration is shaped not only by display-level constraints but also by the action-relevant visual information available within the interaction environment. These findings highlight the need to validate perceptuomotor interaction techniques separately in VR and MR-VPT, even when they are implemented on the same hardware.

</details>


### [241] [Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06151)
*Thomas H. Costello,Nathaniel Rabb,Michael Nicholas Stagnaro,Gordon Pennycook,David Rand*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Conversational dialogues with a large language model significantly reduced belief in emerging conspiracy theories following two real-world assassination events, with effects persisting one to two months later.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conspiracy theories that emerge immediately after major societal events pose a serious challenge, and scalable interventions to counteract them in real time are lacking. The authors sought to test whether LLM-based conversational interventions could effectively reduce such beliefs during their critical formation window.

Method: Two randomized controlled experiments were conducted shortly after real-world crisis events (the July 2024 Trump assassination attempt and the September 2025 Charlie Kirk assassination). U.S. adults holding conspiratorial beliefs (N=472 and N=1035, respectively) were assigned to either a multi-turn conversational dialogue with an LLM prompted to reduce conspiracy belief, or control conditions (discussing an irrelevant topic with an LLM, or viewing a static fact sheet). Beliefs were measured immediately post-intervention and at one- to two-month follow-ups assessing downstream effects on unrelated conspiracies arising from subsequent crises.

Result: The LLM treatment significantly reduced targeted conspiracy beliefs compared to both control conditions in each experiment. Downstream effects were also observed: participants in the LLM condition showed reduced belief in different, unrelated conspiracies one to two months later following subsequent crisis events.

Conclusion: LLM-based conversational interventions offer a scalable, cognitively-focused approach to counteracting conspiracy beliefs during their acute emergence following high-profile events. The persistence and generalization of these effects underscore the promise of this method for real-time misinformation intervention.

Abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1035) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in different conspiracies one to two months later in the wake of subsequent crisis events. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

</details>


### [242] [What Current AI Benchmarks Leave Unmeasured: Modality, Search, Citations, and Implications (for Safety Evaluations)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06202)
*Ro Encarnación,Tina Behzad,Emma Lurie,Danaé Metaxa*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Auditing LLM evaluation assumptions reveals that modality (API vs. chat UI), web search, and repeated runs significantly alter model accuracy, consistency, citation grounding, and abstention behavior—challenging the practice of reporting single-run accuracy as sufficient for safety assessments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
