Motivation: Current LLM benchmark evaluations typically use a single modality (API), single-run prompts, and report only accuracy, ignoring real-world deployment factors like web search and multi-run variability. The authors seek to audit whether these simplifying assumptions obscure important behavioral variation relevant to AI safety.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic audit of ChatGPT (chat UI vs. OpenAI API), with and without web search, using a stratified sample of 401 prompts from BBQ and SafetyBench. They collect 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt and evaluate accuracy, response consistency, text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior.

Result: Chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses with search disabled. Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points and reversed modality performance trends on one benchmark. Up to 21% of prompts produced inconsistent responses across repeated runs. Citation grounding and abstention behavior also differed significantly between modalities.

Conclusion: Single-run accuracy metrics are insufficient for AI safety evaluations. Evaluations should systematically account for access modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to reflect how deployed systems actually operate in practice.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) benchmark evaluations are routinely used to support claims about model safety, reliability, and deployment readiness. Yet most evaluations rely on a single access modality (model APIs), perform a single run per prompt, and report accuracy as the primary outcome metric, without accounting for conditions such as web search that may have effects on model behavior in deployment. We audit these assumptions for one of the most widely-used LLMs, comparing two modalities, ChatGPT's chat UI and OpenAI's API, with and without web search enabled. We use a stratified total sample of 401 prompts from two popular benchmarks, BBQ and SafetyBench, collecting 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt. Beyond standard performance measures, we evaluate model output dimensions including response consistency, response text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior. For instance, chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled. Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points, and even reversed the direction of modality performance trends for one benchmark. Repeated runs of the same prompt produced inconsistent responses in up to 21\% of prompts. The two modalities also grounded answers in different citations, and abstention behavior was also inconsistent across both modalities. These results illustrate that, even within a model family, reporting only simple accuracy metrics can obscure important forms of model behavioral variation relevant to AI safety assessments. We argue that AI safety evaluations should systematically account for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to better reflect how deployed AI systems behave in practice.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [243] [MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05196)
*Adam Simson,Ankush Dutta,Quang Bui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MS-MLB is an open, reproducible benchmark for evaluating machine learning classifiers that distinguish multiple sclerosis patients from healthy controls using whole blood RNA expression data (GSE17048 cohort), with Gradient Boosting achieving the top research score (93.83, AUC-ROC 0.989).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While blood RNA expression may contain MS-associated immune signals, no standardized, reproducible benchmark exists for comparing ML algorithms on this task. The authors aim to fill this gap with a leakage-controlled, rerunnable evaluation framework—explicitly not as a diagnostic replacement but as a research comparison tool.

Method: MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression dataset, framing it as binary classification (MS vs. healthy control). It implements a unified pipeline with nested cross-validation, a stratified untouched holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC/PR analysis, calibration (Brier score), and an exploratory composite metric called the MS Research Score. The framework supports external model submission.

Result: Gradient Boosting ranked first with an MS Research Score of 93.83 on the holdout set, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, F1 score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050.

Conclusion: MS-MLB is the first open benchmark specifically for MS vs. healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA data with a built-in external submission pathway. The scores are for research comparison only and lack clinical validation.

Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

</details>


### [244] [When Do Corrective Features Help? An Agent for Corrective Feature Discovery on Black-Box Forecasters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05207)
*Fangxin Wang,Ziyi Zhang,Diyi Zhuang,Langzhou He,Shiyu Wang,Baichuan Mo,Philip S. Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRAFTER is a post-hoc correction framework that mines interpretable features from a frozen forecaster's residuals using two complementary generators — compositional search and LLM proposals — and applies them via a validation-gated corrector, roughly doubling correction gains across six datasets and six backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frozen pretrained forecasters exhibit structured, recurring failures that are expensive to fix through fine-tuning. Prior feature engineering models the data-generating process, not the model-failure process. The authors argue that targeting the latter — mining corrective features from residuals — offers a more direct and lightweight path to improving frozen forecasters.

Method: CRAFTER keeps the backbone forecaster frozen and mines its residual using two complementary generators: (1) compositional search over raw input channels, and (2) an LLM that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of origin. A validation-selected corrector then applies accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. The source-agnostic pipeline also enables fair comparison of prior feature-engineering systems.

Result: Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget. It roughly doubles the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reduces the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. Gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

Conclusion: Targeting model-failure patterns via corrective feature discovery is more effective than modeling the data-generating process for post-hoc forecast correction. The source-agnostic, gated pipeline of CRAFTER not only delivers state-of-the-art correction performance but also serves as an evaluation instrument for isolating the contribution of feature sources.

Abstract: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to repair through fine-tuning. We study corrective feature discovery: mining interpretable features of a frozen forecaster's residual to drive a lightweight post-hoc corrector. Prior automated feature engineering models the data-generating process; corrective features instead model the model-failure process. We present CRAFTER (Corrective Residual Agent with Feature-based Temporal Exploration and Reasoning), which keeps the backbone frozen and mines its residual with two complementary generators: a compositional search over the raw input channels, and a large language model (LLM) that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of its origin, and a validation-selected corrector applies the accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. This source-agnostic pipeline also allows prior feature-engineering systems to be evaluated under identical conditions, making CRAFTER an instrument for attributing forecast improvements to the feature source alone. Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reducing the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. These gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

</details>


### [245] [PPDL: LLM-Based Flows as Probabilistic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05234)
*Louis Mandel,Guillaume Baudart,Mandana Vaziri,Martin Hirzel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a probabilistic programming language for LLM-based application flows, enabling developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty through multi-call LLM pipelines and experiment with inference scaling techniques declaratively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs produce outputs with unknown confidence, and this uncertainty compounds in multi-step flows involving multiple LLM calls and tool interactions. Developers lack principled mechanisms to quantify and manage this uncertainty, undermining trust in LLM-based applications.

Method: The authors propose a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows. The language allows developers to express flow logic declaratively while the system automatically handles uncertainty quantification and propagation. It also supports experimenting with different inference scaling techniques without code modifications beyond the flow specification.

Result: The paper includes an experimental study demonstrating the language's capability for uncertainty propagation and inference scaling. A case study applies the approach to building a theorem-proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.

Conclusion: A probabilistic programming approach to LLM flows provides a systematic way to handle uncertainty, enabling more reliable LLM-based applications and facilitating experimentation with inference strategies without altering application logic.

Abstract: Building reliable applications that leverage large language models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge. While LLMs offer impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, their outputs often lack accuracy and provide no clear measure of confidence. This uncertainty compounds in flows of multiple calls to LLMs and other tools, making it difficult for developers and end-users to trust the results. This paper introduces a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows. It enables developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty throughout the application's flow, and experiment with different inference scaling techniques without adding a single line of code beyond the flow's logic. We present an experimental study to demonstrate this capability, and a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.

</details>


### [246] [Decoupling Perception from Description: Computation-Grounded Representation Alignment between Multivariate Time Series and Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05238)
*Xinran Feng,Yi Xie,Chao Zhang,Ruikun Li,Wanyun Ling,Ziyue Li,Chenxi Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Existing multimodal time-series-language models face a self-supervision trap where LLM-generated labels cannot exceed the LLM's own perceptual limits, especially for multivariate patterns. CGTime resolves this by decoupling perception (deterministic computation of statistics) from description (LLM verbalization), achieving state-of-the-art multivariate understanding with only 4B parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches for aligning time series with language rely on LLMs to both read series and write descriptions, creating a self-supervision trap — label quality is bounded by the labeling LLM's perceptual skill. This is exacerbated in multivariate settings where cross-channel correlations, lead-lag structures, and co-occurring anomalies appear, precisely where LLMs are weakest. Existing methods face a trilemma: they can be reliable, realistic, or scalable, but never all three simultaneously.

Method: The authors decouple perception from description. Deterministic code computes a comprehensive set of statistical properties from real, open-source multivariate time series. The LLM then verbalizes these precomputed facts, rather than being asked to perceive patterns directly. Computation handles perception (what LLMs do poorly), while the LLM handles only expression. This yields CGTime, a 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model.

Result: CGTime achieves the best multivariate fact score of 0.283 on a held-out benchmark, significantly outperforming GPT-4o-mini (0.173) and GPT-5.4-nano (0.203). These gaps survive Holm-corrected paired significance tests against all baselines. CGTime also generates captions with more accurate verifiable numerical facts and covers a broader range of statistical properties compared to all baselines.

Conclusion: Decoupling computational perception from linguistic expression effectively resolves the self-supervision trap in time-series-language alignment. CGTime demonstrates that a small (4B), computation-grounded model can outperform much larger general-purpose models on multivariate time-series understanding, offering a path toward reliable, realistic, and scalable time-series-language models.

Abstract: Training multimodal models to align time series with language runs into a self-supervision trap. The usual recipe asks an LLM to read a series and write a description, so label quality is capped by the perceptual skill the model is supposed to learn. The data can never teach more than the labeler already knows. A second gap makes this worse: most datasets use a single variable, but the patterns that matter (cross-channel correlation, lead-lag structure, co-occurring anomalies) appear only with several variables, right where the labeling LLM's limits are most exposed. These two problems create a trilemma: existing methods are reliable, realistic, or scalable, but none achieves all three. We resolve this by decoupling perception from description. Deterministic code computes a set of statistics from real, open-source multivariate series; the LLM verbalizes those precomputed facts. Perception, which LLMs do poorly, is handled by computation, while the LLM handles expression. This produces CGTime, our 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model. CGTime outperforms far larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding tasks: it attains the best multivariate fact score on our held-out benchmark (0.283 vs. 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano), a gap that survives Holm-corrected paired significance tests against every baseline. It also states verifiable numerical facts in generated captions more accurately and covers a broader range of statistical properties.

</details>


### [247] [Disentangling 3D Modeling from Spatial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05242)
*Haoze Sun,Jiequan Cui,Qingshan Xu,Richang Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DiSR proposes separating 3D perception from reasoning by using off-the-shelf perception models to extract structured 3D evidence, then fine-tuning an LLM with LoRA to reason over that explicit geometry, achieving competitive spatial reasoning without large-scale end-to-end training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current spatial reasoning approaches jointly learn implicit 3D perception and reasoning through massive training. The authors observe that modern perception models already excel at continuous 3D geometry estimation, while LLMs are strong at compositional/symbolic reasoning. This suggests disentangling these complementary capabilities may be more efficient and interpretable than end-to-end modeling.

Method: The Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR) framework uses off-the-shelf expert perception models to reconstruct the physical world into structured 3D evidence. A LoRA-fine-tuned LLM then performs reasoning exclusively over this explicit geometric evidence. No large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies are required.

Result: DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks compared to end-to-end approaches, while offering improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: Explicitly separating perception from reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative paradigm to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence, suggesting that leveraging specialized expert modules with lightweight LLM adaptation can match or rival monolithic approaches.

Abstract: In this work, we explore an alternative paradigm for spatial reasoning by explicitly disentangling 3D perception from reasoning, rather than jointly acquiring implicit 3D perception and reasoning through large-scale training. Our key observation is that modern perception models excel at estimating continuous 3D geometry, whereas large language models (LLMs) are particularly effective at compositional and symbolic reasoning. Motivated by these complementary strengths, we propose the Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR), a simple yet effective framework that reconstructs the physical world into structured 3D evidence using off-the-shelf expert perception models and fine-tunes an LLM with LoRA to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence. Without large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies, DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks. Beyond its strong performance, DiSR offers improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency, demonstrating that explicit separation of perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative paradigm to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence.

</details>


### [248] [Marginal Matching Does Not License Factorized Sampling: Auditing Conditional Style Leakage in Factorized Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05243)
*Duong Bach,Hai Nguyen Hong,Cuong Do*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that matching a latent style variable's marginal distribution to a Gaussian prior does not guarantee independence from class labels. Class-conditional distributions can remain highly predictive of labels even when the marginal appears perfectly Gaussian. The authors show this leakage persists across multiple settings and propose mitigation strategies, concluding that marginal statistics alone cannot certify style-class independence in factorized generative models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Factorized generative models commonly claim that regularizing the marginal distribution of a style variable z_s to match a Gaussian prior ensures style is independent of class information. The authors challenge this widespread interpretation, arguing that marginal matching imposes no constraint on class-conditional distributions, allowing significant information leakage from style to class labels.

Method: The authors derive an exact decomposition showing that marginal distribution matching is only one of four necessary conditions for proper factorization. They conduct empirical evaluations using a case-study model and four latent baselines, measuring global MMD, linear probe accuracy, clustering accuracy, and externally evaluated class-conditional generation success rates. They test robustness under six independent perturbations (model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, supervision) across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies are evaluated for reducing label leakage, along with post-hoc conditional priors and empirical style banks for improving class-conditional generation.

Result: Models achieve near-zero global MMD while linear probes recover labels with 74-100% accuracy (chance=10%). The case-study model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy but class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage persists under all six perturbations. Mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21-46% but leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior achieves 0.97 class generation on MNIST but only 0.41 on CIFAR-10; an empirical style bank reaches 0.88 on CIFAR-10.

Conclusion: No divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels. Reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the factorization property commonly claimed in factorized generative models. Proper evaluation requires examining class-conditional distributions.

Abstract: Factorized generative models commonly regularize a latent style variable z_s by matching its marginal distribution to a fixed Gaussian prior and interpret this as evidence that the style representation is independent of class information. We show that this interpretation is incorrect. Matching only the marginal distribution places no constraint on the class-conditional distributions, allowing the latent style to remain highly predictive of the label despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate. We derive an exact decomposition showing that this mismatch is one of four conditions required for factorized sampling, and demonstrate that eliminating it is necessary but not sufficient to obtain the intended factorization.
  Empirically, our case-study model and four representative latent baselines achieve near-zero global MMD while still allowing a linear probe to recover class labels with 74%--100% accuracy (10% chance level). Our model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy, whereas externally evaluated class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage remains under six independent perturbations involving model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, and supervision across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%--46%, although they leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior improves externally evaluated class generation to 0.97 on MNIST without retraining but reaches only 0.41 on CIFAR-10, while an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that no divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels, and that reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

</details>


### [249] [IFlowNets: Extending Generative Samplers to Learn Strategies in Incomplete Information Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05422)
*Conor M. Artman,Nicholas Di,Scott Perkins*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Information Flow Networks (IFlowNets), a generalization of Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets) from complete to incomplete information games. The authors prove prior AFlowNet constraints are invalid for incomplete information settings and demonstrate that IFlowNets achieve comparable or superior performance and speed against OSMCCFR and RL baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Few investigations explore generative sampling frameworks for game-theoretic applications in incomplete information games, despite active research blending RL with CFR methods. AFlowNets were originally designed only for complete information games, and their constraints fail when applied directly to incomplete information settings.

Method: The authors extend the Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets) framework, a generative flow network (GFlowNet) variant, to incomplete information games. They formally prove that existing AFlowNet constraints are inadmissible for obtaining valid player strategy densities and a valid training objective in incomplete information settings. The proposed IFlowNets introduces a generalization that resolves these issues, strictly subsuming AFlowNets as a special case.

Result: In preliminary experiments across three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in both performance and computational speed.

Conclusion: IFlowNets successfully extends generative flow networks to incomplete information games, correcting theoretical flaws in prior constraints and demonstrating practical viability against strong baselines.

Abstract: While many algorithms blend reinforcement learning (RL) with counterfactual regret (CFR) methods to leverage tradeoffs in computational speed and performance, there are fewer investigations into generative sampling frameworks in game theoretic applications in incomplete information games. We extend a generative flow network framework, Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets), to incomplete information games, called Information Flow Networks (IFNs). We prove that previously established constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities (corresponding to player strategies) and a valid training objective. We show that our proposed generalization, IFlowNets, alleviates this issue and strictly generalizes AFlowNets. In preliminary results for three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in performance and speed.

</details>


### [250] [PRISM: Priority-aware Rubric Internalization via Structured Multimodal Data Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05249)
*Xiaomin He,Dongling Xiao,Jiahao Xie,Ruiqi Lu,Qianle Wang,Zhongbin Guo,Wanxuan Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PRISM is a data synthesis framework that trains multimodal LLMs to follow prioritized, multi-rule rubrics (not just answer questions). With only 10K synthetic samples, it boosts a 4B model's strict compliance from 9.5% to 30.1% on a new rubric-based benchmark, while preserving general performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world multimodal instructions often contain multiple requirements with unequal priority, but existing training data treats instruction following as answering a single self-contained question. This creates a gap where models lack the ability to handle multi-rule, priority-aware instructions that demand step-by-step verification.

Method: The authors propose PRISM, a four-stage data synthesis framework: (1) generating persona-task pairs for diversity, (2) prefix-guided rule set generation, (3) quality-filtered rubric curation, and (4) structured verification trace creation. They also introduce PRISM-Eval, a benchmark with Loose and Strict metrics that use deterministic matching against fixed labels, eliminating the need for an LLM judge at inference time.

Result: Training Qwen3-VL-4B on only 10K PRISM samples raises Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval from 9.5% to 30.1%, while maintaining average performance on general multimodal benchmarks. The gains transfer across four additional open-source MLLMs spanning both dense and MoE architectures.

Conclusion: Structured rubric supervision is a scalable and effective approach for teaching multimodal models to follow multiple rules with explicit priority, offering a path beyond single-question instruction following without sacrificing general capabilities.

Abstract: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet most multimodal training data still reduce instruction following to answering one self-contained question. We study this gap through \textbf{rubric comprehension}, which casts the model not as a generator measured against rubrics but as an \textbf{executor} that follows them: given an image and a typed, prioritized rubric, the model must verify each rule before producing an overall judgment. To support this setting, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a four-stage data synthesis framework that produces persona--task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. We further introduce \textbf{PRISM-Eval}, whose Loose and Strict metrics use deterministic matching against fixed labels and therefore require no inference-time judge model. With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5\% to 30.1\% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks, and the gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures, suggesting that structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following.

</details>


### [251] [Hybrid-Adaptive Thread Tuning to Mitigate Simulation Execution Bottlenecks in High-Performance Reinforcement Learning Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06025)
*Jiming Su,Hantao Hua,Lujia Yin,Yiping Yao,Feng Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoThread is a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method that uses a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) for thread-count prediction, combined with an M/M/1 queueing model and online fine-tuning, to dynamically optimize thread allocation for RL inference under simulator-side bottlenecks, achieving significant speedup and throughput gains over static and state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RL simulation-in-the-loop systems, simulator-side execution introduces highly dynamic workloads sensitive to thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies fail to adaptively match thread resources before or during execution, leading to resource contention, scheduling overhead, and degraded throughput.

Method: AutoThread combines three components: (1) a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) that serves as a thread-count predictor, (2) a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model that constrains and guides predictions for fast, accurate estimation under dynamic workloads, and (3) load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation in real time.

Result: AutoThread achieves an average speedup of 18.4% over static strategies, delivers 1.7x the throughput of XGBoost and 1.8x that of Reinforcer, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8% compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: The ratio of task execution time to scheduling time is the key factor determining optimal thread count, and AutoThread's hybrid approach—combining PINO-based prediction, queueing-theoretic constraints, and online fine-tuning—effectively mitigates simulation bottlenecks in RL inference under dynamic workloads.

Abstract: In simulation-in-the-loop decision-making systems, reinforcement learning (RL) inference is often constrained by simulator-side execution overhead, where workloads are highly dynamic and sensitive to runtime thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match thread resources before or during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput. Through empirical analysis, we identify the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time as the key factor determining the optimal thread count. Building on this insight, we propose AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method for mitigating simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. AutoThread employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor and incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide prediction, enabling fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It further performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation. Experiments show that AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4\% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8\% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/suchenjm/AutoThread.

</details>


### [252] [Beyond Full-Model Rollback: AuroSFT for Adapter-State Multi-Task Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05250)
*Yue Han,Ziniu Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AuroSFT introduces a parameter-efficient multi-task fine-tuning framework that replaces full-model checkpoints with compact, mergeable adapter states, enabling task-wise rollback at peak performance without costly storage and deployment overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-task SFT treats heterogeneous data as a single optimization problem, but different tasks generalize best at different training stages. Prior work (msft) addresses this via task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but its reliance on full-model checkpoints makes stage transitions expensive in storage, restoration, and deployment. AuroSFT aims to retain msft's overfitting-aware scheduling while drastically reducing the carried state to a compact, parameter-efficient form.

Method: AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only injected adapters. It rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise validation peaks and continues training on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter uses an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer applied to a low-rank weight factor (not the sample representation), keeping the update linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection matrix. This yields a mergeable adapter state that substitutes for full-model snapshots.

Result: Under a retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy versus 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy across all five evaluated backbones.

Conclusion: AuroSFT successfully preserves the benefits of overfitting-aware multi-task scheduling while eliminating the storage and deployment costs of full-model checkpointing, demonstrating consistent accuracy gains across multiple backbone architectures.

Abstract: Multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often casts a heterogeneous data mixture as a single optimization problem, even though different tasks may reach their best generalization at different times. msft exposes this mismatch through task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but its original formulation materializes the scheduler state as full-model checkpoints, making stage transitions costly to store, restore, and deploy. This paper introduces AuroSFT, a parameter-efficient framework that recasts the carried state of overfitting-aware multi-task SFT as a compact, mergeable adapter state. AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone, trains only injected adapters, rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks, and continues on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor rather than to the sample representation. The resulting update remains linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection. Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy, compared with 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy on all five backbones. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroSFT-80D1.

</details>


### [253] [Does Latent Context Help? A Controlled Evaluation of Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Arctic Shipping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06105)
*Vaishnav Vaidheeswaran,Dilith Jayakody,Biruk Ambaw,Jaswanth Kumar,Md Mahbub Alam,Gabriel Spadon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled evaluation on Arctic shipping data shows that adding vessel-specific latent context to inverse reinforcement learning degrades performance; observable route and environmental features already explain most behavioral variation, cautioning against unnecessary latent variables for trustworthy AI deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Meta-IRL methods increasingly use latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity across agents, but it is unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or merely re-encode information already present in observed states. This matters for safety-critical domains like Arctic navigation where interpretability and robustness are essential.

Method: Controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels over nine Arctic shipping seasons. Three models compared: (1) linear shared reward, (2) nonlinear shared reward, (3) latent-context model with same nonlinear architecture. Analysis includes behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation. Models evaluated on held-out likelihood, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer.

Result: Nonlinear shared reward improved held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline. Adding vessel-specific latent context reduced performance by 16.5%. Apparent vessel-level variation was largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Different evaluation metrics (predictive accuracy, route fidelity, reward transfer) produced different model rankings, showing no single metric suffices.

Conclusion: Before introducing per-vessel latent context in IRL, researchers should test whether observable features already explain behavioral variation. This practice supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains like Arctic shipping.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a framework for recovering such rewards from vessel trajectories, while recent meta-IRL methods introduce latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity. However, it remains unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode information already available in the observed state. We conduct a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing a linear shared reward, a nonlinear shared reward, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. The nonlinear reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, whereas adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation show that apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Moreover, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer yield different model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric is sufficient to evaluate learned rewards. These findings motivate testing whether the observed route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation before adding per-vessel latent context. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

</details>


### [254] [Beyond Rotations: AuroOFT for Expressive Quantized Orthogonal Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05253)
*Yue Han,Dianlin Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AuroOFT extends quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) by adding a zero-initialized gated low-rank nonlinear residual branch, enabling input-dependent corrections while preserving quantization compatibility. It outperforms qoft and QLoRA on Qwen2.5 models with fewer trainable parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing qoft is limited to linear orthogonal transformations, which cannot capture input-dependent nonlinear corrections needed for richer task-specific adaptation of low-bit quantized language models.

Method: AuroOFT retains qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch and attaches a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual. Activations are mapped into an RMS-normalized compact latent space with adaptive nonlinear bases and bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up projection ensures functional identity to qoft at initialization, and orthogonality is preserved as a branch-level property rather than a layer-level one.

Result: Under matched protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over qoft by 1.30–2.70% on Qwen2.5 1.5B/3B, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52–10.62%, and saves 32.3–44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA.

Conclusion: AuroOFT effectively combines the stability of orthogonal fine-tuning with nonlinear expressivity via a gated low-rank residual, achieving superior parameter efficiency and accuracy on quantized LLMs.

Abstract: Quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models by learning structured activation rotations before frozen quantized weights. However, its task-specific updates remain constrained to linear orthogonal transformations, limiting input-dependent nonlinear corrections. We introduce AuroOFT, which keeps qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch while attaching a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. AuroOFT maps activations into an RMS-normalized compact latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up projection makes AuroOFT functionally identical to qoft at initialization, while orthogonality remains a branch-level stability property rather than a property of the combined nonlinear layer. Under matched data, optimization, decoding, and parser protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over matched qoft by 1.30-2.70% on the 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA in representative scales. The small exam-style multiple-choice math set is treated only as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroOFT-F3FD.

</details>


### [255] [An Emerging Retail Portfolio Management Application: Personalized, Tax-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Goals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05255)
*Ramin Pishehvar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A fully built RL-based portfolio management application that generates personalized, tax-aware investment recommendations from plain-language goals, integrated with a live brokerage API but not yet deployed to real users. Preliminary validation via 14-day walk-forward backtests is reported alongside practical engineering lessons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retail investors lack access to personalized, tax-aware portfolio management — existing robo-advisors use static rule-based allocation, while institutional systems have prohibitive account minimums and technology requirements. This paper aims to close that gap.

Method: A FastAPI backend + web dashboard that accepts plain-language investment goals, routes them to one of six investment mandates, and generates broker-integrated portfolio recommendations via a three-phase RL system: (1) a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, (2) a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and (3) a lightweight LoRA adapter for personalization from revealed brokerage behavior. The system is integration-tested against Alpaca (paper-trading mode) with multi-user auth, preview-before-apply flows, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain. Validation uses 14-day walk-forward backtests with bootstrapped confidence intervals.

Result: The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end, but has not been opened to real users. Preliminary, pre-deployment validation is reported honestly as such. Several generalizable engineering lessons are documented: silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata.

Conclusion: This is an emerging, pre-deployment application demonstrating a concrete path toward democratizing institutional-grade, personalized portfolio management for retail investors using modern RL techniques. The engineering lessons reported generalize to other applied RL systems relying on external live data.

Abstract: Retail investors lack access to the kind of personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients take for granted -- existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, and institutional-grade systems require account minimums and technology stacks unavailable to individual investors. We present a fully built, integration-tested application that closes this gap: a FastAPI backend and web dashboard that let a user describe an investment goal in plain language (e.g. "I want steady growth but need to sell some shares next month for a down payment"), routes that goal to one of six investment mandates, and produces a live, broker-integrated portfolio recommendation from athree-phase reinforcement learning system -- a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations from an individual's revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against a live brokerage API (Alpaca, paper-trading mode), including multi-user authentication, a trust first preview-before-apply confirmation flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain, but has not yet been opened to real end-users; we report this honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment application with a concrete path to full deployment, alongside 14-day walk-forward backtests (bootstrapped confidence intervals included) as preliminary, pre-deployment validation rather than production performance. We also report several practical engineering lessons -- silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata -- that we believe generalize to other applied RL systems built on external, live data sources.

</details>


### [256] [Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05571)
*Mohammad Asadi,Soheil Hor,Bardiya Akhbari,Jack W. O'Sullivan,Tahoura Nedaee,Layne C. Price,Raviteja Anantha,Euan Ashley,Ehsan Adeli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Align-RAG is a training-free method for retrieval-augmented time series forecasting that uses closed-form amplitude rescaling and phase shifting to align retrieved examples with a query before feeding them into a frozen backbone, outperforming trained retrieval adapters without any learned parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods assume frozen TSFMs cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own and thus rely on trained fusion modules/adapters. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that frozen backbones already possess the capacity for in-context use of retrievals if properly aligned.

Method: Align-RAG applies a closed-form, per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter the frozen backbone's context window. This alignment requires no learning, no gradient updates, and no per-backbone tuning. The method also includes a future-shuffle control to rule out simple futures-averaging as the mechanism.

Result: Align-RAG outperforms the SOTA trained retrieval adapter on a frozen Chronos-Bolt across all 7 standard benchmark datasets (avg -3.75% MSE). It improves zero-shot MSE on 4 additional frozen TSFMs with varying architectures by 2.5%–13.7%. Analysis shows aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor, confirming frozen backbones support dynamic in-context retrieval use.

Conclusion: Frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals when properly aligned. Closed-form alignment (Align-RAG) should serve as the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained, as the gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without training.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented forecasting promises to adapt frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to new domains without fine-tuning, but recent methods typically rely on learned fusion modules, i.e., trained adapters that merge retrieved examples into the backbone's forecast, based on the assumption that frozen backbones cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own. We show this assumption is unnecessary. We introduce Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies a closed-form per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter a frozen backbone's context. With no learned parameters, Align-RAG outperforms the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on a frozen Chronos-Bolt on all seven datasets of the standard benchmark (avg -3.75% MSE), showing that the gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without any training. Align-RAG further improves zero-shot MSE on four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone with no per-backbone tuning. To probe why alignment helps, we compare the frozen backbone's prediction shift under aligned demonstrations to the closed-form ridge prediction shift on the same pairs. We find that aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out a futures-averaging account. Together, these results indicate that frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals, and that closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained. Code available at: https://github.com/masadi-99/align-rag

</details>


### [257] [Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Post-Wildfire Debris-Flow Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05265)
*Quinn Ledingham,Zhengsen Xu,Yimin Zhu,Zack Dewis,Mabel Heffring,Saeid Taleghanidoozdoozan,Motasem Alkayid,Megan Greenwood,Lincoln Linlin Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A systematic evaluation of 15 machine learning models for post-wildfire debris-flow prediction, finding TabPFN achieves the best unaugmented performance (threat score 0.637). SHAP analysis identifies short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation as dominant predictors, while synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples improves most models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-wildfire debris-flow prediction is critical for hazard mitigation, but is complicated by three challenges: (1) overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, (2) the need for model interpretability in safety-critical applications, and (3) limited training data availability.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate 15 machine learning models (including TabPFN) using basin-scale observations across the western United States with repeated stratified cross-validation. Model interpretability is assessed via SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Synthetic data augmentation is performed using TabPFN-generated samples to address data scarcity.

Result: TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented threat score of 0.637, followed closely by tree-based models. SHAP analysis reveals short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation as the most important features, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. Synthetic augmentation improves all models except CNN, with the largest mean threat score increase (+0.041) observed among deep learning models.

Conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive framework combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation to improve post-wildfire debris-flow prediction, demonstrating that TabPFN is a strong candidate for operational deployment.

Abstract: Prediction of post-wildfire debris flows is critical for mitigating hazards to communities, infrastructure, and resources during intense rainfall in recently burned areas. However, identifying reliable machine learning models is complicated by overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, the need for model interpretability, and limited training data. This paper addresses these challenges through a systematic evaluation of machine learning models in terms of predictive performance, feature importance, and synthetic data augmentation. Using basin-scale observations of post-wildfire debris-flow events across the western United States, we compare 15 models, including the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). Repeated stratified cross-validation shows that TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented performance with a threat score of 0.637, closely followed by the best tree-based models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to identify the features driving predictions, revealing that short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation consistently rank highest, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. We further evaluate synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address the scarcity of debris-flow observations. Synthetic augmentation improves the performance of all models except CNN, with the largest mean threat score increase of +0.041 among the deep learning models. By combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation, this work provides a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction.

</details>


### [258] [Rectifying Geometric Misalignment: Online Source-Free Adaptation for Class-Imbalanced EEG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05315)
*Shiwen Chu,Shanglin Li,Motoaki Kawanabe,Reinmar Kobler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OSPDIM is a source-free online unsupervised domain adaptation method for EEG-based BCIs that corrects geometric misalignment caused by label shifts on the Riemannian manifold, using manifold-constrained bias optimization via information maximization, outperforming standard Riemannian alignment in imbalanced online scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Riemannian alignment methods like RCT assume balanced class priors, but real-world online BCI scenarios experience dynamic label distribution shifts (label shift), causing geometric misalignment. Existing solutions are offline and rely on global batch statistics, making them unsuitable for online, source-free adaptation.

Method: OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping of SPD (symmetric positive definite) manifolds. This bias is optimized online via information maximization to correct geometric skew from imbalanced data streams. The method operates source-free and on-the-fly without requiring global batch statistics.

Result: 2D SPD matrix simulations visually confirmed OSPDIM rectifies misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive motor imagery dataset experiments showed OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, especially under severe class imbalance in online adaptation scenarios.

Conclusion: OSPDIM provides a robust, plug-and-play solution for practical online BCI systems by effectively handling label shifts on Riemannian manifolds in a source-free, online manner, overcoming a key limitation of existing Riemannian alignment techniques.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) often require unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to generalize across subjects and sessions. While Riemannian alignment methods like the Riemannian Centering Transformation (RCT) are effective for handling covariate shifts, they implicitly assume balanced class priors. However, in realistic online BCI scenarios, the label distributions vary dynamically (label shift), causing standard alignment techniques to geometrically misalign the target data distributions. In this work, we propose OSPDIM (Online SPD manifold information maximization), a source-free online UDA framework designed to address label shifts on the Riemannian manifold. OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping, which is optimized via information maximization to correct the geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods relying on global batch statistics, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly. Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually demonstrate that OSPDIM successfully rectifies the misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets show that OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, particularly in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance, offering a robust solution for practical, plug-and-play BCI systems.

</details>


### [259] [QEvict: Recoverable Quantized KV Eviction for Attention-Drift-Robust Long-Context Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05326)
*Ayushman Garg,Akshita Gupta,Shaswata Bhattacharya,Abhishek Gupta,Sandeep Kumar,Manoj Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QEvict replaces binary KV-cache eviction with a three-tier recoverable scheme (full-precision, quantized, deleted), enabling previously evicted tokens to be restored when they regain importance during decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard KV-cache eviction policies make irreversible decisions—once a token is discarded it cannot return—but token importance drifts during decoding. The authors demonstrate this brittleness by showing evicted tokens often receive substantial future attention, motivating a recoverable eviction framework.

Method: The authors introduce two diagnostics: Future Missed Mass (future attention assigned to discarded states) and Global LIR (reactivation of historically inactive regions). They then propose QEvict, a three-tier system: (1) high-confidence windows kept at full precision, (2) intermediate windows stored in a quantized recoverable tier, and (3) low-confidence windows deleted entirely. Cumulative attention scores dynamically update window importance; quantized windows that regain importance are dequantized and promoted back to full precision.

Result: QEvict consistently outperforms representative eviction and quantization baselines across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, reducing missed attention and improving information retention under a fixed memory budget.

Conclusion: Recoverable KV-cache eviction via a tiered precision strategy effectively addresses the attention drift problem in autoregressive decoding, preserving broader historical context without sacrificing precision on critical regions.

Abstract: Autoregressive large language model inference is increasingly constrained by the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache. A dominant line of work reduces this footprint by evicting tokens that appear unimportant under attention-derived scores. However, such policies make an implicit irreversible decision: once a token is evicted, it cannot become useful again. We show that this assumption is brittle during decoding. Token and window importance drift as generated queries evolve, causing standard eviction policies to permanently discard states that later receive substantial attention under the full-cache model. To characterize this behaviour, we introduce Future Missed Mass and Global LIR, two diagnostics that measure future attention assigned to discarded states and the reactivation of historically inactive regions. We propose QEvict, a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces binary retain-or-delete eviction with recoverable eviction. QEvict maintains high-confidence windows in full precision, stores intermediate windows in a quantized recoverable tier, and deletes only the lowest-confidence windows. During decoding, cumulative attention scores update window importance and when a quantized window becomes important again, it is dequantized and promoted to the full-precision. Under a fixed memory budget, this design preserves broader historical context while retaining exact full precision for the most important regions. Across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, QEvict consistently improves over representative eviction and quantization baselines, reducing missed attention and improving information retention

</details>


### [260] [DG-FedReuse: Proxy-Gradient-Gated Cached-Update Reuse with Matched Sparse Uplink Accounting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05358)
*Rahil Aftab,Vineet Kumar Rakesh,Soumya Mazumdar,Tapas Samanta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DG-FedReuse proposes a federated learning mechanism where clients reuse age-decayed cached model updates when a gradient discrepancy proxy is below a threshold, combined with adaptive Top-K compression. Under symmetric uplink-only accounting, it achieves 83-85% communication savings versus 77% for Top-K FedAvg, with accuracy drops of -5.29 to -0.14 pp. When downlink is symmetrically accounted, savings fall to ~42%, highlighting sensitivity to accounting boundaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce communication overhead in federated learning by allowing clients to skip transmitting fresh model updates when their local gradient has not changed substantially, thereby reusing cached, age-decayed updates instead.

Method: DG-FedReuse introduces a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy compared against a round-dependent threshold. Clients below the threshold submit age-decayed cached updates; a hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota constrain reuse. Fresh updates employ adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. Experiments use 6 image datasets, 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet(α=0.5) label heterogeneity, and 3 seeds over 90 rounds.

Result: Under uplink-only accounting, DG-FedReuse achieves 83.36-85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink savings vs. 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg, with seed-aligned accuracy differences of -5.29 to -0.14 pp. Best-observed test accuracies (exploratory) range from -2.38 to +0.45 pp. Under symmetric dense-model-downlink accounting, headline saving drops to 41.68-42.71%, with only 3.24-4.27 pp incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg.

Conclusion: The paper characterizes a specific reuse rule in its simulator without establishing generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime/energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods. Results are highly sensitive to whether downlink communication is included in the accounting boundary.

Abstract: Federated learning repeatedly incurs local optimization and model-update transmission. We study DG-FedReuse, a simulator-level mechanism that allows selected clients to contribute age-decayed cached updates when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy remains below a round-dependent threshold. A hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota constrain reuse, while fresh updates use an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. Experiments cover six image-classification datasets, 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5), and three seeds. At a common 90-round budget, DG-FedReuse yields 83.36-85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving, compared with 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg; the seed-aligned accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies obtained under test-controlled checkpointing are retained only as exploratory archival evidence and range from -2.38 to +0.45 percentage points relative to matched FedAvg. A symmetric dense-model-downlink sensitivity reduces the headline saving to 41.68-F42.71% and the incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg to 3.24-4.27 percentage points, demonstrating the dependence of communication conclusions on the accounting boundary. The study characterizes the proposed reuse rule in the implemented simulator; it does not establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime or energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

</details>


### [261] [Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) for Predictive Latent Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05371)
*Hailong Jiang,Emran Hossain,Feng Yu,Jianfeng Zhu,Guilin Zhang,Wulan Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a framework that uses quantum-inspired mathematical structures (complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents) for world modeling, establishing three theoretical properties and evaluating on cellular automata with mixed results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether quantum-inspired mathematical structures—specifically complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latent states—provide useful inductive biases for learning world models, going beyond classical vector, probabilistic, recurrent, or transformer-based latent state representations.

Method: The authors formalize QSWMs with three components: structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. They establish three foundational theoretical properties (classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, structured compactness) and instantiate both complex-valued and density-matrix-like variants, evaluating them on elementary cellular automata prediction tasks against classical baselines.

Result: Complex-valued QSWMs demonstrated promising local predictive performance on elementary cellular automata compared to classical baselines. However, both complex-valued and density-matrix variants exhibited limitations in long-horizon rollout prediction.

Conclusion: Quantum-structured representations show some promise as inductive biases for local prediction in world models, but significant challenges remain for long-horizon forecasting, particularly with density-matrix variants, suggesting that quantum-inspired approaches are not yet a straightforward improvement over classical methods for world modeling.

Abstract: World models learn latent states that summarize interaction histories, evolve over time, and support prediction, simulation, or planning. Most existing world models represent these states using classical vectors, probability distributions, recurrent hidden states, or transformer activations. In this paper, we introduce Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a quantum-inspired framework for predictive world modeling with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. We study whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory, such as complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents, provide useful inductive biases for world modeling. We establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. We then instantiate complex-valued and density-matrix-like QSWM variants and evaluate them on elementary cellular automata against strong classical baselines. Results show promising local predictive potential for complex-valued QSWMs, while also revealing limitations in long-horizon rollout, density-matrix variants

</details>


### [262] [Spectral Distillation: From Nonlinear Dynamics to Linear State-Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05416)
*Liane Galanti,Devan Shah,Shlomo Fortgang,Elad Hazan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides the first end-to-end provable pipeline for learning nonlinear dynamical systems through compact linear state-space representations. It combines a convex method called Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF) to learn an implicit predictor, followed by spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert it into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system, with dimension-free generalization guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning nonlinear dynamical systems typically requires solving non-convex system-identification problems, which lack theoretical guarantees and can be computationally brittle. The authors ask whether a nonlinear system can instead be represented by a compact linear state-space model (LDS) through a provably convex approach, bypassing direct non-convex optimization entirely.

Method: The proposed pipeline has two stages: (1) Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex learning method that produces an implicit spectral predictor competitive with the best linear observer for the unknown nonlinear system; (2) spectral-to-LDS distillation, which converts the implicit spectral predictor into an explicit recurrent LDS. The main theorem decomposes the prediction error into an exponentially small distillation term plus an OSF learning term bounded by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer.

Result: The main theoretical result is a dimension-free guarantee: average prediction error depends on observer complexity rather than the latent dimension of the nonlinear system. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning demonstrate that the train-then-distill pipeline yields compact LDS predictors matching or outperforming directly trained baselines.

Conclusion: This work establishes the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation, with strong empirical validation.

Abstract: Can nonlinear dynamical systems be learned through a compact linear state-space representation, without directly solving a non-convex system-identification problem? We give a provable pipeline for doing so. Starting from observations of an unknown nonlinear dynamical system, we first learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer for the system. We then apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system. Our main theorem shows that the average prediction error of the distilled LDS decomposes into an exponentially-small distillation term and the OSF learning term governed by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free: it depends on observer complexity rather than on the latent dimension needed to represent the nonlinear system. To our knowledge, this yields the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show that the train-then-distill pipeline produces compact LDS predictors that match or outperform directly trained baselines.

</details>


### [263] [Perturbation Sensitivity at Convergence: A Simple Signal for Identifying Spuriously Correlated Samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05419)
*Nilesh Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: After training convergence, samples relying on spurious correlations are classified by a shared, robust rule, while others are fit via fragile, sample-specific configurations. Perturbing inputs flips predictions of the latter more often, enabling detection of spurious-correlation samples without group labels or early-stopping hyperparameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Models trained with empirical risk minimization on data with spurious correlations fail on subpopulations where the correlation breaks. Existing detection methods require early-training signals and group-labeled validation data to select the intervention epoch. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency on group annotations and early-stopping hyperparameters.

Method: The method operates post-convergence. It applies a fixed perturbation to model inputs and observes prediction flips. Samples aligned with the spurious correlation are classified via a shared decision rule and are robust to perturbation. Remaining samples rely on instance-specific, fragile configurations and flip predictions more frequently. This difference is used to identify spurious-correlation samples. The procedure requires only two forward passes per sample, no group labels, and no early-stopping epoch. Detected samples are then used to rebalance training.

Result: On the Waterbirds dataset, using detected samples to rebalance training improved worst-group accuracy from 57.3% to 80.8%, compared to 85.8% achieved with ground-truth group labels.

Conclusion: Post-convergence perturbation sensitivity provides a reliable signal for detecting spurious-correlation samples without group annotations or early-stopping hyperparameters, substantially closing the gap with fully supervised group-label-based methods.

Abstract: Models trained by empirical risk minimization on data containing spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy while failing on subpopulations where the correlation does not hold. Existing methods for identifying the affected samples without group annotations rely on signals from early training, which requires locating the epoch at which to intervene, a hyperparameter typically selected using group-labeled validation data. We show that a usable signal is available after convergence, when loss no longer distinguishes the two populations. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared rule, while the remaining samples are fit through configurations specific to individual inputs and are correspondingly more fragile. Applying a fixed perturbation to a converged model's inputs flips the predictions of the latter far more often than the former. The resulting procedure requires two forward passes per training sample, no group annotations at any stage, and no early-stopping epoch. Using the detected samples to rebalance training raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, against 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

</details>


### [264] [Why the Third Axis Is Freedom](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05423)
*Michael Timothy Bennett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: XM's claimed "third pretraining axis" of exploration is actually freedom — the weakness of behavioral constraints. XM implicitly optimizes for freedom, and explicitly selecting for freedom improves XM under distribution shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the framing of Explorative Modeling (XM) — which produces K outputs per comparison and updates on the closest — as introducing "exploration" as a third pretraining axis. The author argues the real mechanism is freedom (weakness of behavioral constraint), which has known generalization benefits, and that XM should be reframed accordingly.

Method: The author provides a theoretical analysis proving that average XM loss depends on the probability that a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power K. For K>1, match probability increases with freedom. Empirical validation includes (1) Forward XM experiments manipulating K, (2) training XM candidate pools and comparing validation selection against a freedom selector using unlabelled parent contexts, and (3) demonstrating that explicit freedom selection improves XM under distribution shift.

Result: Larger K increased or saturated measured freedom and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. The freedom selector beat validation selection in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is shown to be a mode-count proxy for freedom that discards the extension structure critical to generalization. Prior work showed freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500% in induction experiments.

Conclusion: The "third pretraining axis" is freedom, not exploration. XM is merely a means to the end of freedom optimization. Explicitly selecting for freedom, rather than relying on XM's implicit optimization, yields better performance under distribution shift. Freedom — as a behavioral property independent of parameters, architecture, or MDL — is the likeliest property for generalization.

Abstract: In generative training, a model produces an output and is penalised for its difference from an example. With one output per comparison, a model that produces one common answer can outperform a model retaining a broader repertoire. Explorative Modeling (XM) produces $K$ outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, claiming exploration as a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Here I show the third axis is actually freedom, meaning the weakness of the constraint implied by a model's behaviour. Previous work showed freedom is a property of function rather than form. Parameters, architecture, minimum-description-length (MDL), and data can vary while the behavioural constraint remains unchanged.
