It was formally proved that weakest models are likeliest to generalise, and freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500\% in induction experiments. I prove average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power $K$. For $K>1$, match probability rises with freedom. I then demonstrate empirically that XM optimises for freedom. In a Forward XM experiment, larger $K$ increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. I trained XM candidate pools and compared validation selection with a freedom selector that read unlabelled parent contexts. Freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy for freedom, that discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalisation significance. XM is a means, freedom an end, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.

</details>


### [265] [EvoHarness-RL: Learning Self-Evolving Runtime Harness for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05446)
*Xuying Ning,Dongqi Fu,Tianxin Wei,Hanqing Zeng,Yuanchen Bei,Bingxuan Li,Zihao Li,Qifan Wang,Xiang Shen,Yifan Wu,Jiayi Liu,Hong Li,Yinglong Xia,Xiangjun Fan,Hanghang Tong,Jingrui He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoHarness-RL learns offline harness policies that construct and update external Belief-Progress-Experience (BPE) state during long-horizon task execution. Using supervised fine-tuning plus cost-aware GRPO on a Qwen3-8B model, it achieves 96.9% on ALFWorld, revealing harness annealing and harness evolution dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents need external execution support (state tracking, progress monitoring, tool invocation, outcome verification, experience reuse), but current approaches hand-engineer external workspaces and access policies via prompts/heuristics. The paper addresses the coupled challenges of state formation from noisy traces and runtime control over external-state access by studying whether agents can learn harness policies rather than relying on manual design.

Method: EvoHarness-RL introduces Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. A two-stage training pipeline: (1) supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the agent the harness action space and external state construction; (2) cost-aware GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) explores coordination policies for selectively reading, updating, and consolidating external state. The approach is instantiated on ALFWorld using a Qwen3-8B LLM.

Result: EvoHarness-RL achieves 96.9% success rate on ALFWorld. The paper identifies two key emergent dynamics: (1) harness annealing — training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns, shifting the agent from frequent harness calls to selective external-state access; (2) harness evolution — progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate.

Conclusion: Long-horizon agents benefit substantially from trainable policies that construct and coordinate with external harness workspaces, rather than merely adding stronger tools or larger memories. Learned harness policies enable more efficient and adaptive external-state management.

Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly rely on external execution support to maintain state, track progress, invoke tools, verify outcomes, and reuse experience across interactions. However, effective harness use raises two coupled challenges: state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access. Existing agents usually handle both through prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions, leaving the external workspace and its usage policy manually engineered. To address this, we study the problem of harness policy learning, where agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution. We introduce EvoHarness-RL, which exposes Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, while cost-aware GRPO explores coordination policies to selectively read, update, and consolidate that state during long-horizon interaction. Instantiated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM, EvoHarness-RL reaches 96.9% success and reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into the model policy and shifts the agent from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access, and harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate. These results suggest that long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories.

</details>


### [266] [Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotopes for Identifiable and Refinable Predictive Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05454)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The authors propose the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), a novel prediction head that disentangles three distinct uncertainty sources — discrete mode choice, bounded systematic drift, and stochastic noise — within a zonotope representation, offering closed-form likelihood, identifiability guarantees, and coupled future predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard neural network prediction heads output either Gaussian mixtures or conformal regions, but neither can separate the three distinct sources of uncertainty that arise in real prediction tasks: (1) discrete choice among modes, (2) bounded systematic drift within a chosen mode, and (3) irreducible stochastic noise. Disentangling these sources enables richer uncertainty quantification, coupled multi-step prediction refinement, and per-mode risk analysis.

Method: The HProbZ head represents the three uncertainty sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope. The binary generator captures mode selection, the bounded generator models systematic drift, and the stochastic generator accounts for noise. The likelihood is computed in closed form via convolution of these generators. The bounded generator is shared across prediction steps, coupling future predictions algebraically so that observing one step refines all remaining steps in a single forward pass. The authors prove the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation and that HProbZ densities are representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture.

Result: Empirical evaluation on representative prediction benchmarks shows that HProbZ is competitive with same-encoder mixture baselines while additionally providing structural properties — per-mode risk analysis and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time — that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly offer.

Conclusion: HProbZ provides a principled framework for representing and disentangling distinct uncertainty sources in predictive models, coupling future predictions for efficient refinement, and offering identifiability guarantees. It matches baseline predictive performance while uniquely delivering per-mode risk quantification and multi-modal conformal sets, making it a compelling alternative to Gaussian mixture and conformal prediction heads.

Abstract: Probabilistic prediction heads in neural networks typically output either a Gaussian mixture or a single conformal region. Neither separates the distinct sources of uncertainty often present in real prediction tasks: a discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within the chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. We introduce the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), an output head that represents these three sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, and admits a closed-form likelihood by convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, so observing one step refines the predictive distribution at every remaining step in a single forward pass. We establish that the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and that an HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. The same shared structure provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks supports the effectiveness of the design relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

</details>


### [267] [Matrix Zonotopic Attention: A Context-Adaptive Value Projection for Set Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05472)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies a structural asymmetry in multi-head attention where value projections are input-independent while routing is input-dependent, limiting expressivity for permutation-invariant set functions. It introduces Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) to quantify target complexity, proves depth-separation results, and proposes Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) with context-adaptive value families that recover standard attention at initialization and show selective gains on high-rank combinatorial tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multi-head attention exhibits an architectural asymmetry: the softmax routing over keys/queries is richly input-dependent, yet the value projection matrices are fixed and shared across all inputs. This "context-rigid" design means the linear operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is identical for every sample, potentially limiting the model's ability to represent complex set functions that require input-conditional transformations. The authors aim to formally characterize this limitation and propose a solution.

Method: First, the paper formalizes Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF), a complexity measure counting the number of input-dependent directions needed for exact representation of a target operator. Using this, a depth-separation theorem is proved: context-rigid attention requires depth proportional to TDOF, while a single context-adaptive layer suffices. Second, Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) is introduced, replacing the fixed value projection with a matrix-zonotope family — a learned centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices gated by input-dependent scalars. This preserves permutation equivariance, reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialization (by zeroing gates), and admits a data-driven reachability interpretation via zonotope geometry.

Result: The TDOF-based depth-separation analysis formally proves a representational gap between context-rigid and context-adaptive architectures. Experiments on set-prediction benchmarks show that MZAttn's advantage is selective: it yields meaningful improvements on targets with high-rank, sparsely combinatorial dependence on the input set, while on aggregate-statistic targets (e.g., mean, sum), parameter-matched standard attention remains competitive, consistent with TDOF predictions.

Conclusion: The input-independent value projection in standard multi-head attention is a genuine representational bottleneck for permutation-invariant set functions with high TDOF. MZAttn offers a principled, initialization-compatible remedy with selective architectural advantages precisely where theory predicts, without sacrificing performance on simpler targets.

Abstract: Multi-head attention combines an input-dependent softmax routing with an input-independent linear value projection, so the per-sample operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is the same for every input set. We study the consequences of this asymmetry for permutation-invariant set targets. We introduce the Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) of a target operator, a complexity measure counting the input-dependent directions an exact representation requires, and present a depth-separation analysis showing that context-rigid attention needs depth proportional to the target's TDOF, whereas a single layer with a context-adaptive value family can represent the same target. Building on this analysis, we propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), which replaces the fixed value projection with a context-adaptive matrix-zonotope family: a centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices weighted by input-dependent gates. The construction reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialisation, preserves permutation equivariance, and admits a data-driven reachability interpretation. Experiments on a range of set-prediction tasks are consistent with the TDOF prediction that the architectural advantage is selective: it appears on targets that depend on the input set in a high-rank, sparsely combinatorial way, and is small on aggregate-statistic targets where parameter-matched standard attention is already competitive.

</details>


### [268] [KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05475)
*Zhaowei Han,Xiang Zhang,Bing Han,Kai Liu,Danqi Hu,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KV-Skill introduces a design space of external factorized operators that augment frozen LLMs via a lightweight key-value interface. Skills can be registered from text or learned from rewards, without consuming prompt positions, and consistently outperform text-in-prompt, soft prompting, and LoRA baselines across multiple benchmarks and model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Task knowledge stored as text in prompts is modular but requires repeated interpretation, while weight updates (e.g., fine-tuning, LoRA) make capabilities hard to load, remove, or share independently. The authors seek a representation that combines the modularity of text with the efficiency of parameterized operators, enabling knowledge to be authored, compressed, deployed, and independently managed without modifying the backbone model.

Method: KV-Skill operates via two complementary paths: (1) Registration — converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface that injects skill information into the frozen model's key-value cache; (2) Reward Learning — develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes using reinforcement learning, with or without a source text skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. The operators are factorized, injected at specific layers, and loaded through a lightweight interface, enabling independent loading, removal, and composition of multiple skills.

Result: On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, KV-Skill registration achieves 77.2 accuracy vs. 23.4 for source text, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill wins in 7/8 settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. Post-hoc rank analysis reveals that text-derived operators retain nearly all benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. A single shared interface supports three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting.

Conclusion: KV-Skill demonstrates that task knowledge — whether from text or experience — can be effectively compressed into external factorized operators, deployed separately from the backbone, and independently managed. This offers a compelling middle ground between in-context learning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, combining modularity with performance.

Abstract: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 23.4 for the source text skill, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, one shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill

</details>


### [269] [LC-GRPO: Bridging Train-Inference Gap for Flow-Based GRPO with Langevin Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05600)
*Yingqing Guo,Hui Yuan,Zijian He,Mengdi Wang,Zheng Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LC-GRPO introduces a Langevin-corrected rollout for flow-based GRPO that aligns stochastic training transitions with deterministic ODE inference, improving reward optimization while preserving generation quality across image and video tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GRPO methods for flow models replace the inference-time ODE with an SDE during training, but finite-step SDE discretization produces blurry, mismatched samples relative to the test-time ODE sampler. This mismatch harms the effectiveness of reinforcement learning for fine-tuning flow-based generative models.

Method: LC-GRPO proposes a hybrid transition: each rollout step first applies an inference-aligned ODE Euler step, then a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal at that timestep. The Langevin score is recovered directly from the flow velocity (no additional score model), and the resulting transition is an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood for policy optimization (e.g., PPO/GRPO).

Result: Theoretically, one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step under suitable conditions, and at matched randomness, the proposed transition can be more accurate than the standard Euler–Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Empirically, LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo, preserves generation quality, and narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic ODE inference.

Conclusion: LC-GRPO resolves the train–test mismatch in flow-based GRPO by coupling inference-aligned ODE steps with Langevin corrections, yielding more accurate stochastic rollouts, better reward optimization, and preserved sample quality without requiring extra models.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models are typically sampled by solving a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), whereas online reinforcement learning requires stochastic rollouts for policy exploration and optimization. Existing GRPO methods for flow models therefore replace the inference-time ODE with a stochastic differential equation (SDE) during training. Although the ODE and SDE share the same marginal distributions in continuous time, their finite-step discretizations can differ substantially. In particular, SDE rollouts often become blurry as the exploration noise increases, creating a mismatch between the samples used for reinforcement learning and those generated by the test-time ODE sampler. We introduce LC-GRPO, a flow-based GRPO framework with Langevin correction. Each rollout transition first takes an inference-aligned ODE Euler step and then applies a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The required score is recovered directly from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model, while the resulting transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood for policy optimization. We theoretically show that, under suitable conditions, one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step. At a matched randomness level, we further show that the proposed transition can be more accurate than the standard Euler--Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo demonstrate that LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

</details>


### [270] [GAUGE: Granularity-Adaptive Counterfactual Gating of Evidence for Incomplete Multimodal Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05608)
*Yunping Shi,En Yu,Kairui Guo,Jie Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GAUGE is a lightweight counterfactual gating framework that performs fine-grained evidence modulation for incomplete multimodal classification. It imputes missing modalities, scores counterfactual unit-replacement effects via prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores in a single forward-backward pass, and converts these scores into additive attention-logit biases without altering the backbone, outperforming strong baselines across six benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal classification methods handle missing modalities through imputation and dynamic fusion, but they operate at a coarse modality level. This prevents them from retaining reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, ultimately compromising prediction reliability under input incompleteness.

Method: GAUGE employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) a frozen imputer recovers missing modalities; (2) both observed and recovered inputs are encoded as fine-grained evidence units; (3) rather than explicit per-unit intervention, it computes the counterfactual effect of replacing each unit with a reference representation using prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores derived in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates and converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without modifying the backbone architecture. A Taylor remainder analysis bounds the first-order approximation error relative to exact counterfactuals.

Result: Experiments across six benchmarks show that GAUGE consistently outperforms strong baselines under diverse incomplete-input settings, demonstrating its effectiveness as a fine-grained evidence control framework.

Conclusion: GAUGE establishes itself as a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness. The Taylor remainder theoretical analysis formally characterizes the approximation error, providing rigorous justification for the first-order scoring mechanism.

Abstract: Multimodal classification typically assumes all modalities are available, yet real-world inputs are often incomplete. Imputation and dynamic fusion can mitigate such incompleteness, but existing methods operate at a coarse modality level and thus cannot retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, compromising prediction reliability. To address this issue, we propose GAUGE, a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification. GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes observed and recovered inputs uniformly as fine-grained evidence units. Rather than intervening on each unit explicitly, GAUGE scores the counterfactual effect of replacing every unit with a reference representation through prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores, all obtained in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates, which are converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without altering the backbone architecture. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across diverse incomplete-input settings. Furthermore, a Taylor remainder theoretical analysis characterizes the error of the first-order approximation relative to the exact counterfactual effect, establishing GAUGE as a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness.

</details>


### [271] [Reasoning Errors Have a Region and a Direction in the Residual-Stream Trajectory of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05660)
*Hamed Damirchi,Ignacio Meza De la Jara,Damith Ranasinghe,Yuhang Liu,Javen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a three-stream detector for distinguishing sound vs. flawed reasoning in language models, combining residual-stream displacement ("motion") with two restricted views of the originating state ("region" via VQ and "direction" via normalized multi-layer states). It outperforms displacement-only and single-layer baselines by up to 12% and 21%, respectively, and generalizes to factual tasks, suggesting correctness signals are better read from state-conditioned motion than static states or decontextualized trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As language models are increasingly deployed for verifiable reasoning tasks, reliably detecting flawed reasoning is critical. Existing trajectory-based methods use layerwise residual-stream displacement to capture representational change while attenuating stable token-specific shortcuts. However, displacement alone discards the originating state, while restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. The authors identify a fundamental trade-off between these approaches.

Method: The authors propose a three-stream detector architecture: (1) a **motion** stream capturing residual-stream displacement between layers; (2) a **coarse region reader** using vector quantization to provide a restricted view of the originating state's location; and (3) a **fine direction reader** operating over normalized multi-layer states. These three streams are combined to restore enough state context for interpreting motion without reverting to full-state probing.

Result: On unseen reasoning benchmarks, the three-stream detector improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state-of-the-art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also performs well on factual completion and fact verification, outperforming all compared detectors. Ablations confirm that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals.

Conclusion: Reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone. The three-stream design successfully navigates the trade-off between decontextualized displacement and full-state probing, and the signal it captures appears tied to correctness rather than to a specific kind of reasoning.

Abstract: As language models are increasingly used for tasks that require verifiable reasoning, reliably distinguishing sound reasoning from flawed reasoning has become an important practical problem. Recent trajectory-based methods seek this signal in layerwise residual-stream displacements, which capture how representations change while attenuating some stable, token-specific information. However, displacement omits the state from which an update originates, whereas restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. We identify this trade-off and propose a three-stream detector that combines motion with two restricted views of location. A coarse region reader based on vector quantization and a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This design restores enough state context to interpret the motion without returning to full-state probing. On reasoning benchmarks unseen during training, our method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state of the art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also reads factual completion and fact verification, ahead of every detector we compare against, which places the signal on correctness rather than on a kind of reasoning. Ablations further show that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals. These results suggest that reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone.

</details>


### [272] [Potential Matching Optimal Transport: Continuous Normalizing Flows for Exact $p$-Wasserstein Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05666)
*Lishuo Zhang,Ruizhi Huang,Yang Yu,Lei Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PMOT introduces a potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost optimal transport, parameterizing CNF velocity fields with a scalar potential. It uses self-induced matching along straight bridges and flexible terminal matching, with a zero-loss exactness guarantee: any zero-loss solution recovers the $p$-optimal transport map.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend optimal transport beyond the classical $p=2$ (Wasserstein-2) setting by developing a unified potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost OT, enabling learning of $p$-specific transport maps while maintaining theoretical exactness guarantees.

Method: PMOT parameterizes the Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) velocity field using a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou–Brenier form for exponent $p$. Training employs a self-induced matching loss computed along straight bridges defined by the model's own predicted endpoints, combined with flexible terminal distribution matching (e.g., likelihood-based or MMD-based).

Result: The main theoretical result establishes that under regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou–Brenier optimality system and recovers the $p$-optimal transport map. Empirically, PMOT learns $p$-specific maps aligning with OT references on synthetic benchmarks, remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching via an MMD-based color transformation experiment.

Conclusion: PMOT provides a principled, flexible, and theoretically grounded framework for learning $p$-optimal transport maps across different cost exponents, bridging the gap between dynamic OT formulations and practical deep learning-based transport models.

Abstract: We introduce Potential Matching Optimal Transport (PMOT), a potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost optimal transport with $c_p(x,y)=\|x-y\|^p$. PMOT parameterizes the CNF velocity field with a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou--Brenier form for the chosen exponent $p$. It trains the potential gradient with a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching. Our main result establishes zero-loss exactness: under the stated regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou--Brenier optimality system and recovers the corresponding $p$-optimal transport map and dynamics. On synthetic benchmarks, PMOT learns $p$-specific maps that agree with the corresponding $p$-matched OT references. It also remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and an MMD-based color transformation experiment demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

</details>


### [273] [When Does Consensus Mean Correctness? Measuring the Agreement-Accuracy Coupling with Semantics-Preserving Re-Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05670)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RENDEQ generates render-equivalent scientific figures (semantically identical by construction) to directly measure whether model agreement across perturbations tracks correctness. Re-rendering beats resampling; agreement outperforms token log-probability on 2/3 VLMs; fine-tuning on cross-render consensus unexpectedly reduces accuracy — reversing prior natural-image findings — because rewarding agreement destroys the error diffuseness that makes agreement a useful correctness signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work uses model agreement across perturbed inputs as a reliability signal and self-training target, assuming agreement correlates with correctness. However, this coupling is rarely measured directly because natural-image perturbations only preserve meaning by assumption and lack exact ground-truth answer keys. Scientific figures — programmatically generated from data — solve both problems: redrawing yields images that are semantically equivalent by construction with exact answers.

Method: The authors build RENDEQ, a generator producing render-equivalence sets of scientific figures. They measure the agreement-correctness coupling on three open-weight VLMs, with every finding replicated across three independent instantiations. They compare re-rendering against resampling, benchmark agreement against mean token log-probability (an evidence-carrying baseline), and analyze dispersion across style factors (plotting library, etc.). They also fine-tune models on their own cross-render consensus to test whether self-training with agreement improves accuracy.

Result: Re-rendering outperforms resampling on both accuracy and reliability. Agreement beats the token log-probability baseline on two of three models and ties on the third (reversing an earlier buggy replication). Dispersion is dominated by plotting library choice (>2× the next factor, an order of magnitude above noise). Fine-tuning on cross-render consensus consistently reduces accuracy across all five replication runs — the opposite of published natural-image results.

Conclusion: Agreement certifies correctness only above a threshold set by how diffuse a model's errors are. Optimizing for agreement eliminates that diffuseness, destroying the very property that makes agreement predictive. This explains the inversion: when a model's errors become concentrated (non-diffuse), agreement ceases to track correctness, undermining its utility as a self-training objective.

Abstract: A model's agreement across perturbed inputs is used both as a label-free reliability signal and as a self-training target, on the premise that agreement tracks correctness. That coupling is rarely measured directly: natural-image perturbations preserve meaning only by assumption, and no exact answer key localizes errors. Scientific figures remove both obstacles, a figure is drawn from data by a program, so redrawing it yields images that are semantically equivalent by construction and share a programmatically exact answer. We build RENDEQ, a generator of such render-equivalence sets, and measure the coupling on three open-weight VLMs, checking every finding across three independent instantiations. Re-rendering beats resampling on both accuracy and reliability. Agreement beats an evidence-carrying baseline, mean token log-probability, on two of three models and ties on the third, reversing an intermediate, buggy replication traced to a rendering-pipeline failure. The dispersion behind this is concentrated in one style factor, the plotting library, more than double the next-largest factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Fine-tuning on the model's own cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy falls in every one of five replication runs, the opposite sign to published results on natural images. Agreement certifies correctness only above a threshold set by how diffuse a model's errors are, and an objective that rewards agreement destroys exactly that diffuseness.

</details>


### [274] [Consistency Has a Computable Blind Spot: A Commutation Theory of Label-Free Reliability for Vision-Language Figure Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05675)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a theoretical framework for label-free reliability testing of vision-language models based on invariance and equivariance. It characterizes the blind spot of invariance-based testing—errors that commute with perturbations escape detection—through the algebra of centralizers, proves completeness results for affine and permutation errors, and instantiates the theory as the Equivariance-Consistency Score (ECS), validated across multiple models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing label-free reliability methods for vision-language models rely on invariance to input perturbations, but suffer from a systematic blind spot: certain misreadings survive perturbations unchanged and get falsely certified as correct. The paper aims to characterize this blind spot rigorously, determine which error classes are provably detectable, and develop complementary equivariance-based detection that exploits predictable changes in output when input data is edited.

Method: The authors formalize the blind spot algebraically: an error is invisible to an edit iff the two transformations commute, making the set of undetectable errors the joint centralizer of the edit suite. They prove completeness: two matched affine edits are provably complete for affine reading errors, while no swap-based edit suite is complete for label permutations—a gap partially closed by cyclic relabeling. Complementary equivariance testing checks that editing data produces a computable, predictable change in output. The Equivariance-Consistency Score combines invariance and equivariance metrics, instantiated in the REND-EQUIV benchmark with matched invariance/equivariance sets over identical data.

Result: The predicted ordering (invariance+equivariance outperforming either alone) holds across three vision-language models on a hand-labeled population. A second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot is inherent to the relation, not implementation-specific. Cyclic relabeling delivers the predicted detection gain on matched real samples. The framework also explains a reported inversion in classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is jointly determined by the relation and fault class, never the relation alone.

Conclusion: Label-free reliability testing must account for the algebraic structure of the perturbation-error relationship. Invariance alone has a computable, inescapable blind spot (the centralizer), which equivariance complements. Detectability is a joint property of the test relation and the fault class—a finding that resolves apparent contradictions in prior literature and provides a principled foundation for building more complete reliability suites.

Abstract: Label-free reliability for vision-language models rests on invariance: perturb the input and a faithful reader's answer should not change. This has a known blind spot, a systematic misreading survives the perturbation and gets certified wrong, which we show is computable, not just real: an error is invisible to an edit exactly when the two commute, so the errors a suite cannot reach form its joint centralizer, a set that shrinks as edits are added and can be written down rather than guessed at. We act on the complementary relation, equivariance: edit a figure's data and the correct answer must change by a computable amount. Two matched edits are provably complete for affine reading errors; no suite of swap edits is complete for label permutations, and cyclic relabeling closes most of that gap. We instantiate the theory as the Equivariance-Consistency Score, a label-free, training-free detector, and release REND-EQUIV, pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets over identical data. The predicted ordering holds across three models and a hand-labeled population immune to the one circularity in how it is selected; a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation, not to any implementation; and cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted gain on a matched real sample. The same characterization explains a reported inversion of this ordering in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is a joint property of the relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

</details>


### [275] [SEAM: Global consistency beyond local accuracy in scientific machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05702)
*Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan,Bum Jun Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEAM introduces a generator-agnostic framework that tests whether locally valid scientific explanations can be assembled into a globally consistent account, using a sheaf-theoretic obstruction formalism that locates inconsistency at specific channels and overlaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific machine learning typically validates explanations locally (per subdomain, benchmark split, or single prediction), but cannot determine whether these local explanations cohere into a globally admissible scientific account. There is no existing computable framework for assessing this local-to-global consistency.

Method: SEAM represents each region as a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels plus optional contract metadata. The finite explanation-sheaf instantiation (SEAM-Ω) compares neighboring explanations on overlaps, converting disagreement into a channel-resolved obstruction. This obstruction locates inconsistency and tests competing accounts by restricting repairs to revisions each account permits. Exact feasibility refutes/retains accounts; when unavailable, residual-aware regularized records provide empirical attribution. The framework also separates inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitors generators under distribution shift.

Result: Theorems for minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability are established, along with results for identifiability and closure recoverability. Across 19 experiments on synthetic PDE systems and out-of-distribution FNO monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, attributing failures to specific channels and overlaps.

Conclusion: SEAM provides a global explanation-consistency audit layer that complements existing solvers and learning models, testing whether local explanations form a coherent scientific account. This addresses a critical gap in scientific machine learning validation.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning commonly validates models at the level of a subdomain, a benchmark split, or an explanation for one prediction. Yet such local checks cannot establish whether the resulting explanations can be assembled into one globally admissible explanation. We introduce Scientific Explanation-Admissibility Machines (SEAM), a generator-agnostic framework that makes this local-to-global consistency question computable across regions, sensors, regimes, and model components. The finite explanation-sheaf instantiation SEAM-$Ω$ represents each region by a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels together with optional contract metadata; compares neighboring explanations on their overlaps; and converts disagreement into a channel-resolved obstruction. This obstruction locates inconsistency and tests competing declared accounts by restricting each repair to the revisions that one account permits. Exact feasibility refutes or retains an account; when exact repair is unavailable, residual-aware regularized records provide a separately labeled empirical attribution. The framework also separates inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitors learned generators under distribution shift. We establish theorems for minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability, together with companion results for identifiability and closure recoverability. Across nineteen experiments involving synthetic partial differential equation systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator (FNO) monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, and attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps. SEAM adds a global explanation-consistency audit to existing solvers and learning models, testing whether their local explanations form a coherent scientific account.

</details>


### [276] [Spectral Aliasing Pretext: A novel task for Self-Supervised fault diagnosis in rotating machinery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05705)
*Victor Gialis,Maxime Metz,David Esteve,Abdenour Soualhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAP is a self-supervised pretraining method for machinery fault diagnosis that exploits spectral aliasing by deliberately undersampling vibration signals and training a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum, enabling highly discriminative representations with minimal labeled data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning for machinery fault diagnosis requires extensive labeled data, which is scarce in industrial settings. Existing self-supervised methods often rely on data augmentations that may destroy fault-related signal characteristics. A label-efficient method that learns from unlabeled data without destructive augmentations is needed.

Method: SAP deliberately undersamples vibration signals to create a folded (aliased) spectrum, then trains a Transformer model to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. This pretext task forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults. After pretraining, the model is evaluated via linear probing (frozen encoder + linear classifier) and compared against full fine-tuning and fully supervised training.

Result: On the CWRU dataset, SAP learns stable, highly discriminative representations. Linear probing with SAP achieves very high classification performance using only a small fraction of labeled data with low variance. Full fine-tuning and fully supervised training do not yield more stable or better results than SAP with linear probing.

Conclusion: SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis under limited labeled data, offering a practical solution for real-world industrial applications where labeled data is scarce.

Abstract: Deep learning is a new way for machinery fault diagnosis but requires extensive labeled data, a scarce resource in industrial settings. We propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP), a self-supervised learning method that pretrains models on unlabeled vibration data by exploiting spectral aliasing. We deliberately undersample signals to create folded spectrum, then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. This pretext task forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults, without potentially destructive augmentations. Experiments on the CWRU dataset show that SAP learns stable and highly discriminative representations. In a linear probing setting, SAP quickly achieves very high classification performance with only a small fraction of labeled data and low variance. In contrast, full fine-tuning, including fully supervised training, does not lead to more stable or better results. Overall, these findings suggest that SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis with limited labeled data.

</details>


### [277] [CircuitSteer: Geometrically Aligned Multi-Layer Steering via Sparse Autoencoder Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05732)
*Mehrshad Saadatinia,Parsa Razmara,Ardalan Aryashad,Ali Abbasi,Seyedarmin Azizi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CircuitSteer uses Sparse Autoencoders to identify multi-layer semantic circuits and applies multi-point steering interventions, achieving robust behavioral control across diverse tasks (toxicity, sycophancy, refusal) while preserving text fluency, outperforming single-layer methods like CAA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing steering methods like CAA rely on fixed single-layer interventions from aggregate activation differences, which fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers and perform poorly on semantically diverse inputs and complex behaviors (e.g., sycophancy, refusal). There is a need for a method that isolates coherent, multi-layer circuits responsible for target behaviors.

Method: CircuitSteer leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to construct feature flow circuits by analyzing feature co-activation and geometric alignment of decoder directions across layers. This identifies multi-layer subcircuits responsible for target behaviors. Dense steering vectors are synthesized from these sparse features, and multi-point interventions are applied across layers to guide the model's semantic trajectory.

Result: Across two model families and tasks (toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, refusal), CircuitSteer was the only method to consistently produce fluency-preserving interventions. Competing methods either sacrificed text quality or failed entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal.

Conclusion: Multi-layer circuit steering with geometric alignment of selected features yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions, demonstrating the superiority of circuit-based multi-point interventions for LLM alignment.

Abstract: Controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for AI alignment. Existing steering methods, such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), typically rely on fixed single-layer interventions derived from aggregate activation differences. These methods impose a single intervention across semantically diverse inputs and often fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers, limiting the effectiveness of the steering. In this work, we introduce CircuitSteer, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and manipulate coherent semantic circuits distributed across multiple layers. By constructing a feature flow circuit based on feature co-activation and the geometric alignment of decoder directions, we isolate the specific multi-layer subcircuits responsible for a target behavior. We then synthesize dense steering vectors from these sparse features and apply multi-point interventions to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory. We evaluate CircuitSteer using contrastive examples across a diverse set of tasks, including toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal, spanning two model families. Across all models and datasets, CircuitSteer is the only method to consistently produce fluency-preserving interventions; competing methods either sacrifice text quality or lack coverage, failing entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal. These results demonstrate that multi-layer circuit steering, enabled by enforcing geometric alignment among selected features, yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions. Code is available at https://github.com/mehrshad-sdtn/CircuitSteer.

</details>


### [278] [Multivariate Time Series Forecasting needs Cross Variable Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05742)
*Kuiye Ding,Yifan Hu,Hanchen Wang,Hao Xue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies an "objective gap" in multivariate time series forecasting where Direct Forecasting (DF) fails to constrain cross-variable dependencies among future values. It proposes Cross-Variable Loss (CvLoss), a graph-based structural regularizer that penalizes inconsistent forecast residuals across variables, yielding consistent improvements across diverse forecasting models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multivariate forecasting models focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations but neglect dependencies among future values. The dominant Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm uses point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain the cross-variable structure of multi-step forecasts, creating a mismatch — an "objective gap" — when cross-variable and lagged dependencies are present.

Method: The authors propose Cross-Variable Loss (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that operates on a cross-variable graph. CvLoss penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences across forecast patches, thereby enforcing consistency in both synchronous (same time) and asynchronous (cross-time) interactions among variables. It functions as an add-on to standard DF objectives without requiring architectural changes.

Result: CvLoss consistently improves the performance of competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and demonstrates compatibility with a variety of forecasting backbones.

Conclusion: The DF objective is fundamentally mismatched for multivariate forecasting due to unmodeled cross-variable dependencies in future values. CvLoss effectively bridges this objective gap as a flexible, model-agnostic regularizer, offering a simple yet effective way to enhance multivariate time series forecasting.

Abstract: Multivariate time series forecasting presents unique challenges because future variables often co-evolve under shared system dynamics. While existing studies mainly focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations, dependencies among future values are much less explored. Specifically, modern forecasting models largely follow the Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm, generating multi-step forecasts with point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain cross-variable structure. In this work, we show that the DF objective is mismatched in the presence of cross-variable and lagged dependencies, revealing an objective gap. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{C}ross-\textbf{V}ariable \textbf{Loss} (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that constrains forecast residuals on a cross-variable graph. CvLoss penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions. Our experiments show that CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

</details>


### [279] [Equipment-centric workpiece localization in near real-time using deep learning-based vision and event-driven finite state machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05744)
*Dohyeon Kong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An equipment-centric framework using multi-camera vision and event-driven state machines enables continuous workpiece localization in hot forging environments, achieving 100% event detection and a mean localization error of 317.8 mm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct tracking of workpieces in hot forging is infeasible due to extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. A reliable indirect method is needed for traceability and process coordination.

Method: The framework uses multiple static 2D cameras to monitor handling equipment, estimates 3D equipment coordinates in floorplan space, and recognizes grasp/release activities via a keypoint-guided attention mechanism integrated into a 3D convolutional neural network. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations.

Result: In an operational hot forging factory, the system achieved 100% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, a mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and a mean system latency of 21 seconds.

Conclusion: The framework successfully bridges vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning, enabling visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations in harsh industrial settings.

Abstract: Continuous workpiece localization is essential for traceability and process coordination in hot forging, but direct tracking is unreliable because of extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. This study presents an equipment-centric framework that infers workpiece locations from handling equipment observed by multiple static 2D cameras. The framework estimates floorplan-space 3D equipment coordinates and recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism integrated into a 3D convolutional neural network improves activity recognition by focusing on functionally relevant equipment regions. Evaluation in an operational hot forging factory achieved 100\% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, a mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and a mean system latency of 21 seconds. The framework connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning and supports visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations.

</details>


### [280] [Accelerating nanodrug development in continuous flow systems using informed prediction models based on low-cost surrogate nanoparticles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05761)
*Kai Dahms,Eilien Heinrich,Jochen Schmid,Michael Bortz,Iryna Savych,Regina Bleul*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A shape-constrained predictive modeling approach is introduced to accurately estimate nanoparticle size and PDI across varying process conditions, reducing the need for extensive empirical optimization in nanomedicine manufacturing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Nanoparticle development relies heavily on iterative experimental screening because small changes in process parameters (concentration, flow rates, mixing ratios) significantly affect size and PDI, and no predictive mathematical frameworks exist to guide rational process development.

Method: Liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared using controlled microfluidic methods under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios. A shape-constrained predictive model was then developed, incorporating both experimental data and expert domain knowledge, and validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data.

Result: The shape-constrained model enabled accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, substantially reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows.

Conclusion: Shape-constrained modeling provides a rational, efficient framework for process development in nanomedicine manufacturing, bridging the gap between sparse experimental data and reliable predictive capability.

Abstract: The development of nanotherapeutics often involves extensive empirical optimization due to the sensitivity of nanoparticle properties, such as size and polydispersity index (PDI), to minor changes in process parameters. Factors like formulation concentration, flow rates, and mixing ratios can significantly influence clinical efficacy and therapeutic outcomes. The absence of predictive mathematical frameworks has made iterative experimental screening necessary, increasing both costs and development time.
  This study introduces and validates a predictive modeling approach based on shape constraints, aiming to enhance the estimation of nanoparticle characteristics across various process conditions. Using controlled microfluidic methods, liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios.
  The shape-constrained model, informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge, was subsequently validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data. Results reveal that shape-constrained modeling facilitates accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows. This framework supports rational and efficient process development for manufacturing nanomedicine systems.

</details>


### [281] [Neuro-Symbolic Closed-Loop Control of Laser Powder Bed Fusion with an In-Loop Ontology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05773)
*Gisuk Hong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture for laser powder bed fusion uses an ontology with a description-logic reasoner to dynamically set constraints for a predictive controller, mapping unmeasurable melt pool depth to observable width via a Gaussian process model, successfully eliminating overhang dross in simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overhang dross formation in laser powder bed fusion is governed by melt pool depth, which cannot be measured in real time during the build process. Existing geometry-blind controllers fail to prevent dross, motivating an architecture that can reason about part geometry and dynamically apply appropriate process constraints.

Method: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed with three core components: (1) a standards-aligned ontology that links process objectives and constraints to observable controller signals; (2) a description-logic reasoner that classifies upcoming geometric features and selects active constraints (e.g., lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, monotone guard, energy-density cap); and (3) a constraint-aware predictive controller solving a small quadratic program per scan. The unmeasurable depth-to-width ratio is modeled via a Gaussian process with calibrated uncertainty. Validation uses an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to NIST AM-Bench benchmark data for IN625.

Result: The architecture eliminated dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, maintained zero dross with minimal residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degraded gracefully under deliberate plant-model mismatch, and supported retargeting to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than modifying code.

Conclusion: The results establish architectural feasibility of the neuro-symbolic approach. The principal next step is experimental calibration of the depth-to-width ratio.

Abstract: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which a standards-aligned ontology operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe, and a description-logic reasoner converts them into the references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross, a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality yet cannot be measured during the build, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width, with the ratio and its calibrated uncertainty supplied by a Gaussian process. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints-adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, a monotone guard beyond the calibrated range, and an energy-density cap where a process window is declared while running only on changes of geometric context and otherwise leaving a single small quadratic program on the per-scan path. In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture eliminates the dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code. The results establish architectural feasibility, experimental calibration of the ratio is the principal next step.

</details>


### [282] [GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05783)
*Paweł Batorski,Przemysław Spurek,Paul Swoboda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GROM is a one-shot, closed-form machine unlearning method for LLMs that uses ridge-regularized least-squares optimization to directly update weight matrices, achieving state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs in seconds without iterative fine-tuning, and resisting quantization-based recovery attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing iterative fine-tuning approaches for LLM unlearning (even with LoRA) are computationally expensive, lack analytical formulations, and often merely hide rather than remove targeted knowledge—as evidenced by quantization attacks that restore supposedly forgotten content. A fast, exact, and robust analytical solution is needed.

Method: GROM frames unlearning as a ridge-regularized least-squares problem, deriving a closed-form additive weight update. The method uses only gradient-free forward passes (no backpropagation, no iterative convergence), computing an exact edit to selected weight matrices that suppresses unwanted content while preserving behavior on retained data via a regularization term.

Result: GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News, and WMDP benchmarks. It operates orders of magnitude faster than fine-tuning (seconds vs. hours) and withstands low-bit quantization attacks that recover content from gradient-based baselines.

Conclusion: A direct analytical one-shot approach to machine unlearning is both feasible and superior to iterative gradient-based methods, offering speed, exactness, and robustness against recovery attacks while maintaining model utility. The closed-form nature eliminates convergence uncertainty and computational overhead.

Abstract: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

</details>


### [283] [Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05797)
*Stefan Krsteski,Charlotte Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks, showing that AUC masks poor estimates, token-level entropy is a useful predictive signal, and residual analysis between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws like contamination and infeasibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating task difficulty without costly rollouts is critical for calibrating evaluation benchmarks and constructing progressive training curricula, especially as agents move into long-horizon domains where empirical trial-and-error becomes computationally prohibitive. Prior work is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments with narrow features and inaccurate metrics.

Method: The authors study ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 diverse agentic benchmarks (coding, mathematics, ML, web navigation, function calling, etc.). They evaluate AUC as a metric for difficulty estimation, identify token-level entropy as a predictive signal, and analyze residuals between predicted and observed difficulty to detect environment flaws.

Result: AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, making it an unreliable standalone metric. Token-level entropy emerges as a useful predictive signal for difficulty. Residual analysis between expected and observed difficulty successfully exposes hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

Conclusion: Reliable ex ante difficulty prediction across diverse agentic benchmarks is feasible with better metrics and signals. The proposed residual analysis offers a practical diagnostic tool for benchmark designers to identify flaws without exhaustive rollouts.

Abstract: Task difficulty dictates an agent's likelihood of success, and estimating it without rollouts means forecasting this directly from a task description before executing costly simulations in stateful environments. Reliable estimates would therefore allow environment designers to calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula. This becomes increasingly important as agents move into long-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error is a severe computational bottleneck. Prior work on early prediction is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments, often relying on narrow features and inaccurate evaluation metrics. We study \textit{ex ante} difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We show that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and show how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

</details>


### [284] [Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05819)
*Alfred M. Pastor,Maribel Castillo,Jose M. Badia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A learning-to-rank framework using gradient-boosted models (listwise and pairwise) selects efficient tensor-network contraction plans for quantum circuit simulation on GPUs, outperforming random and MinFill baselines, with rankings showing substantial but imperfect stability across GPU architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits via tensor-network contraction is essential but costly. Contraction plans with similar theoretical complexity can exhibit vastly different GPU performance due to parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. Selecting efficient plans before execution remains an open challenge.

Method: Each contraction plan is represented by structural features extracted from its sequence of pairwise contractions. Gradient-boosted rankers are trained using listwise and pairwise objectives on GPU-measured performance data. The framework is evaluated on diverse circuit families with in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and cross-GPU transfer is assessed by evaluating source-trained models on a second GPU architecture without retraining.

Result: Learned rankers consistently identify better contraction plans than random and MinFill baselines, with the listwise model achieving the strongest overall decision quality. Rankings remain substantially stable across two GPU architectures, and models retain useful decision quality under backend shift, though performance is partly backend-dependent.

Conclusion: Learning to Rank is a practical approach for reducing contraction-plan search cost in tensor-network-based quantum circuit simulation, while acknowledging that plan performance remains partially backend-dependent.

Abstract: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining. The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.

</details>


### [285] [Evidential Rule Learning for Interpretable Classification with Abstention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05859)
*Javier Fumanal-Idocin,Javier Andreu-Perez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FERL introduces an interpretable fuzzy rule learning method that natively produces evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) in a single deterministic pass, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, set prediction quality, and out-of-distribution detection across tabular and vision benchmarks without post-hoc calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interpretable classifiers for real-world deployment must not only predict accurately but also provide transparent evidence for decisions and reliably abstain when uncertain. Existing evidential or calibrated models typically rely on post-hoc techniques, auxiliary heads, held-out sets, or repeated inference, which undermines both interpretability and efficiency. FERL addresses this gap by unifying interpretable rule learning with native evidential reasoning.

Method: FERL learns fuzzy rule models where each rule's antecedent is a conjunction of fuzzy membership functions over input features. The key innovation is that belief and plausibility functions emerge directly from fuzzy memberships in a single forward pass — no auxiliary calibration head, held-out data, or Monte Carlo sampling is needed. The authors also provide a theoretical Lipschitz stability analysis, proving that evidential outputs vary smoothly with input perturbations.

Result: On a 30-dataset tabular benchmark, FERL achieves +2.6% average accuracy over the second-best rule learner (statistically significant). For set-valued predictions, FERL attains utility-discounted accuracy u65/u80 of 0.80/0.83 vs. 0.79/0.80 for the naive credal classifier, with higher set coverage (0.92 vs. ≤0.82). On tabular near-OOD detection, FERL matches dedicated detectors (77.7 vs. 77.4 AUROC). In concept-bottleneck evaluation on CUB and AwA2, it is within 2.3 AUROC points of the strongest detector, achieves best AwA2 AUPR-Out (68.3) and novel-class rejection (57.2), and can name which attributes are anomalous.

Conclusion: FERL demonstrates that native evidential reasoning can be embedded directly into interpretable fuzzy rule learners without sacrificing accuracy or calibration quality. Its combination of competitive predictive performance, built-in abstention, smooth evidential outputs, and the ability to identify anomalous attributes makes it a compelling choice for transparent, trustworthy deployment in safety-critical settings.

Abstract: Interpretable classification often requires more than accurate predictions for real-life deployment: models should be transparent about the evidence behind their decisions and abstain when they cannot decide reliably. We introduce Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL), a method that learns interpretable, accurate fuzzy rule models whose outputs are evidential. Unlike post-hoc calibration, FERL's belief, plausibility, and abstention capabilities arise directly from the fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, with no auxiliary head, held-out set, or repeated inference. Our theoretical analysis further shows that FERL is Lipschitz stable, which means that its evidential outputs vary smoothly with the input. Against state-of-the-art rule learners, FERL is statistically significantly more accurate across a 30 tabular-dataset benchmark ($+2.6\%$ average accuracy over the second best). Its native set predictions attain the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers ($u_{65}/u_{80}=0.80/0.83$ vs.\ $0.79/0.80$ for the naive credal classifier), at higher set coverage ($0.92$ vs.\ $\le0.82$). FERL also matches dedicated out-of-distribution detectors on tabular near-OOD detection ($77.7$ vs.\ $77.4$ AUROC for the strongest baseline). Under detector-class-disjoint concept-bottleneck evaluation, its it is within $2.3$ AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector on both CUB and AwA2, while attaining the best AwA2 AUPR-Out ($68.3$) and novel-class rejection ($57.2$), while being able to name which attributes are anomalous.

</details>


### [286] [Beyond Feature Importance: A Comparative Analysis of Pattern Detection Methods in Cluster Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05880)
