*Benjamin Connor,Anna Jurek-Loughrey,Lu Bai,Muhammad Fahim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comparative evaluation of three post-hoc analysis methods (Random Forest surrogate, LIME, PCA) for detecting structured patterns in clustering results using synthetic datasets with injected patterns. None of the methods consistently recovered all pattern types, revealing a gap between existing explainability tools and pattern-level cluster interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current explainability techniques focus on feature importance or local instance-level explanations, but fail to identify structured patterns within clusters. This gap is especially critical in domains like healthcare, where understanding the semantic structure of clusters is essential for actionable insights.

Method: The authors constructed a suite of synthetic datasets with systematically injected, predefined patterns. They then applied three widely used post-hoc analysis techniques — a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis (PCA) — to evaluate each method's ability to recover the known injected patterns from clustering results.

Result: All three methods successfully recovered relevant features, but none consistently detected all injected pattern types. Each technique exhibited specific strengths and blind spots depending on the nature of the underlying pattern.

Conclusion: A critical gap exists between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation. This motivates the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies tailored to uncovering structured patterns in clustering outcomes.

Abstract: Interpreting clustering outcomes remains a fundamental challenge in data analysis, particularly in domains such as healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. While numerous explainability techniques exist, they are primarily designed to assess feature importance or provide local instance-level explanations rather than to identify structured patterns present within clusters. This work presents a comparative evaluation of commonly used post-hoc analysis methods for pattern detection in clustering results. To enable controlled evaluation, we introduce a suite of synthetic datasets in which predefined patterns are systematically injected. Three widely used techniques are evaluated: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis. Results demonstrate that although each method can successfully recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. These findings high- light a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, motivating the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies.

</details>


### [287] [Alternating Levenberg-Marquardt Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-Enhanced Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05892)
*Yulun Wu,Matthieu Barreau,Miguel Aguiar,Karl H. Johansson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FALM-PINN introduces a bi-level optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting, using Fourier-enhanced bases and Levenberg-Marquardt optimization to overcome spectral bias and representation-coefficient coupling in PINNs, achieving orders-of-magnitude improvement on high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard PINNs struggle with high-frequency/multi-scale solutions and strongly nonlinear PDEs due to two key issues: (1) spectral bias, where neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency features, and (2) representation-coefficient coupling, where the simultaneous learning of basis representations and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization creates severe optimization difficulty.

Method: FALM-PINN formulates a bi-level alternating optimization. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis to enrich the latent space with high-frequency components. The lower-level problem fixes this basis and fits projection coefficients by solving a nonlinear least-squares problem via the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. For linear PDEs, the framework reduces to a single-step convex optimization. Global convergence of the alternating scheme is proved for both linear and nonlinear cases.

Result: Numerical experiments on challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that FALM-PINN achieves relative L² errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: Decoupling representation learning from coefficient fitting, combined with Fourier enhancement and Levenberg-Marquardt optimization, effectively addresses the core failure modes of standard PINNs. The framework is general, provably convergent, and delivers significant accuracy gains on difficult PDE benchmarks.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often fail to accurately resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency or multi-scale solutions, as well as strongly nonlinear problems. Two factors underlie this difficulty: spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to underfit high-frequency features; and representation-coefficient coupling, the entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization objective. In this work, we propose the Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg--Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN), an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, while the lower-level problem resolves the coupling by fitting the projection coefficients on this basis, solving a nonlinear least-squares problem with the Levenberg--Marquardt algorithm. The framework applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems, and reduces to a single-step convex optimization problem for linear PDEs. We prove global convergence of the alternating training scheme in both cases. Numerical examples on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show that FALM-PINN achieves relative $L^2$ errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [288] [CohortHijack: Robustness of Single Cell Annotation to Companion Cell Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05900)
*Arash Vashagh,Yasmin Vashagh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CohortHijack demonstrates that refinement-based single-cell annotation tools can be manipulated by selectively removing non-target cells from the query cohort, altering a target cell's refined label without modifying the target cell itself — exposing query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many single-cell annotation tools apply neighborhood or cluster-level refinement to improve initial cell labels. This paper investigates whether such refinement mechanisms introduce a security vulnerability — specifically, whether an adversary can alter a target cell's final annotation by manipulating only the companion cells in the query cohort, leaving the target cell's expression profile and base prediction unchanged.

Method: The authors introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit framework. Given a fixed classifier, a target cell, and a query cohort, CohortHijack removes selected non-target cells and re-runs refinement. They evaluate random removal, structured removal (based on distance or prediction confidence), and search strategies (greedy, multi-start, beam search). Experiments use logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers on PBMC3K and Paul15 datasets, plus CellTypist majority voting for additional validation.

Result: Structured removal consistently outperformed random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search flipped 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing few cohort cells, with mean collateral changes under 0.4%. Ablations showed the effect vanished when neighborhood refinement was disabled. For CellTypist majority voting, independent predictions remained stable, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals.

Conclusion: Query cohort composition constitutes a genuine, target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation pipelines that employ refinement. The findings highlight a previously unrecognized robustness vulnerability and call for greater scrutiny of post-hoc refinement steps in computational biology tools.

Abstract: Many single-cell annotation tools refine an initial cell label using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. We study whether this refinement can be manipulated without changing the target cell. We introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. We evaluate random and structured removal methods, together with greedy, multi-start, and beam search, on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Structured removal was consistently stronger than random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. We also evaluated CellTypist majority voting, where independent predictions remained unchanged across all evaluations, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals. These findings identify query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation.

</details>


### [289] [BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05928)
*Yuhao Wang,Zelin Zang,Yuxuan Liu,Zhen Lei,Stan Z. Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BioM-JEPA is a self-supervised learning method for single-cell transcriptomics that predicts aggregated representations of gene blocks (defined by protein associations and coexpression) rather than individual genes. A student-teacher JEPA architecture produces embeddings with higher effective rank and lower perturbation error than controls, while linear attention enables significant throughput gains over scFoundation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most self-supervised models for single-cell transcriptomics reconstruct individual genes, which are sparse observations of coordinated biological programs. The authors argue that predicting at the level of gene blocks—groups of functionally related genes—better captures the coordinated nature of biological programmes and mitigates issues like embedding dependency on detected-gene depth.

Method: BioM-JEPA employs a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with a student-teacher design. Gene blocks are constructed from protein-association data and corpus-derived coexpression evidence, connecting genes into graph-structured blocks. The student network predicts target-block aggregate representations from a masked subset of genes (the context), while a slowly updated (momentum) teacher network provides target representations from the full gene set. Linear attention is used to avoid the quadratic complexity of gene-by-gene attention matrices.

Result: Block-level prediction embeddings showed higher effective rank and weaker correlation with detected-gene depth compared to token-prediction, random-block, and reconstruction baselines. On CellBench, frozen embeddings retained expression, pathway, and neighborhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error. Qualitative diagnostics aligned with known pancreatic programmes and compositional perturbation relationships. In a matched hPancreas experiment (batch size 8, one epoch), BioM-JEPA delivered 5.75× higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76× higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation.

Conclusion: Graph-connected gene blocks serve as effective prediction targets for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology, offering improved representation quality and computational efficiency compared to gene-level reconstruction and quadratic-attention alternatives.

Abstract: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes. Here we present BioM-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that instead predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network infers each target-block representation from the remaining genes in a cell, while a slowly updated teacher supplies the corresponding target from the full observed gene set. Under the reported extraction procedure, block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth in the tested diagnostics than token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls. Across CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among the evaluated models. Representation diagnostics were also consistent with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional relationships between genetic perturbations. Linear attention avoids constructing a quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrix; in a matched one-epoch hPancreas experiment at batch size 8, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75-fold higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76-fold higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation. Together, these results support graph-connected gene blocks as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology.

</details>


### [290] [How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05980)
*Sid Ali Hamideche,Louis Adrien Dufrene,Quentin Lampin,Guillaume Larue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tests whether simple linear mappings can translate between heterogeneous text embedding models. Finds partial success for compatible pairs but overall concludes that embedding spaces are not universally relatable by simple transformations, challenging claims of latent universality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether independently trained text embedding models share a common latent structure that can be bridged by simple transformations, enabling AI-to-AI communication without text decoding.

Method: Evaluated nine embedding models varying in architecture, pooling, and training objective. Assessed compatibility using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), downstream transfer performance, embedding fidelity, and retrieval. Tested lightweight translators (linear mappings) for cross-model representation translation.

Result: Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure for some model pairs. However, success is inconsistent — compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Many pairs fail sharply, showing no universal linear relationship.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings, contradicting claims of latent universality prevalent in some literature. Compatibility is conditional on specific model characteristics rather than being a general property.

Abstract: We investigate whether simple transformations can translate representations across heterogeneous text embedding models. Understanding how independently trained models organize semantic information is an enabler for AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text. Focusing on lightweight translators such as linear mappings, we test the literature hypothesis of latent universality in a realistic text setting beyond simplified benchmarks. Across nine embedding models differing in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective, we evaluate compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval. Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Overall, the results show that heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in some literature.

</details>


### [291] [THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05982)
*Pui Chung Siu,Claudia Cabrera,Mani Mudaliar,Arkaitz Zubiaga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG) that captures time-stamped evidence for target-disease links. Using graph propagation, it predicts Phase II to III trial success better than direct-evidence methods, especially for pairs lacking direct evidence, and provides explainable predictions via path-based decomposition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 40-50% of Phase II efficacy failures stem from inadequate target-disease linkage. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows assembling the evidence profile for a target-disease pair as of a past date — i.e., what was known when a clinical programme was initiated. This prevents realistic retrospective validation of target hypotheses.

Method: The authors construct the THBKG with 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, each edge timestamped with the year its evidence changed. They define a decision-aligned benchmark: for each target-disease pair entering Phase II, predict Phase III advancement using only evidence datable before that decision point. Graph propagation (graph neural network encoders) is applied to the time-constrained subgraph. A path-based explainer adapted to the decision-time subgraph decomposes predictions into the underlying evidence landscape.

Result: Graph propagation over THBKG outperforms all direct-evidence baselines under the same decision-aligned protocol, achieving 4.3–4.5 relative success rate in the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. Gains are concentrated on the 72.8% of pairs with no direct target-disease evidence at decision time, where encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance by propagating over intervening biology.

Conclusion: The THBKG enables temporally honest, decision-aligned evaluation of target-disease hypotheses. Propagating over the graph recovers predictive signal even without direct evidence, and path-based explanations make predictions interpretable. The graph is released as a continuously updated resource for retrospective validation in drug discovery.

Abstract: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

</details>


### [292] [Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Reinforcement Learning for Visual Continuous Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05989)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OG-SPR combines multi-step latent self-prediction with next-observation prediction via lightweight adapters, preventing over-constraining of shared representations and achieving state-of-the-art performance on 28 DeepMind Control Suite tasks, especially on challenging dog and humanoid domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual RL methods rely on either latent self-prediction or observation prediction, but neither alone suffices under limited training data. Observation prediction grounds representations in observation dynamics but lacks long-horizon temporal regularization; self-prediction alone can over-constrain shared representations.

Method: OG-SPR is a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that jointly optimizes multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. Crucially, it introduces two lightweight adapter modules for latent self-prediction, decoupling the self-predictive objective from the shared representation to avoid over-constraining it while still benefiting from temporal predictive signals.

Result: Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite demonstrate that OG-SPR outperforms state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL baselines, with particularly significant gains on challenging dog and humanoid domains.

Conclusion: Jointly learning observation-grounded and temporally self-predictive representations via adapter-based decoupling is an effective strategy for sample-efficient visual RL, outperforming methods that rely on either objective in isolation.

Abstract: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Recent dynamics-based representation learning methods have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-free visual RL by learning dynamics-aware representations through auxiliary prediction performed either in latent space (self-prediction) or observation space (observation prediction). However, state-of-the-art methods from both categories still struggle on challenging visual control tasks when training data is limited. We posit that relying on either predictive objective alone may be insufficient. In contrast, observation prediction grounds learned representations in observation-level dynamics, but does not directly regularize the temporal predictability of latent representations over extended horizons. In this paper, we propose Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR), a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation-level dynamics. OG-SPR incorporates two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. We empirically show that directly imposing latent self-prediction on the shared representation may over-constrain it and does not necessarily improve performance. To address this issue, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite show that OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

</details>


### [293] [A Unified Risk View of Uncertainty: Posterior Risk for Disentanglement and Evaluation Beyond Proxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05995)
*Frieder Wizgall,Georg Tirpitz,Moritz Seiler,Kerstin Ritter,Bálint Mucsányi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, then builds a theory-backed benchmark using semi-synthetic data with known generative processes to directly compute oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, enabling fine-grained evaluation without proxy tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing uncertainty quantification literature suffers from (1) inconsistent definitions of epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty across works, (2) lack of ground-truth uncertainty for evaluation, and (3) reliance on proxy tasks like OOD detection that provide limited insight into uncertainty estimate quality and structure.

Method: The authors (1) define uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk—the expected loss under the posterior over plausible ground-truth functions—which unifies Bayesian uncertainty with estimator-dependent deviations (capturing misspecification and optimization error); (2) construct semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes, enabling direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty; (3) use this benchmark for fine-grained comparison of uncertainty quantification methods.

Result: Accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals practically meaningful differences between methods, with some showing better alignment to oracle uncertainty targets, while also exposing sensitivity to dataset characteristics and modeling choices.

Conclusion: A unified risk-based definition of uncertainty, coupled with semi-synthetic oracle benchmarks, provides a principled framework for evaluating uncertainty quantification methods. This approach moves beyond proxy evaluations and reveals that strong predictive performance alone is insufficient for trustworthy uncertainty decomposition.

Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are critical in safety-sensitive applications, where understanding the sources of predictive uncertainty is essential. This often requires disentangling epistemic uncertainty from aleatoric uncertainty, yet these uncertainty types are not defined consistently across the literature, making it difficult to assess whether a method produces accurate uncertainty estimates. Evaluation is further complicated by the fact that ground-truth epistemic uncertainty is typically unavailable. Existing benchmarks therefore mostly rely on proxy tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not provide complete ground-truth uncertainty targets and offer limited insight into the structure and quality of uncertainty estimates. We propose a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, the expected loss of a predictor under the distribution of plausible ground-truth functions given the data. This view combines Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-dependent deviations from the posterior mean, capturing effects such as misspecification and optimization error. This formulation constitutes the foundation of a theory-backed benchmark that enables direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes. By avoiding proxy evaluations, the benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of uncertainty estimates. Empirically, we find that accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals practically useful differences between methods, identifying approaches with meaningful alignment to oracle uncertainty targets while exposing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

</details>


### [294] [Do Tabular Foundation Models Agree with Themselves?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06004)
*Christian Klötergens,Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi,Lars Schmidt-Thieme,Tom Hanika*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies two fundamental consistency requirements—marginalization consistency and factorization consistency—that any multivariate predictive model should satisfy, and demonstrates that existing Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) violate both across all tested datasets and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TFMs are state-of-the-art for tabular prediction but their autoregressive conversion from univariate to multivariate predictors has not been examined for faithfulness. Since the ground-truth posterior is unknown on real-world data, the authors reframe the evaluation question: could a model's predictions derive from any valid joint distribution? This shifts evaluation from fidelity to internal logical consistency.

Method: The authors propose two formal consistency requirements: (1) marginalization consistency—marginalized conditionals must match directly predicted marginals; (2) factorization consistency—different autoregressive factorization orders must yield the same joint distribution. TFMs are tested against these criteria on both classification and regression tasks across multiple datasets.

Result: Every TFM evaluated violates both marginalization consistency and factorization consistency, for both classification and regression, across all datasets tested.

Conclusion: Current TFMs produce predictions that cannot correspond to any coherent joint probability distribution, undermining their reliability as multivariate predictors and highlighting a critical gap between their univariate strengths and multivariate application.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are currently the best approach to tabular prediction problems. They are constructed as transformers that approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution based on a pre-training prior. These univariate predictors can be converted into multivariate ones autoregressively by sampling one target and adding it to the features.
  However, the faithfulness of the resulting joint has not been investigated. Furthermore, TFMs cannot be evaluated against the posterior itself, at least not on real-world datasets, because the ground-truth distribution is unknown. We therefore propose asking a different question: could a model's predictions result from any joint distribution? To answer this question, we pose two requirements that any such model must satisfy. The first is marginalization consistency, which demands that marginalized conditionals are equal to directly predicted marginals. The second is factorization consistency, which demands that different factorization orders result in equal joint distributions. Every TFM that we evaluate violates both of these requirements for both classification and regression across all datasets.

</details>


### [295] [ProDVI: Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06015)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProDVI uses LLM-generated Python programs encoding coarse environment dynamics to pretrain value network representations, improving sample efficiency of model-free RL without needing pre-collected datasets, simulators, or meta-learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL agents are sample-inefficient partly due to random initialization. Existing solutions (pre-collected data, simulators, meta-learning) may be unavailable. The paper aims to leverage LLM-encoded commonsense/domain knowledge as an accessible alternative for informative initialization.

Method: ProDVI prompts a code-generating LLM to produce executable Python functions encoding coarse dynamics hypotheses. These generate synthetic transitions used to construct an auxiliary dynamics prediction objective, pretraining the state-action encoder of an actor-critic value network. The pretrained representation provides dynamics-aware inductive biases. Programs need not faithfully simulate the target environment; online RL with real transitions and rewards corrects inaccuracies.

Result: Experiments on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite demonstrate that ProDVI effectively improves sample efficiency of model-free RL algorithms.

Conclusion: Leveraging LLM-generated programmatic dynamics priors for representation pretraining is a viable and effective approach to improving RL sample efficiency, without requiring traditional prerequisites like datasets or simulators.

Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) is notoriously sample inefficient. One contributing factor is that RL agents are typically initialized from scratch, forcing them to acquire task-relevant knowledge through online interaction. Existing approaches obtain informative initializations through pre-collected datasets, high-fidelity simulators, or meta-learning over related tasks, but these prerequisites may be difficult to access or even unavailable. In this paper, we propose Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization (ProDVI), a framework that leverages the commonsense and domain knowledge encoded in large language models to initialize RL agents without relying on these resources. Specifically, ProDVI prompts a code-generating language model to produce executable Python functions that encode coarse hypotheses about environment dynamics. These functions are then used to generate synthetic transitions. Based on these transitions, we construct an auxiliary dynamics prediction objective to pretrain the state-action encoder of the value network in an actor-critic framework. The learned representation provides dynamics-aware inductive biases before online RL begins. Importantly, the generated programs are used only for representation pretraining and are not required to faithfully simulate the target environment. While the generated programs may be inaccurate, their induced initialization can be corrected through online learning from real transitions and rewards. Experiments on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite tasks show that ProDVI can effectively improve the sample efficiency of model-free RL algorithms.

</details>


### [296] [BioKD: Selective Physiology-to-Video Knowledge Distillation via Reliability Gate for Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06023)
*Bojing Hou,Ruohao Li,Yitong Zhu,Hongjun Liu,Luwen Yu,Yuyang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BioKD is a reliability-aware knowledge distillation framework that uses physiological signals as privileged training information to teach a video-based emotion recognition model, achieving strong performance without requiring physiological sensors at inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video-based emotion recognition suffers from ambiguous or masked behavioral cues, while physiological signals—though more informative—are intrusive and poorly deployable. There is a need for a method that leverages physiological supervision during training but relies only on video at inference, while also addressing the noise and instability inherent in physiological signals.

Method: BioKD employs a teacher-student knowledge distillation paradigm where physiological signals serve as privileged information to guide video-based learning. Key innovations include: (1) a sample-wise reliability-aware gating mechanism that adaptively modulates knowledge transfer strength, and (2) a progressive distillation strategy. Together, these suppress negative transfer from unreliable physiological supervision caused by inter-subject variability, signal artifacts, and temporal inconsistency.

Result: On DEAP and AMIGOS datasets, BioKD consistently outperforms representative baselines under both trial-wise and subject-wise evaluation for valence and arousal recognition. It achieves 68.01% on DEAP (trial-wise arousal) and 65.29% under the more challenging subject-wise setting. Ablation studies confirm BioKD mitigates overconfident teacher errors and surpasses entropy-only weighting, validating the explicit modeling of supervision reliability. The method adds no inference-time overhead.

Conclusion: BioKD successfully bridges the gap between informative but intrusive physiological sensing and deployable video-based emotion recognition through reliability-aware cross-modal distillation. Explicitly modeling supervision reliability is critical for stable knowledge transfer, and the framework eliminates the need for physiological sensors or multimodal synchronization at deployment.

Abstract: To address the limitations of video-based emotion recognition under ambiguous or socially masked behavioral cues, as well as the poor deployability of physiological signals, this paper proposes a reliability-aware physiology-to-video knowledge distillation framework, termed BioKD. The proposed framework leverages physiological signals as privileged information during training to guide a video-based student model in learning deep affective representations, while relying solely on non-intrusive video inputs at inference time. To cope with the high noise and instability of physiological teacher supervision caused by inter-subject variability, signal artifacts, and temporal inconsistency, BioKD incorporates a sample-wise reliability-aware gating mechanism together with a progressive distillation strategy. By adaptively regulating the strength of knowledge transfer, the framework suppresses negative transfer induced by unreliable physiological supervision and enables more stable cross-modal distillation. Experiments on DEAP and AMIGOS show that BioKD consistently outperforms representative baselines under both trial-wise and subject-wise evaluation protocols for valence and arousal recognition. For example, BioKD achieves 68.01\% on DEAP (trial-wise arousal) and 65.29\% under the more challenging subject-wise setting, demonstrating improved performance under a subject-independent evaluation setting. Further analyses show that BioKD effectively mitigates overconfident teacher errors and outperforms an entropy-only weighting strategy, confirming the importance of explicitly modeling supervision reliability. In addition, BioKD introduces no additional inference-time overhead relative to the same video student architecture and removes the need for physiological sensing and multimodal synchronization.

</details>


### [297] [Dynamic Graph Prompting via Topology-Routed Mixed-Curvature Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06031)
*Quanxin Wang,Xuanting Xie,Bingheng Li,Xingtong Yu,Shuo Wang,Ruiyi Fang,Zhao Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CurvPrompt introduces a topology-routed geometry prompting framework for dynamic graphs that maintains a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts with learnable prompts, dynamically routed by local topology to overcome geometry under-adaptation in few-shot learning scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dynamic graph prompting methods operate in a single fixed embedding space, but the authors reveal that temporal shifts in local clustering and degree heterogeneity reorganize the edge curvature spectrum, meaning the optimal representation geometry evolves dynamically with local topology. This creates a mismatch they term "geometry under-adaptation."

Method: CurvPrompt maintains a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each paired with a learnable prompt. A topology-aware gate dynamically routes each node-time instance to a sparse subset of experts, constructing personalized mixed-curvature representations. It uses soft routing during pre-training to build a continuous topology-geometry mapping, then transitions to hard Top-K routing with uniform weights during downstream adaptation for parameter efficiency and stability under label scarcity.

Result: Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that CurvPrompt significantly advances few-shot link prediction and delivers strong, consistent performance on node classification tasks.

Conclusion: The results validate the necessity of geometry-adaptive prompting for dynamic graphs, showing that dynamically adapting representation geometry to local topology is essential for effective few-shot learning on temporal graph data.

Abstract: Dynamic graph prompting freezes a pre-trained temporal backbone and adapts it to label-scarce downstream tasks using lightweight prompts. However, existing methods operate within a single, fixed embedding space. In this work, we reveal that temporal shifts in local clustering and degree heterogeneity actively reorganize the edge curvature spectrum---indicating that the optimal representation geometry dynamically evolves with local topology over time. We formalize this unaddressed mismatch as geometry under-adaptation. To overcome this limitation, we propose CurvPrompt, a topology-routed geometry prompting framework for dynamic graphs. Instead of relying on a single space, CurvPrompt maintains a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each paired with a learnable prompt. A topology-aware gate dynamically routes each node--time instance to a sparse subset of experts, constructing a personalized mixed-curvature representation. To ensure parameter efficiency and training stability under extreme label scarcity, CurvPrompt employs soft routing during pre-training to build a continuous topology--geometry mapping, and transitions to hard Top-K routing with uniform weights during downstream adaptation. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets show that CurvPrompt significantly advances few-shot link prediction while delivering strong, consistent performance on node classification tasks, validating the necessity of geometry-adaptive prompting.

</details>


### [298] [Kastor: An efficient fine-tuning strategy for generative emulation of PDE simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06107)
*Guillaume Couairon,Alexis Jacq,Yu-Han Wu,Renu Singh,Yana Hasson,Quentin Berthet,Romuald Elie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Kastor adapts a deterministic physics foundation model into a generative surrogate for PDE simulations, using a two-stage inference scheme (causal autoregressive + non-causal temporal super-resolution), Mean Prediction Regularization (MPR) to stabilize generative training, and spatial gradient matching for physical fidelity, achieving 42.9% average error reduction over the Walrus baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard autoregressive ML emulators for PDE solving suffer from error accumulation over long time horizons and struggle to capture the inherent stochasticity of complex physical systems. There is a need for efficient, accurate generative surrogates that mitigate these issues.

Method: Kastor proposes three key components: (1) a two-stage inference scheme coupling a large-stride causal autoregressive model with a non-causal temporal super-resolution network to reduce error accumulation cheaply; (2) Mean Prediction Regularization (MPR), a training objective that forces the generative model to predict the deterministic distribution mean under null noise conditioning, applicable to both Functional Generative Networks (FGN) and diffusion-based emulators; (3) spatial gradient matching to improve spectral/physical fidelity as measured by power spectrum density.

Result: On The Well benchmark, Kastor achieves a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting error compared to the Walrus finetuning methodology and outperforms Walrus on 8 of 10 datasets under variance-normalized RMSE (VRMSE), with superior spectral consistency and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed methodology—combining two-stage inference, MPR regularization, and spatial gradient matching—enables deterministic physics foundation models to be effectively adapted into generative surrogates that are both more accurate and more stable than existing approaches, with strong empirical validation across diverse simulation datasets.

Abstract: Machine learning offers a promising avenue to accelerate physical simulations by replacing computationally expensive traditional Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solvers with fast, differentiable surrogate models. However, standard auto-regressive ML emulators often suffer from error accumulation over long horizons and struggle to capture the stochasticity of complex physical systems. In this paper, we propose Kastor, a comprehensive methodology to adapt a deterministic physics foundation model into a highly efficient and accurate generative surrogate. First, we introduce a two-stage inference scheme that combines a large-stride causal auto-regressive model with a non-causal temporal super-resolution network, significantly reducing error accumulation while minimizing computational cost. Second, we present Mean prediction regularization (MPR), a novel training objective that constrains the generative model to predict the deterministic distribution mean under null noise conditioning. This regularization dramatically improves the performance and stability of both Functional Generative Networks (FGN) and diffusion-based emulators. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating spatial gradient matching improves the accuracy and physical fidelity of the simulations as measured by power spectrum density. Extensive evaluations on diverse simulation datasets of the benchmark The Well show that with these components, our model outperforms competing methods in forecasting accuracy, spectral consistency, and computational efficiency. Our model achieves a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting compared to our reference based on the Walrus finetuning methodology, and outperforms Walrus for 8 out of 10 datasets on variance-normalized RMSE (VRMSE).

</details>


### [299] [Is Self-Pretraining really useful to improve diagnosis in medical Time Series?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06122)
*Omar Coser,Antonio Orvieto,Paolo Soda,Loredana Zollo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-PreTraining (SPT) with masking objectives consistently improves transformer performance on medical time series by 0–6 percentage points, with gains increasing for deeper models, even with univariate inputs and limited data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivated by SPT's success on long-context benchmarks in NLP, the authors investigate whether similar pre-training benefits extend to medical time series—spanning multimodal, multivariate, and univariate settings—where labeled data is often scarce.

Method: Transformer models are trained from scratch vs. SPT using four masking-based objectives for temporal/cross-modal representation learning. Evaluated across three medical tasks (rehabilitation robotics, stress detection, Parkinson's gait), with systematic variation of model depth to assess capacity–pre-training interactions.

Result: SPT consistently improves classification accuracy by 0–6 pp across all datasets and configurations. Gains persist in univariate settings and increase with deeper architectures that better exploit enriched temporal representations from pre-training.

Conclusion: SPT is a simple, general, architecture-agnostic strategy that enhances transformer robustness and accuracy on medical time-series tasks, especially in data-limited clinical scenarios.

Abstract: Inspired by recent evidence that transformer architectures benefit from Self-PreTraining (SPT) on long-context benchmarks, we investigate whether similar gains extend to multimodal, multivariate, and even simple univariate medical time series. Our objective is to assess the impact of SPT on the performance and scalability of transformer-based models across diverse medical applications, particularly under limited data conditions. We evaluate transformer architectures on three representative medical time-series tasks: rehabilitation robotics (Camargo dataset), stress detection (Non-EEG Stress), and Parkinson's disease detection (Gait Parkinson's Disease). Models are trained either from scratch or through SPT using four masking-based objectives designed to promote temporal and cross-modal representation learning, and we systematically vary model depth to examine how capacity interacts with pre-training benefits. Across datasets and configurations, SPT consistently improves classification accuracy by 0-6 percentage points depending on masking strategy, dataset and architecture, with gains observed not only in multivariate settings but also when models are restricted to simple univariate inputs. The improvements increase for deeper models that can better exploit the enriched temporal representations learned during pre-training. These findings indicate that SPT is a simple and general strategy that enhances transformer performance on medical time-series tasks without requiring task-specific architectural changes, supporting its potential to improve robustness and accuracy in data-limited clinical settings.

</details>


### [300] [LLM Inference Under Bursty Workload Distribution: Modifying the WAIT Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06135)
*Anjali Gangadhar Katageria,Shobha Rani,Raghu Nandan Sengupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a lightweight extension to the WAIT scheduling algorithm for LLM serving that adapts to time-varying, bursty request arrivals by performing online estimation of arrival intensity from observed interarrival times. Simulation-based evaluation using MMPP workloads shows higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM under low arrival-rate shifts, with comparable latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM serving scheduling algorithms (e.g., Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, vLLM) typically assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates, which fails to capture the bursty, dynamic nature of real-world traffic patterns. This mismatch motivates the need for a scheduling approach that adapts to time-varying arrival rates without requiring prior knowledge of traffic characteristics.

Method: The authors propose a lightweight extension to the state-of-the-art WAIT algorithm that performs online estimation of request intensity based on observed interarrival times. The method adapts dynamically to time-varying arrival rates without prior traffic knowledge. Evaluation uses Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types in a simulation environment.

Result: The proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM in low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.

Conclusion: Online arrival intensity estimation enables LLM serving schedulers to better handle bursty, non-stationary traffic, yielding throughput gains over existing systems without sacrificing latency, particularly under low-rate shift conditions.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude are widely used for information retrieval and problem-solving. Recent work has focused on improving scheduling algorithms to boost throughput while maintaining low latency. However, these approaches often assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates - an assumption that fails to reflect the inherently bursty and dynamic nature of real-world traffic. We propose a lightweight extension to the state-of-the-art WAIT algorithm [1], which adapts to time-varying arrival rates without prior traffic knowledge. The proposed algorithm performs online estimation of request intensity based on observed interarrival times. Using Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types, we conduct a simulation-based evaluation demonstrating that the proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve [2], ORCA [3], and vLLM [4] in the evaluated low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.

</details>


### [301] [SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06137)
*Yi He,Zhengkang Guan,Anpeng Wu,Peng Cui,Fei Wu,Kun Kuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SkillTFM is a training-free adaptation system for tabular foundation models that uses a verifiable, extensible skill bank with gated evolution—coupling boundary evidence identification with skill retrieval and validation—to address distribution shifts and heterogeneous features without fine-tuning, achieving significant AUC gains in both simulated and real-world settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer reusable prediction across diverse datasets but face practical deployment challenges due to distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns. Existing solutions require costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data, limiting their practicality. SkillTFM addresses this gap by enabling TFM adaptation without any parameter updates.

Method: SkillTFM introduces a training-free adaptation framework centered on a verifiable and extensible skill bank. It operates via two mechanisms: (1) boundary evidence identification, which characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns; and (2) gated skill evolution, which retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation. Adaptation is thus shifted from parameter updates to the gated evolution of agentic skills.

Result: Across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142 overall and raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898. Experiments across multiple TFM backbones further confirm its effectiveness and generality.

Conclusion: SkillTFM demonstrates that training-free, skill-based adaptation is a viable and effective alternative to fine-tuning for tabular foundation models, offering robust performance under distribution shifts and across diverse backbones without requiring parameter updates or additional labeled data.

Abstract: Tabular data are ubiquitous in real-world applications and are crucial for data-driven prediction and decision-making across science, industry, finance, healthcare, and public services. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose tabular learning, offering reusable predictors across diverse datasets and substantially reducing the need for task-specific training, tuning, and model development. However, their practical deployment remains constrained by distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns that are difficult to capture without costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data.
  To this end, we propose SkillTFM, a training-free system that shifts TFM adaptation from parameter updates to the gated evolution of agentic skills. The core of SkillTFM is a verifiable and extensible skill bank that couples boundary evidence identification with gated skill evolution: the former characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns, whereas the latter retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation. Across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128--0.142, raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898. Furthermore, experiments across TFM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of SkillTFM.

</details>


### [302] [Threshold-Based Early Stopping of Accumulations in Neural Networks with Binary Activation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06177)
*Quentin Luquet de Saint-Germain,Massil Ait Abdeslam,Jean Pierre David*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Binary neural networks waste computation by fully accumulating sums whose final sign is already predictable. This paper proposes a post-training early-stopping mechanism that halts accumulation once the sign becomes predictable, reducing operations by up to 86.6% in deep convolutions with minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In binary neural networks (BNNs) with binary activations, dot products reduce to sign-controlled additions/subtractions. However, every output channel still accumulates all inputs even though only the sign matters. The running partial sum often drifts far enough from zero that its final sign is predictable long before all terms are accumulated, making subsequent computations wasteful.

Method: The authors propose a post-training early-stopping mechanism that requires no retraining. They characterize the statistical behavior of running accumulations on the training dataset to model when the final sign becomes predictable. Under an idealized weight ordering, accumulation halts as soon as the partial sum's sign is confidently determined, reducing the number of operations. The method is evaluated on VGG11 with CIFAR-10.

Result: On the deepest convolution layer of VGG11 (CIFAR-10), the method removes 86.6% of accumulation terms with only a 0.37-point accuracy drop. When applied simultaneously to the three deepest convolutions, 25% of full-network arithmetic is eliminated at the cost of a 1.36-point accuracy drop.

Conclusion: The proposed early-stopping mechanism effectively exploits the predictability of running accumulation signs in BNNs to significantly reduce computation with negligible accuracy degradation, all without retraining any model parameters.

Abstract: Binary neural networks are very attractive for constrained deployment, enabling small footprint and low-power inference. For binary activations, the dot products become sign-controlled additions or subtractions, but the number of operations is unchanged. Indeed, every neuron or output channel still accumulates all of its input, even though only the sign will be retained, which is often wasteful. As the accumulation progresses, the running partial sum frequently drifts so far from zero that its final sign becomes highly predictable long before the last term is reached; every contribution evaluated after that point changes the value of the sum but not the final output activation. This paper turns this observation into a post-training early-stopping mechanism. We characterize the behavior of the running accumulations on the training dataset and use this information to predict the final sign as soon as possible. No model parameter is retrained. We count the number of operations under an idealized ordering of weights. On VGG11 applied to the CIFAR-10 dataset, the method removes $86.6\%$ of the accumulation terms of the deepest convolution for a $0.37$-point accuracy drop, and $25\%$ of the full-network arithmetic when used on the three deepest convolutions simultaneously, for a $1.36$-point drop.

</details>


### [303] [SAGA: Score-Weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment for Low-Resource Nordic Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06179)
*Hoda Fakharzadehjahromy,Emil Wiman,Andreas Bueff,Hafsteinn Einarsson,Fredrik Heintz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGA introduces a parser-guided preference optimization framework that replaces costly human annotations with dependency-parser supervision to improve grammatical quality in morphologically rich, low-resource languages. Across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål, SAGA yields substantial grammatical improvements without any human preference labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference optimization methods like DPO improve LLMs but depend on expensive human annotations. Extending these methods to morphologically rich, low-resource languages is challenging because such annotations are scarce. The authors aim to replace human labels with automatic, parser-derived supervision.

Method: SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment) uses a dependency parser to generate preference pairs for delta-DPO training. It combines parser quality scores with lexical diversity into a composite reward, filters low-information pairs via a reward-gap criterion, and monitors reward hacking to prevent the model from exploiting the parser rather than truly improving grammar.

Result: Danish parse success rate rises from 69.0% to 93.8%. Icelandic sees a +4.5 pp improvement on an independent Stanza evaluation (mean +3.3 pp over three runs), with native speakers preferring SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons. Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 pp.

Conclusion: Parser-derived supervision is a practical and effective alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers are available.

Abstract: Preference optimisation has proven effective for improving large language models but typically relies on costly human preference annotations. Extending these methods to morphologically rich, low-resource languages remains challenging because such annotations are scarce. We present SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment), a parser-guided preference optimisation framework that replaces human labels with dependency-parser supervision. SAGA converts parser judgements into preference pairs for delta-DPO, combines parser quality with lexical diversity in a composite reward, filters low-information pairs using a reward-gap criterion, and monitors reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision. Across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål using GPT-SW3-1.3B, SAGA consistently improves grammatical quality without requiring human preference labels. Danish parse success increases from 69.0% to 93.8%, Icelandic achieves a +4.5 percentage-point improvement on an independent Stanza evaluation (three-run mean +3.3 percentage points) while native speakers prefer SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons, and Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 percentage points. These results demonstrate that parser-derived supervision is a practical alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers are available.

</details>


### [304] [Continual Learning in Transition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06216)
*Zhiyan Hou,Dan Zhang,Tao Feng,Liyuan Wang,Wei Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Hongyan An,Junfeng Fang,Haokai Ma,Zhaohui Xu,Haiyun Guo,Jinqiao Wang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a tri-axial framework (When, How, Where) to characterize the evolution of continual learning from traditional parameter-centric model adaptation toward system-level adaptation, encompassing on-policy learning, test-time training, and external harness components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional continual learning research has been narrowly focused on parameter-centric mechanisms (training strategies, architectural designs, weight adaptation), but emerging paradigms—on-policy learning, test-time training, and external components like memory and skill libraries—are expanding CL beyond this limited view. There is a need to systematically characterize this broader transition toward system-level adaptation.

Method: The authors develop a tri-axial framework organized around three dimensions: (1) How—off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient optimization mechanics; (2) When—pre-training, post-training, and inference-time stages; (3) Where—updates within internal parameters versus external structural constraints. Using this framework, they systematically survey representative continual learning methods and trace the ongoing paradigm transition.

Result: The survey reveals a clear trajectory from parameter-centric CL toward system-level adaptation, with learning increasingly distributed across the training-inference boundary and across internal/external components. The framework successfully organizes diverse CL methods and highlights underexplored regions in the design space.

Conclusion: Continual learning is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift from static parameter adaptation to dynamic, system-level evolution. The proposed When-How-Where framework provides a unified lens to understand this transition and identifies key challenges and future directions for the field.

Abstract: Classical continual learning (CL) has primarily focused on enabling models to update and retain knowledge through parameter-centric mechanisms, e.g., training strategies, architectural designs, and weight adaptation. However, emerging paradigms are reshaping the scope of CL beyond this traditional model adaptation view. For instance, on-policy learning broadens the space of update mechanisms; test-time training extends CL from the training phase to inference; and external harness components such as memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols extend the evolutionary boundaries of model capabilities far beyond the static parameter space. Collectively, these developments indicate a transition from parameter-centric learning toward system-level adaptation. To characterize this transition, we examine the evolution of continual learning through three dimensions: When, How, and Where learning occurs. The How dimension encompasses off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient optimization mechanics. The When dimension captures evolution across pre-training, post-training, and inference-time stages. The Where dimension delineates updates occurring within internal parameters versus external structural constraints. Anchored by this tri-axial framework, we systematically survey representative methods, trace the ongoing transition of continual learning, and discuss the key challenges, broader implications, and future directions arising from this paradigm shift.

</details>


### [305] [Timestep-Conditioned Transformers for Global Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06241)
*Sam Levang,Fran Bartolic,Ty Dickinson,Chase Dwelle,Paulius Rauba,Viktor Cikojevic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GEM-3 is a probabilistic global weather model using multi-timestep inference, allowing a single model to flexibly operate at different timesteps at inference time to balance short-range and medium-range forecast quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed autoregressive timesteps in ML weather models create a fundamental trade-off: short timesteps (1–6h) resolve diurnal dynamics well but accumulate errors faster over long horizons, while long timesteps (24h) reduce error accumulation but sacrifice short-range sub-daily predictability. No single fixed timestep is optimal across all forecast horizons.

Method: GEM-3 introduces explicit multi-timestep inference, where a single set of trained weights can be configured at inference time to use different timesteps. Mixed-timestep training is employed, which improves rollout stability over timestep-specialist models. The architecture is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer (~134M parameters) on an equirectangular grid with architectural improvements over GEM-2.

Result: Mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability. The model achieves near state-of-the-art medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training and inference, and produces decision-relevant diagnostics.

Conclusion: Multi-timestep inference with mixed-timestep training resolves the timestep trade-off, yielding a practical, flexible, and efficient probabilistic forecasting system competitive with specialized models across multiple forecast horizons.

Abstract: Existing machine-learning weather forecasting models rely on predetermined and fixed autoregressive timesteps. The choice of model timestep involves a fundamental trade-off: shorter timesteps (e.g. 1 to 6 hours) finely resolve atmospheric dynamics within the diurnal cycle but increase error accumulation for a given forecast horizon, while longer timesteps (e.g. 24 hours) reduce error accumulation but limit the usability of short-range forecasts where sub-daily predictability is high. In this work, we present GEM-3, a probabilistic global weather model that addresses this trade-off through explicit multi-timestep inference. With a single set of trained weights, the model timestep can be configured at inference time to balance predictability and usability across a broad forecast horizon. Additionally, we find that mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability relative to timestep-specialist models. Under the hood, GEM-3 is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer with ~134M parameters on an equirectangular grid with a number of architectural advancements beyond its predecessor GEM-2. The result is a practical forecasting system that couples near-SOTA medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training and inference, and decision-relevant diagnostics.

</details>


### [306] [A Six-Dimensional Taxonomy of Post-Training Adaptation Techniques with Applications in AI Governance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06246)
*Fardin Afdideh,Fernando Seoane,Farhad Abtahi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This survey synthesizes the fragmented literature on post-training adaptation (fine-tuning, alignment, unlearning, etc.) by introducing a six-dimensional taxonomy organized by mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, and model type. It clarifies commonly conflated terms, maps technique relationships, and identifies open challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The post-training adaptation literature is fragmented across disjoint technique families, model classes, and deployment contexts, making cross-method comparison and clear description of model modifications difficult. A unifying framework is needed.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature survey and propose a six-dimensional taxonomy: (1) mechanism, (2) goal, (3) data requirement, (4) persistence, (5) structural scope, and (6) model type. They use this taxonomy to disambiguate terms, trace the evolution of adaptation strategies across ML paradigms (traditional ML → deep learning → foundation models → LLMs → multimodal LLMs), and map inter-technique relationships (inheritance, supersession, hybridization, layered stacks).

Result: The taxonomy distinguishes commonly conflated terms (e.g., fine-tuning vs. retrieval augmentation vs. prompting) and reveals how adaptation strategies have evolved. It provides a structured vocabulary useful for technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis. Key open challenges are identified in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware workflows.

Conclusion: A unified six-dimensional taxonomy can organize the sprawling post-training adaptation literature, clarify terminology, and support both technical and governance use cases. Significant open problems remain, particularly around evaluation standards, reproducibility, and governance-aware adaptation pipelines.

Abstract: Post-training adaptation has become central to modern machine learning practice and includes techniques such as retraining, fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, alignment, retrieval augmentation, model editing, unlearning, calibration, and Multimodal Instruction Tuning. However, the literature remains fragmented across technique families, model classes, and deployment contexts, making it difficult to compare methods or describe how a trained model has been modified. This survey synthesizes the post-training adaptation literature and introduces a six-dimensional taxonomy organized by mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, and model type. The taxonomy distinguishes commonly conflated terms such as fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, and prompting, and shows how adaptation strategies evolve from traditional machine learning through deep learning, foundation models, large language models, and multimodal large language models. It also maps relationships among techniques, including inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks. The resulting vocabulary can support technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis. The survey concludes by identifying open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows.

</details>


### [307] [MetaboLLM: a metabolomics-specialized large language model for biochemical knowledge integration and predictive metabolite graph construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06253)
*Dohyun Ku,Min Gu Kwak,Francisco J. Pasquel,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MetaboLLM is a metabolomics-specialized LLM that, together with a graph isomorphism network (MetaboLLM-GIN), converts biochemical descriptions into predictive metabolite graphs, outperforming baselines on knowledge tasks and achieving high AUCs for stress hyperglycemia prediction (0.8616) and hormone-regimen classification (0.8123).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metabolomics knowledge is siloed across heterogeneous databases and formats, making it difficult to translate into unified, predictive representations useful for downstream clinical and biological tasks.

Method: The authors developed MetaboLLM by continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval on metabolomics corpora. They then paired it with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts LLM-generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs that are processed by a graph isomorphism network for patient-level prediction.

Result: MetaboLLM outperformed both base and medically adapted LLMs across four backbone families on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and generalized to an external benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUCs — 0.8616 for stress hyperglycemia prediction post-CABG and 0.8123 for postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification — surpassing conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM setups. Interpretation yielded biologically meaningful findings.

Conclusion: Domain-specialized language models can effectively organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations, advancing both metabolomics informatics and clinical prediction.

Abstract: Metabolomics knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous resources and remains difficult to translate into predictive representations. We developed MetaboLLM, a metabolomics-specialized large language model adapted through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval, together with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using a graph isomorphism network. Across four backbone families, MetaboLLM outperformed corresponding base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction after coronary artery bypass grafting (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs generated from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM configurations. Model interpretation further produced biologically meaningful findings in both applications. These results show that domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations.

</details>


### [308] [RxnCLF: Contrastive Transformation-Aware Reaction Foundation Model for Improved Reactivity Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06259)
*Yiting Zheng,Cheng Fang,Anthony Donofrio,Haote Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RxnCLF is a self-supervised contrastive learning framework that uses a novel condensed reaction graph (CRG) representation to learn chemically meaningful reaction embeddings. Pretrained on 1.7M reactions, it outperforms existing methods on multiple yield prediction benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reaction yield prediction is hindered by scarce labeled data, a combinatorially large reaction space, and sparse population of that space. Existing string-, fingerprint-, and graph-based encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, especially for reactions with complex substrates. A representation that unifies reactants and products into a single, transformation-aware encoding is needed.

Method: The authors propose RxnCLF, a self-supervised contrastive learning framework. Its key innovation is the Condensed Reaction Graph (CRG), which merges reactant and product information into a single unified graph, explicitly encoding atom-mapping and bond changes rather than treating reactants and products as disconnected graphs. The model is pretrained on 1.7 million reactions from the Pistachio dataset using contrastive learning to learn a continuous latent space. It is then fine-tuned on downstream yield prediction tasks.

Result: RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph-based and sequence-based baselines on multiple yield prediction benchmarks: Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, proprietary HTE C-N coupling, and amide formation datasets. It achieves improved R² scores and the best overall performance across these datasets.

Conclusion: The CRG-based RxnCLF shows strong promise as a scalable reaction foundation model. Its chemically interpretable, transformation-aware latent space has potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream tasks such as regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

Abstract: Reaction yield prediction remains challenging because labeled data are scarce and reaction space is both combinatorially large and sparsely populated, limiting the generalization of existing reaction representations. String-, fingerprint-, and graph-based reaction encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, making accurate prediction difficult for reactions with complex substrates. We propose reaction contrastive learning foundation (RxnCLF), a self-supervised contrastive framework for reaction representation learning. RxnCLF is built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that unifies reactant and product information into a single graph, enabling the model to learn explicit and enriched transformation structure rather than disconnected graphs. Pretrained on 1.7 million Pistachio reactions, RxnCLF learns a compact and continuous latent space that captures both reaction-center features and broader side chain contexts, making it transformation-aware and chemically interpretable. Fine-tuned on multiple yield prediction benchmarks, including Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary HTE C-N coupling and amide formation datasets, RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines, improving R2 and achieving the best performance overall.
