Our results highlight the promise of CRG-based RxnCLF as a scalable reaction foundation model, with the potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream reaction informatics tasks, including regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

</details>


### [309] [Hypothesis Testing with Conditional Queries: Learnability and the Value of Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06262)
*Zonghuan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the adaptivity gap in model evaluation under a conditional-query model. It establishes that learnability requires positive separation in conditional probabilities, characterizes the optimal error when separation is zero, and proves that the adaptivity gap is Θ(N²) — interaction yields a quadratic but not exponential reduction in query complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model evaluation strategies differ: some fix all test queries in advance (non-adaptive), while others select later tests based on earlier responses (adaptive). The paper investigates the fundamental trade-off between these approaches, asking when adaptive evaluation provides a genuine advantage and quantifying that advantage precisely.

Method: The authors use a conditional-query model over a finite outcome space of size N. They analyze pairwise conditional probability separation between distribution classes as the key condition for distinguishability. They construct a randomized non-adaptive simulation procedure that approximates any adaptive policy using O(N²(T + log(1/ρ))) pre-fixed pair queries, achieving total variation distance ρ. A matching lower bound family with constant adaptive complexity and Ω(N²) non-adaptive complexity is also constructed, establishing tightness.

Result: Three main results: (1) Two distribution classes are reliably distinguishable iff they have positive separation in pairwise conditional probabilities; zero separation yields optimal worst-case error exactly 1/2 at any finite budget. (2) Any T-query adaptive policy can be simulated non-adaptively with O(N²(T + log(1/ρ))) pre-fixed pair queries. (3) The worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap is Θ(N²), meaning interaction provides a quadratic but not exponential advantage.

Conclusion: Interaction in model evaluation reduces the required number of tests by at most a quadratic factor relative to non-adaptive evaluation. Despite the seemingly exponential branching structure of adaptive procedures, the query advantage is bounded polynomially in the outcome space size, ruling out exponential separations between adaptive and non-adaptive evaluation strategies.

Abstract: Model evaluations may fix all tests before observing any responses or select later tests using earlier responses. We study this choice in a conditional-query model on a finite outcome space $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|=N$. We first ask which pairs of distribution classes can be reliably distinguished. We then ask how many additional queries are required to match an adaptive tester when all queried events must be fixed in advance. We show that learnability holds if and only if the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities. When this separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error is exactly $1/2$ at every finite query budget. For any $T$-query adaptive policy and any $ρ\in (0,1)$, we construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using $O(N^2(T + \log(1/ρ)))$ pair queries chosen before any response is observed. Its simulated transcript is within $ρ$ in total variation of the adaptive transcript, uniformly over all distributions in the model. We also construct a matching family with constant adaptive query complexity and $Ω_\varepsilon(N^2)$ non-adaptive query complexity. Consequently, the worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap is $Θ_\varepsilon(N^2)$. Thus interaction can reduce the required number of tests by a quadratic factor, but the apparent exponential branching of an interactive evaluation does not yield an exponential query advantage.

</details>


### [310] [The Tamed Subgradient Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm beyond Convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06283)
*Iosif Lytras,Nikolaos Makras,Sotirios Sabanis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces SG-TULA, a subgradient-based tamed Langevin algorithm for sampling from non-smooth, non-convex distributions with superlinear gradient growth. It provides explicit non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, improves upon existing subgradient Langevin rates, and demonstrates competitive LLM pretraining performance against AdamW and Muon.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Langevin-based sampling methods either require smooth potentials or struggle with superlinear gradient growth. Subgradient methods exist but have suboptimal convergence rates. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing a provably convergent, explicit scheme that handles non-smoothness, non-convexity, and superlinear growth simultaneously, with practical applicability to large-scale problems like LLM pretraining.

Method: The authors propose the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), which discretises the Langevin diffusion using subgradients directly (bypassing smoothing) and incorporates a taming mechanism to control superlinear gradient growth. They derive non-asymptotic W2 convergence bounds with explicit dimension and temperature dependence, and provide excess risk bounds for the associated optimisation problem. Assumptions are verified for a regularised LLM pretraining potential, and a boosted coordinate-wise variant is tested empirically.

Result: SG-TULA achieves improved non-asymptotic convergence rates over existing subgradient-based Langevin algorithms, with all constants explicitly tracked in terms of dimension and inverse temperature. The boosted coordinate-wise variant pretrains a GPT-2 lineage model competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon — optimisers for which comparable non-asymptotic guarantees do not currently exist.

Conclusion: SG-TULA provides a theoretically grounded, practical sampling algorithm for non-smooth, non-convex potentials with superlinear growth. It bridges the gap between theory and practice by offering explicit convergence guarantees while demonstrating competitive performance in LLM pretraining, a regime where popular optimisers like AdamW and Muon lack comparable theoretical backing.

Abstract: We study the problem of sampling from target distributions whose potentials are simultaneously non-smooth, subject to superlinear gradient growth, and non-convex. We introduce the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discretisation of the Langevin diffusion that operates directly on subgradients, without relying on computationally demanding smoothing procedures. To handle the superlinear regime, taming techniques are employed to produce a stable, explicit scheme. We derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, with all constants tracked explicitly in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving upon the currently known rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms. We further provide excess risk estimates for the associated optimisation problem. We verify the assumptions, with explicit constants, for the regularized pretraining potential of a LLM in the GPT-2 lineage and the boosted coordinate-wise variant of SG-TULA pretrains the former competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees are presently available.

</details>


### [311] [Surv-IPTB: An Attention-Based Model for Estimating Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit with Survival Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06288)
*Lev V. Utkin,Stanislav K. Kogan,Andrei V. Konstantinov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Surv-IPTB is an attention-based framework that reframes individual treatment benefit estimation in survival analysis as a binary classification problem, using pairwise patient comparisons and interval-valued probabilities to handle censoring, demonstrating superior performance over meta-learner baselines in nonlinear settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for estimating individual treatment effects in survival analysis struggle with complex nonlinear relationships between covariates and outcomes, and often handle right-censoring in ad hoc ways. There is a need for a principled, scalable framework that directly estimates the probability that a given patient benefits from treatment in terms of extended survival time.

Method: Surv-IPTB reformulates IPTB estimation as binary classification via pairwise comparisons between treatment and control patients. Right-censored observations are handled through imprecise probability representations (interval-valued probabilities). An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations performs data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons and learns soft class probabilities for censored cases.

Result: On synthetic datasets with spiral, bell-shaped, and circular nonlinear feature spaces, Surv-IPTB consistently outperforms T-learner and S-learner meta-learners using random survival forests, Cox models, and Beran estimators. Performance remains robust across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths, with the largest gains in nonlinear scenarios where baselines degrade significantly.

Conclusion: The attention-based Surv-IPTB framework provides a scalable and statistically principled approach to personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings, effectively handling both nonlinear covariate-outcome relationships and censored observations.

Abstract: This work presents a novel attention-based framework for estimating the Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit (IPTB) in survival analysis contexts. The proposed model, called Surv-IPTB, directly quantifies the probability that a specific patient will experience extended survival time under treatment versus control. We reformulate IPTB estimation as a binary classification problem, leveraging pairwise patient comparisons across treatment and control cohorts. The framework incorporates a principled handling of right-censored observations through imprecise probability representations, where uncertain treatment effects are characterized by interval-valued probabilities. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations enables flexible, data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons, while simultaneously learning soft class probabilities for censored cases. Through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with complex nonlinear structures, including spiral, bell-shaped, and circular feature spaces, we demonstrate that our approach maintains robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths. The model consistently outperforms meta-learner baselines (T-learner and S-learner) equipped with random survival forests, Cox proportional hazards, and Beran estimators, particularly in challenging nonlinear scenarios where conventional methods exhibit significant degradation. The results establish the proposed attention-based framework as a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings. The code implementing the model is publicly available.

</details>


### [312] [BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291)
*Johann Birnick,Rayan Saab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BaKron is an efficient solver for two-sided adaptive rounding in neural network quantization that leverages Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations, reducing computational complexity from O(m²n²) to O(mn(m+n)) while matching GPTQ's cubic scaling and exploiting richer curvature information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPTQ-style adaptive rounding uses only one-sided (input activation) information, missing correlations across output coordinates. Two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations (used by BoA and YAQA) capture this richer curvature, but applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally prohibitive (O(m²n²) work). The need is for an efficient solver that retains the benefits of two-sided information without the computational burden.

Method: BaKron combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction. It operates on m×n weight matrices, using O(m+n) sequential steps and reducing total work to O(mn(m+n)). The method is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator, and includes an efficient technique for computing the required Hessians.

Result: BaKron achieves cubic scaling comparable to GPTQ (O(mn(m+n)) vs. GPTQ's per-row cubic cost) while using richer two-sided curvature information. Practical benchmarks and experimental evaluations demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness across a range of Hessian choices.

Conclusion: BaKron provides a computationally efficient and modular framework for two-sided adaptive rounding in neural network quantization, enabling the practical use of richer Hessian geometry without the prohibitive cost of naive GPTQ application in the vectorized domain.

Abstract: We accelerate a family of algorithms for neural network quantization whose geometry is informed by any Kronecker-factored approximation of the Hessian. GPTQ-style adaptive rounding typically uses one-sided information derived from input activations. Two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations can additionally capture correlations across output coordinates, but applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally expensive. Building on the two-sided adaptive-rounding formulation used by BoA and YAQA, we introduce BaKron, an efficient solver that combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction. For an $m\times n$ weight matrix, BaKron uses $O(m+n)$ sequential steps while reducing the total work from $O(m^2n^2)$ to $O(mn(m+n))$. Thus, it matches the cubic scaling of GPTQ while exploiting richer curvature information. Moreover, BaKron is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator. We also provide practical benchmarks, consider a range of Hessians that BaKron can be called with, find an efficient technique to compute these Hessians, and evaluate the algorithm experimentally.

</details>


### [313] [On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296)
*Yijiang Li,Bingyang Wang,Yijun Liang,Yunjie Tian,Di Fu,Nuno Vasconcelos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: U-OPSD achieves genuine self-distillation for LLMs without external supervision, using only a model's own generations and internal consistency. It constructs pseudo-solutions via majority voting, then distills from the shortest correct solution into the longest incorrect one to enable targeted self-correction, matching or surpassing supervised methods like OPSD and GRPO across math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy (self-)distillation methods (OPD/OPSD) still depend on external supervision such as ground-truth labels, environmental feedback, or larger teacher models, failing to achieve genuine "self"-distillation. The authors aim to eliminate this reliance on external signals and enable a model to improve purely from its own generations.

Method: U-OPSD (Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation) operates in three steps: (1) Sample multiple rollouts from the model and construct a pseudo-solution via majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. (2) Condition a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution (the most confident correct answer). (3) Distill this teacher distribution into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, enabling precise self-correction at points where the model is confidently wrong. No external ground truth or larger model is used.

Result: On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23: U-OPSD improves over base models by 8.5% (4B) and 10.7% (8B) on Qwen3 non-thinking mode, outperforming OPSD by 3.2% and 2.3% on average. In thinking mode, U-OPSD outperforms OPSD by 0.9% at 4B and matches it at 8B, while surpassing GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1%, respectively.

Conclusion: Genuine self-distillation without external supervision is feasible and effective. U-OPSD demonstrates that leveraging internal consistency via majority voting and targeted distillation from correct to incorrect rollouts enables LLMs to self-improve, consistently matching or exceeding supervised counterparts across diverse math reasoning benchmarks and model scales.

Abstract: On-policy (Self-)Distillation (OPD / OPSD) has shown strong potential for post-training large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods still rely heavily on external supervision, including ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or guidance from larger models, and therefore fall short of genuine "self"-distillation. In this study, we show that on-policy self-distillation can be achieved using only a model's own generations via internal consistency. We propose Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation (U-OPSD). U-OPSD first samples multiple rollouts and constructs a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. It then conditions a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution and distills it into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, allowing the model to correct itself precisely where it is confidently wrong. Across diverse benchmarks, base models, and training settings, U-OPSD consistently improves over the base models and matches or surpasses supervised methods with ground truth (GT), such as OPSD and GRPO. On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23, U-OPSD improves over the base model by 8.5% and 10.7% on Qwen3 non-thinking mode at the 4B and 8B scales, respectively, and outperforms OPSD by an average of 3.2% and 2.3%. In thinking mode, U-OPSD remains on par with OPSD, outperforming it by 0.9% at 4B and matching it at 8B, while surpassing GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1%, respectively.

</details>


### [314] [RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310)
*Chenglong Wang,Ziming Zhu,Yifu Huo,Bei Li,Qiaozhi He,Yan Ding,Xiaoyang Hao,Yuxin Gao,Tianhua Zhou,Xiaojia Chang,Tongran Liu,Jingbo Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Generative reward models underperform in RL due to a mismatch between their comparative outputs and RL's scalar reward paradigm. The authors propose Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC), which derives scalar rewards from relative preference rankings via self-competitive and anchor-guided ranking strategies, achieving consistent RL improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative reward models (GRMs) excel at response ranking but fail to deliver proportional gains in reinforcement learning (RL) settings. The root cause is a fundamental mismatch: GRMs are inherently comparative (ranking-based), while RL algorithms expect scalar reward signals. Existing workarounds don't fully exploit GRMs' ranking capabilities.

Method: The authors propose Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) with two strategies: (1) Self-competitive ranking — compares multiple sampled responses from the current policy against each other to derive relative rewards; (2) Anchor-guided ranking — uses a small, fixed set of reference responses as anchors to enable scalable, consistent reward construction without requiring large-scale on-the-fly sampling.

Result: RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches.

Conclusion: Converting generative reward models' comparative ranking signals into scalar rewards via RRC effectively bridges the gap between GRMs and RL, unlocking the potential of generative reward models for policy optimization.

Abstract: Recent advances in reward modeling show a paradigm shift from discriminative reward models to generative reward models. However, despite their strong capabilities in response ranking, generative reward models have not realized their potential in reinforcement learning (RL). Our analysis reveals that this limitation arises from a mismatch between the comparative nature of generative reward modeling and the scalar scoring paradigm adopted by existing RL algorithms. To bridge this gap, we propose a Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) approach, which enables generative reward models to provide more effective RL learning signals by deriving rewards from relative preference rankings. RRC introduces two complementary strategies: self-competitive ranking, which exploits comparisons among sampled responses, and anchor-guided ranking, which enables scalable ranking-based reward construction with a small set of reference responses. Experiments across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches. Our code can be found at https://github.com/wangclnlp/RRC.

</details>


### [315] [CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06352)
*Fanzhe Meng,Guoxin Chen,Jiale Zhao,Shuang Sun,Zhiyu Lin,Wayne Xin Zhao,Ruihua Song,Ji-Rong Wen,Kai Jia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CalibForge is an autonomous system for synthesizing terminal tasks using adversarial solver calibration. It employs multi-solver and contrastive calibration strategies to create tasks in a solver-relative "learnable zone." The resulting 5,431 calibrated tasks yield significant performance gains on Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Pro, and Doc2Repo, demonstrating that solver-relative learnability is an effective target for agent training data construction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing terminal-task synthesis relies on executable validation to establish feasibility, but this does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting — i.e., whether it is appropriately challenging for learning. The authors argue that tasks should occupy a "learnable zone" where they are neither trivially solvable nor impossibly hard for a given solver, and that this requires understanding solver-relative behavior rather than mere executability.

Method: CalibForge uses two adversarial solver calibration strategies: (1) Multi-solver calibration, which targets disagreement among a heterogeneous pool of solvers to identify tasks that are neither universally easy nor universally hard; and (2) Contrastive solver calibration, which targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation between a stronger and weaker solver. Both strategies operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. The system autonomously revises candidate tasks based on verified solver behavior, producing 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks.

Result: Models trained on the full CalibForge collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the base model reach +24.71 pp on Terminal-Bench 2.0, +27.68 pp on SWE-bench Pro, and +30.04 pp on Doc2Repo. Ablations show both calibration strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring with validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback.

Conclusion: Solver-relative learnability is a practical and effective target for constructing agent training data. CalibForge's calibration strategies produce tasks that are both executable and appropriately challenging, leading to strong and transferable improvements across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Training terminal agents requires executable and verifiable tasks that are not merely solvable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Executable validation establishes feasibility, yet does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting. In this paper, we present CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks through adversarial solver calibration. Multi-solver calibration targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, whereas contrastive solver calibration targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation; both operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Using CalibForge, we construct 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Our ablations show that both strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring and validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the corresponding base model reach 24.71 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 points on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 points on Doc2Repo. Together, these results support solver-relative learnability as a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data.

</details>


### [316] [An Optimal Agnostic PAC Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06363)
*Markus Engelund Mathiasen,Jian Qian,Nikita Zhivotovskiy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A learner is constructed for binary classification with VC classes that achieves statistically optimal agnostic PAC risk bounds, matching known lower bounds up to universal constants, thereby settling the sample complexity question.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning for VC classes has long been studied, with existing upper bounds containing gaps relative to known lower bounds (e.g., from Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi). The paper aims to close this gap by constructing a learner that achieves the statistically optimal risk bound, matching the lower bounds exactly up to universal constants at every fixed optimal risk level L*.

Method: The authors construct a learner for a VC class H of finite VC dimension d ≥ 1 over X with labels in {-1, +1}. From an i.i.d. sample of size n, the learner outputs a hypothesis ĥ whose binary risk L(ĥ) satisfies the bound with high probability (1-δ). The bound takes the form L(ĥ) ≤ L* + C·[√(L*(d+log(1/δ))/n) + (d+log(1/δ))/n], with C = 7·10⁸, achieving the optimal dependence on L*, d, n, and δ.

Result: The constructed learner achieves risk bound L(ĥ) ≤ L* + 7·10⁸[√(L*(d+log(1/δ))/n) + (d+log(1/δ))/n] with probability ≥ 1-δ, for any 0 < δ ≤ 1/2. This matches the lower bounds from Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi (1996) up to universal constants, thereby settling the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning for every fixed L*.

Conclusion: The paper definitively settles the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning for VC classes by providing a learner whose risk bound matches the known lower bounds up to universal constants. The result holds at every fixed optimal risk L*, closing a longstanding gap in statistical learning theory.

Abstract: Let $H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^X$ be a class of finite VC dimension $d\ge1$. Writing $L$ for the binary risk and $L^*=\min_{h\in H}L(h)$, we construct a learner achieving the statistically optimal risk bound: from an i.i.d.\ sample of size $n$, for every $0<δ\le 1/2$, with probability at least $1-δ$, \[
  L(\widehat h)
  \le L^*+ 7\cdot10^8\left(
  \sqrt{\frac{L^*(d+\log(1/δ))}{n}}
  +\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}
  \right). \] This settles the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning up to universal constants at every fixed $L^*$, matching the lower bounds of Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi [A Probabilistic Theory of Pattern Recognition, Springer, 1996].

</details>


<div id='cs.MA'></div>

# cs.MA [[Back]](#toc)

### [317] [F$^2$Agent: Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence for Multimodal Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05668)
*Changshuo Liu,Yanzheng Jin,Shangfeng Cai,Peng Fang,Xiaokui Xiao,Beng Chin Ooi*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: F²Agent is a multimodal LLM-based agent for financial trading that uses specialized agents, adaptive cross-modal fusion, and noise-robust regularization to outperform 16 baselines, achieving over 20% relative improvement in annualized returns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based trading agents struggle with (1) limited multimodal modeling that fails to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies, (2) ineffective fusion mechanisms for integrating heterogeneous data sources, and (3) inadequate robustness against market noise. As information sources grow increasingly diverse, a more sophisticated approach to multimodal financial analysis is needed.

Method: F²Agent employs three key components: (1) a hierarchy of specialized agents that independently extract modality-specific signals from diverse data sources; (2) a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism that dynamically captures fine-grained inter-modality dependencies; and (3) noise-robust consistency regularization to generate trading signals resilient to market noise.

Result: Experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets show F²Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics, with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. Specific returns include 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA.

Conclusion: F²Agent demonstrates strong efficacy and robustness across varying market dynamics, validating that hierarchical specialized agents combined with adaptive multimodal fusion and noise-robust regularization form an effective paradigm for financial trading.

Abstract: With increasingly diverse and heterogeneous information sources, effectively leveraging multimodal data is becoming pivotal for high-quality financial trading. Although recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have enabled the ingestion of multimodal inputs, existing methods fail to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies and remain vulnerable to market noise, due to limited multimodal modeling, ineffective fusion mechanisms, and inadequate robustness. To address these challenges, we propose F$^2$Agent, a novel multimodal agentic paradigm driven by the Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence. F$^2$Agent first deploys a hierarchy of specialized agents to comprehensively extract modality-specific signals. It further introduces a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism coupled with noise-robust consistency regularization to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies and generate noise-resilient trading signals. Extensive experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets demonstrate that F$^2$Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics, with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. Notably, F$^2$Agent delivers returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA, demonstrating its efficacy and robustness in varying market dynamics.

</details>


### [318] [A Two-Tier Perspective on Inference-Time Parallelism in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05791)
*Zihan Xu,Haolin Tian,Hai Jiang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: TIPEX is a framework that unifies two levels of parallel execution in LLM-driven multi-agent systems — Replica Parallelism (exploring multiple solution paths) and Structural Parallelism (concurrent execution within a path via task decomposition) — enabling systematic coordination, analysis, and configuration of parallel strategies to improve accuracy and reduce latency at the cost of token usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven multi-agent systems involve multiple model invocations and complex coordination, making inference-time execution strategies critical for accuracy, latency, and cost. While parallelism can improve efficiency, the roles and interrelationships of different parallelism forms (task-level replication vs. intra-path decomposition) lack systematic study regarding unified organization and coordination.

Method: The authors propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that models parallelism at two levels — Replica Parallelism (task-level exploration of multiple complete solution paths) and Structural Parallelism (concurrent execution within a single path via task decomposition) — unified under a common execution semantics. The framework supports systematic combinations and parameterized configurations of different parallel strategies.

Result: Experiments on the GAIA benchmark show that inference-time parallelism significantly improves accuracy and reduces end-to-end latency, though at the cost of increased token consumption. Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with intermediate-difficulty tasks benefiting most from their coordination. Overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

Conclusion: The two levels of parallelism are complementary rather than redundant, and their coordinated application under TIPEX yields the best cost-effectiveness trade-offs, particularly for tasks of intermediate difficulty. Naively maximizing parallelism is not optimal; strategic, controllable coordination is essential.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems typically require multiple model invocations and complex coordination during inference, and their execution strategies directly affect system accuracy, latency, and computational cost. Parallel execution provides a means to improve inference-time efficiency. From the perspective of inference-time execution, this paper models parallelism in multi-agent systems as two distinct levels of decision processes: Replica Parallelism, which explores multiple complete solution paths at the task level, and Structural Parallelism, which enables concurrent execution within a single solution path through task decomposition. However, the roles of different forms of parallelism and their interrelationships still lack systematic study in terms of unified organization and coordination. We therefore propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that unifies these two levels of parallelism and coordinates their roles within the inference process under a unified execution semantics while supporting systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies and parameter configurations. Systematic experiments on the GAIA benchmark demonstrate that inference-time parallelism can significantly improve accuracy and reduce end-to-end latency at the cost of increased token consumption. Further analysis shows that Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with tasks of intermediate difficulty benefiting most from their coordination, while overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

</details>


### [319] [Certifying Collective Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems via Koopman Spectral Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05956)
*Nuzhat Khan,Indrakshi Dey*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper introduces a Koopman operator theory framework for analyzing LLM agent collectives, providing certifiable guarantees on convergence timescales, faction identification, and compressed decision representations, validated with strong empirical results on attention-consensus models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agent collectives that debate and vote improve task accuracy but remain black boxes: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drives decisions. The authors seek to make these systems transparent and certifiable.

Method: The collective is modeled as a nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph. The Koopman transfer operator provides an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics, estimated from interaction traces. Three certificates are derived from the Koopman spectrum: (1) the sub-dominant eigenvalue λ₂ gives a convergence deadline; (2) its eigenvector identifies coherent factions; (3) leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis. Validation uses an attention-consensus model.

Result: The convergence deadline tracks observed convergence with log–log correlation 0.93 and bounds it in 96% of 24 configurations. Attribution is exact when the spectrum certifies metastability. Eight of 32 spectral coordinates preserve decisions at 99.7% fidelity. A certificate learned from 15 debates generalizes to 60/60 held-out debates. Computation runs in minutes on a CPU.

Conclusion: Spectral certification via Koopman operator theory provides a practical, computationally lightweight layer for trustworthy collective reasoning, offering machine-checkable guarantees on convergence, interpretability, and compressed representation of LLM agent debates.

Abstract: Orchestrated collectives of large language model (LLM) agents that debate and vote are an emerging form of computational intelligence: the intelligent behaviour resides in the \emph{interaction}, not in any single agent. They improve task accuracy, yet remain black boxes at the system level: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on the rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drove a decision. This paper develops a novel framework based on Koopman operator theory and validates its theoretical guarantees on multi-agent consensus dynamics. Treating the collective as one nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph, we read its essential behaviour off the spectrum of its Koopman transfer operator, an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics estimated from interaction traces. The spectrum yields three machine-checkable certificates: the sub-dominant eigenvalue $λ_2$ fixes the intrinsic timescale of reasoning and yields a convergence deadline computable \emph{before} the debate runs; its eigenvector names the coherent factions the collective reasons in, and $|λ_2|$ certifies when that explanation is valid; and the leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis. On an attention-consensus model, the deadline tracks observed convergence with log--log correlation $0.93$ and bounds it in 96\% of 24 configurations; attribution is exact whenever the spectrum certifies metastability; eight of 32 coordinates preserve the decision at 99.7\% fidelity; and a certificate learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates. The study runs in minutes on a CPU, making spectral certification a practical layer for trustworthy collective reasoning.

</details>


### [320] [ASGE-RR: Agentic Service Graph Embedding with Revisable Reservations for Dynamic AI-Agent Calls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06033)
*Trond Vatten,Yuming Jiang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: AI-agent workflows expose runtime-revealed dependency calls that form an agentic service graph (ASG). The paper formulates online resource allocation for these graphs as ASGE and proposes ASGE-RR, a controller with revisable reservations that protects capacity for likely future calls, achieving up to 10% more workflow completion value compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In AI-agent workflows, dependency calls to remote models, memory stores, and tools are revealed dynamically at runtime. This creates a resource allocation challenge: committing resources to a currently visible call may starve a future, higher-value call from a different workflow. Traditional service graph embedding assumes full topology knowledge upfront, which does not hold here. The authors identify this as a novel network-control problem where runtime-revealed structure creates both a challenge and an opportunity for smarter capacity reservation.

Method: The authors formalize the problem as Agentic Service Graph Embedding (ASGE), an online network-control problem with capacity, cost, and deadline constraints. They propose ASGE-RR (Revisable Reservations), an online controller that: (1) evaluates candidate replica-and-path mappings against predicted workflow continuations, (2) protects capacity for likely future calls via reservations, and (3) updates these reservations incrementally as new execution information emerges. The approach exploits a key control point — steering runtime-revealed dependency calls before connection establishment.

Result: Evaluation used OpenHands and GPT Researcher workflows with gpt-5.6-luna, replayed across a controlled Docker testbed and a WAN testbed. All evaluated AI-agent tasks exhibited at least one runtime-revealed dependency call steerable before connection establishment. ASGE-RR completed up to 10% more workflow value than a same-information rolling-horizon controller and a current-call steering controller on the WAN testbed.

Conclusion: Runtime-revealed workflow structure in AI-agent systems presents a new network control opportunity. Protecting resources for likely future calls via revisable reservations enables more AI-agent workflows to finish within their deadlines, increasing overall workflow completion value. The results validate that even small-scale deployments can benefit from ASG-aware resource allocation.

Abstract: AI-agent workflows often involve remote calls to models, memory stores, and tools distributed across a network. As execution progresses, these dependency calls collectively form an agentic service graph (ASG). Unlike traditional service requests, many dependency calls are revealed only at runtime. Consequently, allocating resources to a currently visible call may consume capacity later needed by a call from a higher-value workflow. We formulate this challenge as Agentic Service Graph Embedding (ASGE), an online network-control problem that maps runtime-revealed workflow calls to service replicas and network paths under capacity, cost and deadline constraints. We present ASGE-RR, an online ASGE controller with revisable reservations. ASGE-RR protects capacity for likely future calls while enforcing the constraints. ASGE-RR evaluates candidate replica-and-path mappings against predicted workflow continuations and updates reservations as new execution information becomes available.
  We evaluate ASGE-RR using OpenHands and GPT Researcher workflows executed with gpt-5.6-luna and replayed over in two complementary experimental environments, a controlled Docker testbed and a WAN testbed. The investigation shows that all the evaluated AI-agent tasks expose at least one runtime-revealed dependency call that can be steered before connection establishment. Exploiting this control point, even though the experimental environments are small-scale, ASGE-RR already demonstrates noticeable potential: It completes (up to) 10% more workflow value than a same-information rolling-horizon controller and a current-call steering controller on the WAN testbed. The results suggest that runtime-revealed workflow structure creates a new network control opportunity: protecting resources for likely future calls allows more AI-agent workflows to finish in time.
